Context: what polemics is and why the Ch:
This curriculum answers, from the Orthodox faith, everything that stands against it or beside it: Rome and the Reformation, the new movements, Judaism and Islam, the religions of India and the East, the old gods and the New Age, and atheism. Theology teaches the faith from the inside. **Polemics takes the faith outside and puts it beside the other answers people give.**

**The word.** *Polemics* comes from the Greek *pólemos* (πόλεμος), "war". In the schools of the West it became the name of a subject, "polemical theology", the defence of one church's teaching against another's. Russian seminaries taught the same thing under the name *oblichitel'noe bogoslovie*, "theology that exposes" (error). The war, for the Fathers, is never against people. St Paul says it plainly: "we wrestle not against flesh and blood" (Ephesians 6:12, KJV). The enemy is the lie, not the man who believes it.

**Why the Church answers at all.** Three reasons run through the Fathers:

1. **For the sake of the truth.** If Christ is the truth (John 14:6), then what contradicts Him is not one more opinion among many. It matters for salvation, and silence would be a failure of love.
2. **For the sake of the faithful.** Most heresies were answered because they were drawing believers away. St Irenaeus wrote, as you will read in this stage, so that "sheep" would not be "carried off" through his neglect.
3. **For the sake of the other person.** An answer given well is an invitation. The Fathers wrote against Arius and received back the Arians who repented.

**What this curriculum is not.** It is not a list of other people's mistakes, and it is not neutral. History and Philosophy keep the rule of not arriving at a position. Polemics does arrive, but it keeps the fairness: each other position is first given **at its strongest, in its own words**, so that its best defender would say "yes, that is what we believe". Only then comes the Orthodox answer, the other side's best reply, and the one or two premises the whole disagreement rests on.

**How the stages run.**

| Stages | What is answered |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | how the Church answers: words, models, method, and receiving converts |
| 2 | the old heresies, as the pattern later errors repeat |
| 3 | Judaism, the faith closest to the Church's own roots |
| 4–5 | Rome: the schism and what has divided since |
| 6–7 | the Reformation and its heirs |
| 8 | the new movements |
| 9–12 | Islam; India and the East; the old gods and the New Age; atheism |
| 13 | answering in practice |

**What it leans on.** The faith itself is taught in **Theology**: the councils (Theology Stages 7–8), the Fathers (Stage 9), the canons (Stage 1). The arguments for God and against Him are in **Philosophy**; the events, in **History**. This curriculum uses them and points across instead of repeating them.

**The spirit of it.** Answering is part of the Christian life, but it is not the centre of it. **Prayer comes before polemic**, and the last stage returns to that. A man who wins every argument and loses his charity has lost the more important one.
Apologia and polemic: giving an answer f:
Two Greek words describe the Church's speaking to those outside. They overlap, and it helps to keep them apart.

**Apologia.** *Apología* (ἀπολογία) is a defence, the speech a man makes in court to answer a charge. St Peter uses it: "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear" (1 Peter 3:15, KJV). "Answer" there is *apologia*; "reason" is *lógos*. From this comes **apologetics**: showing that the faith is reasonable and answering objections to it. The second-century writers who addressed the emperors, St Justin among them, are called **the Apologists**.

**Polemic.** Polemic goes on the offensive. It examines the other position and shows where it fails. Apologetics says "here is why we believe"; polemic says "here is why that teaching is not true". Both are needed: a defence with no examination of the alternative leaves a person without an answer to the next question, and an attack with no account of one's own hope is only destruction.

**What St Peter's verse requires.** Read closely, 1 Peter 3:15–16 sets four conditions on every answer:

| Phrase | What it asks |
| --- | --- |
| "sanctify the Lord God in your hearts" | the answer begins in prayer, not in cleverness |
| "be ready always" | study beforehand; this curriculum is the readiness |
| "to every man that asketh" | answer the question actually asked, not a speech prepared for someone else |
| "with meekness and fear" | gentleness toward the person, reverence toward God |

The next verse adds "having a good conscience": the life must not contradict the words. **An argument from a man whose life denies it is answered before he speaks.**

**The Church's own name for the work.** The Orthodox Church honours some saints with the title *Isapóstolos* (ἰσαπόστολος), "equal to the apostles", for bringing whole peoples to the faith, and calls others "pillars of Orthodoxy" for defending it: St Athanasius, St Mark of Ephesus, St Gregory Palamas. The two callings belong together. Mission and defence are one love facing in two directions.

**A caution from the Fathers.** St Gregory the Theologian warned against arguing about God as a sport (see Theology Stage 1, "Purity of heart"). The same holds here. The aim of an apologia is not to win but to let the other person see the hope. **If the conversation is going to end in contempt, it is better not to begin it.** Stage 13 comes back to when not to argue.

**In short.** Apologetics answers "why do you believe?"; polemics answers "why not believe this instead?" This curriculum does both, in that order.
Heresy, schism and heterodoxy: the words:
Polemics needs exact words. Calling everything outside the Church "heresy", or nothing at all, makes clear thinking impossible. The Fathers had a precise vocabulary.

**Heresy.** *Haíresis* (αἵρεσις) first meant simply "choice", then "a school" or "party" (the "sect of the Pharisees" in Acts 15:5 is a *hairesis*). In the Church it came to mean **choosing one's own opinion over the faith received**, on a matter of the faith itself: who God is, who Christ is, how we are saved. St Paul tells Titus: "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject" (Titus 3:10, KJV). A heretic is not someone who has a question or makes a mistake; he is one who holds to the error after correction.

**Schism.** *Schísma* (σχίσμα) is "a tear", as in cloth. A schism is **a break in communion over order, discipline or persons**, with the faith itself still shared. Both sides may confess the same Creed and still be out of communion.

**St Basil's three categories.** In his first canonical letter to Amphilochius (Letter 188, written in 374), St Basil the Great sets out the ancient distinction (tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895):

> "By heresies they meant men who were altogether broken off and alienated in matters relating to the actual faith; by schisms men who had separated for some ecclesiastical reasons and questions capable of mutual solution; by unlawful congregations gatherings held by disorderly presbyters or bishops or by uninstructed laymen."

| Category | Greek | What divides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Heresy** | *hairesis* | the faith itself |
| **Schism** | *schisma* | questions of order "capable of mutual solution" |
| **Unlawful congregation** | *parasynagōgḗ* (παρασυναγωγή) | disobedience: a rival assembly under a deposed or rebel cleric |

Basil's point is practical: **how the Church receives a person depends on which category his group is in.** Lesson 17 of this stage shows how.

**Heterodoxy.** *Heterodoxía* (ἑτεροδοξία), "other belief", is the opposite of *orthodoxía*, "right belief" or "right glory". Modern Orthodox writers use "heterodox" as the more general and gentler word for Christians outside the Orthodox Church. It names the fact that their teaching differs without settling, in every case, whether it amounts to heresy in the strict sense.

**Apostasy.** *Apostasía* (ἀποστασία), "standing away", is the abandonment of the faith altogether.

**Why the distinctions matter.** A person raised a Lutheran has not *chosen* anything against the Church; he inherited it. The Fathers condemn heresies and heresiarchs, the men who founded them, but they speak differently of those born into them. **The teaching is judged strictly; the person is met as he is.** Orthodox writers differ on how to name modern Western churches (heresy, schism, or something the old categories did not foresee), and later stages give both views where they arise.
\"There must be also heresies\": why err:
If the Church has the truth, why is there so much error? The Fathers took the question seriously, and their answer shapes how the Church answers.

**St Paul's sentence.** "For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you" (1 Corinthians 11:19, KJV). "Approved" is *dókimoi* (δόκιμοι), "tested and found genuine", the word for metal that has passed the assay. **Heresies, in God's providence, are the occasion on which the truth is tested and made plain.**

**What the Fathers saw.** Three things recur:

1. **Error grows out of truth.** Almost no heresy invents from nothing. It takes one true thing and makes it the whole. Arius took the true teaching that God is one and unbegotten and drew from it that the Son must be a creature. Nestorius took the true teaching that Christ is fully man and divided Him in two. **A heresy is usually a truth cut loose from the rest of the faith.**
2. **Error forces the Church to speak.** Before Arius, the Church had not needed to say *homooúsios* (ὁμοούσιος), "of one essence". Before the iconoclasts, she had not needed to explain why an icon is not an idol. **The definitions of the councils are almost all answers to someone.** The faith did not grow; its fence was built where the attack came.
3. **Error tests the heart, not only the mind.** The Fathers often traced heresy to pride: the wish to know better than the Church, or to be a teacher. St Irenaeus says the Gnostics boasted of a "perfect knowledge" beyond the apostles. This is why the Fathers joined the answer to repentance and prayer.

**The rule of faith.** Against heresies the early Church set the *regula fidei*, Greek *kanṓn tês alētheías* (κανὼν τῆς ἀληθείας), "the rule of truth": the summary of the faith taught to every baptised person, later fixed in the Creed. St Irenaeus describes the Church scattered across the world keeping it "as if occupying but one house" (Against Heresies I.10.2, tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885). **A teaching is tested first by whether it agrees with what the whole Church has always confessed.** Theology Stage 1 teaches this at length (St Vincent of Lérins, the consensus of the Fathers).

**Why this gives confidence without arrogance.** If heresies are permitted for testing, then meeting them is not a disaster. The Orthodox who studies this curriculum should expect hard questions and not be shaken by them. But the same verse cuts the other way: the test is of "you". **Error among others is a test of whether we ourselves hold the faith truly**, in life as well as words.

**How this curriculum uses the point.** For each position it asks: what true thing does this begin from? Where was it cut loose? What does the whole faith say instead? That is the shape of every answer from Stage 2 onward.
Speaking the truth in love: why truth an:
The most common modern objection to polemics is that it is unloving. The most common fault in polemics is that it is. The Fathers held both truth and love, and did not trade one for the other.

**The verse.** St Paul: "But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ" (Ephesians 4:15, KJV). The Greek is one word, *alētheúontes* (ἀληθεύοντες), "truthing", done *en agápē* (ἐν ἀγάπῃ), "in love". **Not truth softened by love, and not love that drops the truth, but truth spoken as an act of love.**

**Two failures.**

| Failure | What it looks like | Why it fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Truth without love** | contempt, mockery, scoring points, enjoying the other's error | it makes the truth repellent and hardens the hearer; it is itself a sin |
| **Love without truth** | "all paths are the same", saying nothing so as not to offend | it withholds what the person most needs; it is indifference wearing a kind face |

**The Fathers' example.** St Gregory the Theologian, who preached the Trinity against the Arians in Constantinople, resigned that throne in 381 rather than let the council divide over his own appointment. St Justin, as the next lessons show, ended a long argument with Trypho the Jew by praying for him and parting as friends. **Firmness in the faith and warmth toward people are found together in the saints.**

**A distinction the Fathers kept.** The teaching is condemned; the person is prayed for. The canons that cut heretics off from communion exist so that the person may see the seriousness of his position and return. The Church's anathemas are not curses wished upon people; they are the Church saying "this is not what we believe, and whoever holds it is outside our communion".

**What love requires in argument.**

1. **Understand before you answer.** Love listens. That is why every lesson in this curriculum gives the other side at its strongest first.
2. **Never misrepresent.** A lie told against a heresy is still a lie.
3. **Admit your own side's wrongs.** Where Orthodox Christians have wronged others, this curriculum says so (Stage 3 on the Jews, Stage 4 on 1182 and 1204).
4. **Want the other person's good, not your victory.** If he would be better served by your silence today, be silent.

**In one sentence.** **Love is the reason to speak the truth, and truth is what love has to give.**
Reading: St Paul at the Areopagus (Acts:
The first Christian speech to a pagan audience that Scripture preserves is St Paul's at Athens. It is the model for every answer to those who do not share the Scriptures.

**The setting.** Paul was waiting in Athens for Silas and Timothy, "his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry" (Acts 17:16). He argued in the synagogue and the market; Epicurean and Stoic philosophers took him to the Areopagus, "Mars' hill", the council that judged new teachings.

**The text** (Acts 17:22–31, KJV):

> "Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious. For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you. God that made the world and all things therein, seeing that he is Lord of heaven and earth, dwelleth not in temples made with hands; Neither is worshipped with men's hands, as though he needed any thing, seeing he giveth to all life, and breath, and all things; And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation; That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us: For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring. Forasmuch then as we are the offspring of God, we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold, or silver, or stone, graven by art and man's device. And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent: Because he hath appointed a day, in the which he will judge the world in righteousness by that man whom he hath ordained; whereof he hath given assurance unto all men, in that he hath raised him from the dead."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"Too superstitious."** The Greek *deisidaimonésterous* (δεισιδαιμονεστέρους) can mean "very religious" as well as "superstitious". Paul chooses a word that is at once a compliment and a diagnosis.
2. **He begins with what they have.** The altar to the unknown God is their own admission that something is missing. **He names their longing before he names their error.**
3. **He quotes their poets.** "For we are also his offspring" is from Aratus, a Stoic poet of the 3rd century BC. "In him we live" is often traced to Epimenides. Paul uses their own best words against their idols.
4. **He does not stop at common ground.** The speech moves from creation, to the absurdity of idols, to repentance, judgement and **the resurrection**. That last word is where they mocked (17:32). He did not drop it to keep them listening.
5. **The result was mixed.** "Some mocked", some wanted to hear more, a few believed, among them **Dionysius the Areopagite** and a woman named Damaris (17:34). Faithfulness, not success, is the measure.

**The pattern for this curriculum.** Find what is true in what they hold; show where it points; show where their system contradicts it; and then say plainly what only the Gospel says. Lesson 7 draws the method out.
The Areopagus method: common ground with:
Paul's speech at Athens gives a method that the Fathers used for centuries. It has two halves, and both are needed.

**First half: begin where they stand.** Paul did not open with the Hebrew prophets, whom the Athenians did not know. He opened with their altar and their poets. The Fathers called this kind of meeting point a **point of contact**. Every serious faith or philosophy has one: the Muslim's reverence for the one God, the Buddhist's seriousness about suffering, the atheist's demand for honesty, the Catholic's love of the Fathers. **To begin there is not compromise; it is respect, and it is accurate.** Those things are really there.

**Second half: say what only the Gospel says.** Paul ended with judgement and the resurrection, the two things the Stoics and Epicureans most rejected. A conversation that finds common ground and stays there has not given an answer. **The point of contact is a door, not a room to live in.**

**The four moves, drawn from Acts 17:**

| Move | In Paul's speech | In practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Acknowledge** | "I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious" | say honestly what is good in their position |
| **Connect** | "him declare I unto you" | show what their good points toward |
| **Correct** | "we ought not to think that the Godhead is like unto gold" | show where their system contradicts its own best insight |
| **Proclaim** | "he hath raised him from the dead" | give what only Christ gives, and call for a response |

**Two errors on either side.**

- **The wall.** Treating the other faith as wholly false and having nothing to learn from it. This is not the Fathers' way: Justin, Clement of Alexandria and Basil all read the Greeks and found truth in them. It is also simply inaccurate, and inaccurate answers fail.
- **The bridge to nowhere.** Treating the common ground as if it were the whole, so that the Gospel becomes one more expression of what everyone already believes. Stage 10 meets the strongest form of this, the claim that "all religions are one".

**The Orthodox reason for the method.** Christ is the *Lógos* (Λόγος), the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Whatever is true anywhere is true because it comes from Him. So the Christian can recognise truth wherever it is found without fear, and can also say that **its fullness is in Christ alone**, because He is its source. The next lesson shows how St Justin built on this.

**A warning.** The method works only for one who knows the faith well. A person who does not know the Gospel cannot tell where the common ground ends. That is why this curriculum sits beside Theology and not before it.
St Justin Martyr: the seeds of the Word:
The first Christian philosopher to answer pagans and Jews at length, and the first to give a theory of why truth is found outside the Church, was St Justin.

**Who.** Justin was born about 100 in Flavia Neapolis (Nablus) in Samaria, of a pagan family. He tried the Stoics, a Peripatetic, a Pythagorean and the Platonists before an old man by the sea showed him the prophets (he tells the story in the opening chapters of the *Dialogue with Trypho*). He taught as a Christian philosopher in Rome and was beheaded there with six companions about 165, under the prefect Rusticus. The Church calls him **St Justin the Philosopher and Martyr**; the Orthodox feast is on 1 June.

**His works.** The *First Apology* (about 155), to the emperor Antoninus Pius; a shorter *Second Apology*; and the *Dialogue with Trypho* (about 160), which Stage 3 reads.

**The seeds of the Word.** Justin's best-known idea is that the divine *Logos* sowed seeds of truth in every people before Christ came. In the *Second Apology*, chapter 13 (tr. Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "For each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word, seeing what was related to it. But they who contradict themselves on the more important points appear not to have possessed the heavenly wisdom, and the knowledge which cannot be spoken against. Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians."

The Greek phrase is *lógos spermatikós* (λόγος σπερματικός), "the seed-bearing Word".

**What it does and does not mean.** Justin is careful. The philosophers had **seeds**, partial truths, and he adds at once that "the seed and imitation impacted according to capacity is one thing, and quite another is the thing itself". They also "contradict themselves on the more important points". **Partial truth is real truth, and it is still partial.** Christ is the whole of which they had fragments.

**His boldest sentence.** In the *First Apology*, chapter 46, Justin says that "those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus". "Reasonably" is *metà lógou*, "with the Logos". Orthodox writers have read this in more than one way: some as a hope for the righteous who lived before Christ, others as a statement only about the truths they grasped. Justin does not say that pagans after Christ need not believe; his whole life was spent calling them to.

**Why he matters for polemics.**

1. **He took his opponents seriously.** He had been a philosopher; he answered as one.
2. **He found the point of contact in the Logos.** This is the theology behind the Areopagus method.
3. **He died for what he argued.** His answer was not only an argument. Before the prefect he refused to sacrifice, and that refusal is the last chapter of his apology.
Reading: St Irenaeus on error dressed as:
The second great model of answering is St Irenaeus of Lyons, and the preface to his great work is the best short statement in the Fathers of why error must be exposed.

**Who.** Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, about 130, and heard St Polycarp of Smyrna, the disciple of St John. He became bishop of Lyons in Gaul after the persecution of 177 and died about 202. Around 180 he wrote five books usually called *Against Heresies* (Greek title: *Exposure and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called*). His target was **Gnosticism**, which Stage 2 explains.

**The text** (Against Heresies, Book I, Preface, sections 1–2; tr. Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "Inasmuch as certain men have set the truth aside, and bring in lying words and vain genealogies, which, as the apostle says, minister questions rather than godly edifying which is in faith, and by means of their craftily-constructed plausibilities draw away the minds of the inexperienced and take them captive, [I have felt constrained, my dear friend, to compose the following treatise in order to expose and counteract their machinations.] ...
>
> Error, indeed, is never set forth in its naked deformity, lest, being thus exposed, it should at once be detected. But it is craftily decked out in an attractive dress, so as, by its outward form, to make it appear to the inexperienced (ridiculous as the expression may seem) more true than the truth itself. One far superior to me has well said, in reference to this point, A clever imitation in glass casts contempt, as it were, on that precious jewel the emerald (which is most highly esteemed by some), unless it come under the eye of one able to test and expose the counterfeit."

(The square brackets are the translators'.)

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"Craftily-constructed plausibilities."** Irenaeus does not say the Gnostics were stupid. He says they were persuasive. **Error that persuades is error that has something attractive in it**, and that is why it needs an answer.
2. **"More true than the truth itself."** A clever falsehood can look more convincing than the plain truth, because it is made to please. The Gnostic systems were elaborate and flattering: they told their followers they were the spiritual elite.
3. **The glass and the emerald.** The image is the heart of the passage. A fake jewel fools everyone except "one able to test". **The answer to counterfeit is not suspicion of all jewels but knowing the real one well.** This is why polemics depends on theology.
4. **"Expose and counteract."** Irenaeus's method has two steps: first set out what they really teach (Book I is a careful description), then refute it (Books II–V). **He described before he answered**, which is the first step of this curriculum's method.
5. **The pastoral motive.** He goes on to say he writes "lest ... some should be carried off, even as sheep are by wolves", because "their language resembles ours, while their sentiments are very different". Shared words with different meanings: every later stage meets this.

**What to take from it.** Know the real thing so well that the imitation shows itself; describe the other side accurately before answering; and answer because people you love are at stake.
St Irenaeus's answer: the rule of faith:
Having described the Gnostics, Irenaeus answered them, and his answer has two parts that the Church has used against every heresy since.

**The problem he faced.** The Gnostics quoted the same Scriptures as the Church. They claimed a **secret tradition** from the apostles, handed to a spiritual few, that gave the true meaning. So Scripture alone could not settle the dispute: both sides read it, and read it differently.

**First answer: the rule of faith.** Irenaeus pointed to the faith the Church confesses everywhere: one God, the Creator; one Christ, His Son, made flesh for our salvation; one Holy Spirit who spoke through the prophets. He describes the Church across the world holding it in agreement (Against Heresies I.10.2, tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "For, although the languages of the world are dissimilar, yet the import of the tradition is one and the same. For the Churches which have been planted in Germany do not believe or hand down anything different, nor do those in Spain, nor those in Gaul, nor those in the East, nor those in Egypt, nor those in Libya..."

**The point:** the Scriptures belong to the Church and are read within her faith. A reading that contradicts the faith every church has confessed is wrong, however clever. Irenaeus's image (Against Heresies I.8.1) is a mosaic of a king taken apart and rearranged by a forger "into the form of a dog or of a fox", while he insists that it is still "the beautiful image of the king". **The same stones, put together without the pattern, give a different picture.**

**Second answer: the succession.** If the apostles had secret teachings, they would have given them to the men they appointed to lead the churches. Those men are known by name, and Irenaeus lists them: the bishops of Rome from Linus to Eleutherius in his own day (Against Heresies III.3). **The public, continuous succession of bishops in the apostolic churches is the guarantee that nothing was hidden.** What they teach openly is what the apostles taught.

**Why both together.** Succession without the faith is a line of names; the faith without succession has no visible guardian. Irenaeus joins them: the bishops guard the rule of faith, and the rule of faith is how one recognises true bishops.

**The passage both sides of the schism quote.** In III.3.2 Irenaeus singles out the church of Rome, "founded and organized at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul", and says "it is a matter of necessity that every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its preeminent authority". Catholics read this as Rome's universal authority; Orthodox read it as Rome's witness in Irenaeus's time, when it held the faith of Peter and Paul, as an example among the apostolic churches he names (he goes on to Smyrna and Ephesus). **Stage 4 weighs the two readings.**

**What this gives the Orthodox answerer.** Against any new teaching, ask two questions: **Does it agree with what the Church has always and everywhere confessed? And who handed it to you?**
St Athanasius: answering the pagans and:
The third model is St Athanasius the Great, who answered two quite different opponents and is the Church's example of standing firm when almost no one else does.

**Who.** Athanasius was born about 296 in Alexandria. As a young deacon he attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 with his bishop, Alexander; he became bishop of Alexandria in 328 and held the see until his death in 373. He was **exiled five times** by four emperors, for about seventeen years in all, for refusing to receive Arius and his party back into communion. The Orthodox Church keeps his feast on 18 January, with St Cyril of Alexandria, and on 2 May.

**His two-part answer to the pagans.** Early in his life (scholars date it variously, from about 318 to the 330s) he wrote one work in two books: *Against the Heathen* (*Contra Gentes*) and *On the Incarnation* (*De Incarnatione*).

| Book | What it argues |
| --- | --- |
| **Against the Heathen** | the soul, turned from God, invented idols; the order of the world shows one Maker; the soul can know Him by turning inward and purifying itself |
| **On the Incarnation** | why the Word became man: to restore the image of God in us and to destroy death; the Resurrection is shown by the changed lives of those who believe |

**The shape of the answer.** Athanasius first shows what is wrong with idolatry on its own terms, then explains the Christian answer from its centre, the Incarnation. **He does not argue only against; he shows what the Gospel is.** On the Incarnation ends with the challenge to "come and see": the martyrs, the ascetics and the converts are evidence that Christ is risen.

**His answer to the Arians.** Against Arius, who taught that the Son was a creature (Stage 2), Athanasius argued from **salvation**: only God can unite us to God. If the Son is a creature, He cannot deify us, and the Gospel is lost. He also argued from **worship**: the Church has always worshipped Christ, and worship of a creature is idolatry. Stage 2 reads him at length.

**"Athanasius against the world."** A later Latin saying, *Athanasius contra mundum*, sums up his reputation. In the 350s, after the councils of Arles (353) and Milan (355), most of the bishops of the West had signed against him under imperial pressure, and much of the East leaned to compromise. He held on, and the Church came back to Nicaea at the Council of Constantinople in 381, eight years after his death.

**What he teaches the answerer.**

1. **Answer from the centre.** Every doctrine is tied to salvation; show the tie.
2. **Numbers do not decide truth.** A majority of bishops can be wrong for a time; the faith is what the Church has always held, and the Church receives it again.
3. **Firmness is not hatred.** Athanasius refused communion with the Arians but worked for reconciliation with those who differed in words and agreed in faith, the "semi-Arians" who accepted the substance of Nicaea, at the Council of Alexandria in 362.
St John of Damascus: On Heresies and the:
The fourth model is St John of Damascus, who gathered the Church's answers into order and was one of the first Christian writers to describe Islam from inside the Muslim world.

**Who.** John was born about 675 in Damascus, then the capital of the Umayyad caliphate, into a Christian family, the Mansur, who had served as financial officials under the caliphs. He served at court himself before becoming a monk at the monastery of St Sabbas near Jerusalem. He died about 749. He wrote against the iconoclast emperors from outside their reach (Stage 2), and he wrote hymns the Church still sings at Pascha. Feast: 4 December. He is one of the Fathers Theology Stage 9 reads in his own words.

**The Fount of Knowledge.** His great work, *Pēgḕ gnṓseōs* (Πηγὴ γνώσεως), has three parts:

| Part | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Philosophical Chapters** | the terms of logic and philosophy that theology needs |
| **On Heresies** | a catalogue of about a hundred heresies, each briefly described |
| **An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith** | the faith itself, set out in order |

**The order is the lesson.** Tools first, then the errors, then the truth. **You know the truth more exactly once you have seen what it is not**, and you cannot name the errors without exact terms.

**On Heresies.** Most of the catalogue is taken from St Epiphanius of Salamis, whose *Panarion* (about 375), "medicine chest", described eighty heresies as poisons with their antidotes. John adds later movements, ending with the iconoclasts. Each entry is short: a name, what it teaches, sometimes where it went wrong. Among the later chapters is the one on the **"religion of the Ishmaelites"**, Islam, usually numbered chapter 100 (101 in some editions). John treats it as a Christian heresy, because it accepts Christ as a prophet and denies His divinity. Stage 9 reads that chapter and asks whether the classification is right.

**What the catalogue does.** It gives a **map**. Heresies repeat themselves: denying Christ's divinity, denying His humanity, dividing Him, confusing Him. A modern movement often turns out to be an old error in new clothes. Stage 2 uses exactly this method.

**Its limits.** The entries are summaries, sometimes from hostile sources, and they do not always give the heretics' own reasons. **This curriculum keeps St John's map but adds what his catalogue usually does not: the other side's case at its strongest, from its own texts.** A Muslim today will notice at once if he is answered from an eighth-century summary rather than from the Qur'an.

**His temper.** John writes plainly and without abuse in most of the work. He was a servant of a Muslim court and a monk among Muslims. His example is one of knowing the other side closely because he lived beside it.
The method of this curriculum: four step:
Every lesson from Stage 2 onward that answers a position follows the same four steps. This lesson sets them out and explains why each is there.

**Step 1. Their case at its strongest.** The position is given **from its own texts and best defenders**: the Catechism of the Catholic Church, the Book of Concord, the Westminster Confession, the Qur'an, the Pali Canon, jw.org, the Book of Mormon, Dawkins. Never from an exposé or a hostile summary. **The test: would its best defender read the description and say "yes, that is what we believe"?** Modern writers call this *steelmanning*, the opposite of a straw man.

**Why it comes first.** Irenaeus spent a whole book describing the Gnostics before answering them. A position learned from its enemies is answered wrongly, and the person across the table notices at once. It also obeys the commandment "Thou shalt not bear false witness" (Exodus 20:16), which applies to opponents.

**Step 2. The Orthodox answer.** From Scripture, the councils, the Fathers and modern Orthodox writers, **saying which**. "The Orthodox say" is not enough; this curriculum says "St Photios says", "the Council of 1848 says", "Fr Georges Florovsky says". The answerer must know where the answer comes from and how much weight it carries: a council's definition is not the same as one writer's opinion.

**Step 3. Their best reply.** Most answers have a reply. A Catholic answers the Orthodox reading of Matthew 16; a Muslim answers the Christian reading of the Trinity. **If you have never heard the reply, you have not finished thinking.** This step is honest about where the argument goes next.

**Step 4. What it finally rests on.** Most long disagreements come down to one or two premises that each side holds and the other denies. Naming them saves hours.

| Disagreement | It rests on |
| --- | --- |
| Papal infallibility | whether Christ's promise to Peter passes to the bishop of Rome alone |
| *Sola scriptura* | whether Scripture can be read rightly apart from the Church that received it |
| Islam on the Trinity | whether God's oneness excludes any distinction within Him |
| Atheism | whether the world explains itself |

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** Some questions are not settled among the Orthodox: how to receive converts, St Augustine's standing, evolution and the age of the earth, ecumenism, and what may be hoped for those outside the Church. On these, each Orthodox view is given at its strongest **without the curriculum taking a side**.

**Where Christians did wrong.** Where Christians, the Orthodox included, have wronged the people being answered, the lesson says so. **An answer that hides its own side's history is weaker, not stronger**, and the other side knows the history.

**What the method protects against.** Pride (assuming we already know what they think), laziness (repeating stock answers), and uncharity (treating the person as his worst arguments).
The fallacies that sink an argument:
An argument can have a true conclusion and still be a bad argument. In polemics, a bad argument for the truth does harm: the other person rejects the truth along with the argument. These are the faults that sink arguments most often, on both sides.

**What a fallacy is.** A *fallacy*, from Latin *fallacia*, "deceit", is a form of reasoning that seems to prove its conclusion but does not. Aristotle catalogued them in *On Sophistical Refutations*. Philosophy teaches logic properly; here are the ones polemics meets.

| Fallacy | What it is | Typical polemical form |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Straw man** | attacking a weaker version of the position than the one held | "Catholics worship Mary"; "Orthodox think icons are magic" |
| **Ad hominem** | attacking the person instead of the argument | "Luther was a bad-tempered man, so justification by faith is false" |
| **Tu quoque** ("you too") | answering a charge by pointing to the accuser's faults | "You criticise the Crusades? What about Byzantine persecution?" |
| **Genetic fallacy** | judging a belief by where it came from rather than whether it is true | "The Trinity came from Greek philosophy, so it is pagan" |
| **Proof-texting** | taking a verse out of its setting to prove a point it does not make | quoting "call no man your father" (Matthew 23:9) against priests while ignoring 1 Corinthians 4:15 |
| **Equivocation** | using one word in two senses | "grace", "church", "tradition" meaning different things to each side |
| **Anachronism** | reading a later situation back into an earlier text | treating a 2nd-century "bishop of Rome" as a 19th-century pope, or the reverse |
| **Argument from silence** | concluding from what a text does not say | "the Fathers never mention X, so they rejected it" |
| **False dilemma** | offering two options when there are more | "either the Pope or the Bible" |

**The one to watch most: equivocation.** Christian disagreements are full of shared words with different meanings. A Lutheran and an Orthodox can both say "we are saved by grace" and mean different things by "saved" and "grace". **Define terms before arguing about them.** Every stage of this curriculum defines its terms first for this reason.

**The fallacy of our own side.** The Orthodox are tempted by particular faults: the **tu quoque** (meeting every charge with a Western sin), the **genetic fallacy** in reverse ("it is Western, so it is wrong"), and the **argument from authority** used carelessly (citing a saint's opinion as if it were a council). An Orthodox who answers well does not use them.

**Not every appeal to authority is a fallacy.** Appealing to a recognised authority on what it is authoritative for is reasonable: the councils on the faith, a historian on dates. The fallacy is appealing to an authority outside its field, or to one the other side does not accept, as if that settled the matter. **With a Muslim, quoting a Father proves nothing; quoting the Qur'an accurately might.**

**The practical rule.** Before using an argument, ask: would it convince me if it were used for the other side? If not, do not use it.
Scripture as common ground: why both sid:
In almost every disagreement between Christians, both sides quote Scripture, and both quote it sincerely. Understanding why is the beginning of answering well.

**The fact.** The Arians quoted "my Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). The iconoclasts quoted "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image" (Exodus 20:4). Catholics quote "thou art Peter" (Matthew 16:18). Jehovah's Witnesses quote "the firstborn of every creature" (Colossians 1:15). **No heresy has ever lacked verses.**

**Why verses alone do not settle it.** Scripture is a large book, written over many centuries, in many genres. Its parts must be read together, and **someone has to decide how they fit**. That decision is made by a framework the reader brings: the rule of faith, a confession, a tradition, or private judgement. Two people with different frameworks will read the same verse differently, and neither can prove his reading from the verse alone.

**The Orthodox position.** Scripture is the written heart of Tradition, and it is read **in the Church**, by the mind of the Fathers and the councils. St Vincent of Lérins (about 434) said exactly this: because heretics interpret Scripture in many ways, Scripture must be read according to what has been believed "everywhere, always, by all". (Theology Stage 1 reads him.) St Paul calls the Church "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15, KJV).

**How this shapes an answer.** With other Christians, an answer usually has three layers:

| Layer | Question | Example (the Theotokos) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The text** | what does the verse actually say, in its context and language? | Luke 1:43: "the mother of my Lord" |
| **The reading** | how did the Church read it before this dispute? | the Fathers and Ephesus (431) |
| **The framework** | why read it that way rather than another? | Scripture in Tradition, not Scripture alone |

**The trap.** Many conversations stay on the first layer: verse against verse, for hours. **The disagreement usually lives on the third.** It is often better to say early: "We read this differently because we read Scripture differently. Can we talk about that?" Stage 6 on *sola scriptura* treats the third layer in full.

**With non-Christians.** With Jews, the shared text is the Old Testament, and the dispute is over how to read it (Stage 3). With Muslims, the Qur'an accepts the Torah and the Gospel in principle but says they have been changed (Stage 9). With atheists, Scripture is evidence to be weighed, not an authority. **Choose the common ground the other person actually accepts.**

**A caution for the Orthodox.** Appealing to Tradition is not a way to avoid the text. The Fathers knew Scripture by heart and argued from it closely. **An Orthodox who cannot show the Scriptural roots of his faith has not yet learned it.**
Akriveia and oikonomia: strictness and m:
Before the Church receives anyone, she has to decide how strictly to apply her rules. The two Greek words for this are taught in Theology Stage 1; here they are applied to the meeting with those outside.

**The words.** *Akríveia* (ἀκρίβεια), "exactness", is applying the canons as written. *Oikonomía* (οἰκονομία), "household management", is the bishop's freedom to relax them for the salvation of a person or the peace of the Church, as a steward does who knows when the rule would defeat its purpose.

**The example in St Basil.** In Letter 188 (374), Basil gives the strict view that the Cathari, as separatists, had lost the grace to baptise. Then he adds (tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 8, 1895):

> "Nevertheless, since it has seemed to some of those of Asia that, for the sake of management of the majority, their baptism should be accepted, let it be accepted."

"For the sake of management of the majority" translates *oikonomías héneka tôn pollôn*. **The strict principle is stated; the merciful practice is allowed; neither cancels the other.**

**How the two relate.** Orthodox writers agree on some points:

1. **Oikonomia is not a change of doctrine.** It applies to practice. The faith itself is never relaxed.
2. **It is exercised by the Church**, through her bishops and synods, not by any individual on his own.
3. **It serves salvation.** It is used when strictness would drive a person away or harm the Church.

**Where they differ.** Orthodox writers disagree about what oikonomia *does* when applied to the sacraments of the heterodox.

| View | What it holds | Representatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oikonomia fills an empty form** | outside the Church there are no sacraments in the full sense; when the Church receives a convert without baptism, her own grace fills the form he brings | St Nikodemos of the Holy Mountain in the *Pedalion* (1800); many Athonite and Greek writers today |
| **Oikonomia recognises something real** | the Church's boundaries in the canons are not identical with the reach of grace; some heterodox sacraments, especially baptism in the Trinity, are not empty | Fr Georges Florovsky, "The Limits of the Church" (1933); many Russian theologians and the long practice of the Russian Church |

**The strongest case for the first view.** The canons speak of one baptism and one Church; grace is not something a body outside the Church can possess and dispense apart from her. Without this, the Church's unity becomes vague.

**The strongest case for the second view.** The Church has received some groups by chrismation or confession for over fifteen centuries; the canons themselves distinguish between groups, which would be pointless if all were equally empty. And the Church has never re-ordained or re-baptised everyone.

**What both agree on.** Whoever comes to the Orthodox Church enters the one Church and receives in her the fullness of grace. The disagreement is over what he had before. **Lesson 17 shows how this works out in practice.**
How the Church receives converts: baptis:
A person who comes to the Orthodox Church from another Christian body may be received in one of three ways. Which way depends on where he comes from, on the canons, and on the practice of the local church. Here Orthodox practice genuinely differs.

**The three rites.**

| Rite | What it is | Used for, in the canons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Baptism** | full baptism by triple immersion, then chrismation | those whose baptism was not in the Trinity or not by triple immersion |
| **Chrismation** | anointing with holy chrism after renouncing errors | those baptised in the Trinity in a form the Church accepted |
| **Confession** (profession of faith) | renouncing errors and confessing the Orthodox faith, then communion | schismatics whose sacraments the Church accepted, sometimes clergy |

**The canons.** The key text is canon 7 of the Council of Constantinople (381), which scholars think was added from a letter of the church of Constantinople in the mid-5th century. It is repeated almost word for word as canon 95 of the Council in Trullo (692). Canon 95 begins (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "Those who from the heretics come over to orthodoxy, and to the number of those who should be saved, we receive according to the following order and custom. Arians, Macedonians, Novatians, who call themselves Cathari, Aristeri, and Testareskaidecatitæ, or Tetraditæ, and Apollinarians, we receive on their presentation of certificates and on their anathematizing every heresy which does not hold as does the holy Apostolic Church of God: then first of all we anoint them with the holy chrism..."

Others (Eunomians baptised with one immersion, Montanists, Sabellians) it receives "as heathen", by baptism. **The ancient Church did not treat all heterodox alike.**

**How Westerners have been received.** History gives no single answer:

- In **1484**, a synod at Constantinople repudiating Florence received Latins by chrismation.
- In **1755**, the *Oros* of Patriarch Cyril V, signed with the patriarchs of Alexandria and Jerusalem, required that Latins and Protestants be baptised. Greek practice largely followed it for a time.
- In **Russia**, a council of 1620 required baptism of Latins; the Great Council of Moscow in **1667** returned to receiving them without baptism.
- Today, practice varies by jurisdiction and often by bishop. **As of November 2026**, many jurisdictions (among them the OCA and the Antiochian Archdiocese in North America) usually receive Christians baptised in the Trinity by chrismation, and Roman Catholics in some churches by confession; Mount Athos and many monasteries, priests and bishops elsewhere, especially in the Greek-speaking churches, baptise all converts.

**The strongest case for baptising all.** Baptism is entry into the Church; outside her there is no baptism in the full sense; the ancient acceptances were oikonomia for particular times. Receiving by baptism removes all doubt, and it is never wrong to give the convert the certainty of the Church's own sacrament. Fr Peter Heers and many Athonite fathers argue this way.

**The strongest case for chrismation.** It is the practice of canon 95 and of most of the Church for most of her history. Baptising someone already baptised in the Trinity can seem to deny that one baptism exists (Ephesians 4:5), and the Fathers forbade rebaptism. Most bishops of the OCA and many Russian and Antiochian theologians argue this way.

**For the convert and the answerer.** This is a matter for the bishop, not for argument with the convert. **Whichever rite is used, the Church receives the whole person into the whole faith.**
Looking back: how the Church answers:
This stage set out the words, the models and the method that every later stage uses. Before going on, gather them.

**The words.**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *apologia* (ἀπολογία) | a defence of the faith, "a reason of the hope that is in you" (1 Peter 3:15) |
| polemic | examining and refuting another position |
| *hairesis* (αἵρεσις) | choosing one's own opinion against the faith received |
| *schisma* (σχίσμα) | a break in communion over order, the faith still shared |
| *parasynagōgē* | an unlawful rival assembly |
| heterodoxy | teaching other than Orthodox; the gentler general word |
| *akriveia* / *oikonomia* | exactness / merciful stewardship in applying the canons |

**The models.**

| Father | What he shows |
| --- | --- |
| **St Paul at Athens** (Acts 17) | begin with their altar and their poets, end with the Resurrection |
| **St Justin** (about 100–165) | truth anywhere is a seed of the Word; the fullness is Christ |
| **St Irenaeus** (about 130–202) | describe the error accurately; answer with the rule of faith and the succession |
| **St Athanasius** (about 296–373) | answer from the centre, salvation; numbers do not decide truth |
| **St John of Damascus** (about 675–749) | know the map of heresies; know the other side by living beside it |

**The method, in four steps.** Their case at its strongest, from their own texts. The Orthodox answer, saying which source. Their best reply. **What it finally rests on.** Where Orthodox writers differ, give each view. Where Christians did wrong, say so.

**The cautions.** Truth without love repels; love without truth abandons. Watch for fallacies, especially equivocation, and especially your own side's. Scripture is common ground with other Christians, but the disagreement usually lies in how it is read. Choose the common ground the other person actually accepts.

**What may be hoped for those outside.** This stage has not settled it, because the Church has not defined it. Orthodox writers hold, on one side, that **the Church alone is the ark of salvation** and that we must not presume on what God has not promised; and, on the other, that **God is not bound by His sacraments** and that we know where the Church is, but not where she is not, a saying often repeated by Orthodox writers in the 20th century. Both agree that the Christian's duty is to proclaim the faith and leave judgement to God. Later stages return to the question where it arises.

**Questions to test yourself.**

1. What is the difference between heresy and schism in St Basil's terms, and why does it matter for receiving a convert?
2. What did Paul quote at the Areopagus, and where did the audience stop listening?
3. What does Irenaeus's image of the glass and the emerald teach about how to answer error?
4. Name the four steps of the method, and give an example of step 4.
5. What are the two Orthodox views of what oikonomia does in receiving converts?

**What comes next.** Stage 2 takes the old heresies one by one, Gnosticism, Marcion, Arius, the modalists, Nestorius and the iconoclasts, and shows how each comes back in a modern form. **The Fathers already answered them once; the answer still works.**
Context: why the old heresies keep comin:
The saying "there is no new thing under the sun" (Ecclesiastes 1:9, KJV) is nowhere truer than in heresy. Almost every modern challenge to the Christian faith from within Christianity repeats an error the Church met and answered in her first eight centuries.

**Why they come back.** The Gospel makes claims that strain the mind: **one God in three persons; one Christ, fully God and fully man; the Creator present in matter.** Each claim can be "simplified" in a few ways, and only a few. Make God one person who wears three masks, and you have the modalists. Make the Son a lesser being, and you have Arius. Divide Christ, and you have Nestorius. Despise matter, and you have the Gnostics and, in another form, the iconoclasts. **The number of ways to get the mystery wrong is small, so the same errors recur.**

**The six patterns of this stage.**

| Ancient heresy | What it simplified | Modern echo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Gnosticism** (2nd century) | salvation as secret knowledge; the world as evil | "lost gospels", spirituality without the body or the Church |
| **Marcion** (about 140) | two gods: the harsh God of the Old Testament, the kind God of Jesus | setting the Old Testament aside as primitive |
| **Arius** (about 318) | the Son as the first and greatest creature | Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians |
| **The modalists** (about 200–220) | one God in three successive roles | Oneness Pentecostals; bad analogies for the Trinity |
| **Nestorius** (428–431) | Christ as God and a man joined, two subjects | "Mary is the mother of Jesus, not of God" |
| **Iconoclasm** (726–843) | images of Christ as idols | the Reformed case against images |

**How each lesson works.** First the ancient teaching at its strongest, in its own words where any survive (much of what we know of the early heretics comes from those who answered them, and the lesson says so). Then the Fathers' answer, and the council that settled it. Then the modern form, given fairly, and why the old answer still applies.

**What this stage does not do.** It does not answer the **Oriental Orthodox** churches (the Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac and Malankara churches), which did not receive the Council of Chalcedon (451). Their history and the modern dialogues are taught in Theology Stages 7 and 12. They are not heirs of any heresy in this stage, and modern dialogues have asked whether the division is over doctrine or over words. Nor does it answer the modern movements in full: Jehovah's Witnesses and Oneness Pentecostals each get their own lesson in Stage 8. **Here they are shown as patterns.**

**What it leans on.** The councils are taught in Theology Stages 7 and 8, and the Fathers in Stage 9. This stage uses them. **It is the Church's history read as a toolkit**: when a new teaching appears, ask which old one it resembles, and the Fathers' answer is already waiting.

**A caution.** Calling a modern person "an Arian" or "a Gnostic" is a description of a teaching, not an insult, and it can be wrong. Many modern movements are not simply the old heresy; they have their own reasons. Each lesson notes where the likeness ends.
Gnosticism: secret knowledge and an evil:
The first great challenge the Church faced from within was a family of movements that offered a higher, secret knowledge. The Fathers called them "Gnostics", and their answer to them shaped how the Church reads Scripture.

**The word.** *Gnōsis* (γνῶσις) is "knowledge". St Paul warns Timothy against "oppositions of science falsely so called" (1 Timothy 6:20, KJV), where "science" translates *gnōsis*. Irenaeus's great work is titled *Exposure and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called*.

**What a Gnostic system taught, at its strongest.** The systems differed, and modern scholars (Michael Williams, Karen King) warn that "Gnosticism" groups movements that did not think of themselves as one. But the great 2nd-century teachers, **Valentinus** (in Rome about 136–160) and **Basilides** (in Alexandria), shared a shape:

| Teaching | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **The true God** | utterly beyond, unknown, the source of a spiritual "fullness" (*plḗrōma*, πλήρωμα) of divine beings (*aeons*) |
| **The fall** | one aeon, Sophia ("Wisdom"), fell through desire, and from her fall came a lesser god |
| **The Demiurge** | *dēmiourgós* (δημιουργός), "craftsman": the ignorant maker of this material world, whom some identified with the God of the Old Testament |
| **The human being** | sparks of the divine trapped in matter; some people are spiritual (*pneumatikoí*), some partly so, some wholly material |
| **Salvation** | Christ comes from the true God to give **knowledge** that awakens the spark and lets it escape the body and the world |

**Why it attracted.** It answered the problem of evil (an ignorant maker explains a broken world); it flattered (the knowers were the elite); and it took Christ seriously as Revealer. Irenaeus admits that it was "craftily decked out in an attractive dress".

**The Fathers' answer.** Irenaeus, Tertullian and Hippolytus answered on four points:

1. **One God is both Creator and Father.** "God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31, KJV). The world is not a prison made by a fool.
2. **The Word was made flesh** (John 1:14). Many Gnostics held that Christ only *seemed* to have a body (*dokeîn*, "to seem", hence **Docetism**). St John had already answered: "every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God" (1 John 4:3, KJV).
3. **No secret tradition.** The apostles taught openly, and their successors are known (Stage 1).
4. **The body will rise.** Salvation is not escape from matter but its transfiguration.

**Irenaeus's image.** The Gnostics quoted the same Scriptures, but, Irenaeus says, like one who takes "a beautiful image of a king" made of jewels and rearranges the stones "into the form of a dog or of a fox" (Against Heresies I.8.1, tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885).

**What it rests on.** **Is the material world the good work of the one God, or the botched work of a lesser one?** Everything else follows from that.
Gnosticism today: the lost gospels and t:
Gnosticism disappeared as an organised movement in late antiquity (the Mandaeans of Iraq are its one surviving relative). But its ideas came back in the 20th century, helped by a discovery in the Egyptian desert.

**Nag Hammadi.** In December 1945 farmers near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt found a jar holding **thirteen leather-bound books** in Coptic, copied in the 4th century. They contained over fifty texts, many Gnostic, among them the *Gospel of Thomas*, the *Gospel of Philip* and the *Gospel of Truth*. For the first time, scholars could read Gnostics in their own words, not only through Irenaeus. In 2006 a further text, the *Gospel of Judas*, was published.

**The modern case, at its strongest.** Popular and some scholarly writers since the 1970s, among them Elaine Pagels in *The Gnostic Gospels* (1979), argued in substance (paraphrased):

- early Christianity was **diverse**, and the "orthodox" party was one group among many that won through politics;
- the Gnostic texts are **as old and as authentic** as the Gospels the Church kept;
- they offer a **more inward, less authoritarian** spirituality, with a larger place for women;
- the canon was **closed to exclude them**.

Novels such as *The Da Vinci Code* (2003) carried a cruder version of this to millions.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Dates.** Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are usually dated by scholars to the second half of the 1st century; the Gnostic gospels, with the possible exception of parts of *Thomas*, to the 2nd and 3rd. **The four Gospels are the earlier witnesses to Jesus**, and Irenaeus already names exactly four about 180.
2. **Diversity is not equality.** That there were many groups is true; the Church never denied it. Irenaeus spent a book describing them. The question is which group kept **what the apostles taught publicly**, and the succession of bishops answers it.
3. **The Gnostic texts are not more liberating.** The *Gospel of Thomas* ends (saying 114, here paraphrased) with Peter asking that Mary Magdalene be sent away because women are not worthy of life, and Jesus answering that he will make her male so that she may enter the kingdom. **The Church, which honours the Theotokos above the cherubim, did not need to be taught the dignity of women by such texts.**
4. **The body and the world.** A spirituality that despises the body and seeks escape is not kinder. Christianity says God made matter good and became flesh.

**Their best reply.** Scholars answer that the "four Gospels" were themselves chosen by a party, so appeal to them begs the question; and that early dating of *Thomas* is possible. **The Orthodox reply**: the Church's choice was not arbitrary; it received the Gospels that had been read in the apostolic churches from the start.

**The everyday form.** More common than the lost gospels is the **spirituality of "spiritual but not religious"**: a private inner path, freed from the body, the Church and her sacraments, known to the few who are awake. **That is the Gnostic shape, with or without the books.** Stage 11 meets it again in the New Age.

**What it rests on.** **Is Christianity a secret inner knowledge, or the public faith handed down by the apostles?**
Marcion: two gods and a shortened Bible:
Marcion is the first Christian teacher known to have produced his own canon of Scripture, and the first to set the God of the Old Testament against the Father of Jesus.

**Who.** Marcion was born late in the 1st century in Sinope, on the Black Sea in Pontus, and became a wealthy shipowner. He came to Rome about 140, gave the church a large gift, and set out his teaching. In **144** the church of Rome excommunicated him and returned his money. His church spread widely and lasted for centuries, especially in the East. His own works, among them the *Antitheses* ("Contrasts"), are lost; we know them from Irenaeus, Tertullian's five books *Against Marcion* (about 207–208), and others.

**What he taught, at its strongest.** Marcion read the Old Testament literally and found a God of **justice, law and war**, who commands slaughter and punishes. He read St Paul and found a God of **grace and love**, revealed in Jesus. He concluded they cannot be the same God. Irenaeus reports (Against Heresies I.27.2, tr. Roberts and Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885) that Marcion declared the God of the law and the prophets "to be the author of evils, to take delight in war, to be infirm of purpose, and even to be contrary to Himself".

| Marcion's | God of the Old Testament | Father of Jesus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nature** | just, severe | good, merciful |
| **Work** | made the world and gave the Law | unknown before Jesus; came to rescue us from the Creator |
| **Scripture** | the Jewish Bible | an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul |

**His canon.** Marcion rejected the whole Old Testament and accepted **one Gospel**, a shortened Luke without the birth narratives, and **ten letters of Paul** (not the Pastorals or Hebrews), cut where they seemed to praise the Law or the Creator. **He made the first New Testament canon by subtraction.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **One God in both Testaments.** Jesus calls the God of Israel His Father, quotes the Law and the Psalms, and says "I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil" (Matthew 5:17, KJV).
2. **Mercy in the Old, judgement in the New.** The God of the Old Testament is "merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness" (Exodus 34:6); the Jesus of the Gospels speaks of hell more than anyone else in Scripture. **Marcion could keep his contrast only by cutting the texts that refuted it.**
3. **The whole Scripture, read in Christ.** The Church reads the Old Testament as pointing to Christ (Theology Stage 5, typology). Its hard passages are read spiritually and as part of a story moving toward the Cross.
4. **The Church's answer was the canon.** Marcion's challenge helped the Church to say clearly which books she had always read, Old and New.

**What it rests on.** **Is the God who made the world and gave the Law the same God who is revealed in Jesus Christ?** If He is, Marcion's whole system collapses. Lesson 5 shows how the question is asked today.
Marcion today: the angry God of the Old:
Marcion's church faded, but his question did not. Today it comes in two forms, one from inside the churches and one from outside them.

**Inside the churches.** In the 19th and 20th centuries some liberal Protestant scholars came close to Marcion. **Adolf von Harnack**, the great German historian, wrote a book on Marcion (1921) in which he argued, in substance (paraphrased), that the early Church was right to keep the Old Testament in the 2nd century, that the Reformation could not yet avoid keeping it in the 16th, but that keeping it as canonical Scripture in modern Protestantism was the result of religious and ecclesiastical paralysis. In 2018 the American evangelical pastor **Andy Stanley** urged Christians, in a sermon series, to "unhitch" their faith from the Old Testament when presenting it to sceptics. He rejected the charge of Marcionism and said he holds the Old Testament inspired; his point was apologetic, that the faith rests on the Resurrection. **The pattern is the same: the Old Testament treated as an embarrassment to be got past.**

**Outside the churches.** Many sceptics argue that the God of the Old Testament is morally unacceptable: the flood, the conquest of Canaan, the commands to destroy whole peoples. Richard Dawkins's description of that God as one of the most unpleasant characters in fiction is the best-known modern form (Stage 12 answers it in full).

**Their case at its strongest.** Some Old Testament texts command or describe violence that seems flatly opposed to "love your enemies". A modern reader cannot simply accept them. Either God changed, or the texts are not fully from God.

**The Orthodox answer, and where Orthodox readers differ in emphasis.**

1. **The Church never read these texts as Marcion did.** The Fathers read the Old Testament **in Christ**, and often spiritually. Origen and St Gregory of Nyssa read the destruction of the Canaanites as the destruction of the passions; Gregory says in his *Life of Moses* that a literal reading of some texts would be unworthy of God. Other Fathers took the history more literally and stressed that God's judgements on particular nations, at a particular time, were just and are not a pattern for Christians.
2. **The same God judges in the New Testament.** The Book of Revelation and Christ's words on judgement are not milder than the prophets. **Mercy and justice are not two gods; they are one God seen from two sides.**
3. **The story moves.** God teaches a people step by step, as a father teaches a child. St Paul calls the Law a "schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ" (Galatians 3:24). What Moses permitted "because of the hardness of your hearts" (Matthew 19:8) is not the final word.
4. **Christ reads the Old Testament as His own.** On the road to Emmaus He began "at Moses and all the prophets" to show them "the things concerning himself" (Luke 24:27). **A Christian who sets the Old Testament aside sets aside the Bible Christ read.**

**Their best reply.** The spiritual reading can look like a way to avoid what the text says. **The Orthodox reply**: the Fathers did not deny the history; they held that its meaning for the Church is found in Christ, and the Church has always read it so.

**What it rests on.** **Is the Old Testament a record of a different God, or of the same God preparing a people for Christ?**
Arius: the Son as the first and greatest:
No heresy shook the Church more than Arius's, and no council is better known than the one that answered it. Theology Stage 7 teaches Nicaea; this lesson gives Arius's case at its strongest and shows the pattern.

**Who.** Arius (about 256–336) was a presbyter in charge of the Baucalis church in Alexandria, an ascetic and a popular preacher, trained in the school of **Lucian of Antioch**. About 318 he began to teach that the Son of God had a beginning. His bishop, St Alexander, condemned him; Arius found support among bishops in Asia Minor and Palestine, above all **Eusebius of Nicomedia**. He set his teaching to verse in a work called the *Thalia* ("Banquet"), of which only fragments survive, in the quotations of his opponents.

**His case at its strongest.** Arius was not trying to lower Christ; he believed he was protecting God.

1. **God is one and unbegotten.** Scripture insists there is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4). If the Son is also God, unbegotten and eternal, there are two Gods.
2. **A son comes after a father.** To be begotten is to have a beginning. So "there was once when the Son was not".
3. **Scripture calls Him created.** Proverbs 8:22 in the Septuagint has Wisdom say "The Lord made me the beginning of his ways for his works" (Brenton's translation, 1844); the Fathers and Arius alike read Wisdom as the Son. Colossians 1:15 calls Christ "the firstborn of every creature"; John 14:28, "my Father is greater than I".
4. **The Son is still unique.** He was made before all ages, by God's will, as the instrument through whom everything else was made. He is "perfect God", Arius wrote, but **not God as the Father is God**.

**The pattern.** Arius took a true thing, **the oneness and the unbegottenness of the Father**, and made it decide everything. The Son had to fall on the creature side of the line between God and creation.

**The Council of Nicaea (325).** The bishops declared the Son "of one essence with the Father", *homooúsios tō Patrí* (ὁμοούσιος τῷ Πατρί), "begotten, not made". They added anathemas against those who say "there was when He was not" and "He was made from things that were not".

**What it rests on.** **Is there one line between God and everything else, and on which side of it is the Son?** Arius said: one God, then creatures, and the Son is the first of them. Nicaea said: the Son is on God's side, begotten of the Father's essence, not made. There is no third category. **A being who is neither God nor creature does not exist.**

**What follows.** If the Son is a creature, worshipping Him is idolatry, and He cannot unite us to God. Lesson 8 reads St Athanasius on exactly this. Lesson 9 shows where Arius's position lives today.
Reading: Arius's letter to Eusebius of N:
Arius's own words survive in only a few places. The most important is a letter he wrote about 318, after his bishop had condemned him, to his most powerful supporter. It is the clearest statement of his teaching in his own voice.

**Where it survives.** The church historian Theodoret of Cyrus (about 393–about 458) copied it into his *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, chapter 4 (in NPNF numbering).

**The text** (Theodoret, Ecclesiastical History I.4; tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 3, 1892):

> "To his very dear lord, the man of God, the faithful and orthodox Eusebius, Arius, unjustly persecuted by Alexander the Pope, on account of that all-conquering truth of which you also are a champion, sends greeting in the Lord. ...
>
> He has driven us out of the city as atheists, because we do not concur in what he publicly preaches, namely, God always, the Son always; as the Father so the Son; the Son co-exists unbegotten with God; He is everlasting; neither by thought nor by any interval does God precede the Son; always God, always Son; he is begotten of the unbegotten; the Son is of God Himself. ...
>
> But we say and believe, and have taught, and do teach, that the Son is not unbegotten, nor in any way part of the unbegotten; and that He does not derive His subsistence from any matter; but that by His own will and counsel He has subsisted before time, and before ages, as perfect God, only begotten and unchangeable, and that before He was begotten, or created, or purposed, or established, He was not. For He was not unbegotten. We are persecuted, because we say that the Son has a beginning, but that God is without beginning."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"Alexander the Pope."** In 4th-century Egypt the bishop of Alexandria was called *Pápas*, "father"; the title is still used by the Coptic and Greek patriarchs of Alexandria. Arius uses it of his own bishop.
2. **He states his opponent's teaching fairly.** "God always, the Son always ... always God, always Son." This is exactly what Nicaea would confirm. **Arius saw clearly where the line ran.**
3. **What he denies.** The Son is not "unbegotten", not "part of the unbegotten", not made from "any matter". Arius is careful: he does not want the Son to be a piece of God (that would divide God) or made of matter (that would make Him like us).
4. **What he affirms.** The Son exists "by His own will and counsel" (the Father's will), "before time, and before ages", "perfect God, only begotten and unchangeable". **This is a very high view of the Son**, and many who heard it thought it pious.
5. **The decisive words.** "Before He was begotten, or created, or purposed, or established, He was not." Arius puts "begotten" and "created" side by side as if they meant the same. **Everything turns on that equation.** "The Son has a beginning, but ... God is without beginning."
6. **"Fellow-Lucianist."** At the end (not quoted above) Arius greets Eusebius as a fellow pupil of Lucian of Antioch: the network behind the teaching.

**What to take from it.** Arius was not a crude unbeliever. He held a sincere, reasoned, high view of Christ that stopped short of saying He is God as the Father is God. **That is why his view keeps returning: it seems to honour both God's oneness and Christ's greatness.** The next lesson reads the Orthodox answer.
Reading: St Athanasius against \"there w:
St Athanasius wrote his *Discourses against the Arians* in exile, about 340 by one common dating (some scholars place them in the 350s). They are the fullest answer the Church gave to Arius. This lesson reads two short passages from the first discourse.

**The text, first passage** (Discourse I against the Arians, §11; tr. John Henry Newman and Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892):

> "At his suggestion then you have maintained and you think, that 'there was once when the Son was not;' this is the first cloke of your views of doctrine which has to be stripped off. Say then what was once when the Son was not, O slanderous and irreligious men? If you say the Father, your blasphemy is but greater; for it is impious to say that He was 'once,' or to signify Him by the word 'once.' For He is ever, and is now, and as the Son is, so is He, and is Himself He that is, and Father of the Son."

**The text, second passage** (§19):

> "Is it not then irreligious to say, 'Once the Son was not?' for it is all one with saying, 'Once the Fountain was dry, destitute of Life and Wisdom.' But a fountain it would then cease to be; for what begets not from itself, is not a fountain."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"Once."** Athanasius seizes on the little word *pote* (ποτέ), "once". To say "once the Son was not" is to put **time before the Son**. But Scripture says all things, time included, were made through Him (John 1:3). The Son cannot come after something that He made.
2. **"Father" is an eternal name.** If the Son had a beginning, then God was once not a Father. **The Father is Father by having the Son**; if the Son is not eternal, God's fatherhood is something that happened to Him. Arius's protection of God ends by changing God.
3. **The fountain.** Scripture calls God "the fountain of living waters" (Jeremiah 2:13) and Christ His Wisdom and Life. A fountain is a fountain because water flows from it. **A God without His Word and Wisdom would be a dry spring.** The Son is not an addition to God; He is what God has always had.
4. **Begotten is not made.** Throughout the discourses, Athanasius separates what Arius had joined. **To beget is to give one's own nature** (a man begets a man); **to make is to produce something of another nature** (a man makes a house). The Son is begotten of the Father's essence, so He is what the Father is. Creation is made, by His will, from nothing.
5. **Why it matters.** Elsewhere Athanasius argues from salvation: a creature cannot deify creatures. **If the Son is not God, we are not saved.**

**Reading the two letters together.**

| Arius | Athanasius |
| --- | --- |
| begotten and created mean the same | begotten gives the Father's own nature; created is from nothing |
| the Son has a beginning; God is without beginning | God was never without His Word; "Father" is an eternal name |
| the Son is "perfect God" by the Father's will | the Son is God by nature, of one essence with the Father |

**What to take from it.** The whole dispute turns on two words, "begotten" and "made", and on whether time can come before the Word. **Athanasius answers with Scripture and with what the names "Father" and "Son" mean.**
Arius today: Witnesses, Unitarians and \:
Arius's view did not end at Nicaea. It ruled much of the empire for half a century, lived on among the Goths until the 6th and 7th centuries, and returned after the Reformation. Today its largest heirs are Jehovah's Witnesses.

**The line of descent (of ideas, not of churches).**

| Movement | Founded | What it holds about the Son |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Socinians** | Poland, 16th century; the *Racovian Catechism* (1605) | Christ a man, raised to divine honour; no pre-existence |
| **Unitarians** | England and New England, 18th–19th centuries | God is one person; Jesus a man, a great teacher |
