| **Jehovah's Witnesses** | Charles Taze Russell's Bible Students, from the 1870s; the name from 1931 | the Son is God's first creation, the archangel Michael before His birth on earth |
| **"Biblical Unitarians"** | small modern groups | God the Father alone; Jesus the human Messiah |

The Witnesses are the closest to Arius: **a pre-existent Son, made before everything else, through whom God made the rest.** Stage 8 answers them in full; here is the pattern.

**Their case at its strongest, from their own texts** (paraphrased from the Witnesses' published teaching on jw.org): Jehovah alone is Almighty God; Jesus is "the firstborn of every creature" (Colossians 1:15, KJV) and "the beginning of the creation of God" (Revelation 3:14, KJV), so He had a beginning; Jesus Himself says the Father is greater (John 14:28) and does not know the day or hour (Mark 13:32); the Trinity is not in the Bible and was settled by councils under emperors. Their *New World Translation* renders John 1:1 "and the Word was a god", arguing that the Greek has no article before *theós*.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **John 1:1.** The Greek reads *kaì theòs ēn ho lógos*. In Greek a predicate noun placed before the verb often lacks the article and still means the full quality: "the Word was God" in nature. **"A god" would make John, a strict Jewish monotheist, teach two gods**, a greater and a lesser. The verse continues: "All things were made by him" (1:3), so He is not one of the things made.
2. **"Firstborn."** *Prōtótokos* (πρωτότοκος) means pre-eminence as well as order: David, the youngest son, is made God's "firstborn" (Psalm 89:27). And Colossians 1:16 says "by him were all things created": the Son is the agent of creation, not part of it.
3. **"Greater."** The Fathers read John 14:28 of the Father as source and of Christ's humanity, not as a difference of nature. A son can be equal in nature to his father and still honour him.
4. **Worship.** Thomas calls Jesus "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), and He accepts it. **Worship of a creature is what Scripture forbids most strongly.**
5. **The councils.** The Trinity was not invented at Nicaea; the councils defended what the Church already prayed, baptising in the one name of Father, Son and Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19).

**Their best reply.** The Witnesses answer that Thomas's words are an exclamation, that the Church fell away early, and that the councils imported Greek philosophy. **The Orthodox reply**: the Church's worship of Christ is older than any philosophy brought to it, and Athanasius's question stands: can a creature save?

**What it rests on.** **Is there any being between God and creation?** Arius and the Witnesses say yes; Nicaea says there is not.
The modalists: Sabellius and the one God:
Arius protected God's oneness by making the Son less than God. An older party protected it the other way: by making Father, Son and Spirit the same person under different names. The Church called them "modalists" or "Sabellians".

**Who.** The teaching appeared in Asia Minor and Rome about 190–220. **Noetus of Smyrna** taught that the Father Himself was born and suffered. **Praxeas** brought a similar view to Rome; Tertullian answered him about 213 in *Against Praxeas*. **Sabellius**, in Rome about 215, gave the view its classic form and was excommunicated by Pope Callistus about 220. Their own writings are lost; we know them from opponents, so care is needed.

**What they taught, at its strongest.**

1. **God is one, absolutely.** "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4, KJV). One God means one person.
2. **Jesus is fully God.** Against those who lowered Christ, the modalists insisted He is God Himself, not a lesser being.
3. **So the Father and the Son must be the same.** Jesus says "I and my Father are one" (John 10:30) and "he that hath seen me hath seen the Father" (John 14:9).
4. **"Father", "Son" and "Spirit" are names of roles.** One God acts as Father in creation and the Law, as Son in the Incarnation, as Spirit in the Church. A later form spoke of three successive "modes", hence **modalism**; Sabellius is reported to have used the word *prósōpon* (πρόσωπον), which can mean "face" or "mask" as well as "person".

**The consequence the Fathers named.** If the Son is the Father, then the Father was born of Mary and the Father suffered on the cross. Hence the Latin name for the view, **patripassianism**, "the Father suffered". Tertullian's summary of Praxeas (Against Praxeas 1, tr. Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885): "he put to flight the Paraclete, and he crucified the Father."

**The Fathers' answer.**

1. **The Gospels show three, speaking to one another.** The Son prays to the Father; the Father speaks from heaven at the Baptism; the Son sends the Spirit "from the Father" (John 15:26). **One person cannot send himself, pray to himself, and glorify himself "with the glory which I had with thee before the world was"** (John 17:5).
2. **"One" in John 10:30 is neuter.** *Hén* (ἕν), "one thing", not *heîs*, "one person": one in essence, not one person.
3. **The names are eternal relations.** God is not Father only in creation; He is eternally the Father of the Son. If the persons are roles, **God in Himself is unknown** behind His masks, and revelation does not show us who He is.
4. **The Church's terms.** The Cappadocian Fathers later made the distinction exact: **one essence (*ousía*), three persons (*hypostáseis*)**. Theology Stage 2 teaches it.

**What it rests on.** **Are Father, Son and Spirit who God is, or only how God appears?** The modalist says how He appears; the Church says who He is.
Modalism today: Oneness Pentecostals and:
Modalism returned in the 20th century in a large movement, and it lives on unnoticed in many ordinary explanations of the Trinity.

**Oneness Pentecostals.** At a Pentecostal camp meeting at Arroyo Seco, near Los Angeles, in 1913, a preacher spoke on baptism "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38). Some hearers, among them Frank Ewart, concluded that the one name of Matthew 28:19 is **Jesus**, and that Father, Son and Holy Spirit are titles of the one God revealed in Jesus. The movement split from the Trinitarian Assemblies of God in 1916. Its largest body in America is the **United Pentecostal Church International** (formed 1945); there are large Oneness churches in Latin America, Africa and Asia. They are sometimes called "Jesus Only", a name they reject.

**Their case at its strongest, from their own teaching** (paraphrased from the UPCI's published "Our Beliefs"): there is **one God**, who has revealed Himself as Father in creation, as Son in the Incarnation, and as Holy Spirit in regeneration; **Jesus is the name** of that one God, and in Him dwells "all the fulness of the Godhead bodily" (Colossians 2:9); the apostles always baptised "in the name of Jesus" (Acts 2:38; 8:16; 10:48; 19:5); the word "Trinity" and "three persons" are not in the Bible.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The same as to Sabellius.** The Son prays to the Father and is sent by Him; the Father loves the Son "before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). **Love needs two.** If God is one person, He was not love before He made someone to love.
2. **"In the name of Jesus" in Acts** means by His authority and into Him; it does not replace the Trinitarian formula. The earliest church order outside the New Testament, the *Didache* (late 1st or early 2nd century), already gives baptism "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit".
3. **"All the fulness of the Godhead"** in Christ means that He is fully God, which the Church confesses, not that He is the Father.
4. **The word "Trinity" is not in the Bible**, and neither is "Incarnation". **A word is not false because it is later; the question is whether it names what Scripture teaches.**

**Their best reply.** Oneness teachers answer that the Son prays to the Father in His humanity, the man speaking to the God who dwells in him. **The Orthodox reply**: then the Son who prays is only a man, and we are back with a divided Christ (Lesson 12). The Son who prays is the eternal Word, who "had glory with the Father before the world was".

**The everyday form: bad analogies.** Many Christians explain the Trinity with analogies that are, strictly, modalist.

| Analogy | What it really teaches |
| --- | --- |
| **water, ice and steam** | one substance in three successive states: modalism |
| **one man who is a father, a son and a husband** | one person in three roles: modalism |
| **a three-leaf clover** | three parts of one thing: each person a third of God, which is also wrong |

**The Fathers' caution.** St Gregory the Theologian tried several images and said that none was adequate. **Every analogy fails somewhere**; the safe course is to say exactly what the Church says: one essence, three persons, each fully God.

**What it rests on.** As with Sabellius: **are Father, Son and Spirit three who are eternally one God, or one who appears three ways?**
Nestorius: two sons and the Theotokos:
The third great Christological controversy began with a title of the Virgin Mary, and it shows how a word about her is really a word about Christ.

**Who.** Nestorius (about 386–451) was a monk and preacher of Antioch, trained in the Antiochene school of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and was made archbishop of Constantinople in **428**. Soon after, he backed a priest who preached against calling Mary *Theotókos* (Θεοτόκος), "she who gave birth to God". Nestorius preferred *Christotókos*, "she who gave birth to Christ".

**His case at its strongest.** Nestorius was defending something real.

1. **God cannot be born, suffer or die.** The divine nature is eternal and impassible. To say "God was born" sounds pagan, like the births of the Greek gods.
2. **Christ's humanity is real and complete.** Against Apollinarius, who had denied Christ a human mind, the Antiochenes insisted that Christ had a full human nature that grew, learned and suffered.
3. **So the two natures must be kept distinct.** Mary gave birth to the humanity, in which the Word dwelt as in a temple. She is the mother of Christ, of the man in whom God was united, not of the Godhead.

**What the Church heard.** St Cyril of Alexandria (about 376–444) saw that Nestorius's language made Christ **two subjects**: the Word, and a man joined to Him by a union of will and honour. If Mary bore only the man, then the one born of her is not the Word, and the one who died on the cross is not God. **We would be saved by a man in whom God dwelt, not by God made man.**

**The Council of Ephesus (431).** The council, led by Cyril, deposed Nestorius and confirmed Mary as **Theotokos**. Cyril's first anathema, which the council received (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900), reads:

> "If anyone will not confess that the Emmanuel is very God, and that therefore the Holy Virgin is the Mother of God (Θεοτόκος), inasmuch as in the flesh she bore the Word of God made flesh [as it is written, The Word was made flesh] let him be anathema."

**Why the title is about Christ.** Mothers give birth to persons, not to natures. **The person born of Mary is the eternal Word.** He was born according to His humanity, but it was He, the Word, who was born. So Mary is truly Mother of God. The Orthodox call this the **communication of properties** (*antídosis tôn idiōmátōn*): what belongs to either nature is said of the one person. "God was born", "God died in the flesh", are true sentences.

**Honest history.** Nestorius died in exile in Egypt about 451. A long defence he wrote late in life, the *Bazaar of Heracleides*, came to light in a Syriac manuscript in the 1890s; some modern scholars argue from it that he was closer to Chalcedon than his enemies allowed. **The Church condemned the teaching his words expressed**, and the council's judgement stands; but the man himself was more careful than the caricature.

**What it rests on.** **Is the one who was born of Mary and died on the cross the eternal Son of God, or a man united to Him?**
Nestorius's pattern today: \"the mother:
Nestorius's name is now attached to a church that hardly fits it, and his pattern appears in places that have never heard of him. This lesson separates the two.

**The Church of the East.** The ancient church of Persia, today the **Assyrian Church of the East** and the **Ancient Church of the East**, did not accept Ephesus and honours Nestorius and Theodore of Mopsuestia as teachers. For centuries it was called "Nestorian". Modern scholars, and the church itself, reject the label: its Christology developed in Syriac in its own way, and it confesses one Christ. In **1994** Pope John Paul II and Patriarch Mar Dinkha IV signed a **Common Christological Declaration** stating that both churches confess the same faith in Christ, while each keeps its own titles for Mary. There is no comparable Orthodox agreement **as of November 2026**, though there have been Orthodox contacts. In 1898 a group of the Church of the East in the Urmia region of Persia, with its bishop, was received into the Russian Orthodox Church. **This church is not the subject of this lesson**; it deserves to be met in its own terms.

**The pattern in the West.** Among some Protestants, the title Theotokos is refused, in words close to Nestorius's (paraphrased from a common objection): Mary is the mother of Jesus' human nature, not of God; God has no mother; calling her Mother of God exalts her above Christ. This comes in good faith, from a wish to guard God's eternity and to avoid honouring Mary too much.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The Reformers kept the council.** The magisterial Reformers accepted the Council of Ephesus; Luther used the title "Mother of God" freely, and the Lutheran Formula of Concord (1577) affirms that Mary is truly the mother of God. **Rejecting the title is not the Reformers' own position; it is a later development.** (Stage 6 gives the evidence.)
2. **"Mother of God" is a statement about Christ.** It does not say Mary is older than God or the source of the Godhead. It says that **the one she bore is God**. Elizabeth already calls her "the mother of my Lord" (Luke 1:43, KJV), and "Lord" there is the title of God.
3. **The alternative divides Christ.** If Mary is mother only of the human nature, then the human nature has a mother but the person does not; or else there are two persons. Either way, the one who died is not the Word. **Every refusal of the title, followed through, leads back to Nestorius's two subjects.**
4. **The honour follows from the faith.** The Church honours Mary highly because of whom she bore. The hymn that calls her more honourable than the cherubim is a hymn about the Incarnation.

**Their best reply.** Many evangelicals answer that they believe Jesus is fully God and that Mary bore Him, but avoid the title because of what they see as excessive devotion in Catholic and Orthodox practice. **The Orthodox reply**: then they hold the doctrine of Ephesus, and the disagreement is not about Christ but about the honour of the Theotokos, a separate question, which Stage 6 treats.

**Another modern echo.** The 19th- and 20th-century distinction between "the Jesus of history" and "the Christ of faith", where a human teacher is separated from the divine Lord the Church worships, is Nestorian in shape: **two Christs, one for the historian and one for the believer.** Stage 12 answers it.

**What it rests on.** **Is the child Mary bore the eternal Word in person?** If yes, the title follows.
The iconoclasts: image and idol:
The last of the heresies settled by an ecumenical council was the attack on icons. It lasted, with a break, over a century, and its defeat is still celebrated on the first Sunday of Great Lent.

**The history in brief.** Theology Stage 8 teaches it in full.

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **726–730** | Emperor Leo III acts against icons; the first iconoclasm |
| **754** | the iconoclast Council of Hieria condemns images |
| **787** | the **Seventh Ecumenical Council, Nicaea II**, restores them |
| **815** | the second iconoclasm under Leo V |
| **843** | Empress Theodora restores the icons: the **Triumph of Orthodoxy** |

**The word.** *Eikṓn* (εἰκών), "image"; *eikonoklástēs*, "image-breaker".

**Their case at its strongest.** The iconoclasts were not secularists; they were zealous Christians with serious arguments.

1. **The commandment.** "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image" (Exodus 20:4, KJV). Moses warned that Israel "saw no manner of similitude" at Horeb (Deuteronomy 4:15).
2. **God cannot be depicted.** He is invisible and uncircumscribable. A picture can show only a body.
3. **The Christological dilemma** (the strongest argument, from the Council of Hieria). An icon of Christ either depicts His divinity, which is impossible, or depicts His humanity alone, which separates it from His divinity, as Nestorius did. Either way it is heresy. **The only true image of Christ is the Eucharist.**
4. **Practice.** Devotion to images had excesses: some scraped paint into the chalice or took icons as godparents.

**The Orthodox answer: St John of Damascus.** Writing about 730 from outside the empire, John answered with the Incarnation (tr. Mary H. Allies, *St John Damascene on Holy Images*, 1898):

> "Of old, God the incorporeal and uncircumscribed was never depicted. Now, however, when God is seen clothed in flesh, and conversing with men, (Bar. 3.38) I make an image of the God whom I see. I do not worship matter, I worship the God of matter, who became matter for my sake, and deigned to inhabit matter, who worked out my salvation through matter."

**The answer in four points.**

1. **The commandment forbids idols, not all images.** The same Law commanded "two cherubims of gold" over the ark (Exodus 25:18). What it forbids is making a likeness of the invisible God and worshipping it.
2. **The Incarnation changed what can be seen.** The invisible God became visible in Christ. To refuse to depict Him is, in effect, to deny that He truly became man.
3. **An icon depicts a person, not a nature.** This answers Hieria: the icon shows the person of the Word, as He was seen in the flesh. It neither depicts the divine nature nor separates it.
4. **Veneration is not worship.** Nicaea II distinguished **latreía** (λατρεία), the worship due to God alone, from **proskýnēsis** (προσκύνησις), reverence, given to icons. Its definition (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900): "the honour which is paid to the image passes on to that which the image represents, and he who reveres the image reveres in it the subject represented." The phrase comes from St Basil.

**What it rests on.** **Did the Incarnation make the invisible God visible, so that He may be depicted as He was seen?**
Iconoclasm today: the Reformed case agai:
The heirs of iconoclasm today are mostly in the Reformed tradition, the churches that follow Zwingli and Calvin. Their case is serious and should be heard at its strongest.

**The history.** In Zürich in 1524, under Zwingli's influence, images were removed from the churches; in the Low Countries in 1566, crowds smashed statues and windows in the *Beeldenstorm* ("image storm"); in England and Scotland, images were destroyed under Edward VI, Elizabeth I and the Puritans. Lutherans, by contrast, kept many images, and Luther opposed the image-breakers.

**Their case at its strongest, from their own texts.** John Calvin, *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, Book I, chapter 11, section 12 (tr. Henry Beveridge, 1845):

> "I am not, however, so superstitious as to think that all visible representations of every kind are unlawful. But as sculpture and painting are gifts of God, what I insist for is, that both shall be used purely and lawfully ... We think it unlawful to give a visible shape to God, because God himself has forbidden it, and because it cannot be done without, in some degree, tarnishing his glory. ... If it be unlawful to make any corporeal representation of God, still more unlawful must it be to worship such a representation instead of God, or to worship God in it."

The Westminster Larger Catechism (1648), on the second commandment, likewise names among its sins "the making any representation of God, of all or of any of the three persons" (question 109). The Reformed argument runs:

1. **The second commandment is a separate command** (in the Reformed numbering) forbidding images in worship, not only idols.
2. **Christ is God**, so a picture of Christ is a picture of God, which is forbidden.
3. **God has chosen how to be known**: through the Word preached and the sacraments, not through images.
4. **Bowing before an image is worship**, whatever distinction one makes in theory.

**Note what Calvin does not say.** He does not forbid all art: he allows historical pictures for teaching. **His objection is to depicting God and to venerating images.**

**The Orthodox answer.** It is Nicaea II's answer, and it meets each point.

1. **On the commandment.** The cherubim on the ark and in the Temple show that God Himself commanded images in worship. The commandment forbids making a likeness of the God who "saw no manner of similitude" at Horeb. **At the Incarnation He showed one.**
2. **On a picture of Christ.** The icon depicts the person of the Word **as He was seen**: in the flesh, with a human face. Calvin's argument, like Hieria's, assumes that to depict Christ is to claim to depict the divine nature. The Orthodox answer is that we depict a person, not a nature.
3. **On the Word preached.** St Basil said, and the Seventh Council repeated, that what the word gives through the ear, painting shows silently through the image (paraphrased). **The Church has never set image against Word.**
4. **On bowing.** Scripture records bowing to honour persons without worshipping them (Abraham before the Hittites, Genesis 23:7). The distinction between *latreia* and *proskynesis* is not a theory added to cover idolatry; it is in the language of the Bible.

**Their best reply.** The Reformed answer that the cherubim were commanded by God and icons were not, and that no human hand can depict the person of the Son without depicting the man as if he were separable. **The Orthodox reply**: the Church depicted Christ from early centuries (the catacombs show Him), and a council of the whole Church judged the question in 787.

**What it rests on.** **Has the Incarnation changed the second commandment's application, because God has now been seen?** Lutherans and Orthodox say yes, in different ways; the Reformed say no.
Looking back: the pattern of the old her:
This stage took six ancient errors and showed how each comes back. Before turning to the faiths outside Christianity, gather the pattern.

**The six, side by side.**

| Heresy | The true thing it started from | Where it was cut loose | The Church's answer | Modern echo |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Gnosticism** | evil is real; Christ reveals | matter evil, salvation secret | one God made all good; the Word made flesh; public tradition | lost gospels; "spiritual but not religious" |
| **Marcion** | God is love, revealed in Christ | two gods, two Testaments | one God in both Testaments, read in Christ | the Old Testament as an embarrassment |
| **Arius** | God is one and unbegotten | the Son a creature | *homoousios*, begotten not made (Nicaea, 325) | Jehovah's Witnesses, Unitarians |
| **Modalism** | God is one; Jesus is fully God | Father, Son and Spirit one person | three hypostases, one essence | Oneness Pentecostals; water-ice-steam |
| **Nestorius** | Christ is fully man; God cannot suffer in His nature | two subjects in Christ | one person, Mary Theotokos (Ephesus, 431) | refusing "Mother of God" |
| **Iconoclasm** | God is invisible; idols are forbidden | no image of the incarnate Christ | images of the person seen (Nicaea II, 787) | Reformed case against images |

**The lesson of the pattern.** **Every heresy is a truth cut loose from the rest of the faith.** That means the answer is always the same kind of answer: show the true thing, then show the whole of which it is a part. It also means one should **grant the true thing freely**. A Witness is right that God is one; a Reformed Christian is right that idolatry is forbidden. The answer begins there.

**The two great lines.** Almost all six heresies fall on one of two lines:

- **The Trinity line**: how God can be one and three (Arius, modalism).
- **The Incarnation line**: how God can be in matter, in flesh, in an image (Gnosticism, Nestorius, iconoclasm; Marcion in another way).

**Most later disputes fall on one of these lines too.** Islam and the Witnesses are on the first; much of the Reformation's quarrel with icons and sacraments is on the second.

**What this stage did not answer.** The **Oriental Orthodox** churches, which did not receive Chalcedon, are taught in Theology Stage 7 with the modern dialogues in Stage 12. The **Church of the East** is not the same thing as Nestorius's teaching, and the 1994 declaration with Rome shows why. Neither is answered here as a heresy.

**Questions to test yourself.**

1. What did the Gnostics mean by the Demiurge, and what verse of Genesis answers them?
2. What canon did Marcion make, and how did it answer itself?
3. In Arius's letter, which two words does he treat as meaning the same, and how does Athanasius separate them?
4. Why is "water, ice and steam" a modalist analogy?
5. Why is the title Theotokos a statement about Christ rather than about Mary?
6. How does the iconoclast "Christological dilemma" go, and how did Nicaea II answer it?

**What comes next.** Stage 3 turns to the faith that shares the Church's Scriptures and her roots: Judaism. **There, the method changes**: it is not a heresy, and the Church's own history toward it must be told honestly.
Context: why Judaism is answered differe:
Judaism is unlike every other faith this curriculum answers. It is not a heresy, not a rival revelation, and not a philosophy. **It is the faith of the people from whom Christ came, and its Scriptures are the Church's Old Testament.**

**What St Paul says.** No one wrote more intensely about the Jews who did not accept Christ than Paul, himself "an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin" (Romans 11:1, KJV). Of his kinsmen he says: "to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever" (Romans 9:4–5, KJV). And he warns the Gentile believers: "Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee" (Romans 11:18). Finally: "the gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (11:29).

**Why the method changes.** The four steps still apply, but three things differ:

1. **The common ground is huge.** The one God, the Creator; the Law and the prophets; the hope of the Messiah; the resurrection of the dead (held by the Pharisees, the ancestors of rabbinic Judaism). **The disagreement is not over whether God spoke to Israel, but over what He said and whether it has been fulfilled in Jesus.**
2. **The question is about one man.** Is Jesus of Nazareth the Messiah promised to Israel, and is He the Son of God? Everything else (the Law, the Trinity, the Temple) follows from that.
3. **The history is heavy.** Christians, the Orthodox among them, have wronged Jews for centuries: in preaching, in law, and in violence. A Jew who hears the Christian case hears it after that history. **This stage tells it plainly** (Lesson 16), and also tells of the Orthodox who stood with Jews (Lesson 17).

**What this stage covers.**

| Lessons | Subject |
| --- | --- |
| 2–4 | what Judaism teaches; how rabbinic Judaism arose; the Talmud |
| 5–6 | which Old Testament: the Septuagint and the Hebrew text; Isaiah 7:14 |
| 7–10 | the Messiah: what is expected; Isaiah 53 read by both sides; Justin and Trypho; Daniel's weeks |
| 11–12 | God: the Shema and the Trinity; the Word and the Angel of the Lord |
| 13–15 | the Law, the sacrifices, and the Jewish case against Jesus |
| 16–17 | the Church's history toward the Jews, told honestly |

**A word on terms.** "Judaism" here means rabbinic Judaism, the faith shaped by the rabbis after the destruction of the Temple in 70 and handed down in the Talmud. It is not identical to the religion of the Old Testament, and Jews say so too. **Christianity and rabbinic Judaism are both heirs of Second Temple Judaism**, each claiming to be its true continuation. That is the real shape of the question.

**What it leans on.** Theology Stage 5 teaches the Septuagint and how the Church reads the Old Testament in Christ (typology). History teaches the events. This stage uses both.

**The aim.** To know Judaism as an observant Jew would recognise it; to give the Church's answer as the Fathers and the apostles gave it, from the Scriptures both sides share; and to do so **as Paul did, "with great heaviness and continual sorrow"** (Romans 9:2), not with triumph.
What Judaism teaches: the Thirteen Princ:
Judaism is a religion of practice more than of creeds, and many Jews say it has no dogmas in the Christian sense. But the most famous summary of Jewish belief, by the greatest medieval Jewish thinker, gives a fair starting point.

**Maimonides.** Rabbi Moses ben Maimon (1138–1204), known as **Maimonides** or by the acronym **Rambam**, was born in Córdoba and died in Egypt, where he was a physician at the court of Saladin's family. He wrote the *Mishneh Torah*, a code of Jewish law, and the *Guide for the Perplexed*. In his commentary on the Mishnah (tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 10), written about 1168, he set out **Thirteen Principles** of faith. In summary (paraphrased):

| # | Principle |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | God is the Creator and sustains all that exists |
| 2 | God is one, with a unity unlike any other |
| 3 | God has no body or bodily form |
| 4 | God is eternal, the first and the last |
| 5 | God alone is to be worshipped |
| 6 | God spoke through the prophets |
| 7 | Moses is the greatest of the prophets |
| 8 | the Torah was given to Moses from heaven |
| 9 | the Torah will not be changed or replaced |
| 10 | God knows the deeds and thoughts of men |
| 11 | God rewards and punishes |
| 12 | the Messiah will come; one should wait for him though he delay |
| 13 | the dead will be raised |

A poetic form of the principles, the hymn *Yigdal*, and a prose form beginning "I believe with perfect faith" (*Ani Ma'amin*) are printed in many Jewish prayer books.

**Notice where Christians agree.** Principles 1, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11 and 13 the Church confesses as well. **Principles 2, 3, 9 and 12 are where the disagreement lies**: God's unity (against the Trinity), God without a body (against the Incarnation), the Torah unchangeable (against the new covenant), and the Messiah still to come.

**The movements today.** Jews differ widely in practice and belief.

| Movement | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **Orthodox** (Haredi, Hasidic, Modern Orthodox) | the written and oral Torah are from God; Jewish law (*halakhah*) binds |
| **Conservative** (Masorti) | the law binds but develops historically |
| **Reform** (Progressive, Liberal) | the ethical core binds; ritual law is a matter of choice |
| **Reconstructionist** | Judaism as the evolving civilisation of the Jewish people |
| **secular Jews** | Jewish by people and culture, often not religious |

**Numbers, as of November 2026.** The most cited demographer, Sergio DellaPergola, put the core world Jewish population at about **15.8 million** in 2025, with Israel holding about 46 percent and the United States most of the rest. Counts with wider definitions are higher.

**Who is a Jew.** In rabbinic law, a Jew is one born of a Jewish mother or converted according to the law; Reform Judaism in America also accepts descent through the father. **Being Jewish is belonging to a people, not only holding a belief**, and many Jews who do not believe are fully Jewish. This matters in conversation: a secular Israeli and a Hasid in Brooklyn need very different answers.

**The answerer's starting point.** Ask which Judaism the person holds. Most of this stage answers religious Judaism, especially Orthodox, because it makes the fullest claims and is the strongest case.
From the Temple to the rabbis: how rabbi:
Christianity and rabbinic Judaism grew from the same root at the same time. Knowing how helps one see why each claims to be Israel's true heir.

**Before 70.** In Jesus' time, Judaism had several parties. The Jewish historian Josephus (about 37–100) names four:

| Party | What it held |
| --- | --- |
| **Sadducees** | priestly; only the written Torah; no resurrection |
| **Pharisees** | the written Torah with the "tradition of the fathers"; resurrection; angels |
| **Essenes** | a strict separatist community, probably linked to the Dead Sea Scrolls |
| **the "fourth philosophy"** | revolutionaries who would accept no king but God |

The followers of Jesus were, at first, another group within Judaism, worshipping in the Temple (Acts 2:46) and called "the sect of the Nazarenes" (Acts 24:5).

**The disaster of 70.** The Jewish revolt against Rome (66–70) ended with the **destruction of the Temple** by Titus in 70. Sacrifice stopped. The Sadducees, whose life was the Temple, disappeared. Of the parties, the **Pharisees** and the **Christians** survived, and both had answers to the loss of the Temple.

**Yavneh.** According to rabbinic tradition, Rabbi **Yohanan ben Zakkai** escaped the siege and founded an academy at **Yavneh** (Jamnia) on the coast. There the sages rebuilt Judaism around **the Torah, prayer and study**, without a Temple. A second revolt under **Bar Kokhba** (132–135), whom the great Rabbi Akiva hailed as the Messiah, ended in a further catastrophe; Jews were banned from Jerusalem.

**The parting of the ways.** Modern historians stress that the separation was gradual and uneven, taking a century or more in some places. Some points along the way:

1. The Christians did not join Bar Kokhba, whom they could not accept as Messiah.
2. A blessing against "heretics" (*minim*) was added to the daily Jewish prayer; whether it targeted Christians from the start is debated by scholars.
3. Gentile believers soon outnumbered Jewish ones, and the Church stopped keeping the ritual Law (Acts 15).

**Two answers to the same loss.**

| Question | Rabbinic answer | Christian answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where is God's presence without the Temple? | in the Torah studied and the commandments kept | in Christ, "the temple of his body" (John 2:21), and in the Church |
| How are sins forgiven without sacrifice? | repentance, prayer, deeds of love | the sacrifice of Christ, once for all |
| Who is Israel? | the Jewish people, keeping the covenant | all who are in Christ, the Messiah of Israel |

**Why this matters.** Neither faith is simply "the religion of the Old Testament". **Both read the same Scriptures through a centre**: the rabbis through the oral Torah, the Church through Christ. The real argument is over which centre is the true one.

**What it rests on.** **Did the history of Israel reach its goal in Jesus, or is it still waiting?**
The Talmud and the Oral Torah:
For Orthodox Jews, the Torah given at Sinai came in two forms: the written Torah, the five books of Moses, and an **oral Torah** that explains it. The oral Torah was later written down in the Mishnah and the Talmud. It is the heart of rabbinic Judaism.

**The claim, at its strongest.** The written Torah cannot be kept without explanation. It commands rest on the Sabbath but does not define work; it commands *tefillin* but does not say how to make them. Therefore, Orthodox Judaism holds, **God gave Moses the explanation along with the text**, and it was handed down from teacher to pupil. The tractate *Pirkei Avot* ("Sayings of the Fathers") opens (paraphrased): Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and the prophets to the men of the Great Assembly.

**The books.**

| Work | When | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mishnah** | edited about 200, by Rabbi Judah the Prince | the oral law in six orders: agriculture, festivals, women, damages, holy things, purity |
| **Jerusalem Talmud** | about 400, in Galilee | discussion (*Gemara*) of the Mishnah |
| **Babylonian Talmud** | about 500–600, with later editing, in Babylonia | the larger and more authoritative Talmud |
| **Midrash** | 3rd century onward | interpretation of Scripture, legal and narrative |

Talmud means "study" or "learning". Its pages place the Mishnah in the centre, the Gemara around it, and commentaries (above all **Rashi**, 1040–1105) around them. The Talmud counts **613 commandments** in the Torah.

**What the Orthodox Christian should notice.** The rabbinic claim is close in shape to the Church's own: **Scripture cannot be read rightly apart from a tradition received with it.** An Orthodox Christian cannot answer the Talmud by saying "Scripture alone". The question is not whether there is an oral tradition but **which tradition is the true one.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Christ's judgement on "the tradition of the elders".** In Mark 7:8–13 Christ rebukes the Pharisees for "laying aside the commandment of God" to hold "the tradition of men", giving the example of a vow used to avoid supporting one's parents. **He does not reject tradition as such; He judges a tradition that sets God's word aside.**
2. **The apostles' tradition.** The Church holds that the true tradition of the meaning of Scripture is the one given by Christ, who "opened ... their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures" (Luke 24:45), and handed down by the apostles (2 Thessalonians 2:15).
3. **The test of the centre.** The rabbis' tradition reads the Law as the centre; the apostles' tradition reads Christ as the centre of the Law and the prophets.

**Their best reply.** The rabbis answer that the Christian tradition is a later reading imposed on the Hebrew Scriptures, and that the continuity of the Jewish people keeping the commandments is the living proof of theirs. **The Orthodox reply**: both traditions are continuous; the question is which one the prophets pointed to, and Lessons 7–10 take that up.

**A caution about the Talmud.** It is a vast record of argument, including minority opinions and folklore. A few passages speak harshly of a "Yeshu"; scholars debate whom they mean and when they were written (Peter Schäfer, *Jesus in the Talmud*, 2007). **Quoting stray passages to shock is the polemic of the medieval burnings of the Talmud, not of the Fathers.** Read it, if at all, as its own students read it.
The Septuagint and the Masoretic text: w:
Before any argument from prophecy, one question must be settled: which text of the Old Testament? The Church and the synagogue read different ones, and some disputed prophecies depend on the difference.

**The Septuagint.** About the 3rd century BC, Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated the Torah into Greek; the rest of the Scriptures followed over the next two centuries. The *Letter of Aristeas* tells that seventy-two elders made the translation, hence the Latin name **Septuagint** (*Septuaginta*, "seventy"), abbreviated **LXX**. It was the Bible of Greek-speaking Jews and of the apostles: most quotations of the Old Testament in the New are from it. **It is the Old Testament of the Orthodox Church** (Theology Stage 5).

**The Masoretic text.** The Hebrew text used by Jews today was fixed by about the end of the 1st century and later furnished with vowels and notes by scholars called the **Masoretes** (from *masorah*, "tradition"), working from about the 7th to the 10th century. Its best manuscripts are the **Aleppo Codex** (about 930) and the **Leningrad Codex** (1008).

**What changed after Christ.** As Christians used the Septuagint against them, Jewish teachers turned away from it. About 130, a convert to Judaism named **Aquila** made a new, very literal Greek translation for Jewish use. St Justin, about 160, accused the Jewish teachers of rejecting the Septuagint and even removing passages from it (Dialogue with Trypho 71–73). **Some of Justin's specific charges cannot be supported from the manuscripts**, and honesty requires saying so.

**The Dead Sea Scrolls.** Found from 1947 near Qumran, the scrolls include Hebrew texts a thousand years older than the Masoretic manuscripts. They show that **in the time of Christ there was more than one form of the Hebrew text**. Some scrolls agree with the Masoretic text; some agree with the Hebrew from which the Septuagint was translated.

| Passage | Masoretic text | Septuagint | Dead Sea Scrolls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Deuteronomy 32:8** | nations divided "according to the number of the children of Israel" | "according to the number of the angels of God" | a Qumran scroll reads "sons of God", the Hebrew behind the Septuagint |
| **Deuteronomy 32:43** | short | longer, including "let all the angels of God worship him" (quoted in Hebrews 1:6) | a Qumran scroll has the longer form in part |
| **Jeremiah** | longer | about one-eighth shorter, in a different order | Hebrew fragments of the shorter form were found |

**The Jewish case.** The Masoretic text is the careful, sacred transmission of the Hebrew original; a translation can never outrank its original.

**The Orthodox answer.** The Septuagint was made by Jews, before Christ, from Hebrew texts sometimes older than the Masoretic; the apostles used it; and the Holy Spirit guided its reception in the Church. **It is not a Christian corruption, and in places it preserves the older Hebrew.** Orthodox scholars also use the Hebrew and do not regard every Septuagint reading as superior.

**What it rests on.** **Which text did God give the Church?** The answer affects Isaiah 7:14, the next lesson.
Isaiah 7:14: almah and parthenos:
No single verse has been argued over between Christians and Jews longer than Isaiah 7:14. It shows exactly how the textual question works out in practice.

**The texts.**

| Version | Isaiah 7:14 |
| --- | --- |
| **JPS 1917** (Jewish) | "Therefore the Lord Himself shall give you a sign: behold, the young woman shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." |
| **Brenton's Septuagint** (1844) | "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name Emmanuel." |
| **KJV** (1611) | "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." |

St Matthew quotes it of the birth of Christ: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us" (Matthew 1:23, KJV).

**The Jewish case, at its strongest.**

1. **The word.** The Hebrew is *‘almah* (עַלְמָה), "young woman", a girl of marriageable age. Hebrew has a word for virgin, *betulah* (בְּתוּלָה), which Isaiah did not use.
2. **The context.** Isaiah speaks to King Ahaz about 735 BC, when Syria and Israel threatened Judah. The sign is that before the child knows good from evil, the two enemy kings will be gone (7:16). **A birth seven centuries later would be no sign to Ahaz.**
3. **The Greek is not decisive.** The Septuagint uses *parthenos* of Dinah after Shechem had lain with her (Genesis 34:3), so even the Greek word did not always mean a virgin in the strict sense.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Jews translated it "virgin" before Christ.** The Septuagint translators were Jewish scholars two centuries before the Nativity. **They read *‘almah* here as *parthenos*.** The Christian reading was not invented to prove a point.
2. ***‘Almah* is not clearly used anywhere in the Hebrew Bible of a married woman.** Its other uses (Rebecca before her marriage in Genesis 24:43, Miriam as a girl in Exodus 2:8) are of unmarried young women, who in that society were presumed virgins.
3. **"The Lord himself shall give you a sign."** A young woman having a baby is no sign; the language prepares for something extraordinary. And the passage continues into Isaiah 9, where the child born is called "The mighty God" (9:6, KJV).
4. **Prophecy has more than one fulfilment.** The Fathers accept that the sign spoke to Ahaz's time and also beyond it. St Matthew's "that it might be fulfilled" means the full meaning of the prophecy, not its only one.

**Their best reply.** Jewish scholars answer that Isaiah 9:6 is a royal name praising God ("a mighty God is the planner"), not calling the child God, and that Christians read the Old Testament backward from the New. **The Orthodox reply**: the Church reads it backward deliberately, in the light of Christ, as the apostles did (Luke 24:27); the question is whether that light is true.

**What it rests on.** **Is the meaning of a prophecy limited to what its first hearers could see, or can God's word mean more than its first fulfilment?**

**A note for conversation.** Isaiah 7:14 alone will not convince anyone. **It belongs with the whole pattern** of a promised son of David, "God with us", born in an extraordinary way.
The Messiah: what Judaism expects and wh:
The heart of the disagreement is the Messiah. Jews and Christians agree that God promised one; they disagree about what he would do and whether he has come.

**The word.** *Mashiach* (מָשִׁיחַ), "anointed one", in Greek *Christós* (Χριστός). Kings and priests were anointed in Israel; the prophets promised a king from David's line who would restore Israel.

**The Jewish expectation, at its strongest.** Maimonides, in the *Mishneh Torah* (Laws of Kings, chapters 11–12), gives the standard account (paraphrased):

1. The Messiah will be **a king from the house of David**, learned in the Torah and observant of it.
2. He will **compel Israel to walk in the Torah** and fight the wars of the Lord.
3. He will **rebuild the Temple** in Jerusalem.
4. He will **gather the exiles** of Israel.
5. In his days the whole world will **serve God together** in peace.
6. If a man does all this, he is the Messiah. **If he does not succeed, or is killed, he is not the one promised.**

Maimonides names Jesus in this passage (in uncensored manuscripts) as a man who was thought to be the Messiah and was killed, and whose followers changed the Torah. He adds that God used Christianity and Islam to spread knowledge of the Scriptures and of the Messiah through the world.

**The argument against Jesus.** By that standard, the case is short: **the Temple is destroyed, not rebuilt; the exiles were scattered further; the world is not at peace; and Jesus was killed.** So he is not the Messiah. The Christian "second coming" looks to a Jew like a way of postponing a failure.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The prophets speak of suffering as well as glory.** Isaiah 53, Psalm 22 (21 in the Septuagint), Zechariah 12:10 ("they shall look upon me whom they have pierced") and Daniel 9:26 ("shall Messiah be cut off") speak of a figure who suffers and dies. **Two kinds of prophecy require either two figures or two comings.** The Church says one figure, two comings, as St Justin argued to Trypho (Dialogue 32).
2. **The Temple.** Christ said "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up", meaning "the temple of his body" (John 2:19, 21). The Temple's purpose, God dwelling with man, is fulfilled in the Incarnation.
3. **The ingathering is wider than Israel.** The Servant is given "for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth" (Isaiah 49:6, KJV). The nations coming to worship the God of Israel, which Maimonides himself notes, **is the Messiah's work happening.**
4. **The peace begins.** The kingdom comes first in the hearts of those who believe; its fullness is at His return. **The prophets themselves joined the two**: "the desire of all nations shall come" to the Second Temple (Haggai 2:7, KJV).

**Their best reply.** Jewish writers answer that the "suffering" texts are about Israel, not the Messiah (Lesson 8), and that the plain sense of the messianic prophecies is a political and visible restoration, not a spiritual one. **The Orthodox reply**: the Church does not spiritualise away the visible restoration; she expects it at Christ's return, together with the resurrection, which Maimonides also expects.

**What it rests on.** **Did the prophets foretell a Messiah who would suffer and die before he reigned?**
Reading: Isaiah 52:13–53:12 in the Jewis:
The Fourth Servant Song of Isaiah is the passage Christians cite most often to Jews, and the one Jewish teachers have answered most carefully. Read it in the Jewish Publication Society's translation, so that the text is the one a Jew would use.

**The text** (Isaiah 52:13–53:12, selections; JPS 1917):

> "Behold, My servant shall prosper, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high. ...
>
> He was despised, and forsaken of men, a man of pains, and acquainted with disease, and as one from whom men hide their face: he was despised, and we esteemed him not. Surely our diseases he did bear, and our pains he carried; whereas we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded because of our transgressions, he was crushed because of our iniquities: the chastisement of our welfare was upon him, and with his stripes we were healed. All we like sheep did go astray, we turned every one to his own way; and the LORD hath made to light on him the iniquity of us all. He was oppressed, though he humbled himself and opened not his mouth; as a lamb that is led to the slaughter, and as a sheep that before her shearers is dumb; yea, he opened not his mouth. ...
>
> Therefore will I divide him a portion among the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the mighty; because he bared his soul unto death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors."

**The rabbinic reading, at its strongest** (paraphrased from the medieval commentators Rashi, Ibn Ezra and David Kimchi):

1. **The servant is Israel.** Isaiah names the servant elsewhere: "Thou art My servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified" (Isaiah 49:3, JPS 1917).
2. **The speakers are the nations.** In 53:1–9 the kings of the earth (52:15) speak in astonishment: "we" thought this despised people was punished by God for its own sins, but it suffered because of ours, at our hands.
3. **The tense.** The song describes Israel's sufferings in exile, and its future exaltation.

**Older Jewish readings.** The Aramaic paraphrase called the **Targum of Jonathan** names the servant of 52:13 as the Messiah, though it turns the suffering onto Israel's enemies. A passage in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) gives as one of the Messiah's names "the leper", from 53:4. **So a messianic reading existed among the rabbis themselves**, though it was not the dominant medieval one.

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"He opened not his mouth."** The servant is silent and willing. Israel's history includes martyrs, but the prophets constantly rebuke Israel for sin; **this servant has "done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth"** (53:9).
2. **"For the transgression of my people"** (53:8, JPS). If "my people" is Israel, the servant suffers *for* Israel and so cannot simply *be* Israel.
3. **Vicarious suffering.** "The LORD hath made to light on him the iniquity of us all." The servant does not suffer alongside the guilty; **he bears what they deserve, and they are healed.**
4. **Death and life after it.** He "bared his soul unto death" and is "numbered with the transgressors", buried "with the wicked", and then "shall see his seed, prolong his days" (53:10). **This is a death followed by life.**
5. **The New Testament reads it of Christ.** Philip begins with this passage to preach Jesus to the Ethiopian (Acts 8:32–35).

**The honest conclusion.** The collective reading is not foolish; Isaiah does call Israel the servant. **The question is whether this servant, sinless, silent, dying for "my people" and living again, fits a nation or a person.** The next lesson reads how the first great Christian apologist argued it.
Reading: St Justin's Dialogue with Tryph:
The oldest surviving Christian dialogue with a Jew is St Justin's *Dialogue with Trypho*, written about 160. It records, or reconstructs, a conversation at Ephesus soon after the Bar Kokhba war. Trypho is a cultured Jew, a refugee from that war. It is a model of how the argument can be held: long, close to the Scriptures, and courteous.

**Who was Trypho?** Justin presents him as a Jewish teacher who had fled the war (Dialogue 1). Some scholars have identified him with Rabbi Tarfon of the Mishnah; most think the identification uncertain. Whether or not he existed as described, **Justin gives him real arguments.**

**The text** (Dialogue with Trypho 89; tr. Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885):

> "Trypho: Be assured that all our nation waits for Christ; and we admit that all the Scriptures which you have quoted refer to Him. ... But whether Christ should be so shamefully crucified, this we are in doubt about. For whosoever is crucified is said in the law to be accursed, so that I am exceedingly incredulous on this point. It is quite clear, indeed, that the Scriptures announce that Christ had to suffer; but we wish to learn if you can prove it to us whether it was by the suffering cursed in the law.
>
> Justin: If Christ was not to suffer, and the prophets had not foretold that He would be led to death on account of the sins of the people, and be dishonoured and scourged, and reckoned among the transgressors, and as a sheep be led to the slaughter, whose generation, the prophet says, no man can declare, then you would have good cause to wonder. But if these are to be characteristic of Him and mark Him out to all, how is it possible for us to do anything else than believe in Him most confidently?"

And in chapter 90 Trypho presses again: "prove to us whether He must be crucified and die so disgracefully and so dishonourably by the death cursed in the law. For we cannot bring ourselves even to think of this."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **What Trypho grants.** In Justin's account, Trypho admits that the Scriptures foretell a suffering Christ. **His objection is narrower: why a crucifixion?** It is a serious objection. Deuteronomy 21:23 says "he that is hanged is accursed of God".
2. **Justin's first answer** is the pattern of prophecy: Isaiah 53 ("reckoned among the transgressors", "as a sheep") marks Him out. **What scandalises Trypho is exactly what the prophets foretold.**
3. **His second answer**, in chapter 90 onward, is from types: Moses praying with outstretched arms while Joshua (in Greek, *Iēsous*) defeated Amalek (Exodus 17), and the bronze serpent lifted up (Numbers 21). **Justin reads the Law as full of the shape of the cross.**
4. **Paul's answer to the same objection.** "Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree" (Galatians 3:13). **The curse is not denied; it is taken on.**
5. **The tone.** Trypho speaks freely and Justin listens. At the end of the dialogue (chapter 142), Trypho says he has been "particularly pleased with the conference" and asks Justin to "remember us as friends"; Justin prays for them as they part.

**What to take from it.** The crucifixion is the hardest point for a Jew, and it was so from the beginning ("unto the Jews a stumblingblock", 1 Corinthians 1:23). **Justin does not soften it; he shows it was foretold.** And he argues for days without contempt. Elsewhere in the dialogue his words about the Jews are sharp; this curriculum takes that up in Lesson 16.
Daniel's seventy weeks and the sceptre o:
Besides prophecies of what the Messiah would do, Christians have pointed to prophecies of **when** he would come. These are among the most argued texts in the whole dispute.

**The sceptre of Judah.** Jacob blesses Judah: "The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be" (Genesis 49:10, KJV). The Septuagint reads "until there come the things stored up for him; and he is the expectation of nations" (Brenton). **The Christian reading**: Judah's rule would last until the Messiah, and the nations would gather to him; Judah lost its last self-rule under Rome in Christ's lifetime.

**Daniel's seventy weeks.** Daniel 9:24–26 (KJV):

> "Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city, to finish the transgression, and to make an end of sins, and to make reconciliation for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal up the vision and prophecy, and to anoint the most Holy. ... And after threescore and two weeks shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself: and the people of the prince that shall come shall destroy the city and the sanctuary..."

**The Christian reading.** "Weeks" are weeks of years: 70 × 7 = 490 years from a decree to rebuild Jerusalem. Counted (in one common reckoning) from the decree of the 5th century BC, they reach to the time of Christ. **An anointed one is "cut off", and then the city and the sanctuary are destroyed**, which happened in 70.

**The Temple must still stand.** Two further prophecies place the coming before the Second Temple's fall: "The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former" (Haggai 2:9, KJV), and "the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple" (Malachi 3:1, KJV). **That house was destroyed in 70. If the Messiah was to come to it, he came before then.**

**The Jewish case, at its strongest.**

1. **Daniel is about the 2nd century BC.** Jewish commentators (and most modern critical scholars) read the "anointed one cut off" as a high priest, often identified with **Onias III**, murdered about 171 BC, and the desolation as Antiochus IV's profanation of the Temple in 167 BC.
2. **The arithmetic is not certain.** There were several decrees to rebuild; the starting point and the kind of year are disputed, and Christian writers have not agreed among themselves. **A calculation that needs adjusting proves little.**
3. **"Shiloh"** is an obscure word, read by some as a place, and the sceptre did depart from Judah long before Christ, at the Babylonian exile.
4. **The Talmud warns** (Sanhedrin 97b, paraphrased) against those who calculate the end, because when the date passes people lose hope.

**The Orthodox answer.** The Fathers did differ on the arithmetic, and honesty says so. But the **pattern** is not arithmetic: Daniel says an anointed one is cut off and then the city and sanctuary fall; Haggai and Malachi say the Lord comes to the Second Temple. **Whatever the exact count, the window closed in 70.** The rabbis' own warning against calculating arose, the Fathers would say, precisely because the expected time had passed.

**Their best reply.** Jewish scholars answer that the Second Temple's "glory" (Haggai) refers to its splendour under Herod, and that Malachi's "temple" can be the Temple at any time God chooses. **The Orthodox reply**: Herod's gold is a thin fulfilment of "the desire of all nations shall come".

**What it rests on.** **Do the prophets fix the Messiah's coming before the destruction of the Second Temple?**
The Shema and the Trinity: is God one?:
For a religious Jew, the Trinity is the greatest obstacle after the Cross. It seems to break the first words every Jewish child learns.

**The Shema.** "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one" (Deuteronomy 6:4, JPS 1917). The Hebrew is *Shema Yisra'el, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad*. It is recited morning and evening, and with one's last breath. Martyrs died with it on their lips.

**The Jewish case, at its strongest.**

1. **God is one, absolutely.** Maimonides' second principle (paraphrased): God's unity is not that of a species with many members, nor of a body with parts, but a unity unlike any other.
2. **The Trinity is three gods, or a God with parts.** However subtle the Christian formulas, a Jew hears either three gods (Father, Son and Spirit) or one God divided into three.
3. **God has no body.** The third principle excludes the Incarnation: "God made man" is to a Jew what idolatry looks like.
4. **Scripture is clear.** "I am the LORD, and there is none else" (Isaiah 45:5); "I am the first, and I am the last" (Isaiah 44:6).

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The Church confesses the Shema.** When asked for the first commandment, Christ answered "Hear, O Israel; The Lord our God is one Lord" (Mark 12:29, KJV). The Creed begins "I believe in one God". **The Trinity is not a denial of the Shema but a statement of who the one God is.**
2. **Not three gods.** The Father, the Son and the Spirit are not three beings sharing a species, as three men share humanity. They have **one essence, one will, one operation**, and the Son and Spirit come eternally from the Father, the one source. **One God, because one Father, with His Word and His Spirit** (Theology Stage 2).
3. **Not a God with parts.** Each person is wholly God, not a third of God. The Church teaches God's simplicity as firmly as Maimonides.
4. **Paul re-reads the Shema.** "But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him" (1 Corinthians 8:6, KJV). The Greek words of the Shema, "God" and "Lord", are distributed to the Father and to Christ, inside the confession of one God.
5. **The Incarnation is not God becoming a creature.** The Son takes a human nature without ceasing to be God. **God remains without a body in His nature**; the Word takes a body in His person.

**A weak argument to avoid.** Some Christians argue that *echad* means a "compound unity", pointing to "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). The word means simply "one"; the argument proves little and irritates Jewish hearers. **Answer from who God has shown Himself to be, not from the grammar of one word.**

**Their best reply.** Jewish thinkers answer that Christian talk of "one essence, three persons" is Greek philosophy that no prophet taught, and that Paul's re-reading is exactly the change they reject. **The Orthodox reply**: the terms came later, but the Father, the Word and the Spirit are already in the Scriptures Israel kept (the next lesson).

**What it rests on.** **Can the one God have His Word and Spirit within Him, eternally, without ceasing to be one?**
The Word and the Angel of the Lord: plur:
The Fathers answered the charge that the Trinity is foreign to Israel by pointing to Israel's own Scriptures and to Jewish thought before Christ. Modern scholarship has made this argument more interesting, not less.

**The Angel of the Lord.** Several Old Testament passages describe a figure called "the angel of the LORD" who speaks as God. To Hagar he says "I will multiply thy seed" (Genesis 16:10), and she calls him God. At the burning bush "the angel of the LORD appeared unto him in a flame of fire", and then "God called unto him out of the midst of the bush" (Exodus 3:2, 4). Jacob wrestles with "a man" and says "I have seen God face to face" (Genesis 32:30).

**The Fathers' reading.** St Justin argued to Trypho (Dialogue 56–62) that the one who appeared to Abraham at Mamre, to Jacob and to Moses was, in Justin's words, "another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things; who is also called an Angel" (Dialogue 56, tr. Dods and Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885). Justin's wording is his own, older than Nicaea, but his point is that this is **another person, distinct from the Father who sent Him: the Word before His Incarnation.** The Orthodox Church sings of Christ as the Angel of Great Counsel, from Isaiah 9:6 in the Septuagint. **The invisible Father is never seen; the Son, who reveals Him, is the one who appears.**

**Wisdom and Word.** Proverbs 8 describes Wisdom beside God at creation. The Wisdom of Solomon (in the Septuagint) calls Wisdom "a pure influence flowing from the glory of the Almighty" (Wisdom 7:25, Brenton). The Jewish philosopher **Philo of Alexandria** (about 20 BC–about 50 AD) wrote of the divine *Logos* as God's firstborn and instrument. The Aramaic Targums often put "the Word (*Memra*) of the LORD" where the Hebrew has "the LORD" acting in the world. **John 1 speaks into this world of thought: "In the beginning was the Word."**

**"Two powers in heaven."** The Jewish scholar Alan Segal (*Two Powers in Heaven*, 1977) studied how the rabbis came to condemn, as a heresy, the view that there were two divine powers in heaven. Daniel Boyarin (*The Jewish Gospels*, 2012) argued that the idea of a second divine figure, such as the "son of man" of Daniel 7, was at home in Second Temple Judaism before the rabbis rejected it. **These are modern scholars, not Christians, and their conclusions are debated**; but they suggest that the Christian confession of the Son did not come from outside Judaism.

**The Jewish case.** The rabbis answer that the angel of the Lord is a created messenger who speaks in God's name, as an ambassador speaks for a king; that Wisdom and Word are figures of speech for God's own action; and that the "two powers" view was rightly rejected as a corruption of monotheism.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The ambassador reading strains the texts.** The angel at the bush says "I am the God of thy father" (Exodus 3:6), and Moses hides his face "for he was afraid to look upon God". **A messenger does not receive worship as God.**
2. **Christ is not a second god.** The Church does not teach "two powers" but one God: the Word is God's own Word, eternally with Him, and the Spirit His own Spirit.
3. **The rabbis' rejection came later.** If the plural pattern was present in Israel's Scriptures and in Jewish thought before Christ, its rejection was a decision, not the only possible reading.

**What it rests on.** **When God appears and speaks in the Old Testament, is it the Father Himself, a created angel, or His eternal Word?**
The Law: was the Torah given for ever?:
After the Messiah and the Trinity, the third great question is the Law. Christians do not keep the Sabbath, the food laws or circumcision. To an observant Jew this is not a detail; it is breaking the covenant.

**The Jewish case, at its strongest.**

1. **The Torah is eternal.** Maimonides' ninth principle: the Torah will not be changed, and no other will come from God. Many commandments are given as "a statute for ever" (Leviticus 16:31, KJV, and many others).
2. **Jesus himself said so.** "Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled" (Matthew 5:18, KJV). **Jesus kept the Law; Paul and the Church abandoned it.**
3. **A prophet who changes the Law is false.** Deuteronomy 13 warns against a prophet who leads Israel away from the commandments, even with signs.
4. **The commandments are a joy.** Psalm 119 sings of delight in the Law. To keep the Sabbath is not a burden but a gift, a sanctuary built in time, as the Jewish theologian Abraham Joshua Heschel described it in *The Sabbath* (1951).

St Justin heard the same objection: Trypho says the Christians claim to worship God but do not keep the Sabbath, the feasts or circumcision (Dialogue 10).

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The prophets promised a new covenant.** "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel ... Not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers ... I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts" (Jeremiah 31:31–33, KJV). **The new covenant is God's own promise, in Israel's Scriptures.** Hebrews draws the conclusion: "In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old" (Hebrews 8:13).
2. **"Till all be fulfilled."** Christ does not abolish the Law; He fulfils it (Matthew 5:17). What the Law pointed to, He is: the Passover lamb, the sacrifice, the Temple, the Sabbath rest. **A shadow is not abolished when the body arrives; it is fulfilled.**
3. **The moral Law remains.** The Church keeps the Ten Commandments and Christ's summary of the Law: love of God and of neighbour. The ritual laws that marked Israel off from the nations were fulfilled when the nations were brought in.
4. **The apostles decided it together.** At the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), the apostles and elders ruled that Gentile believers need not be circumcised or keep the Law of Moses. **This was not Paul against Peter; it was the apostolic Church.**
5. **"For ever" in Hebrew.** *Le-olam* means "for an age", "perpetually", and is used of things that ended, such as the Aaronic priesthood's duties in a Temple now gone. Rabbinic Judaism itself cannot keep the Temple commandments today.

**Honest history.** St Justin told Trypho that Jewish believers in Christ who kept the Law while not requiring it of others could be saved, though some Christians would not associate with them (Dialogue 47). **The early Church did not at first demand that Jewish believers abandon the Law.** Later Church councils forbade Christians to keep Jewish observances, and Lesson 16 shows how that was sometimes enforced.

**Their best reply.** Jews answer that Jeremiah's new covenant is the same Torah written on the heart, not a different law, and that Christians interpret "fulfil" to mean "end", which is not what the word means. **The Orthodox reply**: the Law written on the heart is exactly what the Spirit gives; and its ritual parts were, as Hebrews says, "a shadow of good things to come" (Hebrews 10:1).

**What it rests on.** **Was the ritual Law given as Israel's permanent way of life, or as preparation for the Messiah, to be fulfilled when he came?**
Atonement without a Temple: repentance,:
The Torah commands sacrifice for sin. Since 70 there has been no Temple and no sacrifice. How are sins forgiven? Christianity and Judaism answer differently, and both answers claim the prophets.

**The Christian argument.** "For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul" (Leviticus 17:11, KJV). The Day of Atonement (*Yom Kippur*) required the blood of a goat brought into the Holy of Holies (Leviticus 16). **Without the Temple, the Law's own means of atonement is gone.** Christians say God provided the true sacrifice in Christ, "the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world" (John 1:29), shortly before the Temple fell.

**The Jewish case, at its strongest.**

1. **Repentance was always the heart.** The prophets taught that God desires the heart more than the offering: "For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice" (Hosea 6:6, KJV). "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD ... so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips" (Hosea 14:3, JPS 1917). **Prayer takes the place of sacrifice.**
2. **The rabbinic tradition.** A well-known story (in *Avot de-Rabbi Natan*, paraphrased) tells that when a disciple wept over the ruined Temple, where Israel's sins were atoned for, Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai answered that they had another atonement as great: **deeds of lovingkindness**, quoting Hosea 6:6.
3. **Forgiveness without sacrifice.** Nineveh repented and was spared (Jonah 3). Ezekiel 18 says the wicked who turns from his sin "shall surely live". **God forgives the repentant directly.**
4. **The sacrifices had limits.** Most sin offerings were for unintentional sins; deliberate sin was dealt with by repentance. **The Cross answers a question the Torah did not ask.**
5. **Human sacrifice is abhorrent to the Torah.** The death of a man for others' sins looks to a Jew like what the Torah forbids.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Repentance is not the rival of sacrifice.** The Church also teaches that God desires the contrite heart (Psalm 51:17), and the whole life of repentance (Theology Stage 10). **The prophets rebuke sacrifice without repentance, not sacrifice as such.** Hosea and Psalm 51 were written while sacrifice was offered.
2. **Why the Temple fell.** Christ foretold the Temple's fall (Matthew 24:2). If God had meant sacrifice to end with no fulfilment, He would have left His people without the Day of Atonement He commanded "for ever". **The Church's answer is that it was fulfilled.** "For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins" (Hebrews 10:4, KJV); they pointed to the one offering that could.
3. **Not human sacrifice.** Christ is not a man offered by men to placate God. **He is God made man, offering Himself**, and raising the human nature He offered. The Orthodox understanding of the Cross is not chiefly penal but victory over death and healing of nature (Theology Stage 3).
4. **Isaiah 53 again.** The Servant's life is made "an offering for sin" (53:10, KJV; JPS "restitution"). **The prophets themselves joined a person's death to the bearing of sin.**

**Their best reply.** Jews answer that the Christian reading of Hebrews reads the Torah through a later Christian lens, and that the God of Israel never required a mediator's death to forgive. **The Orthodox reply**: the Torah itself required blood for atonement, and Daniel 9 foretold that sacrifice would cease when an anointed one was cut off.

**What it rests on.** **Did the sacrifices of the Law point beyond themselves to a final sacrifice, or were they a provision that repentance could replace?**
The Jewish case against Jesus, and the C:
Beyond the particular texts, Jewish teachers have made a general case against Jesus' claims. It should be heard whole, at its strongest, because a Jewish friend will make it whole.

**The case, as modern Jewish writers make it** (paraphrased from popular Jewish explanations such as those on jewfaq.org and from the long tradition of Jewish apologetics):

1. **He did not do what the Messiah must do.** No Temple, no ingathering, no peace (Lesson 7).
2. **His genealogy fails.** The Messiah must descend from David through his father. Matthew's genealogy runs through Joseph, who on Christian teaching was not Jesus' father; and it includes Jeconiah, of whose seed Jeremiah said "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David" (Jeremiah 22:30, KJV).
3. **The prophecies are misread.** The Gospels use texts out of context (Hosea 11:1, "out of Egypt", is about Israel; Isaiah 7:14 is about Ahaz's time).
4. **The divine claims are not Jewish.** A man claiming to be God, or worshipped as God, is exactly what the Torah forbids.
5. **The fruits.** Christianity, for much of history, persecuted Jews. **A Messiah whose followers did that has not brought peace.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **On the Messiah's work.** The two comings (Lesson 7), and the nations turning to the God of Israel, which Maimonides himself acknowledged.
2. **On the genealogy.** The Fathers answer that Luke's genealogy is probably Mary's line, so Jesus is of David's blood; and that legal sonship through Joseph was full sonship in Jewish law, as adoption is. Jeremiah's curse on Jeconiah's line was not on Mary's. Some rabbinic tradition itself holds that Jeconiah repented in exile and the decree against him was eased.
3. **On "out of context".** Matthew reads Israel's story as recapitulated in the Messiah, Israel's representative: as Israel came out of Egypt, so did He. **This is typology, not a misreading.** It is how Jewish exegesis of the time also worked.
4. **On the divine claims.** Christ's claims are made in Jewish terms: the Son of Man of Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds (Mark 14:62), the one who forgives sins (Mark 2:7: "who can forgive sins but God only?"). **The scandal was felt in Jewish terms because the claim was made in Jewish terms.**
5. **On the fruits.** This is the hardest point and should be granted. **Christians who persecuted Jews disobeyed Christ**, who prayed for those who crucified Him (Luke 23:34). The sins of Christians are a charge against Christians, not against Christ; but a Jew is right to feel the force of them. The next lesson tells that history.

**Messianic Jews and Hebrew Christians.** Some Jews have accepted Jesus as Messiah, from the apostles to St Paul to modern converts (among Orthodox Christians, for example, Fr Alexander Men, born to a Jewish family in Moscow and murdered in 1990). Most Jewish bodies regard Jews who accept Jesus as having left Judaism. Some Messianic congregations keep Jewish customs; the Orthodox Church receives Jewish converts into the one Church, as in the apostolic age.

**What it rests on.** **Is Jesus the son of David, foretold by the prophets, whose kingdom has begun?** Every particular objection leads back to that.

**In conversation.** A Jewish friend may never have heard the Christian case except as part of a history of being pressured. **Make the case gently, once, and leave room**; St Paul's hope for his people (Romans 11:26) was in God's hands, not his own.
The Church's own record toward the Jews,:
This lesson tells what Christians, the Orthodox included, have said and done to Jews. It is not a digression. A Christian who makes the case for Christ to a Jew while ignorant of this history speaks into a wound he cannot see.

**The preaching.** Already in the 2nd century, **Melito of Sardis**, in his Paschal homily *On Pascha* (about 170, rediscovered in the 20th century), accused Israel of murdering God (paraphrased): the one who hung the earth in its place was hung on a tree, and Israel killed him. The charge of **deicide**, "God-killing", against the Jewish people as a whole, entered Christian preaching. Holy Week hymns still speak harshly of "the lawless" and those who crucified Christ.

**St John Chrysostom.** In Antioch in **386–387**, Chrysostom preached **eight homilies** usually called *Against the Jews*. Their target was Christians who attended synagogue and kept Jewish feasts, but his language about the Jews themselves was violent: he called the synagogue a brothel and a den of thieves and said the Jews were fit for slaughter (paraphrased; the standard English translation is in copyright). **These words were quoted, centuries later, by people who harmed Jews.**

**How Orthodox writers read it.** Here Orthodox writers differ:

| View | Its case |
| --- | --- |
| **Context first** | Chrysostom used the rhetoric of invective (*psógos*) common in his day; his aim was to stop Christians from Judaizing, not to incite violence; he is a saint for his whole life and teaching, not for every sentence (see Robert Wilken, *John Chrysostom and the Jews*, 1983) |
| **Plain judgement** | whatever the context, the words were wrong and did harm; a saint's sins are not part of his holiness, and the Church should say so plainly |

Both views agree that **the words are not the Church's teaching and must never be used against Jews.**

**The law.** The Christian Roman Empire restricted Jews: they could not hold certain offices, own Christian slaves, or build new synagogues. Justinian in 553 interfered in the reading of Scripture in the synagogue (Novel 146). **Several Byzantine emperors ordered forced baptisms**: Heraclius in the 630s, Leo III in the 720s, Basil I in the 870s, Romanos I in the 930s. The Church's canons forbid forced baptism, and some bishops resisted, but it happened.
