**Russia.** Catherine II confined most Jews to the **Pale of Settlement** (from 1791). After the assassination of Alexander II, **pogroms** swept the south in 1881–1884. At **Kishinev** at Easter **1903**, after a newspaper spread a ritual-murder accusation, a mob killed 49 Jews. The **Black Hundreds**, nationalist groups with Orthodox language, organised violence after 1905. In **1913** the Kiev trial of Menahem Mendel **Beilis** for ritual murder ended in acquittal. The *Protocols of the Elders of Zion*, a forgery, was first published in Russia in 1903.

**Elsewhere.** The ritual-murder libel led to violence in Corfu in 1891. In Romania, the **Legion of the Archangel Michael** (the Iron Guard) joined Orthodox imagery to violent antisemitism in the 1930s; Jews were murdered in the Bucharest pogrom of January 1941 and the Iași pogrom of June 1941.

**In the West.** The Latin Church's record includes the Crusaders' massacres of the Rhineland Jews in 1096, the burning of the Talmud in Paris in 1242, expulsions from England (1290) and Spain (1492), and ghettos. **The guilt is not only Orthodox, but the Orthodox share is real.**

**What the Church teaches.** The canons forbid forced conversion; St Paul forbids Gentile boasting over Israel; Christ prayed for His crucifiers. **Christ died for the sins of all mankind**, and the Church's own hymns say it was our sins that crucified Him. Those who hated Jews in the Church's name disobeyed her Lord.

**For the answerer.** Know this history; do not deny it, minimise it or answer it with the sins of others. **It is the first thing many Jews will think of, and they are right to.**
Orthodox Christians who stood with the J:
Lesson 16 told the darkness. This lesson tells of Orthodox Christians who, often at the cost of their lives, protected Jews. It does not cancel the first; it shows what the faith asks.

**The Bulgarian Church, 1943.** Bulgaria was allied with Nazi Germany, and in March 1943 the government began to deport its Jews. The **Holy Synod of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church**, led by **Metropolitan Stefan of Sofia** and **Metropolitan Kiril of Plovdiv** (later Patriarch), protested publicly, together with members of parliament and citizens. Kiril is remembered as having told the authorities that he would lie down on the railway tracks before the trains. The deportations from Bulgaria proper were stopped, and about **48,000 Jews** in Bulgaria survived. **Honest history:** the same government deported about 11,000 Jews from the Bulgarian-occupied lands of Thrace and Macedonia in March 1943, and nearly all were killed. Both facts belong together. Yad Vashem has recognised both metropolitans as Righteous Among the Nations.

**Archbishop Damaskinos of Athens.** In March 1943 Archbishop Damaskinos and leading Greek figures sent a written protest to the occupying authorities against the deportation of the Jews of Thessaloniki. He ordered clergy to help Jews and issued false baptismal certificates. He is honoured by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations. On Zakynthos, **Metropolitan Chrysostomos** and the mayor, Loukas Karrer, are remembered for refusing to hand over a list of the island's Jews; the island's Jewish community survived the war.

**St Maria Skobtsova and her companions.** Mother Maria (Elizabeth Skobtsova, 1891–1945), a Russian émigré nun in Paris, ran a house for the poor on the rue de Lourmel. Under the German occupation she, **Fr Dimitri Klepinin**, her son **Yuri**, and **Ilya Fondaminsky** hid Jews and gave them baptismal certificates. All four died in Nazi camps; Mother Maria died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945. Yad Vashem recognised Maria and Fr Dimitri as Righteous Among the Nations in 1985, and the **Ecumenical Patriarchate canonised all four in 2004.**

**Vladimir Solovyov.** The Russian philosopher Vladimir Solovyov (1853–1900) wrote and petitioned against the persecution of Jews in the 1880s and 1890s, and argued that a Christian state that persecutes Jews denies Christ.

**Where Orthodox writers are divided.** Not every Orthodox figure is simple. St Nikolai Velimirović, a saint of the Serbian Church who was himself imprisoned in Dachau, wrote passages about Jews that many Orthodox regard as antisemitic; others say they are taken out of context, and point to testimony that he helped a Jewish family. **This curriculum states the dispute and does not settle it.** The same goes for proposals to revise or explain some Holy Week hymns: some Orthodox theologians have asked for it, others hold that the liturgical texts must not be changed and are rightly read as being about all who reject Christ, ourselves included. **As of November 2026 no pan-Orthodox decision on the question has been made.**

**What these saints show.** None of them stopped believing that Jesus is the Messiah of Israel. Mother Maria wrote of Christ in every person she sheltered. **Their witness was not to soften the faith but to live it**: love of neighbour, at any cost, without asking whether the neighbour shared it.

**For the answerer.** When a Jew raises the Church's history, the honest Orthodox answer is twofold: **yes, it happened, and it was a betrayal of Christ; and here are those who were faithful to Him.**
Looking back: Judaism and the Church:
This stage met the faith closest to the Church's roots. Before turning to Rome, gather what it found.

**The common ground.** One God, the Creator; the Law and the prophets; the hope of the Messiah; the resurrection of the dead. Most of Maimonides' Thirteen Principles the Church confesses too.

**The four points of division.**

| Question | Judaism | The Orthodox answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Messiah** | still to come; must rebuild the Temple, gather the exiles, bring peace | Jesus, in two comings: suffering (Isaiah 53, Daniel 9) and glory |
| **God** | one, with no distinction within; no body | one God: the Father with His eternal Word and Spirit; the Word took flesh |
| **The Law** | eternal and unchanging | fulfilled in Christ; the new covenant promised by Jeremiah |
| **Atonement** | repentance, prayer and deeds of love | repentance joined to the one sacrifice of Christ, to which the Law pointed |

**The key texts.**

| Text | The Christian reading | The Jewish reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Isaiah 7:14** | a virgin (LXX *parthenos*) | a young woman (*‘almah*) in Ahaz's day |
| **Isaiah 52:13–53:12** | the Messiah suffering for "my people" | Israel suffering among the nations |
| **Daniel 9:24–27** | the Messiah cut off before the city falls | a high priest in the 2nd century BC |
| **Genesis 49:10** | Judah's rule until the Messiah | obscure; the sceptre left Judah long before |
| **Deuteronomy 6:4** | the one God who is Father, Son and Spirit | one God without distinction |

**What it all rests on.** **Did Israel's Scriptures foretell a Messiah who would suffer, die and rise before he reigned, and is that Messiah Jesus?** Every other question follows.

**The history.** The Church's record toward the Jews includes preaching of deicide, Chrysostom's homilies, forced baptisms, pogroms in Orthodox lands, and the Iron Guard. It also includes the Bulgarian Synod, Archbishop Damaskinos, and St Maria Skobtsova and her companions. **A Christian who answers a Jew must know both.**

**The manner.** St Paul wrote of his people with "great heaviness and continual sorrow", wishing himself "accursed from Christ" for their sake (Romans 9:2–3). Justin argued with Trypho for days and parted as a friend. **The answer to Judaism is given as to an elder brother**, never with triumph.

**Questions to test yourself.**

1. Which of Maimonides' principles divide Christians from Jews, and why?
2. Why does the Septuagint matter for Isaiah 7:14, and what is the Jewish reply about Dinah?
3. Give the rabbinic reading of Isaiah 53 and two features of the text that strain it.
4. What did Trypho find hardest, and how did Justin answer?
5. Why do Haggai 2:9 and Malachi 3:1 matter for the time of the Messiah?
6. How do Orthodox writers differ over Chrysostom's homilies?

**What comes next.** Stage 4 turns to Rome, the church closest to Orthodoxy in faith and order, and to **the questions of the schism**: the filioque, the papacy, and the councils that tried and failed to heal the break.
Context: Rome, the nearest of the separa:
Of all the Christian bodies outside the Orthodox Church, the Roman Catholic Church is the nearest. **She has bishops in apostolic succession, the seven sacraments, the Creed, the first seven councils, the Fathers, the veneration of the Theotokos and the saints, and icons.** That nearness is exactly why the division is so painful, and why it must be understood precisely.

**The size.** As of November 2026, the Catholic Church counts about **1.4 billion** members, by her own statistics the largest Christian body in the world. Most are of the Latin rite; about 18 million belong to the **Eastern Catholic** churches, which keep Eastern rites in communion with Rome (Stage 5 treats them).

**Two stages on Rome.** The questions divide naturally in two.

| Stage | Questions |
| --- | --- |
| **4. The questions of the schism** | the filioque; the papacy, primacy and supremacy; Vatican I and infallibility; the azymes; 1054, 1182 and 1204; the councils of Lyons and Florence; St Mark of Ephesus |
| **5. The questions since** | created grace and the energies; original sin and St Augustine; purgatory and indulgences; the Immaculate Conception; scholasticism; the sacraments; the Unia; Vatican II and the dialogues; what a Catholic says back |

**The two that matter most.** The Orthodox have usually named two questions as decisive: **the filioque** (a change to the Creed, and a question about the Trinity) and **the papacy** (who has authority in the Church). St Mark of Ephesus at Florence, the Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848) and Patriarch Anthimos's reply to Pope Leo XIII (1895) all put these first. The others (the azymes, the calendar of fasts, married priests) were argued over hotly in the 11th century, but most Orthodox writers since have treated them as secondary.

**The method, applied to Rome.** Rome's case is made **from her own texts and best defenders**: the *Catechism of the Catholic Church* (1992, paraphrased here, because it is in copyright), the councils she counts as ecumenical, St Augustine, St Thomas Aquinas, and the modern Catholic theologians of the dialogue. A Catholic should recognise his faith in every summary. Then the Orthodox answer, from St Photios, St Gregory Palamas, St Mark of Ephesus, the Encyclicals of 1848 and 1895, and modern writers. Then Rome's reply.

**History told honestly.** The schism was not one event and not one side's fault. **Latin crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204; a Byzantine mob massacred the Latins of Constantinople in 1182.** Both are told in this stage.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** Orthodox writers disagree about **how serious some of the differences are** (is the filioque a heresy or a theological opinion badly expressed?) and about **ecumenism and dialogue** with Rome. Some, like St Justin Popović in *The Orthodox Church and Ecumenism*, saw the dialogues as a betrayal; others, like Metropolitan Kallistos Ware and Metropolitan John Zizioulas, took part in them as a duty of love and truth. **Both are given at their strongest where they arise.**

**What it leans on.** Theology Stage 8 tells the history of 1054 and of St Photios; Theology Stage 2 teaches the Trinity and the monarchy of the Father; History tells the Crusades. This stage uses them.

**The spirit.** Rome is not a stranger. For a thousand years the Church of Rome was one of the great patriarchates of the one Church, and the Orthodox calendar keeps many Western saints of that time: St Leo the Great, St Gregory the Great, St Benedict. **The question is not whether Rome was once Orthodox but what changed, and whether it can be healed.**
How the Catholic Church sees herself and:
Before the particular questions, it helps to know how the Catholic Church understands herself and how she regards the Orthodox. Her position has developed, and it is more generous to the Orthodox than many Orthodox realise, and less than many Catholics assume.

**Her self-understanding, at its strongest** (paraphrased from the *Catechism*, paragraphs 816 and 880–882, and Vatican II's *Lumen Gentium* 8): the one Church of Christ, which the Creed confesses, **"subsists in" the Catholic Church**, governed by the successor of Peter and the bishops in communion with him. Christ made Peter the visible foundation of His Church; the Pope, as Peter's successor, is **the perpetual and visible source and foundation of the unity** of the bishops and the faithful, and has **full, supreme and universal power** over the whole Church.

**"Subsists in."** Vatican II (1964) chose "subsists in" (*subsistit in*) rather than "is". The phrase was meant to allow that **elements of sanctification and truth exist outside her visible structure**. Catholic theologians have argued since over how much it changes; the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith said in 2007 that it affirms the full identity of the Church of Christ with the Catholic Church while recognising elements of the Church elsewhere.

**How she regards the Orthodox, at its strongest** (paraphrased from Vatican II's decree *Unitatis Redintegratio*, 1964, §§14–15, and the declaration *Dominus Iesus*, 2000):

1. The Orthodox churches have **true sacraments**, above all, by apostolic succession, **the priesthood and the Eucharist**.
2. They are **true particular Churches**, though "wounded" by lacking communion with Rome.
3. Some sharing in the sacraments with the Orthodox is **permitted and even encouraged** in certain circumstances (Catholics may receive from Orthodox priests when their own are unavailable, and Orthodox may receive in Catholic churches if they ask).
4. The Eastern churches' theological traditions are **complementary** to the Latin, not contradictory.

**The Orthodox answer.** Orthodox writers receive this with gratitude for its charity and with reservations about its theology.

1. **The Orthodox do not regard Rome the same way in return.** The Orthodox Church does not, as a rule, permit communion with Catholics, because **communion is the expression of a shared faith, not a means to it.** Orthodox canon law forbids sharing the Eucharist with the heterodox.
2. **"Wounded" by lacking Rome.** From the Orthodox side the wound is the other way: Rome departed from the faith and order of the first millennium.
3. **Complementarity can hide disagreement.** To call the filioque or infallibility "complementary" to Orthodox teaching is, to most Orthodox writers, to leave the real questions unanswered.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** Some Orthodox theologians (for example in the North American dialogue) speak of Rome as a sister Church with real sacraments, separated but not empty. Others, in line with the stricter view of Stage 1, hold that **sacraments outside the Church's canonical bounds are not to be recognised** and that "sister churches" language is a confusion. The word "sister churches" was used in the 1960s by Patriarch Athenagoras and Pope Paul VI; the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith restricted its use in 2000, and many Orthodox also reject it.

**What it rests on.** **Is the one Church defined by communion with the bishop of Rome, or by the faith and order of the first millennium, kept by the Orthodox?** Every question in this stage is a part of that one.
The filioque: what the Creed says and wh:
The oldest of the questions is one word, *filioque*, Latin for "and the Son". It was added in the West to the Creed's article on the Holy Spirit.

**The Creed of 381.** The Council of Constantinople (381) completed the Nicene Creed with an article on the Spirit. In the translation printed by Philip Schaff (*The Creeds of Christendom*, vol. 2, 1877), with the Western addition in his brackets: "And [I believe] in the Holy Ghost, the Lord and Giver of Life; who proceedeth from the Father [and the Son]; who with the Father and the Son together is worshiped and glorified; who spake by the Prophets." The Greek is *tò ek toû Patròs ekporeuómenon* (τὸ ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς ἐκπορευόμενον), "who proceeds from the Father". It echoes Christ's words: "the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father" (John 15:26, KJV).

**The Latin addition.** The Latin Creed came to read *qui ex Patre Filioque procedit*, "who proceeds from the Father **and the Son**". The Orthodox Creed has never contained the words.

**Two questions in one word.** The dispute is really two disputes, and it helps to keep them apart.

| Question | Kind | The Orthodox objection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The addition** | canonical | one part of the Church altered the common Creed of an ecumenical council without an ecumenical council |
| **The doctrine** | theological | to say the Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as the Father confuses the persons and undermines the Father as the one source |

**The canonical question.** The Council of Ephesus (431), in its seventh canon, decreed that it is unlawful "to bring forward, or to write, or to compose a different (ἑτέραν) Faith" as a rival to that of Nicaea (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900). Orthodox writers argue that this binds every later council and church: **the Creed belongs to the whole Church, and no part may change it.** Catholics reply that the canon forbids a *contrary* faith, not a clarification, and that the councils themselves expanded Nicaea in 381.

**The theological question.** Two words in Greek matter.

| Greek | Meaning | Latin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| *ekporeúesthai* (ἐκπορεύεσθαι) | "to proceed" as from the ultimate source, used only of the Father | *procedere* |
| *proïénai* (προϊέναι) | "to go forth", "come forth", used more broadly | also *procedere* |

Latin has one verb, *procedere*, for both. **What a Latin meant by "proceeds from the Son" was not always what a Greek heard.** The Catholic Church itself acknowledged this in a 1995 clarification (see "The filioque since 1995" below).

**What each side means.**

- **The Latin meaning, at its best**: the Father is the source of the whole Godhead; He gives the Son everything, including being the one from whom the Spirit comes; so the Spirit proceeds from the Father **and** from the Son, but from the Son **as having received this from the Father**. Augustine says the Spirit proceeds from the Father "principally" (the next lesson but one).
- **The Orthodox meaning**: the Father alone is the **cause** (*aitía*, αἰτία) of the Son and the Spirit. This is the **monarchy of the Father** (*monarchía*, "one source"), taught by the Cappadocians (Theology Stage 2). The Son and the Spirit are both from the Father, the Son by begetting and the Spirit by procession. The Spirit rests on the Son and is sent by the Son into the world, but **does not have His existence from the Son.**

**What it rests on.** **Is the Father the sole source of the Spirit's existence, or the source together with the Son?** And: **may part of the Church change the common Creed?**
From Toledo to 1014: how \"and the Son\":
The filioque was not added by one decision. It spread in the West over four centuries, and Rome itself was the last to accept it into the Creed.

**Spain, 589.** At the **Third Council of Toledo** (589), King Reccared of the Visigoths renounced the Arian faith of his people. The council's creed, in the form that has come down, includes the filioque. In Spain, the phrase seems to have been meant **against Arianism**: if the Spirit proceeds from the Son as from the Father, the Son is equal to the Father. Scholars debate whether the word was in the original text of 589 or added soon after.

**The Franks.** The Frankish church under **Charlemagne** took up the filioque with zeal. About 790 the Frankish theologians of the *Libri Carolini* accused the Patriarch Tarasius of Constantinople of heresy for confessing that the Spirit proceeds from the Father **"through the Son"**, the Greek formula. The creed with the filioque was sung in Charlemagne's chapel at Aachen. A council at **Aachen in 809** affirmed the filioque.

**Pope Leo III refuses.** The Franks asked Pope **Leo III** (795–816) to approve the addition to the Creed. According to the account of the meeting of 810 and the *Liber Pontificalis* (the papal chronicle), Leo agreed with the doctrine but **refused to add the words to the Creed**, and had the Creed **without the filioque engraved in Greek and Latin on two silver shields** and set up in St Peter's. **The Pope of Rome himself defended the unaltered Creed.**

**St Photios.** In 867 Patriarch Photios of Constantinople wrote an encyclical letter to the Eastern patriarchs condemning the Frankish missionaries in Bulgaria for, among other things, teaching the filioque. It was the first time the East formally named it a heresy. The council of **879–880** in Constantinople, with the legates of Pope John VIII present, confirmed the Creed without any addition and anathematised those who would change it. Some Orthodox count this council as the eighth ecumenical council; the Catholic Church instead counts the council of 869–870, which had deposed Photios.

**Rome, 1014.** The Creed was not even sung at Mass in Rome until the coronation of Emperor **Henry II** in **1014**, when, at the emperor's request, Pope **Benedict VIII** allowed it to be sung, with the filioque, as in the German lands. From then on **the filioque was in the Creed of the Roman Church.**

**The timeline.**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **381** | Constantinople I: "who proceeds from the Father" |
| **431** | Ephesus, canon 7: no "different faith" to be composed |
| **589** | Toledo III, Spain: filioque in the creed (text debated) |
| **about 790** | the *Libri Carolini* attack "through the Son" |
| **809–810** | Aachen affirms the filioque; Leo III refuses to add it; the silver shields |
| **867** | Photios's encyclical condemns it |
| **879–880** | council in Constantinople with Roman legates upholds the unaltered Creed |
| **1014** | Benedict VIII: the Creed with filioque sung in Rome |

**What the history shows.** **The addition came from the local churches of Spain and the Franks, not from an ecumenical council, and Rome resisted it for two centuries.** That is the Orthodox case on the canonical question in one sentence.

**The Catholic reply.** Catholics answer that the doctrine was taught by Latin Fathers long before (Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine), that the addition was a legitimate clarification against Arianism, and that Rome, once it accepted the doctrine, had authority to sanction the wording. **Here the filioque question becomes the papacy question.**
The Latin case for the filioque: Augusti:
The Latin doctrine of the filioque has its classic source in St Augustine of Hippo. To answer it rightly, one must first hear it as its best defenders give it.

**Augustine's text.** In *On the Trinity*, Book XV, chapter 17, section 29 (written about 416–420; tr. Arthur West Haddan, NPNF 1st series vol. 3, 1887):

> "And yet it is not to no purpose that in this Trinity the Son and none other is called the Word of God, and the Holy Spirit and none other the Gift of God, and God the Father alone is He from whom the Word is born, and from whom the Holy Spirit principally proceeds. And therefore I have added the word principally, because we find that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son also. But the Father gave Him this too, not as to one already existing, and not yet having it; but whatever He gave to the only-begotten Word, He gave by begetting Him."

**What Augustine says.** The Father is the source; the Spirit proceeds from Him "principally" (*principaliter*, "as from the first principle"). The Spirit proceeds from the Son too, but **the Son has this from the Father**, by being begotten. Augustine is not setting up two sources.

**The Latin case, at its strongest** (from Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas, and the Catechism's paragraphs 246–248, paraphrased):

1. **Scripture calls the Spirit the Spirit of the Son.** "God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts" (Galatians 4:6, KJV); "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9). The Son sends the Spirit (John 15:26; 16:7) and breathes Him on the apostles (John 20:22).
2. **The Spirit receives from the Son.** "He shall receive of mine, and shall shew it unto you. All things that the Father hath are mine" (John 16:14–15, KJV). **If all that the Father has is the Son's, then being the source of the Spirit is the Son's too**, except being the Father.
3. **The persons are distinguished by relations of origin.** The Father and the Son are distinct because one begets and the other is begotten. If the Son and the Spirit had no relation of origin between them, Anselm and Aquinas argue, **nothing would distinguish them.**
4. **One principle, not two.** The Second Council of Lyons (1274) defined that the Spirit proceeds from Father and Son not as from two principles but as from one principle (paraphrased), and Florence (1439) that the Greek "through the Son" and the Latin "and the Son" mean the same.
5. **The Spirit as the love of Father and Son.** Augustine's image: the Spirit is the mutual love, the bond, between the Father and the Son. A bond is from both whom it binds.

**Catholics today.** The Catechism (paraphrased) says that the Latin tradition confesses the Spirit's procession from the Father and the Son, while the Eastern tradition expresses that the Father is the first origin; these, being legitimately complementary, do not affect the identity of faith, provided the Latin form does not deny the Father as the source.

**What to keep from it.** The Latin doctrine at its best **does not intend two sources** and does intend the Father as the first. **The Orthodox objection must meet this best form**, not a crude "two-source" version. The next lesson gives the strongest Orthodox objection.

**The question it raises.** If the Father gives the Son "all things" including spirating the Spirit, why does He not give Him being Father? Augustine answers: because the Son is begotten. **The Orthodox will ask whether "being the source of the Spirit" is a property of the Father's person, or of the essence the Father shares with the Son.** That is the turning point.
St Photios and the Mystagogy: the Orthod:
The first full Orthodox answer to the filioque was written by St Photios the Great, Patriarch of Constantinople, and it remains the backbone of every later answer.

**Who.** Photios (about 810–about 893), the most learned man of his age, was a layman when he was made patriarch in **858**. He was deposed in 867, restored in 877, and resigned in 886. The Orthodox Church keeps his feast on **6 February**. His last major work, the *Mystagogy of the Holy Spirit* (about 886), answered the Latin doctrine point by point. (No public-domain English translation exists; it is paraphrased here.)

**His argument, in six points** (paraphrased):

1. **Christ's own words.** The Lord said the Spirit "proceedeth from the Father" (John 15:26). He did not say "from the Father and from me", though He spoke of Himself sending the Spirit in the same verse. **The Church should not say more than Christ said about the Spirit's eternal origin.**
2. **The monarchy of the Father.** In the Trinity, what is common to the three belongs to the essence (being God, eternity, power); what is unique belongs to a person (the Father's being unbegotten and the source; the Son's being begotten; the Spirit's proceeding). **Being the source of the Spirit is either common or personal.** If common, the Spirit would be the source of Himself. If personal to the Father, then it cannot also belong to the Son without the Son being the Father.
3. **Two sources or a confused Father and Son.** If the Spirit proceeds from both, either there are two sources (a division of the Godhead), or Father and Son act as one source, merging their persons, which **tends toward Sabellius**.
4. **The Spirit made less.** If the Father and Son each give something the Spirit does not (being a source of another person), the Spirit alone is poorer. **The equality of the three is damaged.**
5. **The sending is not the origin.** The Son sends the Spirit into the world in time (the economy); that tells us about the mission, not the eternal origin (theology). **The Latin argument confuses the two.**
6. **The Latin Fathers.** Photios answers the appeal to Ambrose and Augustine by saying that if they wrote this, they erred as men do, and their holiness elsewhere is honoured; **the Church follows the councils, not a Father's single error.** He also cites popes (Leo III and others) who kept the Creed unaltered.

**Point 2 at the heart.** This is the strongest argument and it meets Augustine at the turning point of the last lesson. **For Photios, "being the source of the Spirit" is a property of the Father's person**, like "being unbegotten". It cannot be "given" to the Son without making the Son a second Father.

**The Latin reply.** Latin theologians answer that Photios's dilemma is false: the Father gives the Son the power to spirate along with the essence, **so it is common to Father and Son but not to the Spirit**, because the Spirit is what is spirated. A property can be shared by two persons and not the third, since persons are distinguished only by opposed relations. **The Orthodox reply**: that makes the Spirit's origin an act of the essence and not of a person, which is exactly what the Cappadocians denied: in God, persons, not the essence, beget and send forth.

**Later Orthodox writers who built on Photios.** St Gregory of Cyprus (1285), St Gregory Palamas (14th century), St Mark of Ephesus (1439). The next lesson follows the line that looked for agreement.

**What it rests on.** **Is causing another person a property of the Father's person alone, or of the divine essence shared with the Son?**
\"Through the Son\": St Maximus, Gregory:
Not every Orthodox answer to the filioque has been a flat no. A line of Orthodox Fathers looked for what is true in the Latin teaching, and their answers are the basis for every hope of agreement.

**St Maximus the Confessor and the Letter to Marinus.** In the 640s or 650s (scholars differ on the date), St Maximus the Confessor (about 580–662), who had lived in the West and defended Rome's orthodoxy against the Monothelites, wrote to the priest Marinus of Cyprus about a letter of Pope Theodore that had been criticised for teaching that the Spirit proceeds from the Son. Maximus defended the Romans (paraphrased): **they do not make the Son the cause of the Spirit**, for they know the Father is the one cause of Son and Spirit; they mean that the Spirit comes forth *through* the Son, showing the unity and identity of essence. He added that the Romans had been asked to explain themselves, and that their language was a difficulty of translation.

**What Maximus shows.** In the 7th century, an Orthodox saint **judged the Latin teaching orthodox in the sense its defenders explained** and distinguished two things: the Father as the one cause, and the Son as the one through whom the Spirit shines forth. **This is the Orthodox reading of "through the Son".**

**Gregory of Cyprus and the Council of Blachernae (1285).** After the failed union of Lyons (1274; see its lesson below), Patriarch **Gregory II of Cyprus** (patriarch 1283–1289) had to answer the unionist John Bekkos, who argued that the Fathers' "through the Son" proved the filioque. The **Council of Blachernae** (1285) and Gregory's *Tomos* drew a distinction:

| | What it is | From whom |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The Spirit's existence** (*hýparxis*) | His being as a person | **from the Father alone** |
| **The Spirit's eternal manifestation** (*ékphansis aḯdios*, ἔκφανσις ἀΐδιος) | His eternal shining forth | **through and from the Son** |

**So the Fathers' "through the Son" is true, but it speaks of an eternal manifestation, not of the origin of the Spirit's existence.**

**St Gregory Palamas.** In the 14th century, Palamas (about 1296–1359) wrote two *Apodictic Treatises* on the procession. With the distinction between God's essence and His uncreated energies (Theology Stage 2), he could say: **the Spirit's person is from the Father alone; the Spirit's grace and energy flows eternally from the Father through the Son, and even from the Son.** He wrote, in substance (paraphrased), that the Spirit is the Father's and the Son's, as the love between them, a sentence that comes close to Augustine's image while keeping the monarchy of the Father.

**Why this matters.** These three show that the Orthodox objection is **not to every connection between the Son and the Spirit**, but to making the Son a cause of the Spirit's existence. **That narrows the disagreement to its exact point.**

**The Latin reply.** Catholic theologians since the 20th century have welcomed this line, and some argue that the Latin filioque, rightly understood, means no more than Gregory of Cyprus's eternal manifestation. **The Orthodox reply**: if so, Rome can say so and remove the addition from the Creed; the definitions of Lyons and Florence, which make the Son with the Father "one principle", say more.

**What it rests on.** **Can the Son's role be confined to the Spirit's eternal manifestation, with His existence from the Father alone?** If Rome accepts that, much of the doctrinal dispute falls away; the canonical dispute remains.
The filioque since 1995: clarifications,:
In the last thirty years the filioque has been discussed more calmly than at any time since Florence. This lesson gives the present state of the question and where Orthodox writers differ, **as of November 2026**.

**The 1995 Clarification.** In 1995 the Vatican's Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity published *The Greek and Latin Traditions regarding the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. In substance (paraphrased), it acknowledged that the Greek **ekporeusis** expresses the Spirit's origin from the Father as the sole source; that the Latin **procedere** has a broader sense; that the Creed of 381 in its Greek form is normative for the whole Church; and that the filioque must not be understood as denying the Father as the one source. Metropolitan John Zizioulas responded that it was a positive step, while asking for further clarity.

**North America, 2003.** The North American Orthodox–Catholic Theological Consultation issued an agreed statement, *The Filioque: A Church-Dividing Issue?* (2003). It concluded that the question need no longer divide, and recommended that **the Catholic Church use the original Greek text of the Creed, without the filioque**, in catechesis and liturgy, and declare that the anathemas of Lyons II (1274) against those who deny the filioque no longer apply. It is a regional statement, not binding on either church.

**Nicaea, 2025.** On **28 November 2025**, at Iznik (ancient Nicaea), for the 1,700th anniversary of the First Council, Pope **Leo XIV** and Ecumenical Patriarch **Bartholomew** recited the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed together in its original form, **without the filioque**. Leo XIV had also used that form at an ecumenical service in Rome earlier in 2025, and earlier popes had done so on occasion. Catholic commentators disagree over whether this signals anything doctrinally; the Latin liturgy still contains the filioque.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** On how grave the filioque is, Orthodox theologians have taken positions that should both be heard.

| View | Its case | Representatives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The root of the division** | the filioque reflects a whole Western theology that subordinates the Spirit and puts the essence before the persons; it is a heresy and the source of other errors | Vladimir Lossky (*The Procession of the Holy Spirit in Orthodox Trinitarian Doctrine*, 1948); Fr John Romanides; St Justin Popović; most Orthodox polemical writers since Photios |
| **A Western opinion, wrongly made dogma** | Augustine's teaching was a theological opinion (*theologoumenon*) of a Western Father, compatible with the faith if not imposed; the real offence is the change to the Creed and its imposition | V. V. Bolotov (*Theses on the Filioque*, 1898, arguing it is not an absolute impediment to communion); some modern dialogue theologians |

**The strongest case for the first view.** Photios's argument (in the Mystagogy lesson) shows that the doctrine, not only the wording, confuses the persons; councils of 1285 and later condemned it; and a doctrine that has been defined at Lyons and Florence cannot be reduced to an opinion without Rome repudiating those councils.

**The strongest case for the second view.** St Maximus judged the Roman teaching orthodox in its explained sense; the Fathers' "through the Son" leaves room for it; and treating every Latin formula as heresy makes the Orthodox position depend on the worst reading of the other side, which the method of this curriculum forbids.

**What both views agree.** **The addition to the Creed was unlawful**; the Father is the sole cause of the Spirit's existence; and **Rome's definitions at Lyons and Florence go beyond what Orthodoxy can accept.**

**What it rests on now.** **Would Rome remove the filioque from the Creed and explain her doctrine as the eternal manifestation through the Son?** As of November 2026, she has not done so in her liturgy.
Peter in the New Testament: the rock, th:
The papacy is the second great question. It begins with three Gospel texts about St Peter. The Catholic case from them is strong and should be heard in full.

**The three texts** (KJV):

1. **The rock and the keys.** "And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven" (Matthew 16:18–19).
2. **Strengthening the brethren.** "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren" (Luke 22:32).
3. **Feeding the sheep.** "Feed my lambs ... Feed my sheep ... Feed my sheep" (John 21:15–17).

**The Catholic case, at its strongest** (from the Catechism, paragraphs 552–553 and 881–882, Vatican I, and Catholic exegetes, paraphrased):

1. **Peter is the rock.** Jesus gives Simon a new name, *Kêphas* in Aramaic (John 1:42), "rock", Greek *Pétros*. In Aramaic there is no difference between "Peter" and "rock": "you are Kepha, and on this kepha I will build". **The rock is Peter himself**, as many Protestant scholars now agree.
2. **The keys.** The image comes from Isaiah 22:22, where the keys of the house of David are given to the king's steward, who opens and shuts. **The keys mark an office** of authority over the household, and offices have successors.
3. **Peter alone.** In Matthew 18:18 all the apostles receive the power to bind and loose; **only Peter receives the keys**, the name of rock, and the charge to strengthen and to feed.
4. **Peter first.** He is always named first in the lists of the Twelve (Matthew 10:2: "The first, Simon, who is called Peter"), speaks for them, preaches at Pentecost, opens the Church to the Gentiles (Acts 10), and speaks first at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15).
5. **Succession.** The Church is built to last until the end; so the foundation must last. **Peter's office continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome**, where he was martyred.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Peter's primacy among the apostles is real.** The Orthodox do not deny it. The Church calls him *koryphaîos*, "the leader" of the apostles, and keeps his feast on 29 June. **The question is not whether Peter was first but what passes to whom.**
2. **The rock.** The Fathers read "this rock" in several ways (next lesson): Peter's faith and confession, Christ, Peter as representative of all who confess. **None of them reads the text as founding a Roman jurisdiction over other bishops.**
3. **The keys belong to all.** The power of binding and loosing is given to all the apostles (Matthew 18:18) and the power to forgive sins to all (John 20:22–23). The foundation of the Church is "the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone" (Ephesians 2:20), and the New Jerusalem has "twelve foundations, and in them the names of the twelve apostles" (Revelation 21:14).
4. **Peter's chair is in every bishop.** St Cyprian (next lesson) taught that the one episcopate begun in Peter is held by every bishop. **Peter's successors are all the orthodox bishops**, not one.
5. **Why Rome?** Peter was bishop at Antioch before Rome, by tradition. The New Testament says nothing about Peter's successors at Rome. **Rome's honour came from Peter and Paul together and from Rome's being the capital** (Chalcedon, canon 28; see the lesson on the canons).
6. **Peter could be corrected.** Paul "withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed" (Galatians 2:11, KJV). At Jerusalem, James gave the final judgement: "my sentence is" (Acts 15:19).

**What it rests on.** **Did Christ give Peter a personal office of authority over the other apostles that passes to the bishops of Rome alone?**
The Fathers on the rock: Origen, Cyprian:
Both sides appeal to the Fathers on Matthew 16. The Fathers do not speak with one voice on what "this rock" is, and that itself is the Orthodox point: **no single reading was the Church's dogma**, and none supports universal jurisdiction.

**Origen** (about 185–254), *Commentary on Matthew* XII.10 (tr. John Patrick, ANF vol. 9, 1896):

> "And if we too have said like Peter, You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, not as if flesh and blood had revealed it unto us, but by light from the Father in heaven having shone in our heart, we become a Peter, and to us there might be said by the Word, You are Peter, etc. ... For a rock is every disciple of Christ..."

**St Cyprian of Carthage** (died 258), *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 4 (tr. Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 5, 1886):

> "Assuredly the rest of the apostles were also the same as was Peter, endowed with a like partnership both of honour and power; but the beginning proceeds from unity."

And in chapter 5: "The episcopate is one, each part of which is held by each one for the whole."

**St John Chrysostom** (about 347–407), *Homily 54 on Matthew* (tr. George Prevost, revised by M. B. Riddle, NPNF 1st series vol. 10, 1888), on "upon this rock": "that is, on the faith of his confession".

**St Augustine** (354–430) read the rock in more than one way. Late in life, in his *Retractations* (I.21, paraphrased), he wrote that he had once explained the rock as Peter, but more often as Christ, whom Peter confessed, and left the reader to choose which is more probable.

**The four readings.**

| Reading | Who | What the rock is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Peter's confession of faith** | Chrysostom and many Greek Fathers | the faith that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God |
| **Christ Himself** | Augustine (often) | "other foundation can no man lay" (1 Corinthians 3:11) |
| **every believer who confesses** | Origen | each disciple who receives the Father's revelation is a "Peter" |
| **Peter as the type of the one episcopate** | Cyprian | Peter, as the beginning of the unity all bishops share |

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest.**

1. **The readings are not exclusive.** A Father can say the rock is Peter's faith and also honour Peter's see. Chrysostom elsewhere calls Peter the leader of the apostles and entrusted with the world.
2. **Cyprian's other text.** Cyprian's chapter 4 survives in two versions. The other, called by scholars the **"Primacy Text"**, adds that **"primacy is given to Peter"** and speaks of "the chair of Peter". The Catholic scholar Maurice Bévenot argued that Cyprian himself wrote both, the Primacy Text first. Cyprian also called Rome "the chair of Peter, the principal church" in a letter (Letter 54, numbered 59 in some editions).
3. **The Fathers in practice.** Even Fathers who read the rock as faith appealed to Rome in crises (Athanasius in exile went to Rome; Chrysostom wrote to Pope Innocent I when deposed).

**The Orthodox reply.**

1. **The Primacy Text** fits Cyprian's ecclesiology too: Peter is the *beginning* of unity, and "the chair of Peter" is shared by every bishop. And Cyprian **resisted Pope Stephen** in 256 over rebaptism, calling a council in Carthage against him. **His actions show he did not think Rome could decide for Carthage.**
2. **Appeals to Rome were appeals to a great orthodox see**, as appeals were also made to Alexandria and Antioch. Chrysostom wrote not only to Innocent but also to the bishops of Milan and Aquileia.

**What it rests on.** **Is the "rock" a faith and an office shared by all orthodox bishops, or an office held by one see?** The Fathers' variety is the Orthodox evidence that no Petrine jurisdiction was dogma in the first centuries.
Rome's place in the first millennium: Ig:
The Orthodox do not deny that Rome held the first place among the churches for a thousand years. The question is what that first place meant. This lesson gives the strongest Catholic evidence and the Orthodox reading of it.

**St Ignatius of Antioch** (died about 107), writing to the Romans on his way to martyrdom, calls their church the one "which also presides in the place of the region of the Romans" and "which presides over love" (Epistle to the Romans, salutation, tr. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson, ANF vol. 1, 1885). Greek: *prokathēménē tês agápēs* (προκαθημένη τῆς ἀγάπης).

**St Irenaeus** (about 180): "it is a matter of necessity that every Church should agree with this Church, on account of its preeminent authority" (Against Heresies III.3.2, ANF vol. 1, 1885; see Stage 1).

**St Leo the Great** (pope 440–461) taught that Peter speaks in his successor. When his *Tome* was read at the **Council of Chalcedon** (451), the bishops cried out (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900): "Peter has spoken thus through Leo. So taught the Apostles. Piously and truly did Leo teach, so taught Cyril."

**The Formula of Hormisdas** (519). To end the Acacian schism (484–519) between Rome and Constantinople, Pope Hormisdas required Eastern bishops to sign a formula affirming (as quoted in Pastor Aeternus, tr. Manning, 1871) that "in the Apostolic See the Catholic religion and her holy and well-known doctrine has always been kept undefiled". The Patriarch of Constantinople, John II, and many Eastern bishops signed.

**St Maximus and St Theodore the Studite** praised Rome in strong terms when Rome stood for orthodoxy against Monothelite and iconoclast emperors (paraphrased): Maximus spoke of Rome as holding the keys of the faith; Theodore wrote to the popes as to the chief shepherd.

**The Catholic case.** These are not Latin claims alone; **Greeks said them.** A Roman primacy of teaching and of final appeal was recognised in the East long before 1054.

**The Orthodox reading.**

1. **"Presides over love."** Ignatius praises Rome's charity, not jurisdiction. In the same letter he does not mention a bishop of Rome at all, though he insists on bishops in every other letter.
2. **Irenaeus's "preeminent authority"** rests on Rome's apostolic founding by Peter *and Paul* and its witness to the faith in his day; and Irenaeus himself **rebuked Pope Victor** about 190 when Victor tried to excommunicate the churches of Asia over the date of Easter.
3. **"Peter has spoken through Leo"** was said **after** the Tome had been examined and found to agree with Cyril. The acclamation praises the orthodoxy of the letter; the council judged it. And the same council passed canon 28 (next lesson), which Leo rejected.
4. **Hormisdas.** The formula was signed under imperial pressure to end a schism, and its claim was **historically false**: the same Apostolic See later had a pope, Honorius, condemned by an ecumenical council (see his lesson).
5. **Maximus and Theodore** praised Rome *because* it was orthodox. **Maximus also said at his trial, in substance, that he would not enter communion with heresy even if the whole world did.** Praise for orthodoxy is not a doctrine that the see cannot err.

**What the first millennium shows.** **Rome had a real primacy of honour and a great moral authority, and was often the rock of orthodoxy.** It did not exercise immediate jurisdiction over the Eastern churches, appoint their bishops, or define dogma without councils.

**What it rests on.** **Was Rome's first-millennium authority the authority of an orthodox see first in honour, or of a see that cannot err and governs all?**
The canons on the great sees: Nicaea, Co:
The councils of the first millennium regulated the place of the great sees in canons. They are the best evidence of what the whole Church thought Rome's place was.

**Nicaea, canon 6 (325)** (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "Let the ancient customs in Egypt, Libya and Pentapolis prevail, that the Bishop of Alexandria have jurisdiction in all these, since the like is customary for the Bishop of Rome also. Likewise in Antioch and the other provinces, let the Churches retain their privileges."

Alexandria's authority over its region is justified **by comparison with Rome's over its own region**. Rome is a model of regional authority, not the source of others'.

**Constantinople, canon 3 (381)** (paraphrased): the bishop of Constantinople shall have the prerogative of honour after the bishop of Rome, **because Constantinople is New Rome**.

**Sardica (343)**, a Western council, allowed a deposed bishop to appeal to the bishop of Rome, in honour of the memory of St Peter (paraphrased), who could order a rehearing. Rome later cited these canons as if they were Nicene.

**The Apiarius affair (418–424).** When the priest Apiarius, deposed in Africa, appealed to Rome, Popes Zosimus and Celestine cited the Sardican canons as canons of Nicaea. The African bishops checked the Nicene canons in Constantinople and Alexandria, found no such canons, and wrote to Celestine (about 424) asking him not to receive appeals from Africa, since **the Nicene canons left each province to judge its own clergy**.

**Chalcedon, canon 28 (451)** (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "For the Fathers rightly granted privileges to the throne of old Rome, because it was the royal city. And the One Hundred and Fifty most religious Bishops, actuated by the same consideration, gave equal privileges (ἴσα πρεσβεῖα) to the most holy throne of New Rome, justly judging that the city which is honoured with the Sovereignty and the Senate, and enjoys equal privileges with the old imperial Rome, should in ecclesiastical matters also be magnified as she is, and rank next after her..."

**What the canons say.** The Orthodox read them together:

1. **The order of the sees is set by councils.** Rome, Constantinople, Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem: the order called the **pentarchy** was fixed by canons, not by a pope.
2. **Rome's first place had a political reason**: "because it was the royal city". **Not one canon grounds it in succession from Peter.**
3. **Rome is first in honour, Constantinople second**, and "equal privileges" are granted to New Rome.

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest.**

1. **Pope Leo rejected canon 28.** He held that the sees' rank came from their apostolic founding, especially Rome's from Peter, not from politics. Rome did not accept canon 28 for centuries (it acknowledged Constantinople's second place in 1215, under the Latin Empire).
2. **The canons concern patriarchal administration**, not the universal office of Peter's successor, which comes from Christ, not from councils.
3. **Sardica shows the West recognised appeals to Rome** already in the 4th century.

**The Orthodox reply.** Chalcedon is an ecumenical council, and its canon was received in the East; **if a pope could annul an ecumenical council's canon, then Vatican I's doctrine was already assumed**, which is the question. And the Africans' answer to Rome in the Apiarius affair is first-millennium evidence that Western churches too did not accept appeals to Rome as of right.

**What it rests on.** **Does a see's rank in the Church come from the councils and the cities, or from Peter's succession by divine right?**
Pope Honorius: a pope condemned by an ec:
If the bishop of Rome cannot err in defining the faith, what of a pope whom an ecumenical council condemned as a heretic? The case of Honorius was central at Vatican I, and remains the hardest historical test of infallibility.

**The history.** In the 630s, Patriarch **Sergius** of Constantinople promoted a compromise with the anti-Chalcedonian churches: Christ has two natures but **one will** (*thélēma*), the teaching later called **Monothelitism**. He wrote to Pope **Honorius I** (pope 625–638). Honorius replied, in letters that survive, approving the formula that Christ has **one will** (paraphrased): he confessed "one will of our Lord Jesus Christ", meaning, he said, that Christ's human will did not war against the divine.

**The council.** The **Sixth Ecumenical Council, Constantinople III (680–681)**, defined that Christ has **two wills**, divine and human, the human freely obedient to the divine, as St Maximus the Confessor had taught. It condemned the Monothelite leaders, and with them Honorius. The bishops' acclamations at the end read (tr. Henry Percival, NPNF 2nd series vol. 14, 1900):

> "To Theodore of Pharan, the heretic, anathema! To Sergius, the heretic, anathema! To Cyrus, the heretic, anathema! To Honorius, the heretic, anathema! To Pyrrhus, the heretic, anathema!"

**Pope Leo II** (pope 682–683) confirmed the council and its condemnation of Honorius. In his letter he said, in substance (paraphrased), that Honorius had not purified the apostolic Church by the teaching of the apostolic tradition, but **allowed its spotless faith to be stained**. The condemnation of Honorius was repeated at the Seventh Council (787) and by later popes in their profession of faith for centuries.

**The Orthodox case.** Here, an ecumenical council, received by Rome itself, **anathematised a bishop of Rome as a heretic for what he taught about the faith in official letters** to a patriarch. **If popes cannot err when teaching the whole Church on faith, Honorius is inexplicable.** The council's judgement also shows that councils judged popes, not the reverse: the Sixth Council examined both Honorius's letters and Pope Agatho's, approving Agatho's and condemning Honorius's.

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest** (from the Vatican I debates and later Catholic historians):

1. **Honorius did not speak *ex cathedra*.** His letters were private replies to Sergius, not definitions binding the whole Church. Vatican I's conditions (see the reading of Pastor Aeternus) were not met.
2. **He may have been orthodox in meaning.** Honorius meant that Christ had no sinful, rebellious will, not that He lacked a human will; his successor Pope John IV defended him on these lines, and so, in his way, did **St Maximus**.
3. **Leo II condemned negligence**, not heresy: Honorius failed to extinguish the heresy rather than teaching it.

**The Orthodox reply.** The council called him "the heretic", in the same breath as Sergius; Rome repeated it for centuries; and **if the infallibility of popes has to be protected by conditions that an official letter on the central controversy of the day did not meet**, the doctrine protects very little. The debate at Vatican I itself shows how serious the case was: the minority bishops, among them Bishop Hefele, the great historian of the councils, raised Honorius against the definition.

**What it rests on.** **When an ecumenical council and a pope disagree on the faith, who judges whom?**
Reading: St Gregory the Great against th:
The strongest witness against papal supremacy may be a pope. St Gregory the Great, honoured by the Orthodox as **St Gregory Dialogos**, rejected the title "universal" in words the Orthodox have quoted ever since.

**The setting.** About 588 the patriarch of Constantinople, **John IV the Faster**, used the title *oikoumenikós patriárchēs*, "ecumenical patriarch". Pope Pelagius II objected; Gregory (pope **590–604**) took up the protest. "Ecumenical" probably meant "imperial", patriarch of the empire's capital; Gregory understood it, or chose to treat it, as "universal", **bishop of the whole Church**. In 595 he wrote to John, to the emperor Maurice, and to the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch.

**The text, first passage** (Letter to the Emperor Maurice, Book VII, Letter 33, 597; tr. James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series vol. 12, 1895):

> "Now I confidently say that whosoever calls himself, or desires to be called, Universal Priest, is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist, because he proudly puts himself above all others."

**Second passage** (Letter to Eulogius of Alexandria and Anastasius of Antioch, Book V, Letter 43, 595):

> "For, as your venerable Holiness knows, this name of Universality was offered by the holy synod of Chalcedon to the pontiff of the Apostolic See which by the providence of God I serve. But no one of my predecessors has ever consented to use this so profane a title; since, forsooth, if one Patriarch is called Universal, the name of Patriarch in the case of the rest is derogated."

**Third passage** (Letter to Eulogius of Alexandria, Book VIII, Letter 30, 598), when Eulogius addressed Gregory himself as "Universal Pope":

> "For if your Holiness calls me Universal Pope, you deny that you are yourself what you call me universally. But far be this from us. Away with words that inflate vanity and wound charity."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"Precursor of Antichrist."** Gregory's language is strong. He does not object to a word but to **one bishop setting himself above all others.**
2. **"The name of Patriarch in the case of the rest is derogated."** His argument is about the other bishops: **if one is universal, the others are not truly bishops** but his delegates. This is exactly the Orthodox objection to Vatican I's "immediate" jurisdiction over every church.
3. **He applies it to himself.** "If your Holiness calls me Universal Pope, you deny that you are yourself what you call me." **Gregory refuses the title for Rome as well.**

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest.** In the same controversy Gregory wrote of Peter (Book V, Letter 20, to Maurice): "the care and principality of the whole Church is committed to him, and yet he is not called the universal apostle." Catholics argue that Gregory **claimed and exercised Peter's care for the whole Church**, intervening in the East, while refusing a title that seemed to deny other bishops' office. Vatican I itself says that papal jurisdiction does not diminish the ordinary power of bishops. **The objection is to a word, not to the primacy.**

**The Orthodox reply.** Gregory names the very thing Vatican I defined: a bishop whose power over every church and every believer is "ordinary and immediate". **If that is not being "universal bishop", the phrase has no meaning.** And Gregory says the title would leave the Church fallen if its bearer fell: "when he who is called Universal falls" (Book V, Letter 20).

**What to take from it.** A pope of Rome, a saint of both churches, **refused for himself and for every bishop the kind of authority later defined at Vatican I.** The Catholic reply is real, but the Orthodox have rightly made Gregory a witness.
From primacy to supremacy: the Dictatus:
Between Gregory the Great and Vatican I, the Roman claims grew. The Orthodox name the change: from **primacy**, the first place among brothers, to **supremacy**, authority over all. Two medieval documents show it most clearly.

**The Gregorian Reform.** In the 11th century a reform movement, named after Pope **Gregory VII** (pope 1073–1085), fought to free the Church from control by emperors and lords. It succeeded in much, and **it made the papacy the centre of the Western Church** as never before. It was in these same decades that the break with the East hardened.

**The Dictatus Papae (1075).** A list of 27 propositions in Gregory VII's register. Some scholars think he wrote it; others that it was compiled from canon-law collections. Some of its propositions (tr. Ernest F. Henderson, *Select Historical Documents of the Middle Ages*, 1910):

> "That the Roman pontiff alone can with right be called universal. That he alone can depose or reinstate bishops. ... That of the pope alone all princes shall kiss the feet. ... That the Roman church has never erred; nor will it err to all eternity, the Scripture bearing witness. ... That he who is not at peace with the Roman church shall not be considered catholic."

**Compare St Gregory the Great** (the reading above): "whosoever calls himself ... Universal Priest, is in his elation the precursor of Antichrist". **Five centuries later, a pope's register claims exactly the title a pope had refused.**

**Unam Sanctam (1302).** Pope **Boniface VIII** (pope 1294–1303), in a quarrel with King Philip IV of France, issued the bull *Unam Sanctam*. It teaches (paraphrased) that there is one Church, outside of which there is no salvation; that she has one head, Peter and his successor; that both the spiritual and the temporal swords belong to the Church; and it ends with a solemn definition that **it is altogether necessary for salvation for every human creature to be subject to the Roman pontiff.**

**The Orthodox reading.** These documents show a development the first millennium did not know:

| First millennium | After the Gregorian Reform |
| --- | --- |
| Rome first among the patriarchates, by canon | Rome alone "universal" |
| councils judge doctrine and bishops | the pope judges all and is judged by none |
| bishops elected locally, patriarchs confirm | the pope may depose any bishop |
| communion with the orthodox Church | subjection to the Roman pontiff necessary for salvation |

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest.**

1. **The Dictatus is not a dogmatic text.** It is a list in a register, and its political claims (the imperial insignia, princes kissing the feet) belong to medieval circumstances, not to doctrine.
2. ***Unam Sanctam*'s definition** is read by Catholic theologians today as teaching that salvation comes through the Church of which the pope is the visible head, not as requiring every person to be juridically subject. Vatican II teaches that those who without fault do not know the Church may be saved.
3. **Development is not corruption.** The papacy, like doctrine, developed in response to need; Newman's *Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine* (1845) argues that a true development preserves the type and principles of its origin.

**The Orthodox reply.** If development can turn Gregory the Great's "precursor of Antichrist" into Gregory VII's "alone universal", **"development" means whatever the later Church says.** St Vincent of Lérins's test (Theology Stage 1) is growth in understanding of the same doctrine, not a change of meaning.

**What it rests on.** **Was the growth of papal power a legitimate development of Peter's primacy, or a change of the Church's order?**
Vatican I (1869–1870): the council and i:
The claims of the medieval papacy were defined as dogma at the First Vatican Council. It is the council most often named by the Orthodox as the decisive barrier, and its history matters.

**The setting.** Pope **Pius IX** (pope 1846–1878) had lost most of the Papal States to the new Kingdom of Italy. In Europe, liberalism and nationalism challenged the Church's place. In 1864 he issued the *Syllabus of Errors*. Many Catholics, the **ultramontanes** ("beyond the mountains", looking to Rome), wanted the pope's authority defined; others, the **Gallicans** and many German and French bishops, resisted.

**The council.** Pius IX opened the council on **8 December 1869**, with about 700 bishops. It first passed the constitution on faith, *Dei Filius* (24 April 1870). Then it debated the papacy. **The Orthodox patriarchs had been invited** by a letter of 1868 to attend if they submitted; they declined, Patriarch Gregory VI of Constantinople refusing to receive the letter, which had been published before it was delivered.

**The minority.** A considerable minority of bishops opposed defining infallibility, mostly not because they denied the pope's authority but because they thought a definition **inopportune** or historically indefensible. They included Archbishop Darboy of Paris, Bishop Dupanloup of Orléans, Bishop **Hefele** of Rottenburg (the historian of the councils), Archbishop Kenrick of St Louis, and Bishop Strossmayer of Đakovo. They raised Honorius, the councils, and the Eastern churches.

**The vote.** At a preliminary vote on 13 July 1870, 88 bishops voted against. Rather than vote against the pope in his presence, **about 60 of the minority left Rome** before the final session. On **18 July 1870**, *Pastor Aeternus* was approved by **533 votes to 2**. The two (Bishop Riccio of Caiazzo and Bishop Fitzgerald of Little Rock) submitted at once.

**What happened next.** On 19 July France declared war on Prussia; French troops left Rome; on 20 September Italian troops took the city. The council was suspended on 20 October 1870 and never resumed. **All the minority bishops eventually accepted the definition.** The German historian **Ignaz von Döllinger**, who refused, was excommunicated in 1871. Groups who rejected the council formed the **Old Catholic** churches (the Union of Utrecht, 1889). In 1875 John Henry Newman, who had thought a definition inopportune, defended it in his *Letter to the Duke of Norfolk*, stressing its narrow conditions.

**The Orthodox reading.**

1. **The decisive vote was taken without the East** and without the minority, which left so as not to vote no. **The Orthodox ask how a council can define, by the vote of one part of one patriarchate, a dogma about the whole Church.**
2. **The minority's arguments were the Orthodox arguments**: Honorius, the councils judging popes, the Eastern Fathers.
3. **Its own reception.** A council's ecumenicity is shown by its reception (Theology Stage 1). The minority submitted under obedience to a definition already made, which made reception a formality.

**The Catholic reply.** Every council has had a minority, including Nicaea; what matters is the definition, which the whole Catholic episcopate received. The Orthodox were invited. **And the conditions of the definition are narrow**, as the next lesson shows.

**What it rests on.** **Can a council of the Latin Church alone, called and confirmed by the pope, define a dogma about the pope's authority over the whole Church?**
Reading: Pastor Aeternus on the infallib:
The text that most divides Orthodox and Catholics is the fourth chapter of Vatican I's *Pastor Aeternus*. Read it in the English translation that Archbishop Henry Edward Manning, one of the leaders of the majority, published in 1871.

**First, the jurisdiction** (chapter 3; tr. Manning, *Petri Privilegium*, 1871, as printed in Philip Schaff, *The Creeds of Christendom*, vol. 2, 1877):

> "Hence we teach and declare that by the appointment of our Lord the Roman Church possesses a superiority of ordinary power over all other churches, and that this power of jurisdiction of the Roman Pontiff, which is truly episcopal, is immediate; to which all, of whatever rite and dignity, both pastors and faithful, both individually and collectively, are bound, by their duty of hierarchical subordination and true obedience, to submit not only in matters which belong to faith and morals, but also in those that appertain to the discipline and government of the Church throughout the world..."

**Then, the limit** (chapter 4):

> "For the Holy Spirit was not promised to the successors of Peter, that by his revelation they might make known new doctrine; but that by his assistance they might inviolably keep and faithfully expound the revelation or deposit of faith delivered through the Apostles."

**Then, the definition** (chapter 4):

> "Therefore faithfully adhering to the tradition received from the beginning of the Christian faith, for the glory of God our Saviour, the exaltation of the Catholic religion, and the salvation of Christian people, the sacred Council approving, we teach and define that it is a dogma divinely revealed: that the Roman Pontiff, when he speaks ex cathedra, that is, when in discharge of the office of pastor and doctor of all Christians, by virtue of his supreme Apostolic authority, he defines a doctrine regarding faith or morals to be held by the universal Church, by the divine assistance promised to him in blessed Peter, is possessed of that infallibility with which the divine Redeemer ... willed that his Church should be endowed for defining doctrine regarding faith or morals; and that therefore such definitions of the Roman Pontiff are irreformable of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **The conditions.** Infallibility applies only when the pope (a) speaks *ex cathedra*, "from the chair", (b) as pastor and teacher of all Christians, (c) with his supreme apostolic authority, (d) defining a doctrine of faith or morals, (e) to be held by the whole Church. **Most of what popes say is not infallible**, and Catholics usually name only two definitions since 1870 as clearly *ex cathedra*: the Assumption (1950) and, before the council, the Immaculate Conception (1854; Stage 5).
2. **"Not ... new doctrine."** The pope is to guard and explain the deposit of faith, not add to it. **This is the Catholic answer to the charge of innovation**, and the Orthodox should give it its full weight.
3. **"That infallibility with which the divine Redeemer ... willed that his Church should be endowed."** The pope has the Church's own infallibility, not a separate one.
4. **"Of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church."** In Latin, *ex sese, non autem ex consensu Ecclesiae*. **This is the heart of the Orthodox objection.** In Orthodox teaching, a definition is known to be true by its reception by the whole Church (Theology Stage 1). Here, the pope's definitions need no reception.
5. **"Ordinary ... immediate ... truly episcopal."** In chapter 3, the pope's jurisdiction reaches every believer directly, **as if every diocese had two bishops**: its own and the pope. Compare Gregory the Great, read earlier in this stage.
6. **The anathema.** Chapter 4 ends: "But if any one ... presume to contradict this our definition: let him be anathema." **By this text every Orthodox Christian is under anathema**, a point Orthodox writers since 1870 have not missed.

**What to take from it.** The definition is narrower than many Orthodox assume, and the Catholic Church holds that it adds nothing new. But **two phrases, "immediate" jurisdiction over all and definitions irreformable "of themselves, and not from the consent of the Church"**, state exactly what the Orthodox deny. The next lesson gives the Orthodox answer and the Catholic reply.
Infallibility answered: the Encyclicals:
The Orthodox answered the papal claims in formal documents before and after Vatican I. Two encyclicals of the Eastern patriarchs are the classic statements.

**The Encyclical of the Eastern Patriarchs (1848).** In January 1848 Pope Pius IX addressed a letter to the Eastern Christians inviting them to return to Rome. In May 1848 the four Eastern patriarchs (Anthimos VI of Constantinople, Hierotheos II of Alexandria, Methodios of Antioch, Cyril II of Jerusalem) and their synods answered with an encyclical "to the Orthodox everywhere". Its main points (paraphrased):

1. The filioque and the papal claims are **innovations**, contrary to the councils and the Fathers.
2. The bishop of Rome's primacy in the ancient Church was one of honour among equal patriarchs, given by the councils because of the city, and lost when Rome departed from the faith.
3. **The most famous sentence**: among the Orthodox, neither patriarchs nor councils could introduce novelties, because **the guardian of the faith is the very body of the Church, that is, the people themselves**, who want their faith unchanged.

**The Patriarchal Encyclical of 1895.** In 1894 Pope **Leo XIII** issued an apostolic letter, *Praeclara gratulationis*, inviting the Eastern churches to reunion. In 1895 Patriarch **Anthimos VII** of Constantinople and his synod replied. In substance (paraphrased):

1. Union is desired, but **only in the faith of the seven councils**, as it was before the schism.
2. Rome's innovations are listed: the filioque, the azymes, sprinkling instead of immersion in baptism, purgatory, the Immaculate Conception, and **the papal primacy and infallibility**.
3. The ancient Church knew a **bishop of Rome first in honour**, judged by councils, and the Eastern churches governed themselves. Papal supremacy and infallibility are unknown to the Fathers.
4. **Return to the faith of the undivided Church** is the only way to union.

**The Orthodox answer, gathered.**

| Point | Orthodox teaching |
| --- | --- |
| **Who is infallible?** | the Church as a whole, Christ's body, guided by the Spirit, not one bishop |
| **How is a definition known to be true?** | by its agreement with Tradition and its **reception** by the whole Church |
| **What is primacy?** | a primacy of honour and service, first among equals, within councils |
| **Who judges a bishop of Rome?** | a council, as at Constantinople III with Honorius |

**The Catholic reply, at its strongest.**

1. **The Orthodox have no way to settle a dispute.** If reception decides, then no one knows at the time whether a council is true; Ephesus II (449) was ecumenical in form and rejected later. **Infallibility is the answer to the question "who decides?"**, and the Orthodox, without it, have no council since 787 that all accept as ecumenical.
2. **The Orthodox divisions prove it.** The break between Moscow and Constantinople in 2018 over Ukraine, as of November 2026 still unhealed, shows a communion with no final arbiter. **Unity needs a visible centre.**
3. **The people as guardian** is beautiful but vague: the people of Constantinople accepted iconoclasm for decades.
4. **Development.** The papacy's powers developed as the Church grew, as the canon and the Creed did.

**The Orthodox reply.**

1. **The Church lived without infallible popes for a thousand years** and held seven ecumenical councils. Truth was known then as it is now: by the Spirit in the whole Church, over time. **God has not promised a mechanism that removes the need for faithfulness.**
2. **Orthodox divisions are real and a sin**, but they are divisions of administration among churches holding one faith. Rome's unity of administration did not prevent the Reformation.
3. **Infallibility does not settle disputes either.** Catholics disagree about which papal statements are infallible.

**What it rests on.** **Did Christ give His Church a single visible organ that settles the faith infallibly, or did He give the Spirit to the whole Church, known through councils and reception?**
Primacy in the Orthodox view today: Rave:
The Orthodox reject papal supremacy, but they do not reject primacy. What a primacy would look like, and who holds it now, is one of the live questions of the dialogue and among the Orthodox themselves, **as of November 2026**.

**Orthodox theologians on primacy.** In the 20th century, émigré theologians in Paris reopened the question.

- **Fr Nicholas Afanasiev** (1893–1966) developed a **eucharistic ecclesiology**: wherever the Eucharist is celebrated with the bishop, the whole Church is present. Primacy is a primacy among churches, of witness and love, not of power over them.
- **Fr Alexander Schmemann**, in "The Idea of Primacy in Orthodox Ecclesiology" (1960), argued that **some form of universal primacy is part of the Church's order**, and that the Orthodox have neglected it.
- **Metropolitan John Zizioulas** (1931–2023) argued that the Church at every level needs both a **"first"** and a **synod**: no first without the many, and no many without a first (Apostolic Canon 34).

**The joint commission's documents.** The Joint International Commission for Theological Dialogue between the Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church has issued three relevant texts:

| Document | Year | What it said (paraphrased) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ravenna** | 2007 | primacy and conciliarity are interdependent at every level, local, regional and universal; in the first millennium Rome held the first place (*taxis*) among the sees; the role of the bishop of Rome in that communion is still to be studied |
| **Chieti** | 2016 | in the first millennium, primacy and synodality were interdependent; Rome's place was recognised, but it **did not exercise authority over the Eastern churches as in the West** |
| **Alexandria** | 2023 | surveyed the second millennium and how East and West diverged on primacy and synodality |

The Moscow Patriarchate's delegation **left the Ravenna meeting** over the presence of the Estonian church under Constantinople. Since **2018**, after the dispute over Ukraine, **Moscow has not taken part** in the commission. In June 2026 the commission's coordinating committee met at Pannonhalma in Hungary and worked on a draft text on **infallibility**.

**Rome's side.** Pope John Paul II, in *Ut Unum Sint* (1995), asked other Christians to help him find a way of exercising the primacy that would be open to a new situation (paraphrased). In **2024** the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity published a study document, *The Bishop of Rome*, gathering the responses and suggesting, among other things, a "re-reception" or new interpretation of Vatican I and a clearer distinction between the pope's role as patriarch of the West and as universal primate.

**Where Orthodox churches differ: the quarrel over "first".**

| View | Its case |
| --- | --- |
| **Moscow (2013)** | the Russian Church's Holy Synod, in a statement on primacy (December 2013), held that **at the universal level primacy is one of honour only**, grounded in the diptychs (the order of commemoration), not in a "first" with powers; since 1054 the first place belongs to Constantinople, but without authority over other autocephalous churches |
| **Constantinople** | Metropolitan **Elpidophoros Lambriniadis**, in an essay "First without Equals" (2014), argued that the Ecumenical Patriarch has a real **primacy with responsibilities** (receiving appeals, granting autocephaly, convening councils), grounded in the canons, and that a "first among equals" with no powers is a contradiction |

The quarrel came to a head in **2018–2019**, when Constantinople granted autocephaly to the Orthodox Church of Ukraine and Moscow broke communion with Constantinople. **Theology Stage 12 tells that story**; it matters here because **a Catholic will point to it**, as the previous lesson showed.

**What it rests on.** **What kind of "first" does the Church need: an honour, a service with real responsibilities, or a jurisdiction?** The Orthodox agree against the third; they disagree about the first two.
The azymes: leavened and unleavened brea:
In the 11th century the most heated argument between Greeks and Latins was not about the Creed but about bread. Western churches used **unleavened bread** (*ázymos*, ἄζυμος, "without leaven") for the Eucharist; the Greeks used **leavened** bread (*ártos*, ἄρτος).
