**6. The poor are not deceived lightly.** In Africa above all, the prosperity gospel draws people who are desperate. Its preachers often grow rich from the offerings of the poor. **This is the harshest charge, and the most important**: it is not only a theological error, it harms the poor it promises to help.

**Their best reply.** "Your Church has gold domes and rich bishops." **A fair point, to be heard.** The Orthodox answer: the gold of the temple is given **to God** for the beauty of worship, open to the poorest, not to an individual; and **bishops who live in luxury are judged by the same Fathers**. The Church's own saints, from St Nicholas to St John of Kronstadt, gave everything away.

**What it finally rests on:** **whether God's blessing is chiefly material success in this life, or communion with Him through the Cross, with wealth held for others.**
African Independent churches: Kimbangu,:
**African Independent** (or **Initiated**, or **Instituted**) **Churches**, AICs, are churches founded by Africans, independent of the European missions. They began around **1890** and now number thousands of bodies and tens of millions of members. Most Christians in parts of southern and western Africa belong to them.

**Three broad types**, following the Swedish missionary scholar **Bengt Sundkler** (*Bantu Prophets in South Africa*, 1948) and later writers:
| Type | Character |
| --- | --- |
| **"Ethiopian"** | broke from mission churches over African leadership; kept mission doctrine and worship (from Ps 68:31, "Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God") |
| **"Zionist" and "Apostolic"** | prophetic and healing churches; white robes, water, the Spirit (Lesson 16) |
| **"Spiritual"** churches | West African prophetic churches: the **Aladura** ("praying people") of Nigeria |

**Three founders.**
- **Simon Kimbangu** (about 1887–1951), a Baptist catechist in the Belgian Congo, began a **healing ministry in April 1921** at Nkamba. Crowds came; the Belgian authorities arrested him, sentenced him to death, commuted it, and kept him in prison for thirty years until his death in **1951**. **His church**, the *Église de Jésus-Christ sur la terre par son envoyé spécial Simon Kimbangu*, was recognised in **1959** and joined the World Council of Churches in **1969**. In **2021** the WCC ended its membership on doctrinal grounds, over teaching that Kimbangu is the Holy Spirit promised in John 14 and that later leaders are incarnations of Christ.
- **Isaiah Shembe** (about 1865–1935), a Zulu prophet, founded the **Nazareth Baptist Church** (*iBandla lamaNazaretha*) in **1910** near Durban, keeping the Saturday sabbath and Zulu forms of worship in dance and dress. Shembe and his successors are honoured as prophets; some members, by many accounts, regard Shembe as more than a prophet, a teaching scholars and members describe differently.
- **The Aladura** grew in **Nigeria** after the **1918 influenza**: the **Cherubim and Seraphim** (1925, Moses Orimolade and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon), the **Christ Apostolic Church** (with the revivalist Joseph Babalola, 1930s) and the **Celestial Church of Christ** (Samuel Oshoffa, founded at Porto-Novo in Dahomey, now Benin, in 1947). Prayer, fasting, holy water, visions and healing are central.

**Their case at its strongest.**
1. **The Gospel in African form.** The missions often brought European culture with Christ, and refused African leadership. **The AICs gave Africans churches of their own**, with African music, dress and authority, a generation before the missions did.
2. **Healing and the spiritual world.** Africans live with sickness, witchcraft and spirits. The missions often answered with hospitals alone; the AICs answer with **prayer, prophecy and deliverance**, as the New Testament does.
3. **Resistance to colonialism.** Kimbangu suffered thirty years for his ministry; many AICs fostered African dignity under colonial rule.

**An Orthodox connection.** Orthodoxy in East Africa came partly **through** an independent church. In **Uganda**, **Reuben Mukasa Spartas** (1899–1982) and **Obadiah Basajjakitalo**, looking for a church apostolic but free of colonial missions, founded an "African Orthodox Church" in **1929** through a body linked to the American African Orthodox Church. Learning it was not canonical, they sought the true Orthodox Church, and were received by the **Patriarchate of Alexandria in 1946**. Theology, Stage 12, "Orthodoxy in Africa", tells the story.

**The Orthodox answer.** The next lesson answers the Zionist and Apostolic churches together with the AICs. In outline: **the Orthodox Church honours African Christianity under African leadership**, as Alexandria's own history (St Athanasius, St Cyril, the Desert Fathers) shows Africa to be one of Christianity's oldest homes. But **a church is not made apostolic by being independent**; it is apostolic by the apostles' faith and succession. And where a prophet is given the place of the Holy Spirit or of Christ, as in some Kimbanguist teaching, **the faith of the Creed is lost**.
The Zionist and Apostolic churches of so:
The largest family of independent churches in southern Africa are the **Zionist** and **Apostolic** churches. A reader in South Africa or Zimbabwe will meet them everywhere: congregations in white or coloured robes worshipping under trees, by rivers and on hillsides.

**The Zionists.** The name comes from **Zion City, Illinois**, founded by the Scottish-Australian healer **John Alexander Dowie** (1847–1907). His missionaries reached South Africa in **1904**, baptising by triple immersion and preaching divine healing. African leaders took up the movement and made it their own. The largest is the **Zion Christian Church (ZCC)**, founded by **Engenas Lekganyane** about **1924–25**, with its headquarters at **Moria** in Limpopo; millions gather there at **Easter**. Members wear a star or dove badge, keep food laws, and avoid alcohol, tobacco and pork.

**The Vapostori.** In **Zimbabwe** the **Apostolic** churches (Shona *vapostori*, "apostles") began in **1932** with two prophets:
- **Johane Masowe** (Shoniwa Masedza, about 1914–1973), who after a vision preached repentance, the burning of charms, and the rejection of witchcraft; his followers, the **Masowe** churches, wear white and worship in the open.
- **Johane Marange** (Muchabaya Momberume, 1912–1963), founder of the **African Apostolic Church**, whose great **Passover** (*Pasika*) gatherings draw tens of thousands.

**Their practices.** Prophecy and healing with **holy water**, prayed-over stones, ropes or cords; **baptism in rivers** ("Jordans"); fasting; strict rules of dress and diet; and in some churches, **polygamy** permitted and a suspicion of hospitals and medicine. Prophets in these churches commonly **renounce the *n'anga* and *sangoma*** (the traditional healers and diviners), whom they see as working with spirits; yet the role they fill is often similar. Stage 11 answers the traditional religion and the ancestors directly.

**Their case at its strongest.**
1. **The Old Testament and the Spirit together.** They read Scripture as Africans close to its world: sacrifices, prophets, purity laws, dreams, healing.
2. **A church that fights witchcraft.** Where people live in fear, the prophet's prayer gives protection in Christ's name.
3. **Discipline.** Sobriety, hard work and mutual aid have lifted many families.
4. **Independence.** Christianity without white control, at home in African life.

**The Orthodox answer.**
1. **The fear is real, and Christ is the answer to it.** The Orthodox Church has its own prayers of **exorcism** at every baptism, the **blessing of water** at Theophany, the holy oil, and the cross. **She does not mock African fear of evil spirits**; the Gospels take them seriously. But protection comes from **Christ in the mysteries of the Church**, not from objects a prophet empowers, which can become charms by another name.
2. **The prophet is not the apostle.** Authority in the Church passes by **apostolic succession** and is tested by **the faith of the councils**, not by the gift of a single founder whose successors are his sons. "Believe not every spirit" (1 John 4:1).
3. **The Law fulfilled.** Food laws, sabbaths and purity rules were fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Acts 15). **Christians keep the fasts of the Church, but no food is unclean** (Mark 7:19).
4. **Marriage.** The Church blesses the marriage of one man and one woman (Matthew 19:4–6); polygamy, accepted for the patriarchs, is not the Gospel's pattern.
5. **Medicine is God's gift.** "Honour a physician" (Sirach 38:1, KJV Apocrypha). The Unmercenary Healers were physicians.

**History told honestly.** Missions often treated African culture as pagan wholesale, and colonial governments persecuted prophets. **The Orthodox must not repeat that contempt.** The best Orthodox answer in Africa has been an **African Orthodox Church**, worshipping in Shona, Zulu, Swahili and Luganda.

**What it finally rests on:** **whether the power of God against evil is given through the prophets of a new church, or through Christ in the apostolic Church and her mysteries.**
Liberal Protestantism: Schleiermacher, H:
**Liberal Protestantism** is the movement, from the late eighteenth century, that **reinterprets Christianity in the light of modern thought**, treating doctrine as the historical expression of religious experience rather than revealed truth, and reading the Bible by the methods of historical criticism. It shaped the old "mainline" Protestant churches of Europe and North America.

**The great names.**
| Who | When | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Friedrich Schleiermacher** | 1768–1834 | *On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers* (1799); *The Christian Faith* (1821–22): religion is the **"feeling of absolute dependence"** on God |
| **Albrecht Ritschl** | 1822–1889 | Christianity as ethical: the **Kingdom of God** as a moral community |
| **Adolf von Harnack** | 1851–1930 | *History of Dogma*; *What is Christianity?* (1900) |
| **Rudolf Bultmann** | 1884–1976 | *New Testament and Mythology* (1941): **"demythologising"** |

**Schleiermacher's case.** Speaking to educated Germans who had rejected religion, he argued that religion is **neither a set of doctrines nor morality**, but an immediate feeling of being utterly dependent on the Infinite. Doctrines are **descriptions of Christian experience**. Christ is the one in whom **God-consciousness** was perfect, and who communicates it to us.

**Harnack's case.** In *What is Christianity?* (lectures given in Berlin in 1899–1900), Harnack asked what is the **kernel** of the Gospel beneath its **husk**. His answer, in paraphrase: **the Fatherhood of God, the infinite value of the human soul, and the commandment of love**. The Gospel, he said, is about the Father, not the Son. In his *History of Dogma* he argued (paraphrased) that dogma was the work of the Greek spirit on the soil of the Gospel: the **Hellenisation** of a simple faith. **This is a direct attack on the Orthodox Church**, whose dogma Harnack saw as the fullest Hellenisation.

**Bultmann's case.** The New Testament's world of heaven above and hell below, demons, miracles and a bodily resurrection is **myth**, which modern people cannot believe. "We cannot use electric lights and radios... and at the same time believe in the New Testament world of spirits and miracles" (paraphrase). The task is to **interpret the myth existentially**: the Resurrection means the rise of faith in the disciples, the call to authentic existence.

**Their case at its strongest.**
1. **Honesty.** If historical study shows that the Bible's books have human histories, and science that the world is old and miracles rare, then faith must be **intellectually honest** or it will be lost.
2. **The heart of faith** was always love and trust in God, not metaphysics.
3. **Tolerance.** Doctrine divided Christians and caused wars; experience and ethics can unite them.

**The Protestant critics.** Liberalism was answered first from within Protestantism. **J. Gresham Machen**, in *Christianity and Liberalism* (1923), argued that it is **not a form of Christianity but another religion**. **Karl Barth** broke with his liberal teachers in **1914**, when most of them signed a manifesto supporting the German war; his *Epistle to the Romans* (1919, rewritten 1922) proclaimed God's word **against** human religion.

**Where it stands today, as of November 2026.** The mainline churches shaped by liberalism have declined sharply in membership across Europe and North America, while evangelical, Pentecostal and African churches have grown. Many have changed their teaching on sexuality and marriage. The **World Council of Churches** (1948) includes many of them, and the Orthodox churches that remain in it (Stage 5, Lesson 25) have repeatedly protested at the direction of its theology.

The next lesson gives the Orthodox answer.
Liberal Protestantism answered: the fait:
**The Orthodox answer: Christianity is not a feeling or an ethic, but the revelation of God in Christ, risen in the body, and the dogmas are the Church's witness to that revelation, not a Greek disguise over it.**

**1. Harnack answered: the Fathers did not Hellenise the Gospel; they baptised the Greek language.** **Fr Georges Florovsky** (1893–1979) argued that the Fathers used Greek philosophical words to say what **no Greek philosopher believed**: that God creates from nothing, that the Logos became flesh, that the body rises. The Greeks thought matter base and the divine impassible and remote. **Nicaea's *homoousios* says the opposite of Hellenism**: that the man Jesus is God. Florovsky called this "Christian Hellenism", a Hellenism **converted** (Theology, Stage 12). The creeds are not the husk; **they protect the kernel**, which is Christ Himself.

**2. Bultmann answered: the Resurrection is the Gospel.** "If Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain" (1 Corinthians 15:14, KJV). **The apostles did not preach a new self-understanding; they preached an empty tomb and a risen Lord they had touched** (Luke 24:39; 1 John 1:1). The Church's whole life, every Sunday a Pascha, rests on it. Stage 12 of this curriculum takes up the historical case for the Resurrection.

**3. Schleiermacher answered: experience is real, but it is not the source.** The Orthodox would agree with Schleiermacher that faith is lived, not merely believed. But **experience is tested by revelation, not the other way round**. The saints' experience of God **confirms** the dogmas: St Symeon the New Theologian saw the uncreated light and taught the Trinity. When experience is made the norm, **each generation's feeling decides what Christianity is**, and it becomes the religion of the age. St Paul: "be not conformed to this world" (Romans 12:2, KJV).

**4. Miracles and the modern world.** The claim that modern people cannot believe in miracles is a **philosophical premise**, not a result of science. Philosophy (Hume on miracles) and Stage 12 here take it up. The Orthodox note that **miracles continue** in the life of the Church, and that millions of educated people believe in them.

**5. "The faith which was once delivered unto the saints"** (Jude 3, KJV). The faith is **given**, not made. The Church does not improve it in each century; she **guards** it and lives it. **St Vincent of Lérins** (434): what has been believed everywhere, always and by all. St Paul: "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8, KJV).

**6. The fruit.** The churches that followed liberalism have, by and large, emptied. **A Christianity that asks nothing and promises nothing beyond this life gives people no reason to come.** The churches growing fastest believe in the supernatural.

**Their best reply.** "You are fundamentalists in vestments: you refuse what scholarship shows." The Orthodox answer that the Church **welcomes true scholarship**, and that Orthodox scholars use historical methods (as Florovsky, Meyendorff and many biblical scholars did), but **refuses the philosophical premise** that God cannot act in history. The question is not "Do you accept scholarship?" but "Do you accept that God can raise the dead?"

**What it finally rests on:**
**Is Christianity a revelation of God given once in history and kept by the Church, or the developing religious experience of humanity, to be reinterpreted in each age?**
The Old Catholics: Utrecht, Döllinger an:
**The Old Catholics** are Western Catholic churches that broke with Rome but kept the Catholic faith, liturgy and bishops, and **reject papal infallibility and universal jurisdiction**. They have long been the Western church most hopeful of union with the Orthodox.

**Two origins.**
1. **Utrecht.** The ancient see of Utrecht in the Netherlands quarrelled with Rome in the early eighteenth century, partly over Jansenism (a strict Augustinian movement condemned by Rome). In **1723** the chapter elected **Cornelius Steenoven** archbishop without papal approval; he was consecrated in **1724** by a French missionary bishop, **Dominique-Marie Varlet**. The **Church of Utrecht** has had its own bishops ever since.
2. **After Vatican I (1870).** Many German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics refused the dogma of papal infallibility (taught in Stage 4). The great church historian **Ignaz von Döllinger** (1799–1890) of Munich was **excommunicated in 1871**. Communities formed; **Joseph Hubert Reinkens** was consecrated bishop for them by a bishop of the Utrecht church in **1873**.

**The Union of Utrecht (1889).** The Old Catholic churches of the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland joined in the **Declaration of Utrecht** (1889), accepting the faith of the **first millennium** and the ecumenical councils, and rejecting Vatican I and the Immaculate Conception. The Old Catholics later removed the filioque from the Creed.

**The Bonn conferences.** Döllinger convened **Reunion Conferences at Bonn in 1874 and 1875**, with Old Catholics, Anglicans and Orthodox (Russian, Greek and Romanian theologians). In **1875** they agreed on a statement on the procession of the Holy Spirit drawn from **St John of Damascus**: the Spirit proceeds from the Father **through** the Son. **It was the most hopeful Orthodox–Western moment of the nineteenth century.**

**The Old Catholic case at its strongest.** "We are what the West was before the papacy grew: catholic, sacramental, conciliar, with married clergy and the liturgy in the people's language. **We hold what you hold about the first millennium.**"

**The official dialogue.** A **Joint Orthodox–Old Catholic Theological Commission** worked from **1975 to 1987**, producing agreed texts on the Trinity, Christ, the Church, the sacraments and the last things, concluding (at Chambésy, 1987) that there was **no dogmatic obstacle** to communion in the matters treated. **Communion did not follow.**

**Why not.** Two reasons:
1. **Full communion with the Anglicans** (Bonn Agreement, **1931**), whose Articles and later changes the Orthodox could not accept.
2. **The ordination of women**: the German Old Catholic church ordained women priests from **1996**, and others followed. The Union of Utrecht allowed member churches to decide for themselves (2003). The **Polish National Catholic Church** of America **left the Union in 2003** over this question.

**The Orthodox answer.** **Where the Old Catholics hold the faith of the first millennium, the Orthodox recognise it.** But a church that agrees on paper while changing the apostolic order of ministry by its own decision has not received the Tradition whole. **The same lesson as the Nonjurors** (Stage 6, Lesson 23): union is the reception of the whole faith, not agreement on a minimum.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** Some see the 1975–1987 texts as a model of what dialogue can achieve, and grieve the opportunity lost. Others see the Old Catholic story as proof that **only the Church's living Tradition, not a reconstruction of the first millennium**, keeps a church from drifting.

**What it finally rests on:** **whether agreeing on the faith of the first millennium is enough for union, or whether union means entering the one living Church that has kept it.**
Orthodox converts from Protestantism: th:
In the last half-century a steady stream of Protestants, above all evangelicals and Anglicans, have become Orthodox. This lesson tells their story and the question every convert raises: **how is he received?**

**The Evangelical Orthodox.** In the 1960s and 1970s a group of former **Campus Crusade for Christ** leaders, among them **Peter Gillquist** (1938–2012), Jack Sparks and Jon Braun, set out to find the New Testament Church by reading the Fathers. They moved, step by step, to liturgy, the sacraments and bishops, and formed the **Evangelical Orthodox Church** in **1979**. In **February 1987** about two thousand of them were received into the **Antiochian Orthodox Christian Archdiocese of North America** under Metropolitan **Philip (Saliba)**. Gillquist told the story in ***Becoming Orthodox*** (1989).

**Others.** Converts include the writer **Frederica Mathewes-Green**, from the Episcopal Church, and the scholar **Jaroslav Pelikan** (1923–2006), the great historian of doctrine, a Lutheran pastor who became Orthodox in **1998**. Many Anglican clergy have also come. As of November 2026, Orthodox parishes in the United States and Britain have reported **growing numbers of enquirers and converts**, many of them young men; the numbers are small but much discussed.

**Why they come.** Converts most often name: **the Fathers**, and the discovery that the early Church was liturgical and sacramental; **the Eucharist**; **stability** against changing doctrine and morals; **theosis**; and **beauty** in worship.

**How the Orthodox receive Protestants: where Orthodox writers differ.** This is one of the live questions (Stage 1, and Theology, Stage 4, "Receiving converts").

| Practice | Who | Reasoning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **By chrismation**, if baptised in water in the Trinitarian name | most of the Antiochian Archdiocese and the OCA; the Russian Church's usual practice; many Greek dioceses in the past | the Second Ecumenical Council's canon 7 (381) and the Quinisext canon 95 (692) received some heretics by chrismation; the form of baptism is there, and **chrismation and the Eucharist give it grace** (some say: fill an empty form) |
| **By baptism** | Mount Athos; many Greek and Romanian dioceses today; ROCOR since its decision of **1971**, in principle; Fr **Peter Heers** and others | **akriveia**: outside the Church there are no mysteries; St Cyprian and the Apostolic Canons 46–47; the 1755 decree of Constantinople; Protestants often baptise without the Church's faith in baptism |

**The arguments at their strongest.**
- **For chrismation (oikonomia):** The canons themselves receive some by chrismation. Insisting on baptism can imply that the Church's practice for centuries was wrong. **Florovsky** argued that the Spirit's work is not wholly absent where the form of baptism is kept, though it is completed only in the Church.
- **For baptism (akriveia):** St Nikodemos the Hagiorite (*Pedalion*, 1800) argued that *oikonomia* is a pastoral **exception** for a particular good, not a recognition of heterodox baptism, and that the Church may at any time return to strictness. **Many converts ask for baptism themselves**, wanting no doubt about their entry.

**All agree** that the convert's previous baptism is not simply the same as Orthodox baptism; that the bishop decides; and that the convert should **obey his bishop** rather than choose the rite he prefers. **Lesson 21 asks what liturgy he joins.**

**Their best reply, from the Protestant side.** "You call yourselves the one Church, yet you cannot agree on whether I am baptised." The Orthodox answer: the disagreement is about **pastoral practice at the threshold**, not about the faith inside. **All Orthodox agree on what the Church is**; they differ on how to welcome those who were outside it.

**What it finally rests on:** **whether a baptism performed outside the Church is an empty form the Church can fill by chrismation, or no baptism at all.**
The Western Rite: Overbeck, the Antiochi:
**The Western Rite** is the use, within the Orthodox Church, of **Western liturgies** (forms of the Latin Mass or the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, corrected to Orthodox doctrine) by communities of converts. It is small, and much argued over.

**The history.**
| When | Who | What |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1860s | **J. J. Overbeck** (1821–1905) | a German ex-Catholic priest, then Lutheran, received into Orthodoxy (1865); proposed a "Western Orthodox Catholic Church"; the Russian Holy Synod gave cautious approval in principle (about 1870), but the plan lapsed |
| 1904 | **the Russian Holy Synod** | at the request of St Tikhon, then bishop in America, examined the Anglican Book of Common Prayer and noted what would need correcting for Orthodox use |
| 1936–1993 | **the *Église catholique orthodoxe de France*** | a French Western Rite church under Evgraf Kovalevsky, under Moscow, then ROCOR, then the Romanian Patriarchate (1972–1993), with a reconstructed "Gallican" liturgy |
| **1958** | **the Antiochian Archdiocese** of North America | Metropolitan **Antony Bashir** created the **Western Rite Vicariate**; its parishes use the **Liturgy of St Tikhon** (from the Prayer Book) and the **Liturgy of St Gregory** (from the Roman Mass) |
| 2000s–2013 | **ROCOR** | received Western Rite parishes; in **2013** its Synod halted new ordinations for them and placed them directly under the First Hierarch |

**The case for, at its strongest.**
1. **The West was Orthodox for a thousand years.** The Roman liturgy, the Gallican, the Mozarabic and the Celtic were Orthodox liturgies. St Gregory the Great is an Orthodox saint. **Orthodoxy is not Byzantine culture**; it is a faith that can pray in Western forms, as it does in Slavonic, Arabic and Swahili.
2. **Mission.** Many Western Christians could more easily enter the Church if they did not have to leave their whole tradition of prayer at the door.
3. **Precedent.** In the first millennium Rome, Milan and Spain had their own rites in communion with the East. Some cite the **Liturgy of St Peter**, a Byzantine-Roman hybrid used by some Greek monks in the Middle Ages, and Orthodox in Italy before the schism.

**The case against, at its strongest.**
1. **The Western rites did not stop in 1054.** The Roman Mass of today, or the Prayer Book, grew for centuries **outside** the Church, shaped by scholastic and Protestant theology. **Correcting the words does not remove the theology built into the structure**: the Latin rite's centre on the words of institution rather than the epiclesis (Stage 5, Lesson 21), or the Prayer Book's Reformation shape.
2. **A liturgy is lived Tradition, not a text.** The Orthodox liturgy is one with the Church's calendar, fasts, iconography and the whole life of the people. **Fr Alexander Schmemann** and others warned that a Western Rite risks becoming a museum or a halfway house, an "Orthodoxy" of converts kept apart from the Orthodox people.
3. **The Church's own order.** Since the twelfth century, the Orthodox Church has used the **Byzantine rite** almost everywhere, and Patriarch **Theodore Balsamon** (12th century) argued that all churches in communion with Constantinople should do so. **The ROCOR decision of 2013** reflects this caution.

**Where things stand, as of November 2026.** The Antiochian Western Rite Vicariate continues, with a few dozen parishes in North America. ROCOR's Western Rite parishes continue under its First Hierarch's direct care, without new ordinations since 2013. **No Orthodox church outside these has adopted it.** Most converts from Protestantism enter the Byzantine rite.

**Both sides agree** that **the faith is primary**: a Western Rite parish must hold the whole Orthodox faith, commune with Orthodox bishops, and keep the Orthodox calendar and fasts. The disagreement is whether a **Western form** can be filled with it without losing something.

**What it finally rests on:** **whether a liturgy is a neutral form that can be corrected and filled with Orthodox faith, or itself a part of Tradition, so that a rite grown outside the Church carries what it grew in.**
Looking back: the Reformation's heirs:
This stage answered the movements that grew from the Reformation, and the converts who come from them. Looking back:

**The movements, side by side.**
| Movement | Their heart | The Orthodox answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Baptists** | believers' baptism; the gathered church | baptism is God's new birth, given to children too (Gregory, Oration 40) |
| **Methodists** | grace for all; perfect love | the goal is theosis, but by lifelong healing, not a moment |
| **Holiness** | entire sanctification as a second blessing | the gift is given in chrismation and uncovered by struggle |
| **Pentecostals** | baptism in the Spirit, with tongues | the Spirit is given in the mysteries; the sign is holiness and love; test the spirits |
| **Evangelicals** | conversion, Bible, cross, mission | personal faith lived in the Body of Christ |
| **Prosperity gospel** | faith brings health and wealth | the Cross; wealth belongs to the poor |
| **African independent churches** | African Christianity, prophecy, healing | honour Africa's faith; but the Church is apostolic by faith and succession, and Christ, not the prophet, protects |
| **Liberal Protestantism** | religion as experience; dogma as history | revelation given once; the Resurrection is the Gospel |
| **Old Catholics** | the faith of the first millennium | agreement on paper is not reception of the whole living Tradition |

**The premises underneath.** Three run through the stage:
1. **Scripture alone**, inherited from Stage 6.
2. **The individual's experience** as the place where salvation is known: the decision, the second blessing, tongues, the feeling of dependence.
3. **The Church as the company of believers**, which each founder can begin anew.

**The Orthodox reply to all three** is the same: **the Church is the Body of Christ, given once, with the apostles' faith, mysteries and ministry**; experience is real and precious, but it is **tested by** the Church's faith, and **given within** her life.

**What the Orthodox should learn from them.** These movements are not only errors. They show the Orthodox what people hunger for and what the Orthodox Church already has: **a living experience of the Spirit** (St Seraphim, St Symeon), **holiness for all** (Chrysostom), **love of Scripture**, **mission**, **healing**, and **a church at home in every people**, Africa included. Where Orthodox communities are nominal, these movements will fill the gap.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** On how to receive converts (chrismation or baptism); on the Western Rite; on how to judge charismatic experience (Rose's severity or a gentler view); on dialogue with the Old Catholics and Anglicans. **Each was given at its strongest.**

**In conversation.** With a Baptist, begin with **Romans 6** and ask what baptism does. With a Pentecostal, begin with **St Seraphim** and the acquisition of the Spirit. With an evangelical, answer "Yes" to the personal relationship, and show where you meet Him. With a Zionist or Apostolic neighbour, take the fear of evil seriously and point to Christ in the Church's prayers. With a liberal, ask about the **empty tomb**.

**Next.** Stage 8 turns to the new movements that left historic Christianity's creeds altogether: the Jehovah's Witnesses, the Latter-day Saints, the Adventists, Christian Science and the Oneness Pentecostals.
Context: the new movements, and why they:
This stage takes up the movements that grew out of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Protestant America and then claimed to be something more than another denomination: **a restoration of the true Church after a long falling away**, or a new and final light on Scripture. They are the people most likely to knock on a door.

**What makes them "new".** The churches of the Reformation (Stages 6 and 7) changed much, but most kept the Creed of Nicaea and Constantinople and the doctrine of the Trinity. The movements in this stage either **reject the Trinity outright**, or **add a new prophet or a new scripture**, or both. That is why the Orthodox Church receives a convert from most of them by baptism, not by chrismation: their baptism is not into the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit as the Church confesses Them. (On how converts are received, and where Orthodox practice differs for Trinitarian Protestants, see Stage 1.)

| Movement | Founded | Their own name | The main question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Jehovah's Witnesses** | 1870s, Pennsylvania | Jehovah's Witnesses | Is the Son a creature? |
| **Latter-day Saints** | 1830, New York | The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints | Did the Church fall? Is God an exalted man? |
| **Seventh-day Adventists** | 1863, Michigan | Seventh-day Adventist Church | Sabbath, 1844, and a prophetess |
| **Christian Science** | 1879, Boston | Church of Christ, Scientist | Is matter real? |
| **Oneness Pentecostals** | 1913–1916, California | e.g. United Pentecostal Church International | Is God one person? |

**Three things to keep in mind.**

1. **The old patterns return.** Stage 2 taught Arius, Gnosticism and the modalists as patterns. Here they come back: the Witnesses repeat Arius, the Oneness Pentecostals repeat the modalists, Christian Science has something of the Gnostic distrust of matter. This stage refers back and does not re-teach those heresies.
2. **They are not all alike.** The Adventists confess the Trinity and are, for most purposes, conservative Protestants with particular teachings. The Witnesses and the Latter-day Saints do not, and their differences from the Church go to the doctrine of God Himself.
3. **The people are usually admirable.** Witnesses are known for discipline and courage under persecution; Latter-day Saints for family life and generosity; Adventists for health and hospitals. **The answer is to the teaching, never to the person**, and it begins by stating their case as they would state it.

**Names.** Each lesson uses the name the body uses for itself. Since 2018 the Latter-day Saints have asked not to be called "Mormons" or "the LDS Church"; these lessons say "Latter-day Saints" or give the full name.

**Numbers, as of November 2026**, come from each body's own reports and are given in the lessons.
The Watch Tower: Russell, Rutherford and:
The Jehovah's Witnesses began as a Bible study group and became one of the most organised religious bodies in the world.

**Charles Taze Russell (1852–1916)**, a Pittsburgh businessman, gathered a group of "Bible Students" in the 1870s. He rejected eternal hell, the immortality of the soul and the Trinity, and drew on Adventist ideas about dates. In **1879** he began the magazine *Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence*, and in 1881 founded the society later incorporated as the **Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society**. His six-volume *Studies in the Scriptures* set out his scheme of history.

**Joseph Franklin Rutherford (1869–1942)** led the society after Russell's death. He centralised it, made door-to-door preaching the duty of every member, and in **1931** gave the movement the name **Jehovah's Witnesses**, from Isaiah 43:10: "Ye are my witnesses, saith the LORD" (KJV). Under his successors came the **New World Translation** of the Bible (New Testament 1950, whole Bible 1961, revised 2013) and today's leadership by a small **Governing Body** in Warwick, New York.

**What they hold, in their own terms** (from jw.org, paraphrased):

| Teaching | In brief |
| --- | --- |
| **God** | one person, Jehovah, the Father alone |
| **Jesus** | God's first creation, the archangel Michael before his human life; God's Son and the Messiah, but not God Almighty |
| **The holy spirit** | God's active force, not a person |
| **1914** | the year Christ began to rule invisibly in heaven; the "last days" began then |
| **Salvation** | 144,000 rule with Christ in heaven; a "great crowd" will live for ever on a paradise earth |
| **The dead** | unconscious; no immortal soul, no hellfire |
| **Practice** | preaching, neutrality in politics and war, no blood transfusions, no birthdays or Christmas |

**Their numbers, as of November 2026.** The Witnesses' 2025 service year report gives a peak of about **9.2 million** active "publishers" in 241 lands, and about **20.6 million** at the yearly Memorial of Christ's death.

**Their strongest case.** Witnesses present themselves as people who simply read the Bible without the later "pagan" additions of the creeds: the Trinity, the immortal soul, hell, the cross as a symbol, Christmas. They point to their moral seriousness, their refusal of violence, and their courage. **That courage is real.** Under the Nazis they wore the purple triangle in the camps and many died rather than give the Hitler salute or serve in the army. In the Soviet Union whole families were deported to Siberia in 1951.

**History told honestly.** Witnesses have also suffered at Orthodox hands. In **2017 the Supreme Court of Russia declared their organisation "extremist" and banned it**; since then hundreds have been searched, tried and imprisoned, and some Orthodox anti-sect campaigners supported the ban. Whatever the Church thinks of their teaching, **the Fathers answered heretics with argument, not prisons**, and an Orthodox answer to the Witnesses should say so.

The next three lessons take their teaching on Christ, their Bible and their hope in turn.
Jehovah's Witnesses on Christ: Michael,:
The centre of the Witnesses' disagreement with the Church is the person of Christ. **Stage 2 ("Arius today") has already given the pattern and the main answer**: the Son is not "firstborn" as first-created (Psalm 89:27); all things were made through Him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16); Thomas called Him "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28). This lesson does not repeat that. It takes the three points where the Witnesses go **beyond** Arius, or where their practice shows what their doctrine means.

**1. Jesus as Michael the archangel.** *Their case* (jw.org, "The Archangel Michael: Who Is He?", paraphrased): 1 Thessalonians 4:16 says the Lord descends "with the voice of the archangel"; Michael leads the angels against the dragon in Revelation 12:7, the work of the Messiah; so Michael is the name of God's Son before and after his life on earth.

*The Orthodox answer.* The verse says the Lord comes **with** an archangel's voice, as He comes "with the trump of God", which does not make Him a trumpet. And Hebrews 1 is written to show the Son is **above** the angels: "unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son?" (Hebrews 1:5, KJV). Michael "durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee" (Jude 9); Christ rebukes Satan in His own name (Matthew 4:10). **No Father, and no Christian writer before the nineteenth century, identified Christ with Michael.**

**2. Worship.** *Their case.* The Greek *proskynéō* means to bow down, which may be done to kings; so the *New World Translation* has angels "do obeisance" to the Son at Hebrews 1:6, where the King James has "worship". **Witnesses honour Jesus but worship only Jehovah.**

*The Orthodox answer.* Scripture shows the difference in practice. When John falls at an angel's feet, the angel forbids it: "See thou do it not... worship God" (Revelation 22:9). When Cornelius falls at Peter's feet, Peter says "Stand up; I myself also am a man" (Acts 10:26). When the women hold the risen Christ's feet and worship Him (Matthew 28:9), **He does not forbid it**. And in heaven "every creature" gives the same "blessing, and honour, and glory, and power" to "him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb" (Revelation 5:13). **One worship, given to both.**

**3. Prayer.** *Their practice.* Witnesses pray to Jehovah **through** Jesus, never **to** Jesus.

*The Orthodox answer.* Stephen, dying, prays to Him: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). Paul writes to "all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord" (1 Corinthians 1:2), using the Old Testament phrase for calling on the LORD (Joel 2:32). Christ Himself says: "If ye shall ask any thing in my name, I will do it" (John 14:14). **The first Christians prayed to Christ**, and the Jesus Prayer continues it.

**Their best reply.** Stephen saw Jesus in a vision and spoke to him, which is not regular prayer; "call upon the name" can mean to confess him; and Jesus taught his disciples to pray "Our Father", not "Our Jesus".

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the one who receives the worship and prayer of the first Christians can be a creature.** If He can, the Witnesses are right to refuse Him worship. If worship belongs to God alone, as both sides agree, then the apostles' practice shows who they knew Him to be.
John 1:1 and the New World Translation:
The verse a Witness and an Orthodox Christian will most often argue over is the first verse of St John's Gospel. Stage 2 gave the short answer; this lesson gives the full argument, as it runs in a real conversation.

**The Greek.** *En archē ēn ho Lógos, kai ho Lógos ēn pros ton Theón, kai Theós ēn ho Lógos.* The King James renders it: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The **New World Translation** has: **"and the Word was a god."**

**Their case at its strongest.** In the second clause, "with God" has the article (*ton Theon*, "the God"); in the third, *Theos* has none. Greek has no indefinite article ("a"), so translators supply one where sense requires: in Acts 28:6 the islanders say Paul is "a god" with the same bare *theos*. The Witnesses argue that John deliberately marks a difference: the Word is with *the* God and is *divine* or *a god*, not the God he is with. They can cite non-Witness scholars whose translations rendered the clause "the Word was divine" (James Moffatt in 1913, Edgar Goodspeed in 1923), to show the reading is not only theirs.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Word order and the article.** In Greek a predicate noun placed before the verb often drops the article without becoming indefinite; the rule is associated with E. C. Colwell (1933). More importantly, a noun without the article in that position is usually **qualitative**: it says *what* the Word is. John is saying **the Word has the nature of God**, while not being the same person as the One He is with. That is precisely the Orthodox doctrine: one nature, distinct persons.
2. **Inconsistency.** The New World Translation does not render other articleless *theos* in John 1 as "a god": "There was a man sent from God" (1:6), "power to become the sons of God" (1:12), "No man hath seen God at any time" (1:18) all lack the article in Greek.
3. **"A god" is impossible in Scripture's own terms.** God says: "before me there was no God formed, neither shall there be after me" (Isaiah 43:10, KJV) and "beside me there is no God" (Isaiah 44:6). If the Word is "a god" alongside Jehovah, He is either a false god or a second true god. **Scripture allows neither.**
4. **The Fathers read it so from the start.** St Irenaeus (about 180) and St Athanasius (fourth century) quote John 1:1 as plain proof that the Word is God. The Greek-speaking Church, whose language this was, never read it as "a god".

**Their best reply.** Moffatt and Goodspeed were not Witnesses and still wrote "divine". The Witnesses themselves now argue that the articleless *theos* is qualitative, and cite scholars such as Jason BeDuhn: the Word has a godlike quality without being the God he is with. Isaiah 9:6 calls the Messiah "The mighty God", they note, but never "Almighty". Colwell's rule tells you a predicate noun *may* be definite, not that it must. And Psalm 82:6, quoted by Christ in John 10:34, shows Scripture can call beings other than God "gods".

**The Orthodox reply to that.** Psalm 82 calls human judges "gods" in irony, then says "ye shall die like men" (82:7). No one creates the world through them. **"Divine" in the sense of "having God's nature" is the Orthodox meaning, not a halfway house.**

**What it finally rests on.** **Grammar alone does not settle John 1:1; the doctrine of God does.** If there can be only one God, the clause must mean that the Word shares His nature. If there can be lesser gods, "a god" is possible. So the conversation always returns to Isaiah 43–44 and to John 1:3.
The Witnesses' hope: 1914, the 144,000 a:
After the person of Christ, the Witnesses' most distinctive teachings concern the end: when it began, who goes where, and what Christians must refuse in the meantime.

**Their case at its strongest** (jw.org, paraphrased).

- **1914.** Reading Daniel 4 and Luke 21:24 ("the times of the Gentiles"), Witnesses calculate 2,520 years from what they date as the fall of Jerusalem in 607 BC to **1914**. In that year Christ was enthroned invisibly in heaven and Satan was thrown down to the earth; the First World War is the sign. We live in the "last days", and Armageddon is near.
- **Two hopes.** Revelation 7:4 and 14:1 speak of **144,000** sealed. Witnesses take this as the literal number of those "anointed" to rule with Christ in heaven. Revelation 7:9 speaks of "a great multitude, which no man could number": these are the **"other sheep"** (John 10:16), most Witnesses, who will live for ever in a restored **paradise on earth**. Only the anointed eat the bread and drink the wine at the yearly Memorial; in 2025 about 24,600 did.
- **The cross.** Jesus died on a *stauros* (σταυρός), which they translate "torture stake": a single upright pole. The cross is a pagan symbol and is not used.
- **Blood.** "Abstain... from blood" (Acts 15:29, KJV) forbids taking blood into the body in any way; since 1945 that has included transfusions, though some blood fractions are now left to conscience.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Dates.** Christ said: "of that day and hour knoweth no man" (Matthew 24:36, KJV). The movement's own history bears this out. Russell first taught that Christ's invisible presence began in **1874** and expected the end of the age in **1914**; Rutherford's 1920 lecture *Millions Now Living Will Never Die* pointed to **1925**; a 1966 Watch Tower book suggested that six thousand years of human history would end around **1975**. Each was revised. **Deuteronomy 18:22 gives the biblical test of a prophet whose word "follow not, nor come to pass"**, and Orthodox writers apply it here, while granting that the Governing Body does not claim to be inspired prophets.
2. **The 144,000.** In Revelation 7 the number is twelve thousand from each tribe of Israel, and in 14:4 they are virgin men. Witnesses take the number literally but not the tribes or the virginity. The Fathers read the book's numbers as symbols of fullness. And **the New Testament knows one hope, not two**: "There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling" (Ephesians 4:4, KJV); all who believe are to eat Christ's flesh and drink His blood (John 6:53).
3. **The cross.** *Stauros* can mean a stake, but the earliest Christian witness is to a crossbeam: Justin Martyr (about 155) finds the shape of the cross in a ship's sail and mast and in a plough (*First Apology* 55), and the Epistle of Barnabas sees it in the letter T, which only a crossbar makes. And the cross was a Christian sign long before Constantine.
4. **Blood.** The Council of Jerusalem's rule concerned **eating** blood. Orthodox moral theology treats a transfusion as giving life, not consuming it, and does not forbid it.

**Their best reply.** The tribes in Revelation 7 are "spiritual Israel", the Church of the anointed, so the number can be literal while the tribes are not. The anointed are a small group because Christ spoke of a "little flock" (Luke 12:32); the date calculations were honest attempts, now refined; blood is sacred to God in every form.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether one organisation, the "faithful and discreet slave" of Matthew 24:45 (their rendering; the KJV has "faithful and wise servant"), is God's channel for interpreting Scripture today.** Witnesses believe the Governing Body is that slave. If it is, its revisions are "new light". If it is not, the dates, the two hopes and the blood rule have no authority beyond its own.
The Latter-day Saints: Joseph Smith and:
The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is the largest and most confident of the new movements, and its claim is the boldest: **the Church Christ founded was lost, and God restored it through a modern prophet.**

**The story as they tell it.** In **1820**, in western New York, the fourteen-year-old **Joseph Smith (1805–1844)** prayed to know which church to join. In what Latter-day Saints call the **First Vision**, God the Father and Jesus Christ appeared to him and told him to join none, for all had strayed. In 1823 an angel, **Moroni**, showed him buried golden plates. Smith translated them "by the gift and power of God" and published the **Book of Mormon** in **1830**: the record of Israelites who sailed to the Americas about 600 BC, and of the risen Christ's visit to them. On **6 April 1830** the Church was organised. Smith received further revelations, gathered in the **Doctrine and Covenants**, and was killed by a mob at Carthage, Illinois, on **27 June 1844**. Brigham Young led most of the Saints to Utah in 1847.

**Their scriptures.** The Bible (in the King James Version), the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants and the Pearl of Great Price. The eighth Article of Faith (1842): "We believe the Bible to be the word of God as far as it is translated correctly; we also believe the Book of Mormon to be the word of God."

**What they hold** (from churchofjesuschrist.org, paraphrased):

| Teaching | In brief |
| --- | --- |
| **The Godhead** | three distinct beings, one in purpose: the Father and Son with glorified bodies, the Holy Ghost a spirit |
| **Premortal life** | every person lived as a spirit child of Heavenly Parents before birth |
| **The Restoration** | priesthood authority restored by John the Baptist and by Peter, James and John in 1829 |
| **Living prophets** | a President of the Church, with twelve apostles, receives revelation for the whole Church |
| **Temples** | eternal marriage, and baptism and other ordinances done on behalf of the dead |
| **Exaltation** | the faithful may progress to become like God, as heirs |

**Their numbers, as of November 2026.** The Church's report for 2025 gives **about 17.9 million members** and 204 temples in operation. Its President since **October 2025** is **Dallin H. Oaks**, its eighteenth.

**Their strongest case.** Latter-day Saints offer what many Protestants lack: **authority, continuing revelation, and a living apostleship**. They point out, with Orthodox and Catholics, that "Bible alone" Christianity splinters endlessly; that the New Testament Church had apostles and prophets; and that a God who spoke then might speak now. Their missionaries invite people to read the Book of Mormon and pray about it (Moroni 10:4, read in Lesson 17 of this stage; the next lesson weighs the book itself). They are known for strong families, welfare work, and the discipline of the young men and women who serve as missionaries.

**The Orthodox starting point.** On authority and succession, the Orthodox and the Latter-day Saints ask the same question. **The disagreement is about the answer: did that authority die out, or has it continued unbroken?** Lesson 8 takes that up; Lesson 10 takes the doctrine of God.
The Book of Mormon: its claims and the e:
A Latter-day Saint will not usually begin with the doctrine of God. He will begin with a book, and ask you to read it.

**What it claims to be.** The **Book of Mormon**, published in **1830**, presents itself as an ancient record engraved on golden plates by prophets in the Americas and translated by Joseph Smith. It tells of **Lehi**, who left Jerusalem about 600 BC; of his descendants, the **Nephites** and **Lamanites**; of their wars and prophets; and, at its climax (3 Nephi 11), of **the risen Christ appearing to them** and teaching them as He taught in Galilee. Its last prophet, **Moroni**, buried the plates about AD 421. Eleven witnesses signed statements, printed in the book, that they had seen the plates. The Church subtitles it "**Another Testament of Jesus Christ**".

**Its strongest case** (from the Church and its best defenders, notably **Hugh Nibley** (1910–2005) and the scholars of Brigham Young University's Maxwell Institute, paraphrased).

1. **It is a book about Christ.** Much of it is plainly Christian preaching: faith, repentance, baptism, the atonement. Its language about God is, on its own, close to traditional Protestant language; the more distinctive doctrines of Lesson 10 come from Joseph Smith's later revelations.
2. **It is hard to explain as the work of a young farmer.** Smith dictated it in about three months. Defenders point to Hebrew-like features such as **chiasmus** (inverted parallel structures, as in Alma 36), and to names they match to the ancient Near East, such as **Nahom** (1 Nephi 16:34), which they link to a tribal name in Yemen.
3. **The witnesses did not deny their testimony**, even those who later quarrelled with Smith and left the Church.
4. **The spiritual test.** The book itself asks the reader to pray about it (Moroni 10:4, read in Lesson 17).

**The Orthodox answer.** The Church's answer does not depend on archaeology, but the evidence should be stated fairly.

1. **The historical record.** Mainstream archaeologists and historians, including many who are not hostile, find **no trace in the Americas** of the Nephite civilisation, its Hebrew language, or the Old World animals and metals the book describes, and genetic studies trace the ancestry of Native Americans to Asia. Latter-day Saint scholars reply with a "limited geography" in Mesoamerica and argue that absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. **The Church does not need to settle this to answer the book.**
2. **The decisive test is the faith once delivered.** St Paul gives it: "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed" (Galatians 1:8, KJV). A book brought by an angel is judged by the apostolic faith, not the reverse.
3. **A feeling is not a test of truth.** "Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world" (1 John 4:1). The Fathers of the desert warn that the enemy can counterfeit consolation as well as stir fear; the Orthodox test is agreement with the Church's faith, not inward warmth alone. Theology Stage 10 teaches the discernment of spirits.
4. **What the book leads to.** The Book of Mormon opens the door to Joseph Smith's later teaching, and the real disagreement lies there: the apostasy (next lesson) and the nature of God (Lesson 10).

**Their best reply.** The Orthodox also trust the witness of the Spirit and of holy people; the eleven witnesses are as good as much ancient testimony; and the Bible, too, lacks archaeological confirmation for parts of its history.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether a new scripture can be tested by prayer alone, or must be tested by the faith already delivered to the Church.** The Latter-day Saint answers the first; the Orthodox the second, and then asks whether the book's message, and what follows from it, agrees with the apostles.
The Great Apostasy: did the Church fall?:
Every restoration movement rests on one claim: that the Church Christ founded fell away, so that it needed restoring. Latter-day Saints call this the **Great Apostasy**. It is the hinge of their case, and it is where the Orthodox answer is strongest.

**Their case at its strongest** (from the Church's *Gospel Topics* and *Preach My Gospel*, paraphrased). The New Testament itself predicts a falling away: "that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first" (2 Thessalonians 2:3); Paul warns of "grievous wolves" (Acts 20:29); Amos foretold "a famine... of hearing the words of the LORD" (Amos 8:11). After the apostles were killed, there was no one with authority to receive revelation. Within a few centuries the Church had borrowed Greek philosophy, defined God in the abstract language of the creeds (*ousia*, "substance"), changed baptism and grown worldly under Constantine. **The keys of the priesthood were taken from the earth** until God restored them through Joseph Smith.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Christ promised the opposite.** "Upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:18, KJV). "Lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world" (Matthew 28:20). The Spirit "will guide you into all truth" (John 16:13). **A total apostasy would mean Christ's promise failed.** Individuals and whole regions have fallen; the Church as such has not.
2. **The "falling away" texts describe a falling away within or from the Church**, not its disappearance: Paul in 2 Thessalonians goes on to tell the same Church to "hold the traditions which ye have been taught" (2:15).
3. **The evidence of the second century.** St Ignatius of Antioch, writing on his way to martyrdom (about 107), already describes a Church with bishops, presbyters and deacons gathered around one Eucharist. St Irenaeus (about 180) lists the bishops of Rome from the apostles down to his day to show that the apostolic teaching has been kept. **There is no gap in the record where the apostasy should be.** This continuity, and the councils it produced, are taught in Theology Stages 1 and 7.
4. **Greek terms were a fence, not a new faith.** The Fathers used *ousia* and *hypostasis* to guard what Scripture says against Arius, not to replace it (Theology Stage 2).

**Their best reply.** Continuity of offices is not continuity of authority: a body can keep bishops and lose the keys. The early Church's own quarrels and the later corruptions in East and West show it had lost its way. And restoration is not new: the Old Testament also had long gaps without prophets before God spoke again.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** Israel's silence between prophets was never a loss of the covenant, the priesthood or the Temple. And if authority can be lost while every visible sign of it remains, **no one could ever know where it is**, including in a modern Church.

**What it finally rests on.**

**Did Christ's promise to keep His Church hold, or fail?** If it held, the Church must still exist, recognisable by apostolic succession and apostolic faith, and needs no restoration. If it failed, a restoration is possible, and the question becomes whether Joseph Smith's is the true one. Every conversation with a Latter-day Saint missionary comes back here.
Reading: Doctrine and Covenants 130 on t:
This reading is from the Latter-day Saints' own scripture, the **Doctrine and Covenants**. Section 130 records instructions Joseph Smith gave at Ramus, Illinois, on **2 April 1843**, and it is the plainest canonical statement of how they understand God. The text is quoted from the edition on churchofjesuschrist.org.

**Verses 1–3:**

> "When the Savior shall appear we shall see him as he is. We shall see that he is a man like ourselves. And that same sociality which exists among us here will exist among us there, only it will be coupled with eternal glory, which glory we do not now enjoy. John 14:23—The appearing of the Father and the Son, in that verse, is a personal appearance; and the idea that the Father and the Son dwell in a man's heart is an old sectarian notion, and is false."

**Verse 22:**

> "The Father has a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's; the Son also; but the Holy Ghost has not a body of flesh and bones, but is a personage of Spirit. Were it not so, the Holy Ghost could not dwell in us."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **"A man like ourselves."** Verse 1 takes 1 John 3:2 ("we shall see him as he is") and adds that what we will see is a man like us. The risen Christ does have a human body, as the Orthodox also confess. But verse 22 says the same of **the Father**.
2. **"Tangible as man's."** This is meant literally. The Godhead is three distinct beings, and two of them are embodied. The verse explains the Holy Ghost's difference from them by a physical reason: a being with a body could not dwell in us.
3. **"An old sectarian notion."** Verse 3 rejects the Christian reading of John 14:23 ("we will come unto him, and make our abode with him") as an indwelling of the Father and Son. For the Latter-day Saint, God dwells *with* us, as one person visits another; He does not dwell *in* us.
4. **Why it matters to them.** If God has a body, then the gap between God and man is not one of kind but of degree and glory. Their teaching on exaltation (Lesson 10) follows from this. Another revelation of the same year says of the exalted: "Then shall they be gods, because they have no end" (Doctrine and Covenants 132:20).

**What a Latter-day Saint would want said.** That this is not a crude picture but a hopeful one: **God is a real, personal Father, not an abstraction**, and His children may grow into His likeness. They would point to Genesis 1:26 ("Let us make man in our image") and to the risen Christ's words: "handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have" (Luke 24:39, KJV).

**What to notice for the answer.** Christ says that to the disciples about His own risen body, the body He took from the Virgin. The Orthodox Church agrees that the Son, since the Incarnation, has a glorified human body. The question is whether **the Father**, and the divine nature as such, is embodied. The next reading gives St Gregory the Theologian's answer.
Exaltation and the plurality of gods: th:
The deepest disagreement with the Latter-day Saints is not about church history but about **who God is**.

**Their case at its strongest.** In his **King Follett sermon** (April 1844), Joseph Smith taught, in paraphrase, that God was once a man as we are now and became exalted, and that we too may become as He is. Lorenzo Snow, the Church's fifth President, summed it up in a couplet often repeated since, which says the same in two lines. The Church today teaches it more cautiously but holds the substance: we are literally God's spirit children; we lived with Heavenly Parents before birth; and **through Christ's atonement and the temple ordinances, the faithful may be exalted** and become heirs of all the Father has, "gods" (Doctrine and Covenants 132:20). Matter and intelligence were never created: "Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be" (Doctrine and Covenants 93:29). God organised the world from eternal elements.

**Their best text is the Orthodox one.** Latter-day Saint writers often quote the Fathers on **theosis**, deification. St Athanasius: God became man that man might become god (*On the Incarnation* 54, paraphrased). "Ye are gods" (Psalm 82:6, quoted by Christ in John 10:34). "Partakers of the divine nature" (2 Peter 1:4). They say: the early Church taught exaltation, and the later creeds forgot it.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **God is not a man.** "God is not a man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:19, KJV); "I am God, and not man" (Hosea 11:9); "God is a Spirit" (John 4:24). The Son *became* man in time; the Father never did.
2. **Creation from nothing.** The Church teaches that God made all things *ex nihilo*, from nothing (Theology Stage 2). There are not two eternal realities, God and matter, but **one uncreated God and everything else created**. Doctrine and Covenants 93 makes intelligence and elements co-eternal with God, which makes God an organiser, not a Creator.
3. **Theosis is by grace, not by nature.** For the Fathers, and for St Gregory Palamas (Theology Stage 2), man is deified by **participating in God's uncreated energies**, His life and glory, **never in His essence**. The deified saint becomes god *by grace*, and remains for ever a creature united to the Creator. The Latter-day Saint exalted person becomes the same *kind* of being as God, as a child grows into the same kind as its father. The words are alike; **the doctrines are opposite**.
4. **One God, not a species of gods.** "Beside me there is no God" (Isaiah 44:6). The Trinity is not three gods of one kind but one God, one nature, in three persons (Theology Stage 2).

**Their best reply.** Orthodox theosis also says man becomes "god"; the line between "by grace" and "by nature" is a philosophical refinement. And "creation from nothing" is not stated in so many words in the Bible; it was worked out in the second century.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** The distinction is not a refinement but the whole point: in Orthodox teaching **the saint never becomes another source of divinity**, never has worlds and children of his own as God does. And creation from nothing is the plain sense of "In the beginning God created" and of Romans 4:17, God who "calleth those things which be not as though they were".

**What it finally rests on.**

| Question | Latter-day Saints | Orthodox |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is God the same kind of being as man? | yes, exalted | no, uncreated |
| Is anything eternal besides God? | intelligence and elements | nothing |
| What is deification? | becoming what God is | sharing God's life by grace |

**It rests on the line between Creator and creature.** Orthodoxy draws it absolutely; the Latter-day Saint faith does not draw it at all.
Reading: St Gregory the Theologian on wh:
This is the Orthodox answer to Doctrine and Covenants 130, written fourteen centuries before it. St Gregory of Nazianzus preached his **Second Theological Oration (Oration 28)** in Constantinople in 380. He was not answering Latter-day Saints, but anyone who imagines the divine nature as bodily. The text is from the translation by Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, second series, volume 7 (1894), on New Advent.

**Section 7:**

> "Is He a body? How then is He the Infinite and Limitless, and formless, and intangible, and invisible? Or are these attributes of a body? What arrogance for such is not the nature of a body! Or will you say that He has a body, but not these attributes? O stupidity, that a Deity should possess nothing more than we do. For how is He an object of worship if He be circumscribed? Or how shall He escape being made of elements, and therefore subject to be resolved into them again, or even altogether dissolved?"

**Section 9:**

> "And thus we see that God is not a body. For no inspired teacher has yet asserted or admitted such a notion, nor has the sentence of our own Court allowed it. Nothing then remains but to conceive of Him as incorporeal."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **The first argument: infinity.** Scripture calls God limitless and invisible. A body has edges, a place, a shape. **"Tangible", the word of Doctrine and Covenants 130:22, is the very word Gregory says cannot be said of God.**
2. **The second: worship.** "How is He an object of worship if He be circumscribed?" A being contained in a place is one being among others, however glorious. We worship the One who contains all things, not one who is contained.
3. **The third: composition.** A body is made of parts. What is made of parts can come apart. **God cannot come apart, so He has no parts, so He has no body.** Gregory says the argument works "going back from last to first": no dissolution, so no strife, so no composition, so no body.
4. **The appeal to Scripture and the Church.** In section 8 he quotes "Do not I fill heaven and earth? saith the LORD" (Jeremiah 23:24). In section 9 he says no inspired writer and no judgment of the Church ever allowed God to be bodily.
5. **His tone.** "O stupidity" is aimed at an idea, in a sermon for Christians, in the rough style of ancient rhetoric. **We keep his argument, not his scorn**, when we speak with a Latter-day Saint.

**And the body of Christ?** Gregory confesses, with the whole Church, that the Son took a real human body, which He has for ever, risen and glorified. That body is the body of His human nature, received from the Virgin. **The divine nature, which the Father, the Son and the Spirit share, has no body.** That is why Christ's words in Luke 24:39 do not support the claim of Doctrine and Covenants 130 about the Father.

**Side by side.**

| | Doctrine and Covenants 130 | Gregory, Oration 28 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The Father | "a body of flesh and bones as tangible as man's" | "formless, and intangible, and invisible" |
| God in us | "an old sectarian notion" | God "pervades all things and fills all" |
| The gap between God and man | degree and glory | uncreated and created |
The Seventh-day Adventists: Ellen White:
The Seventh-day Adventists are the most orthodox of the movements in this stage: they confess the Trinity, the full deity of Christ and salvation by grace. What sets them apart is a date, a day and a prophetess.

**The story.** **William Miller (1782–1849)**, a Baptist farmer in New York, calculated from Daniel 8:14 ("Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed", KJV) that Christ would return about 1843–1844. His followers settled on **22 October 1844**. When nothing happened, they called it the **Great Disappointment**. One group concluded that the date was right but the event misunderstood: on that day **Christ entered the most holy place of the heavenly sanctuary** to begin a final work of judgment. Among them were Joseph Bates, who brought the seventh-day Sabbath, and **Ellen G. White (1827–1915)**, whose visions guided the movement. The church was formally organised at Battle Creek, Michigan, in **1863**.

**What they hold** (from the *28 Fundamental Beliefs* on adventist.org, paraphrased):

| Teaching | In brief |
| --- | --- |
| **God and Christ** | the Trinity; Christ fully God and fully man |
| **Salvation** | by grace through faith in Christ |
| **The Sabbath** | the seventh day, Saturday, is the Lord's day of rest for all time |
| **The sanctuary** | since 1844 Christ has carried out an **investigative judgment** in heaven before His return |
| **The dead** | unconscious until the resurrection; the wicked are finally destroyed, not tormented for ever |
| **Ellen White** | had the gift of prophecy; her writings are a "continuing and authoritative source of truth", though Scripture is the standard |
| **Health** | the body is a temple; many are vegetarian; no alcohol or tobacco |

**Their numbers, as of November 2026.** The General Conference reported about **24 million** baptised members at the end of 2025, with large churches in Africa, Latin America and the Pacific. Their hospitals and schools are among the largest Protestant networks in the world.

**Their strongest case.** Adventists see themselves as completing the Reformation: Luther restored justification, others restored believers' baptism, and they restore the Sabbath and the biblical teaching on death. **They take the Ten Commandments seriously, all ten**, and ask why Christians who keep nine have dropped the fourth.

**The Orthodox answer on 1844.** The Letter to the Hebrews says Christ, "by his own blood... entered in once into the holy place, having obtained eternal redemption for us" (Hebrews 9:12), and entered "into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God for us" (9:24). **He entered the heavenly sanctuary at His Ascension, not in 1844.** The investigative judgment is a reading of Daniel 8 built to explain a failed prediction. The Fathers knew nothing of it, and it has troubled Adventists too: in **1980** the Adventist theologian **Desmond Ford** challenged it from Hebrews and lost his ministerial credentials.

**Their best reply.** The doctrine is in Daniel and Leviticus 16 (the Day of Atonement) when read as prophecy; Ellen White's gift is shown by her fruit; and Ford's case shows the church takes Scripture seriously enough to argue about it.

**Where Orthodox practice differs.** Because Adventists baptise by immersion in the name of the Trinity, some Orthodox churches receive them by chrismation and others by baptism (Stage 1).

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether God gives the Church a new prophet after the apostles.** Remove Ellen White's authority and 1844 has no foundation; keep it and Adventism becomes a church with an extra voice beside Scripture.
The Sabbath and the Lord's Day:
The question an Adventist neighbour will most often raise is why Christians worship on Sunday.

**Their case at its strongest.** "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy... the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God" (Exodus 20:8–10, KJV). The Sabbath was made at creation (Genesis 2:2–3), before Israel, so it is for all mankind. It is one of the Ten Commandments, written by God's finger; the other nine are still binding. Christ kept the Sabbath and said "The sabbath was made for man" (Mark 2:27). Nowhere does the New Testament command a change. Sunday came later, from **Constantine's law of 321** making the day of the Sun a day of rest, and from church councils such as **Laodicea** (fourth century), whose **canon 29** told Christians not to rest on the Sabbath but to honour the Lord's day. In classic Adventist teaching, enforced Sunday worship will be part of the "mark of the beast" at the end.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Sunday is older than Constantine by two centuries.** The disciples gathered "upon the first day of the week... to break bread" (Acts 20:7, KJV); John was "in the Spirit on the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10). St Ignatius of Antioch, about 107, writes of Christians "no longer observing the Sabbath, but living in the observance of the Lord's Day, on which also our life has sprung up again by Him and by His death" (*To the Magnesians* 9, tr. Roberts and Donaldson, ANF 1, 1885). St Justin Martyr, about 155: "Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly, because it is the first day on which God... made the world; and Jesus Christ our Saviour on the same day rose from the dead" (*First Apology* 67, tr. Dods and Reith, ANF 1, 1885).
2. **Laodicea witnesses the change; it did not make it.** A canon forbidding Christians to Judaise assumes Sunday was already the Christian day.
3. **The Sabbath was a sign and a shadow.** "Let no man therefore judge you... in respect of... the sabbath days: Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ" (Colossians 2:16–17). The Sabbath was the sign of the covenant with Israel (Exodus 31:13).
4. **The Orthodox Church has not abolished the Sabbath.** She keeps **Saturday as a day of rest from strict fasting** (except Holy Saturday), the day of commemorating the dead and the saints, and **Holy Saturday as the great Sabbath on which Christ rested in the tomb**. Sunday is the **eighth day**, the day of the new creation. **The Sabbath is fulfilled, not cancelled**: Christ is our rest (Hebrews 4:9–10, Matthew 11:28).

**Their best reply.** Ignatius is about Jewish Christians and may mean "living according to the Lord's life"; the Greek text is disputed. Colossians 2 concerns ceremonial feasts, not the Decalogue. And the Orthodox keep fasting rules no one finds in Scripture, so why not keep God's own day?

**The Orthodox reply to that.** Even if Ignatius were taken away, Justin's account is unambiguous, from Rome, about 155. And the Church fasts and feasts on the authority Christ gave her, the same authority that knew Sunday from the first generation.

**What it finally rests on.**

**Whether the moral law includes the seventh-day ceremony, or whether the Sabbath's purpose, rest in God, is fulfilled in Christ's resurrection.** Adventists answer from the Decalogue read alone; the Church answers from the Decalogue read in Christ, as the apostles and their disciples kept it.
Soul sleep and annihilation: what happen:
The Jehovah's Witnesses and the Seventh-day Adventists agree on one teaching the Church rejects: **the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, and the unrepentant are finally destroyed, not punished for ever.** The usual names are **soul sleep** and **conditional immortality**.

**Their case at its strongest.** In the Hebrew Bible, a "soul" (*nephesh*, נֶפֶשׁ) is a living being, not a ghost inside a body: "man became a living soul" (Genesis 2:7). "The dead know not any thing" (Ecclesiastes 9:5, KJV). Death is called "sleep" again and again (John 11:11, 1 Thessalonians 4:13). The immortal soul is a Greek idea from Plato, imported into the Church. Only God "hath immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16); eternal life is a gift given at the resurrection (Romans 6:23). As for hell, "the wages of sin is death", not endless torment: the wicked are burned up and cease to be (Malachi 4:1). An endless hell would make God crueller than any tyrant. Both bodies insist that **the hope of the Bible is resurrection, not escape of the soul**, and on that last point the Orthodox agree.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The soul survives the body's death.** "Fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul" (Matthew 10:28, KJV). To the thief: "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43). Paul desires "to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better" (Philippians 1:23): if death were unconsciousness until the end, it would not be better. The souls of the martyrs cry out under the altar (Revelation 6:9–10). At the Transfiguration, Moses speaks with Christ.
2. **"Sleep" describes the body** and the peace of the righteous, not the extinction of the person. Ecclesiastes speaks of what the dead know "under the sun".
3. **The soul's immortality is a gift, not a property.** The Fathers agree with the Witnesses and Adventists that only God is immortal by nature. **The soul is immortal by God's grace**, because He holds it in being. St John of Damascus says it of the angels: "It is immortal, not by nature but by grace" (*Exposition of the Orthodox Faith* 2.3, tr. S. D. F. Salmond, NPNF 2/9, 1899), and the Fathers say the same of the soul. So 1 Timothy 6:16, God "who only hath immortality", is not a contradiction.
4. **The Church prays for the dead and asks the saints to pray**, because they are alive in Christ: "he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him" (Luke 20:38). The intermediate state is taught in Theology Stage 4.
5. **Hell.** Christ speaks of "everlasting punishment" and "life eternal" in one sentence (Matthew 25:46). The Orthodox Fathers often describe hell not as God's cruelty but as the same love of God experienced as fire by those who refuse it (St Isaac the Syrian).

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** The Church teaches that the punishment is everlasting, as Christ says. A few Fathers (St Gregory of Nyssa) hoped for the restoration of all, and some modern Orthodox writers voice that hope as a prayer, while others warn that it was rejected by the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553). **What no Orthodox writer teaches is annihilation**, because God does not unmake what He made in His image.
