> "Now that which is that subtile essence (the root of all), in it all that exists has its self. It is the True. It is the Self, and thou, O Svetaketu, art it."

The Sanskrit ***tat tvam asi***, "thou art that", became one of the great sayings of Hinduism.

**Society: dharma and caste.** Classical Hinduism teaches a person's **dharma**, duty, according to his **varṇa** (the four classes: Brahmin priests, Kshatriya warriors, Vaishya merchants, Shudra labourers) and stage of life. Outside the varnas were those once called "untouchables", today **Dalits**. Caste discrimination is outlawed in India's constitution, and many Hindus reject it as a corruption, but it remains a social reality. **The Orthodox should speak of it with care**: Christians in India have their own caste divisions, and conversion movements among Dalits are politically sensitive.

**Their strongest case.** Hindus see their tradition as **the oldest living religion**, tolerant of many paths, rich in philosophy, and able to include all true insights. Many say: we do not need to reject Christ; we can honour Him as one of many great teachers or as a divine descent.

**The Orthodox starting point.** The Upanishads' search is real: they seek the One behind the many, and the Self behind the passing self. St Paul at Athens honoured such searching: God made men "That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us" (Acts 17:27, KJV). **The question is what is found.** The next lesson takes the most influential answer, that the Self and the Absolute are one.
Brahman and Atman: Shankara's Advaita Ve:
Of the schools that interpret the Upanishads (*Vedānta*, "the end of the Veda"), the most famous in the West is ***Advaita***, "non-duality". It is the philosophy most Westerners mean when they say Hindus believe "all is one".

**Who.** **Adi Shankara** (traditionally 788–820; many scholars place him in the eighth century) wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the *Gita* and the *Brahma Sutras*, and founded monastic orders that still exist.

**What he taught.**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Brahman*** | the one Reality: being, consciousness, bliss (*saccidānanda*); **without attributes** (*nirguṇa*) in its highest truth |
| ***Ātman*** | the true Self, pure consciousness, **identical with Brahman** |
| ***Māyā*** | the power by which the One appears as many; the world is not simply unreal, but not ultimately real either |
| ***Avidyā*** | ignorance: taking oneself to be the body, the mind, a separate individual |
| ***Mokṣa*** | liberation: the realisation, by knowledge (*jñāna*), that one is and always was Brahman |
| ***Īśvara*** | the personal Lord: real at the level of the world, but not the highest truth |

**Their strongest case.** Advaita is a **rigorous philosophy**, not a vague feeling. It argues that only what never changes is fully real; that consciousness is the one thing we cannot doubt; that the sense of a separate self is the root of fear and craving. Its teachers, such as **Ramana Maharshi** (1879–1950), asked one question, "Who am I?", and are revered for their peace. And it says it can include all religions: the personal God of devotion is a true but lower level of the same Reality.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Creator and creation are not one.** The Church confesses that God made the world **from nothing**, freely, by love (Theology Stage 2). The world is not an appearance of God but **a real other, which God loves**. "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31, KJV). **The difference between God and creature is not ignorance to be overcome but a gift to be crowned.**
2. **The person is not an illusion.** In Advaita the individual self is finally dissolved into the impersonal Self. In Orthodoxy the person, made in God's image, **is the crown of creation and lasts for ever**. Theosis is union with God **without confusion**: as iron in fire glows with fire and stays iron, the saint shines with God and remains himself (St Maximus, St John of Damascus).
3. **God is personal at the highest level, not the lowest.** For Shankara the personal Lord is a lower truth. For the Church, **the highest truth about God is personal**: Father, Son and Spirit, a communion of love. The apophatic Fathers (Theology Stage 2) also say God is beyond all names, but they never make Him less than personal.
4. **Love needs two.** If all is one Self, there is finally no one to love and no one to be loved. "God is love" (1 John 4:8) means otherness is not a fall but the condition of love.

**Their best reply.** The Orthodox "beyond all names" sounds like *nirguṇa Brahman*; the mystics of every faith, Eckhart included, speak of union without distinction; personal language is a concession to our weakness.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether otherness and personhood are illusion or gift.** Advaita says the many are finally the One; the Church says God made the many to share His life without ceasing to be themselves.
Vishnu, Shiva and bhakti: the devotional:
Most Hindus are not Advaita philosophers. They worship a personal God with love, in temples and homes, and their theologians have argued against Shankara for a thousand years. **To answer Hinduism only as "all is one" is to miss most Hindus.**

**The great traditions.**

| Tradition | God worshipped as supreme | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Vaishnavism** | **Vishnu**, and his descents, above all **Krishna** and **Rama** | the largest; includes ISKCON (the "Hare Krishna" movement, founded in New York in **1966** by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada) |
| **Shaivism** | **Shiva**, the ascetic Lord of destruction and grace | strong in South India and Kashmir |
| **Shaktism** | **the Goddess** (*Devī*, *Śakti*): Durga, Kali | Bengal, Assam |

**Bhakti**, "devotion", is the way of loving surrender to a personal God, sung by saint-poets across India from about the seventh century onward.

**The theologians.**

- **Ramanuja** (traditionally 1017–1137) taught ***Viśiṣṭādvaita***, "qualified non-duality": souls and the world are **real**, distinct from God, but inseparable from Him **as the body is from the soul**. God (Vishnu) is personal, full of good qualities; liberation is eternal loving service of Him, by **grace** given to those who surrender (*prapatti*).
- **Madhva** (1238–1317) taught ***Dvaita***, "duality": God, souls and matter are **eternally distinct**; God alone is independent; souls depend on Him wholly.
- **Chaitanya** (1486–1534), in Bengal, taught ecstatic love of Krishna through chanting the divine names, the root of ISKCON.

**Their strongest case.** Here Hinduism speaks of **a personal God of grace, love and self-giving**. Some bhakti theology speaks of God's grace in ways close to Christian language: one school of Ramanuja's followers compared the soul to a kitten carried by its mother, saved by God's grace alone. A devotee will say: **we already know the God of love; Krishna is our Christ.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Welcome what is true.** A personal God, grace, love, surrender, the singing of the divine name: **these are real goods, and the Orthodox should recognise them gladly** (Lesson 27 on the "seeds of the Word").
2. **But the God of bhakti is not the Creator from nothing.** For Ramanuja and Madhva, souls and matter are **eternal** alongside God; they depend on Him but were never created out of nothing. The biblical God is the source of all being, and the world began (Theology Stage 2).
3. **Many gods, or one?** Hindu theologians often say the many deities are forms of the One; popular worship honours many gods with images (*mūrti*). The Church honours icons as images of real persons, Christ and the saints, **not as dwellings of a deity** (Theology Stage 6).
4. **Krishna is not Christ.** The Christian claim is not that God shows love, but that **God became one particular man, in history, died and rose bodily** (Lesson 6). Krishna's stories belong to epic and legend; Christ's to the time of Pontius Pilate.

**Their best reply.** History is a Western obsession; what matters is the truth of the divine love, not the date. And Christians, too, have many saints and images.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether God's love is shown in many descents of myth, or given once in history, in flesh, on a cross.** On grace and devotion, bhakti and Orthodoxy are close; on creation and the Incarnation, they part.
The Bhagavad Gita: Krishna, duty and dev:
The ***Bhagavad Gītā***, "the Song of the Lord", is the most read Hindu scripture in the world. It is a short section of the epic *Mahābhārata*, probably composed between about the second century BC and the second century AD.

**The story.** On the battlefield of **Kurukshetra**, before a war between cousins, the warrior prince **Arjuna** loses heart at the thought of killing his kin. His charioteer, **Krishna**, who is God in human form, teaches him across eighteen chapters, and at the climax (chapter 11) reveals his cosmic form.

**The three ways (*yoga*s) of the Gita.**

| Way | Sanskrit | Teaching |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Action** | *karma-yoga* | do your duty without attachment to its fruits |
| **Knowledge** | *jñāna-yoga* | know the Self as eternal, beyond birth and death |
| **Devotion** | *bhakti-yoga* | love and surrender to the Lord; the highest way |

**The deathless Self.** Krishna tells Arjuna that the Self is never born and never dies, and passes from body to body as a man changes clothes (chapter 2).

**Devotion.** The Gita ends (chapter 18) with Krishna's call to abandon all duties and take refuge in him alone. In Sir Edwin Arnold's verse translation, *The Song Celestial* (1885), the line runs: "Rites and writ duties! Fly to Me alone!"

**Their strongest case.** The Gita joins **duty, wisdom and love** in one vision. Gandhi spoke of it as his mother. It teaches selfless action, freedom from greed, and surrender to a gracious God, and many Christians have admired it. Hindus often say its Krishna and the Gospels' Christ teach the same: love God, serve without selfishness.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **There is real moral wisdom here.** Acting without craving for reward, offering one's work to God, inner freedom amid duty: the Fathers teach these too (Theology Stage 10). **The Church does not need to deny them.**
2. **The answer to Arjuna's grief.** Krishna consoles Arjuna that killing is not real killing, because the Self cannot be slain. **The Gospel does not console death away; it defeats it.** "The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death" (1 Corinthians 15:26, KJV). Christ wept at Lazarus' tomb before He raised him. **Death is an enemy, not an illusion, and the body matters.**
3. **The changing of bodies.** The Gita's Self passes through many bodies; the Church teaches that each person is **one soul and one body** made together, and that the same body will rise (Lessons 7–10).
4. **Surrender to whom?** The Christian is also called to leave all and follow (Matthew 19:27–29). The question is **who calls**: a figure of epic poetry, or the One who was crucified under Pilate and rose.

**Their best reply.** The Gita's Krishna is as real to devotees as Christ to Christians; the warrior's battle is the soul's battle, read allegorically, as Gandhi read it; and the eternal Self is what Christians call the immortal soul.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the Self is eternal and passes through bodies, or whether each person is created, body and soul together, and saved by resurrection.** The ethics are often close; the picture of the person differs.
The avatars and the Incarnation:
When a Hindu hears that God became man in Jesus, he often says: "Of course. God has done so many times." The Hindu doctrine of the **avatar** is the nearest thing in any religion to the Incarnation, and the difference must be seen exactly.

**The doctrine.** *Avatāra* means "descent". Vishnu descends into the world in many forms to restore dharma. The traditional ten (*daśāvatāra*) include a fish (Matsya), a tortoise, a boar, the man-lion Narasimha, the dwarf Vamana, **Rama**, **Krishna**, often **the Buddha**, and **Kalki**, still to come at the end of this age. The *Gita* gives the classic statement. Krishna speaks (4.5–8, in Sir Edwin Arnold's translation, *The Song Celestial*, 1885):

> "Manifold the renewals of my birth
> Have been, Arjuna! and of thy births, too!
> But mine I know, and thine thou knowest not,
> O Slayer of thy Foes! Albeit I be
> Unborn, undying, indestructible,
> The Lord of all things living; not the less--
> By Maya, by my magic which I stamp
> On floating Nature-forms, the primal vast--
> I come, and go, and come. When Righteousness
> Declines, O Bharata! when Wickedness
> Is strong, I rise, from age to age, and take
> Visible shape, and move a man with men,
> Succouring the good, thrusting the evil back,
> And setting Virtue on her seat again."

**Their strongest case.** God's love does not leave the world alone; **He comes again and again** wherever He is needed. Why should He have come only once, in one small country? Many Hindus, from Ramakrishna onward, have honoured **Jesus as an avatar** alongside Krishna.

**The Orthodox answer: five differences.**

| | Avatar | The Incarnation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **How often** | "from age to age", many times | **once**, "once in the end of the world" (Hebrews 9:26) |
| **What is taken** | a "visible shape" by *māyā*; in some schools the body is not truly material | a **real human nature**, body and soul, from the Virgin (Theology Stage 3) |
| **For how long** | for the task; then withdrawn | **for ever**: the risen Christ keeps His body and ascends with it |
| **Death** | the avatar does not truly die as a victim | Christ **dies** and is buried |
| **Purpose** | to restore dharma, protect the good, destroy the wicked | to **unite God and man** in one person, destroy death and raise man to God |

**The key point.** Arnold's Krishna says he takes shape "By Maya, by my magic". **The Church insists the Word did not appear as a man; He became man.** That is why she fought the Docetists (Stage 2) who said His body only seemed real. An Incarnation that was only a visible shape would save nothing, because, as St Gregory the Theologian says, **"what has not been assumed has not been healed"** (Letter 101, paraphrased).

**Why "once".** The Incarnation is not a repeated visit but **a permanent union**: from the moment of the Annunciation, God is man for ever. **There is nothing to repeat**, as a marriage is not repeated each year.

**Their best reply.** The once-for-all claim is the arrogance of one culture; and the Gita too says Krishna is "unborn" yet born, as the Creed says the Son is eternal yet born in time.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether God's descent is a recurring appearance or a real and permanent union of God and man in one person.** If the second, Christ cannot be one avatar among many.
Karma and rebirth: the Hindu and Buddhis:
**Karma** and **rebirth** are the bedrock of the Indian religions: Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh. They are also the Eastern ideas that have most spread in the West: by some surveys, a substantial minority of people in Western countries say they believe in reincarnation.

**The teaching.**

| Term | Sanskrit (Pali) | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Karma** | *karman* (*kamma*) | "action": every intentional act leaves a seed that bears fruit |
| **Rebirth** | *punarjanma* | after death, a being is born again, in a higher or lower state, as human, animal, god or in a hell |
| **The round** | *saṃsāra* | "wandering on": the beginningless cycle of birth, death and rebirth |
| **Liberation** | *mokṣa* (*nibbāna*) | release from the cycle |

**How it differs between them.** For Hindus, **the Self (*ātman*) passes from body to body** (*Gita* 2). For Buddhists there is **no permanent Self** (Lesson 13), so what continues is a stream of causes, "as a flame lights another flame". For Jains, karma is a **fine matter** that clings to the soul. For most, **karma is not a judge's punishment but a natural law**, like cause and effect.

**Their strongest case.**

1. **It explains inequality.** Why is one child born healthy and rich, another sick and poor? Karma answers: not by chance or by an arbitrary God, but by their own past actions.
2. **It is just.** Everyone reaps what he sows; no one is condemned for ever for the sins of a single short life.
3. **It is hopeful.** No soul is lost for ever; each has countless lives to grow toward liberation.
4. **Memory.** Some children are reported to remember past lives; researchers such as Ian Stevenson (1918–2007) collected such cases.
5. **Some say the Bible teaches it.** "Elias, which was for to come" (Matthew 11:14), and the disciples' question, "who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" (John 9:2, KJV), and they claim Origen.

**Where Christians agree.** "Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Galatians 6:7). **Actions have consequences that shape the soul**: the Fathers teach this of the passions (Theology Stage 10).

**Where the disagreement lies.** The questions the Orthodox answer must face are: **Is a person one soul in one body, or a traveller through many? Is the end escape from the body, or the resurrection of the body? Is the world governed by an impersonal law of deeds, or by a personal God of justice and mercy?**

The next two lessons read the case and the answer side by side: first the oldest statement of karma and rebirth, from the *Brihadaranyaka Upanishad*; then St Gregory of Nyssa's argument against the passing of souls. Lesson 10 then gives the Orthodox answer in full.
Reading: the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad on:
The ***Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad***, "the Great Forest Teaching", is among the oldest Upanishads. In its fourth book, the sage **Yajnavalkya** teaches King Janaka of Videha what happens at death. This is one of the earliest statements of karma and rebirth anywhere. The translation is **F. Max Müller's**, *Sacred Books of the East*, volume 15 (1884); his footnote numbers are left out.

**Book 4, chapter 4, verses 3–6:**

> "And as a caterpillar, after having reached the end of a blade of grass, and after having made another approach (to another blade), draws itself together towards it, thus does this Self, after having thrown off this body and dispelled all ignorance, and after making another approach (to another body), draw himself together towards it."

> "Now as a man is like this or like that, according as he acts and according as he behaves, so will he be:--a man of good acts will become good, a man of bad acts, bad. He becomes pure by pure deeds, bad by bad deeds. 'And here they say that a person consists of desires. And as is his desire, so is his will; and as is his will, so is his deed; and whatever deed he does, that he will reap."

> "So much for the man who desires. But as to the man who does not desire, who, not desiring, freed from desires, is satisfied in his desires, or desires the Self only, his vital spirits do not depart elsewhere,--being Brahman, he goes to Brahman."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **The caterpillar.** The Self does not let go of one body until it has reached toward the next. **Death is a step from body to body**, not an end and not a judgment.
2. **"According as he acts... so will he be."** This is karma in its first form: not reward handed out by a judge, but **becoming what one does**. The chain runs **desire → will → deed → fruit**. A person "consists of desires".
3. **The way out is the end of desire.** The one "freed from desires", who "desires the Self only", does not go anywhere at death: "being Brahman, he goes to Brahman". **Liberation is not a better rebirth but no rebirth.**
4. **The body.** The next verse (4.4.7) compares the body left behind to "the slough of a snake" lying "dead and cast away" on an ant-hill. **The body is shed, not saved.**

**What a Hindu would want said.** That this is **not fatalism**. The text makes the person responsible: as you desire and will, so you become. It is a call to purify desire and know the true Self, and the goal is not endless wandering but rest in Brahman. Many Hindus would add that God's grace (in the bhakti schools) can lift a soul out of the round.

**What to notice for the answer.**

| Point | Brihadaranyaka 4.4 | To compare in the next reading |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The person** | a Self that moves between bodies | one human being, soul and body together |
| **The body** | a slough to be cast off | made with the soul, to be raised |
| **The law** | deed becomes fruit | ? |
| **The goal** | no more birth | ? |

St Gregory of Nyssa did not know the Upanishads. He knew the Greek doctrine of the passing of souls, from Pythagoras, Empedocles and Plato, which is remarkably similar. His answer is the next lesson.
Reading: St Gregory of Nyssa against the:
St Gregory of Nyssa (about 335–395), brother of St Basil the Great, wrote ***On the Making of Man*** about 379. In chapter 28 he answers those who taught that souls exist before bodies and pass from one body to another, the Greek form of rebirth, which some Christians influenced by Origen had flirted with. The translation is **H. A. Wilson's**, *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, second series, volume 5 (1893), on New Advent.

**Chapter 28, section 3:**

> "Those who stand by the former doctrine, and assert that the state of souls is prior to their life in the flesh, do not seem to me to be clear from the fabulous doctrines of the heathen which they hold on the subject of successive incorporation: for if one should search carefully, he will find that their doctrine is of necessity brought down to this. They tell us that one of their sages said that he, being one and the same person, was born a man, and afterwards assumed the form of a woman, and flew about with the birds, and grew as a bush, and obtained the life of an aquatic creature."

**Section 5:**

> "Strict inference points to the complete destruction of the soul; for that which has once fallen from the exalted state will be unable to halt at any measure of wickedness, but will pass by means of its relation with the passions from rational to irrational, and from the latter state will be transferred to the insensibility of plants."

**Chapter 29, section 1:**

> "But as man is one, the being consisting of soul and body, we are to suppose that the beginning of his existence is one, common to both parts, so that he should not be found to be antecedent and posterior to himself..."

**Reading it closely.**

1. **The sage** is the Greek philosopher **Empedocles** (fifth century BC), who said he had been a boy, a girl, a bush, a bird and a fish. **It is the same picture as the caterpillar in the Upanishad.**
2. **The argument from the passions.** If the soul is bound to bodies by its passions, and lower bodies are more passionate, then a soul that falls should keep falling, from man to beast to plant, down to nothing. **There is no inner reason it should ever climb back.** In the Upanishad, too, liberation needs something beyond karma itself: knowledge, or grace.
3. **"Man is one."** The heart of the answer is in chapter 29: soul and body **begin together**, in one act of God. A person is not a soul who visits a body. **This is why a soul cannot pass into another body: that body would make another person.**
4. **His tone.** In section 3 Gregory goes on to call such doctrines fit "for the chatter of frogs or jackdaws". That was the polemic of his age against Greek philosophers. **We keep the argument and leave the insult**, especially with Hindu or Buddhist friends.

**Side by side.**

| | Brihadaranyaka 4.4 | Gregory of Nyssa 28–29 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The person** | a Self moving between bodies | "man is one, the being consisting of soul and body" |
| **The body** | "the slough of a snake" | begun together with the soul, by God |
| **Where the passions lead** | to rebirth, until desire ends | downward, with no inner way back |
| **What saves** | knowledge of the Self, or grace | God, who made soul and body together and will raise them |

The next lesson gathers the Orthodox answer to karma and rebirth.
Karma and rebirth answered: one life, th:
After the two readings, here is the Orthodox answer in full.

**1. One life, then judgment.** "It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Hebrews 9:27, KJV). The Church teaches **one earthly life** for each person, after which the soul awaits the resurrection. Christ's parable of the rich man and Lazarus speaks of "a great gulf fixed" after death (Luke 16:26), not of return.

**2. One person, soul and body.** As Gregory of Nyssa argued, the soul and body **begin together** and belong together (Lesson 9). That is why the Christian hope is not escape from the body but **the resurrection of the same body**, transfigured: "It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption" (1 Corinthians 15:42). The risen Christ is the first fruits. **Rebirth gives a soul many bodies; resurrection gives a person his own body back, glorified.**

**3. The biblical texts.** "This is Elias" (Matthew 11:14) means John came "in the spirit and power of Elias" (Luke 1:17); John himself denied being Elijah (John 1:21), and Elijah never died, so could not be reborn. To the question "who did sin... that he was born blind?" Christ answered: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him" (John 9:3). **Christ rejects the very explanation karma gives.**

**4. Origen.** Origen (about 185–253) speculated that souls existed before bodies, but **he did not teach rebirth into animals**, and the pre-existence of souls was condemned by the Church, at Constantinople in 543 and in the anathemas associated with the Fifth Ecumenical Council (553).

**5. Justice and mercy.** Karma explains suffering by **past deeds the sufferer cannot remember**. The Church refuses to tell the sick child that he deserves his illness. **Suffering in Scripture is not always punishment**; it may be the place where God's works are shown, and God Himself entered it on the cross. And where karma is an impersonal law, the Gospel proclaims **mercy that breaks the chain**: the thief on the cross, with a lifetime of evil deeds, hears "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43).

**6. The hope.** Karma promises many chances; the Church promises **one Saviour**. The Orthodox do not say that one short life is a harsh test: **God's mercy, the prayers of the Church for the dead, and Christ's descent into Hades** speak of a love that seeks every person (Theology Stage 4).

**Pointing across.** Stage 11 reads **St Irenaeus**'s argument against transmigration from memory: if we had lived before, we would remember (*Against Heresies* 2.33). It is put there against Theosophy; it applies here as well.

**Their best reply.** One life is unjust to those who die as infants or never hear the Gospel; past-life memories are evidence; and the Hindu bhakti schools and Pure Land Buddhists (Lesson 15) also speak of grace that breaks karma.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** The Church entrusts infants and those who never heard to God's mercy, which is not bound by our knowledge (Lesson 27). Reports of past-life memories are contested and can be explained in other ways; the Fathers would add that not every spiritual experience comes from God. **And where Eastern faiths speak of grace, the Church rejoices to agree.**

**What it finally rests on.**

| Question | Karma and rebirth | Orthodoxy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is a person? | a Self or stream passing through bodies | one soul and body, made together |
| Why do we suffer? | past deeds | a fallen world, and sometimes God's hidden purpose |
| What breaks the chain? | knowledge, the end of desire, or grace | **Christ's death and resurrection** |
| The end? | no more birth | the resurrection of the body |
Yoga in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali:
In the West "yoga" usually means exercise and stretching. In Indian tradition it is something else: **a discipline of body and mind aimed at liberation**. A Christian should know the classical teaching before deciding what to say about the modern practice.

**The word.** *Yoga* comes from the root *yuj*, "to yoke" or "to join". In the *Gita* it means a spiritual way (Lesson 5). As a school of philosophy it is set out in the ***Yoga Sūtras* of Patanjali**, a short text of about 195 aphorisms, whose date is disputed (scholars propose dates between about the second century BC and the fifth century AD).

**The definition.** Sutra 1.2: ***yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ***, "yoga is the stilling (*nirodha*) of the fluctuations (*vṛtti*) of the mind (*citta*)". When the mind is still, the seer abides in his own nature.

**The eight limbs** (*aṣṭāṅga*, Sutra 2.29):

| Limb | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| *yama* | restraints: non-violence, truth, not stealing, chastity, non-greed |
| *niyama* | observances: purity, contentment, austerity, study, devotion to the Lord (*Īśvara*) |
| *āsana* | posture, a steady, comfortable seat for meditation |
| *prāṇāyāma* | control of the breath |
| *pratyāhāra* | withdrawal of the senses |
| *dhāraṇā* | concentration |
| *dhyāna* | meditation |
| *samādhi* | absorption |

**The goal: *kaivalya*, "isolation".** Classical Yoga rests on the **Samkhya** philosophy: there are two realities, **spirit** (*puruṣa*, pure consciousness) and **matter** (*prakṛti*, including the mind). Suffering comes from confusing them. **Liberation is the spirit's isolation from matter**, its standing alone. *Īśvara*, the Lord, is a special spirit untouched by karma, an object of devotion and an aid, but not the Creator.

**Their strongest case.** Yoga is **a precise science of attention**. It disciplines the body, quiets the passions, and produces peace that people in the restless modern world crave. Its ethical rules (*yama*, *niyama*) are admirable. Its practitioners say it needs no belief, only practice.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The goal is different.** Patanjali seeks the **isolation** of spirit from matter; the Church seeks the **union** of the whole person, body included, with God. The Orthodox ascetic stills the mind not to rest in himself but to turn the *nous* to Christ (Theology Stage 10).
2. **Technique and grace.** In Yoga, stillness is reached by method; for the Fathers, **methods of posture and breath serve prayer but never produce grace**. St Gregory Palamas defended the hesychasts' bodily posture, but as a help to attention, not as a way to God (Lesson 23).
3. **Powers.** Book 3 of the *Yoga Sutras* describes supernatural powers (*siddhi*) that arise from practice, and warns that they can become obstacles. **The Fathers warn more strongly: such experiences can come from the enemy**, and are never the goal.

**Pointing across.** Whether Orthodox Christians may practise yoga postures as exercise, and the occult side of modern yoga, are taken up in **Stage 11**.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether liberation is spirit freed from matter by discipline, or the whole person, body and soul, united with God by grace.**
The Buddha and the Four Noble Truths:
Buddhism began not with a revelation from God but with **a man who sat down under a tree and resolved not to rise until he understood suffering**.

**The life, as Buddhists tell it.** **Siddhārtha Gautama**, of the Shakya clan, was born at Lumbini (in modern Nepal), probably in the fifth century BC (traditional dates are 563–483 BC; many scholars now prefer about 480–400). Raised in luxury, he met an old man, a sick man, a corpse and a wandering ascetic, and left home at twenty-nine to seek release. After years of severe austerity he rejected it, and at **Bodh Gaya** he attained awakening (*bodhi*). He became **the Buddha**, "the awakened one", taught for forty-five years, and died at Kushinagar at eighty.

**The first sermon.** At the deer park near Varanasi he taught five former companions. *Rolling Forth the Wheel of Dhamma* (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 56.11, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, SuttaCentral, CC0):

> "Mendicants, these two extremes should not be cultivated by one gone forth. What two? Indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is low, crude, ordinary, ignoble, and pointless. And indulgence in self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and pointless. Avoiding these two extremes, the Realized One understood the middle way of practice, which gives vision and knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, awakening, and extinguishment."

> "Now this is the noble truth of suffering. Rebirth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; being coupled with the disliked is suffering; separation from the liked is suffering; not getting what you wish for is suffering. In brief, the five grasping aggregates are suffering."

**The Four Noble Truths.**

| Truth | Pali | In brief |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Suffering** | *dukkha* | life as we cling to it is unsatisfactory |
| **Its origin** | *samudaya* | **craving** (*taṇhā*): for pleasure, for existence, for non-existence |
| **Its cessation** | *nirodha* | craving can end: this is *nibbāna* |
| **The path** | *magga* | the **Noble Eightfold Path**: right view, purpose, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, immersion |

**The Three Jewels.** A Buddhist "takes refuge" in **the Buddha, the Dhamma (his teaching) and the Sangha (the community)**.

**Their strongest case.** The Buddha's teaching is **practical, honest and verifiable**: it begins with what everyone knows, suffering, and offers a path to test. It needs no belief in a creator, and the Buddha refused to answer speculative questions that did not lead to peace (*Majjhima Nikāya* 63). Its ethics of non-harm and compassion are admired worldwide.

**The Orthodox answer, in outline.** The Church agrees that **the world as fallen is full of suffering**, and that **disordered desire is its root in us**: the Fathers' teaching on the passions is close to the Buddha's on craving (Theology Stage 10). The middle way between indulgence and harsh austerity is also the Fathers' discretion (*diákrisis*). **The differences come at the third and fourth truths: what the end of suffering is, and who brings it.** The next lessons take them.
No-self (anatta) and the person:
The most radical Buddhist teaching, and the one that most separates it from Christianity and from Hinduism, is ***anattā***, **"not-self"**.

**The teaching.** A person is made of **five aggregates** (*khandha*): form (the body), feeling, perception, choices (mental formations), and consciousness. None of them is permanent; none is under our control; so none can be "my self". The Buddha's second sermon, *The Characteristic of Not-Self* (*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 22.59, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, CC0):

> "Mendicants, form is not-self. For if form were self, it wouldn't lead to affliction. And you could compel form: 'May my form be like this! May it not be like that!' But because form is not-self, it leads to affliction."

And of each aggregate: "But if it's impermanent, suffering, and perishable, is it fit to be regarded thus: 'This is mine, I am this, this is my self'?" "No, sir." So one should see every form, feeling and thought "with right understanding: 'This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.'"

**The three marks of existence.** All conditioned things are **impermanent** (*anicca*), **unsatisfactory** (*dukkha*) and **not-self** (*anattā*).

**What it is not.** Buddhists do not say "you do not exist". They say there is **no unchanging owner** behind the changing stream. A person is like a river or a flame: real as a process, but with no fixed core. Rebirth continues as a stream of causes, not as a soul moving house.

**Their strongest case.** Look within: you will find thoughts, feelings, sensations, but no "self" apart from them. **Clinging to a self is the root of fear, pride and greed**; letting go of it brings peace and compassion. Modern psychology and neuroscience, Buddhists say, confirm that the self is a construction of the brain.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Much is true about the false self.** The Fathers also teach that **the ego, the self-love (*philautía*) that grasps and fears, is the root of the passions**, and must die. St Paul: "I am crucified with Christ: neverthless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Galatians 2:20, KJV). **The Christian also lets go of the self that clings.**
2. **But "neverthless I live".** For the Church, the self that dies is the false, grasping ego; **the person, made in God's image, is not an illusion but God's gift, and is found, not lost, in God**. "He that loseth his life for my sake shall find it" (Matthew 10:39).
3. **The person is not a thing among the aggregates.** The Buddha rightly says the person is none of the five aggregates. Orthodox theology agrees: **the person (*hypóstasis*) is not any of his parts or properties**. But it concludes the opposite: not that there is no one, but that **the person is a mystery known in relationship, as God the Trinity is three persons in communion**. Personhood is the deepest thing, not the shallowest (Theology Stage 2).
4. **Who is freed?** If there is no self, who is liberated, who loves, who is compassionate? Buddhists have answered this subtly; the Orthodox press it gently.

**Their best reply.** The Christian "person" is the very clinging the Buddha diagnosed, given a theological name; and compassion is easier when the walls of the self are down.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the deepest truth about a human being is an empty stream or a person made for communion.** The Buddha found no self within; the Church says the self is found in the face of Another.
Nirvana and the Kingdom:
What is the end of the Buddhist path, and how does it compare with the Christian hope of the Kingdom of God?

**The word.** *Nibbāna* (Pali), *nirvāṇa* (Sanskrit), means **"blowing out"** or "extinguishment", as a fire goes out when its fuel is gone. **What is blown out is craving, hatred and delusion**, the three fires. With them the round of rebirth ends.

**What the Buddha said of it.** Very little in positive terms. He described it by what it is not. From the *Udāna* 8.3 (tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, CC0):

> "There is, mendicants, freedom from rebirth, freedom from what has been produced, made, and conditioned. If there were no freedom from rebirth, freedom from what has been produced, made, and conditioned, then you would find no escape here from rebirth, from what has been produced, made, and conditioned."

Asked whether the awakened one exists after death, does not exist, both, or neither, **the Buddha set the question aside** as not leading to peace (*Majjhima Nikāya* 63).

**Two moments.** Nirvana is reached **in this life** by the *arahant*, the one who has extinguished craving, who still lives in a body; at death comes ***parinibbāna***, complete nirvana, with nothing left to be reborn.

**Their strongest case.** Nirvana is **peace beyond all suffering**, the "unconditioned", not a heaven of pleasures that would itself be impermanent. It is honest about what words cannot say. It is reached through ethics, meditation and wisdom, and its fruits in this life are visible: calm, kindness and freedom from fear.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Agreement on the negative.** The Fathers also speak of God and the age to come by negation (apophatic theology, Theology Stage 2): "Eye hath not seen, nor ear heard" (1 Corinthians 2:9). Freedom from passion (*apátheia*) is a Christian goal too. **The Church can recognise in nirvana a real longing for what is beyond change and death.**
2. **But the Kingdom is a communion, not an extinction.** The Christian end is not the blowing out of desire but its **fulfilment in God**: not less love but perfect love; "then face to face" (1 Corinthians 13:12, KJV). **Desire is not the enemy; disordered desire is.** St Gregory of Nyssa teaches that in the age to come the soul will **go on for ever from glory to glory** (*epéktasis*), always desiring God more.
3. **A Kingdom with persons and bodies.** The Kingdom is a feast, a city, a marriage; it includes **the resurrection of the body and a new heaven and earth** (Revelation 21). "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death" (Revelation 21:4). Suffering ends not because the sufferer ceases, but because **death itself is destroyed**.
4. **Not unconditioned emptiness, but the uncreated God.** The Buddha found "the unconditioned" beyond all that is made. The Christian says: **beyond all that is made is not a state but the Maker**, the uncreated God, who gives Himself to be known.

**Their best reply.** A heaven of persons and bodies is still conditioned and so cannot be final; "glory to glory" is still craving; and the Buddha's silence is wiser than speculation.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the final good is the end of all desire and becoming, or the eternal fulfilment of persons in love.** It returns to the question of the last lesson: is the person an illusion to be seen through, or a gift to be perfected?
The Mahayana: the bodhisattva, emptiness:
Most Buddhists in the world are not Theravada Buddhists of the Pali Canon but followers of the ***Mahāyāna***, the "Great Vehicle", which spread to China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam from about the first century AD.

**The three great streams of Buddhism today.**

| Stream | Where | Scriptures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Theravāda**, "the teaching of the elders" | Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia | the **Pali Canon** |
| **Mahāyāna**, "the Great Vehicle" | China, Korea, Japan, Vietnam | the Mahayana sutras (*Lotus*, *Heart*, *Diamond*), in Chinese |
| **Vajrayāna**, "the Diamond Vehicle" | Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan | Tibetan canon (Lesson 17) |

**Three Mahayana ideas.**

1. **The bodhisattva.** In the Pali ideal, the *arahant* attains nirvana for himself. The Mahayana ideal is the ***bodhisattva***, "awakening being", who vows **to delay final nirvana until all beings are saved**. Compassion (*karuṇā*) becomes as important as wisdom.
2. **Emptiness.** ***Śūnyatā***, "emptiness", taught by **Nagarjuna** (about the 2nd century AD): nothing has independent, fixed existence (*svabhāva*); everything arises in dependence on everything else. Even nirvana and samsara are, finally, "not two". The *Heart Sutra*, chanted daily across East Asia, says "form is emptiness, emptiness is form" (paraphrased).
3. **Buddhas beyond history.** The Mahayana honours many Buddhas and bodhisattvas, in heavenly realms, who hear prayers: **Avalokiteshvara** (Guanyin, Kannon), the bodhisattva of compassion; and **Amitabha**, the Buddha of Infinite Light.

**Pure Land.** **Pure Land** Buddhism, the most popular form in China and Japan, teaches that Amitabha vowed to bring to his "Pure Land" all who call on his name in faith. In Japan **Hōnen** (1133–1212) and **Shinran** (1173–1263) taught that in this degenerate age no one can save himself by "self-power"; one must rely wholly on **"other-power"** (*tariki*), Amitabha's grace, by reciting ***Namu Amida Butsu***, "I take refuge in Amida Buddha".

**Their strongest case.** The Mahayana shows that Buddhism is not cold self-salvation: it is **a religion of compassion, prayer, grace and self-giving**, in which saints renounce their own rest for others. Pure Land in particular sounds, to Christians, astonishingly like salvation by grace through faith.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Rejoice in the likeness.** The bodhisattva's compassion and Shinran's grace are **real lights**, and the Orthodox should honour them (Lesson 27). The likeness has struck Protestant theologians too.
2. **But the compassion of the bodhisattva is not the cross.** The bodhisattva delays his own entry into rest; **Christ, God Himself, enters death and Hades** to raise others. Compassion in the Mahayana flows from seeing that beings are empty; in the Gospel it flows from **God's love for persons who are real**.
3. **Amitabha is not a historical saviour.** Shinran himself treated Amitabha's vow as a truth beyond history. **The Gospel's grace has a name, a date and a tomb.** Christ is not a symbol of compassion but the Compassionate One in person.
4. **Emptiness and creation.** That things do not exist "by themselves" the Church agrees: **nothing exists from itself except God**; all depends on Him. But dependence on God makes creatures **real and good**, not empty.

**Their best reply.** Historical facts are themselves empty and conditioned; what saves is the reality to which the name points; and Christians too say Christ's grace works beyond history.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether grace is a timeless principle that a name expresses, or the act of a Person in history, which the name proclaims.**
Zen: sitting, koans and seeing one's own:
**Zen** is the form of Buddhism best known in the West, and the hardest to answer, because it claims not to be a doctrine at all.

**The name and the history.** *Zen* is the Japanese form of the Chinese ***Chán***, from the Sanskrit *dhyāna*, "meditation". Tradition traces it to **Bodhidharma**, an Indian monk who came to China about the fifth or sixth century. The Chinese patriarch **Huineng** (638–713) taught **sudden awakening**. In Japan, **Dōgen** (1200–1253) founded the **Sōtō** school, centred on "just sitting" (*shikantaza*); the **Rinzai** school uses ***kōan***, paradoxical sayings ("What is the sound of one hand?") to break the grip of ordinary thought. In the twentieth century **D. T. Suzuki** (1870–1966) brought Zen to Western readers, and many Western Zen centres followed.

**What Zen teaches.**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Zazen*** | seated meditation, the heart of practice |
| ***Satori*** or ***kenshō*** | awakening; "seeing one's own nature" |
| **Buddha-nature** | the teaching that all beings already have the nature of a Buddha, to be realised |
| **"A special transmission outside the scriptures"** | a traditional saying: truth passed from mind to mind, not by words |

**Their strongest case.** Zen offers **direct experience** instead of doctrines: sit, breathe, see. It cuts through the endless talk of religion, and its art (gardens, ink painting, poetry) shows a simplicity and attention many Christians envy. Its teachers say it is compatible with any religion, and some Catholic monks have practised it.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Attention and silence are Orthodox too.** The hesychast tradition (Theology Stage 10) values stillness, watchfulness (*nēpsis*), and a prayer beyond words. **An Orthodox Christian can respect Zen's discipline.**
2. **But it is not "beyond doctrine".** Zen rests on doctrine: Buddha-nature, emptiness, no-self, the Mahayana sutras. **"Seeing one's own nature" assumes that one's nature is the Buddha-nature**, that awakening is discovering what one already is. The Christian path is not discovering an inner divinity but **turning to a God who is other, and receiving grace**.
3. **Experience needs discernment.** The Fathers taught that not every experience in prayer is from God, and that the mind emptied of all content is not yet filled with God. **St Gregory of Sinai and the Philokalia** warn against cultivating states for their own sake; the test is humility and love, and the end is Christ, not a state of mind.
4. **"Compatible with any religion."** For the Orthodox, prayer is not a neutral technique that can be fitted to any belief (Lesson 23). **How one prays shapes what one becomes.**

**Their best reply.** Buddha-nature is not a doctrine to believe but a pointer to test; words like "God" and "grace" are exactly the concepts Zen asks us to drop; and the Christian mystics, too, spoke of the "cloud of unknowing".

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the deepest thing in prayer is to see one's own nature or to meet Another.** Zen and Orthodoxy both value silence; for Zen the silence is the goal, for the Orthodox it is the place where the Word speaks.
Tibetan Buddhism and the Dalai Lama:
Tibetan Buddhism, the **Vajrayāna**, is the third great stream of Buddhism, and through the **Dalai Lama** the best-known face of Buddhism in the modern world.

**What it is.** Tibetan Buddhism joins Mahayana philosophy and monastic discipline with the **tantras**: esoteric texts and practices using visualisation of deities, sacred sounds (*mantras*, such as *Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ*), gestures, and ritual, under the guidance of a teacher, the ***lama***. The goal is Buddhahood for the sake of all beings, reached faster by these methods. There are four main schools: **Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug**.

**Reincarnate lamas.** Tibetans hold that some great teachers are reborn, by choice and compassion, and can be found as children: the ***tulku***. The best known is the **Dalai Lama**, head of the Gelug school and once the ruler of Tibet, regarded as an emanation of **Avalokiteshvara**, the bodhisattva of compassion.

**The fourteenth Dalai Lama.** **Tenzin Gyatso**, born on **6 July 1935**, was recognised as a child. After China's army entered Tibet (1950) and the uprising of **1959**, he fled to India, where he lives at **Dharamsala**. He received the **Nobel Peace Prize in 1989**. In **July 2025**, before his ninetieth birthday, he declared that the institution of the Dalai Lama will continue and that **his own trust alone will have authority to recognise his successor**; the Chinese government insists that it must approve any reincarnation. **As of November 2026 he is living, and the succession remains a political as well as a religious question.**

**Their strongest case.** Tibetan Buddhism has preserved a vast library of Indian Buddhist philosophy, a rigorous training in logic and meditation, and a culture of compassion under persecution. The Dalai Lama speaks of kindness, non-violence and dialogue with science, and is admired across religions.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Honour the suffering and the courage.** Tibetans have endured great suffering under occupation, and **the Church should never be indifferent to persecution of any people**.
2. **The tantras and spiritual powers.** Visualising and identifying with deities is central to Vajrayana practice. **The Orthodox Church warns against seeking contact with spiritual beings other than God, His angels and saints**, and holds that not every spirit is good (1 John 4:1). Some Orthodox writers (notably Fr Seraphim Rose) have been sharp here; others speak more cautiously. All agree that **these practices are not compatible with Orthodox prayer**.
3. **Reincarnation and the person.** The *tulku* teaching applies rebirth to particular individuals; the Orthodox answer is in Lessons 7–10.
4. **Compassion without a Creator.** The Dalai Lama often says one does not need religion, only kindness. **The Church honours kindness wherever it is found**, but believes love comes from God and is made perfect in communion with Him (1 John 4:7).

**Their best reply.** The deities of Vajrayana are understood by the trained as expressions of one's own mind, not external spirits; and Christianity has its own sacramental "technology" of icons, chant and incense.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the spiritual realm is a projection of mind to be used on the way to awakening, or a world of real persons, good and fallen, before the one God.**
The Buddha and Christ: the answer to Bud:
Having set out Buddhism, this lesson gathers the Orthodox answer in one place, by setting **the Buddha beside Christ**. Both are honoured; the comparison shows where the paths part.

**Where they are alike.** Both taught through parables and example; both called for the end of greed, hatred and self-centredness; both lived poor and taught compassion; both founded communities of monks and laity. **Orthodox Christians can admire the Buddha's moral seriousness** and should say so. Some Christians in history even honoured a saint, **Josaphat**, whose legend (the story of Barlaam and Josaphat, long attributed to St John of Damascus) is a Christianised life of the Buddha; that tale shows how deeply his story moved Christians.

**Where they differ.**

| | The Buddha | Christ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Who he claimed to be** | a man who awakened and showed the way | "the way, the truth, and the life" (John 14:6) |
| **Suffering** | to be escaped by ending craving | to be entered and overcome by love; He suffers |
| **God** | set aside as not leading to peace | revealed as Father |
| **The self** | not-self | the person, found in God |
| **Death** | the end of rebirth for the awakened | **defeated by resurrection** |
| **The goal** | nirvana, the end of becoming | the Kingdom, the resurrection of the body |
| **Salvation** | by one's own effort (Theravada) or grace beyond history (Pure Land) | by grace in history: the cross and the empty tomb |

**The heart of the answer.** The Buddha saw truly that **the world as we grasp it is full of suffering, and that craving is its root**. The Gospel agrees, and says more: **suffering is not only our own clinging but the fruit of a fall from communion with God**, and the remedy is not to stop desiring but to desire God. And **God did not wait for us to escape suffering; He came into it.** "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death" (Hebrews 2:14, KJV).

**The cross and the lotus.** The Buddha is shown seated in peace on a lotus, above the waters; Christ is shown on a cross, in the depths. **The Buddhist path rises out of suffering; the Christian God descends into it.** The Paschal troparion says why: He tramples down death by death.

**Their best reply.** The Buddha did not need to die for others because suffering is not a debt but a misunderstanding; a God who must suffer to save is a strange God; and Buddhists also have bodhisattvas who descend into hells to save beings.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** The bodhisattva's descent is a teaching about compassion; **Christ's descent into Hades is proclaimed as an event**, on Holy Saturday, by those who saw Him risen. And a God who comes down in love is not strange: it is what love does.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether suffering is finally a misunderstanding to be seen through, or a wound to be healed by a God who shares it**, and whether there is One who has come back from death to tell us.
Jainism: the soul, karma and non-violenc:
**Jainism** is one of the oldest religions of India, small in numbers but great in influence, above all through its teaching of **non-violence** (*ahiṃsā*), which shaped Gandhi.

**The founder, or rather the last teacher.** Jains honour twenty-four ***tīrthaṅkaras***, "ford-makers", who have crossed the river of rebirth and shown the way. The last, **Vardhamāna Mahāvīra** ("great hero"), traditionally lived 599–527 BC; many scholars place him a little later, as an older contemporary of the Buddha. Like the Buddha, he left a princely life, practised severe austerity, and attained omniscience (*kevala*). His followers are called **Jains**, from *jina*, "conqueror": one who has conquered the passions.

**What Jains hold.**

| Teaching | In brief |
| --- | --- |
| **No creator** | the universe is eternal and uncreated; there is no God who made or rules it |
| **Souls** | countless eternal souls (*jīva*), in humans, animals, plants, even earth and water |
| **Karma as matter** | karma is a fine substance that sticks to the soul through passion and action, weighing it down |
| **Liberation** | by burning off karma through austerity, the soul rises to the top of the universe and rests there in omniscient bliss for ever |
| **Ahiṃsā** | the first vow: harm no living being. Jain monks sweep the path before them, strain water, and some wear mouth cloths to avoid harming tiny creatures |
| **Many-sidedness** | *anekāntavāda*: reality is complex; every view sees only a part |

**Two orders.** The **Digambaras** ("sky-clad"), whose monks go naked, and the **Śvetāmbaras** ("white-clad"). Lay Jains are often merchants, famous for honesty, vegetarianism and charity.

**Their strongest case.** Jainism takes **every living being seriously** and the moral law with total seriousness. It asks no belief in a God who might seem arbitrary; it says liberation is each soul's own work. Its "many-sidedness" offers a philosophy of tolerance.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Reverence for life is Christian too.** "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast" (Proverbs 12:10). The Orthodox desert saints lived at peace with animals, and the Church's fasting is largely vegetarian. **Jain gentleness is a rebuke to the cruelty of modern life**, and the Orthodox should admit it.
2. **No Creator, no grace.** Without God, the soul must free itself by its own austerities. **The Church teaches that no one can save himself**; ascetic struggle is real but is a response to grace, not a substitute for it (Theology Stage 10).
3. **The soul freed from the world.** The Jain liberated soul leaves matter for ever and rests alone. **The Christian hope is not a soul freed from creation but creation itself freed**: "the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the glorious liberty of the children of God" (Romans 8:21, KJV).
4. **Many-sidedness.** That each view sees only a part is true of human views; it does not follow that **God cannot show the whole**, as He has in Christ.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether there is a Creator who gives grace, or only eternal souls freeing themselves by discipline.** Jain ethics often shame Christians; Jain metaphysics leaves the soul alone.
Sikhism: the one God and the Gurus:
**Sikhism** is the youngest of the great Indian religions and, of them all, **the closest to biblical monotheism**. It is often counted the fifth-largest religion in the world, with **about 25–30 million followers**, most in the Punjab and a large diaspora in Britain, Canada and the United States.

**The Gurus.** **Guru Nānak** (1469–1539), born in the Punjab, had a vision of God at about thirty and is remembered for declaring, in a saying tradition attributes to him, that there is neither Hindu nor Muslim, only God's children. He was followed by nine more Gurus, ending with **Guru Gobind Singh** (1666–1708), who in **1699** founded the **Khalsa**, the community of initiated Sikhs, with the **five Ks** (uncut hair, a comb, a steel bracelet, a short sword, and special undergarments). Before he died he declared that the Guru would henceforth be **the scripture itself**, the ***Guru Granth Sahib***, compiled first by Guru Arjan in **1604**.

**What Sikhs hold.**

| Teaching | In brief |
| --- | --- |
| **One God** | ***Ik Oṅkār***, "One Creator", without form, never incarnate, Truth by name, without fear or hatred, timeless, beyond birth, self-existent, known by the Guru's grace (the opening *Mūl Mantar*, paraphrased) |
| **The Name** | salvation through meditation on God's Name (*nām simran*) and His grace (*nadar*) |
| **Against empty ritual** | rejects idols, caste, pilgrimages and ascetic withdrawal |
| **Life in the world** | work honestly, share with others (the free kitchen, *langar*, in every gurdwara), remember God |
| **Rebirth** | souls pass through rebirth until united with God by grace |

**Their strongest case.** Sikhism takes **the best of Hindu devotion and Muslim monotheism** and rejects what divides them: caste, idolatry, priestcraft. It is a faith of equality (all eat together in the langar), courage, service and practical holiness. **Sikhs will say they worship the same one God Christians worship.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Much common ground.** One Creator, grace, the remembrance of God's Name, the rejection of idols, service of the poor: **the Orthodox can recognise these with warmth**. The Sikh *nām simran* resembles, on the surface, the Jesus Prayer.
2. **"Never incarnate."** The *Mūl Mantar* calls God beyond birth, and Sikh teaching explicitly denies that God takes flesh. **This is the precise point of difference with the Gospel**, as with Islam (Stage 9): "the Word was made flesh" (John 1:14).
3. **Grace without a Mediator.** In Sikhism grace comes through the Guru's word and God's free gift. **In the Gospel, grace has a face**: "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6).
4. **Rebirth.** Sikhism keeps the Indian picture of rebirth (Lesson 10).

**History honestly.** Sikhs have suffered greatly: at the hands of Mughal emperors (Guru Arjan and Guru Tegh Bahadur were executed), and in modern times, including the killings of thousands of Sikhs in Delhi in **1984**. **They also suffer in the West from being mistaken for others.** An Orthodox Christian should know their story and treat it with respect.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the one God remains always beyond flesh, or has become man.** Sikhism is closer to the Church than any other Indian faith on God's oneness and grace, and further than any on the Incarnation.
Taoism: the Way that cannot be named:
**Taoism** (or Daoism) is the native religious philosophy of China, the source of yin and yang, *tai chi* and much of what the West calls "Eastern wisdom".

**The text.** The ***Tao Te Ching*** (*Dàodéjīng*), "the Classic of the Way and its Power", is traditionally ascribed to **Laozi** (Lao-tzu), "the Old Master", said to be an older contemporary of Confucius in the sixth century BC. Most scholars think the text was compiled later, perhaps by the fourth century BC. Its eighty-one short chapters begin (tr. James Legge, *Sacred Books of the East* 39, 1891):

> "The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name. (Conceived of as) having no name, it is the Originator of heaven and earth; (conceived of as) having a name, it is the Mother of all things."

And chapter 25:

> "There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth. How still it was and formless, standing alone, and undergoing no change, reaching everywhere and in no danger (of being exhausted)! It may be regarded as the Mother of all things. I do not know its name, and I give it the designation of the Tao (the Way or Course)."

**Key ideas.**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Tao*** (道) | "the Way": the nameless source and order of all things |
| ***Te*** (德) | "virtue", power: the Way at work in a thing |
| ***Wu wei*** (無為) | "non-action": acting without forcing, as water yields and wears down stone |
| **Yin and yang** | the complementary forces whose balance makes the world |

**Philosophical and religious Taoism.** Beside the *Tao Te Ching* and the *Zhuangzi* stands **religious Taoism**, with temples, priests, gods, rituals for long life and immortality, and the Celestial Masters tradition, traced to Zhang Daoling in the second century AD.

**Their strongest case.** The Tao is beyond words; the sage lives simply, humbly, without grasping; force fails and gentleness wins. This is a wisdom of **humility and harmony** that the restless modern world needs.

**The Orthodox answer, and where Orthodox writers differ.**

1. **The sharper view.** Many Orthodox writers stress that the Tao is **impersonal**, a principle, not a Person who loves, speaks, judges and saves; *wu wei* is not the same as obedience to God; and religious Taoism's spirits and techniques for immortality are outside the Church.
2. **The more generous view.** **Hieromonk Damascene**, a disciple of Fr Seraphim Rose, in ***Christ the Eternal Tao*** (1999), argued that Laozi saw dimly the eternal **Logos**, and that the first verse of St John can be read in Chinese as "In the beginning was the Tao" (as Chinese Bible translations render it). He presents Christ as **the fulfilment of the Tao**: the nameless Way became a man with a name. Others have answered that this risks blurring the difference.

**Both views agree** that the *Tao Te Ching* has true insights, that the Way is not itself a revelation of the Trinity, and that **the Way, for the Christian, is a Person**: "I am the way" (John 14:6).

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the nameless Source is an impersonal order or the Father, who has spoken His Word.** The Tao "cannot be named"; the Christian says the Word has a name, and it is Jesus.
Confucius, the ancestors and the Orthodo:
**Confucianism** is less a religion of God than a way of ordering life: family, society, government and ritual. It has shaped China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam more than any other teaching.

**Confucius.** **Kong Fuzi** (551–479 BC), a teacher and minor official in the state of Lu, gathered disciples and taught the way of the ancient sages. His sayings were collected as the ***Analects***. He spoke little of gods or the afterlife; asked about serving spirits, he is reported to have said that we do not yet know how to serve men (*Analects* 11.12, paraphrased).

**His teaching.**

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| ***Rén*** (仁) | humaneness, benevolence: the root virtue |
| ***Lǐ*** (禮) | ritual propriety: the right forms of conduct, from bowing to sacrifice |
| ***Xiào*** (孝) | filial piety: honour and care for parents, living and dead |
| ***Jūnzǐ*** (君子) | "the gentleman", the person of moral cultivation |
| ***Tiān*** (天) | Heaven: the moral order above all; in early texts close to a personal Lord |

**The ancestors.** Chinese families honour their ancestors with tablets, offerings of food and incense, and visits to graves, above all at the Qingming festival. For many this is respect and remembrance; for some it includes the belief that the dead need offerings and can bless or harm.

**Their strongest case.** Confucius taught a humane, reasonable ethic that kept a civilisation together for two thousand years: **reverence, loyalty, learning, care for family and the dead**. Many Chinese say: this is our culture, not a rival religion, and a Christian should not be asked to despise his parents.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Much is good.** "Honour thy father and thy mother" is the fifth commandment. The Church, too, has ritual, reverence and care for the dead. **Confucian virtue is a schoolmaster** of the kind St Justin and St Clement saw in Greek philosophy (Lesson 27).
2. **The dead: prayer, not offerings.** The Orthodox Church remembers the dead constantly: memorial services (*panikhida*, *mnēmósyna*), boiled wheat (*kollyva*), prayers at the grave. **This gives the Chinese love of ancestors a Christian home**: we pray *for* the dead, and ask the saints to pray *for us*, but we do not feed or appease spirits.
3. **Heaven and the Father.** Confucius' "Heaven" can be a bridge to the God who made heaven, as St Paul spoke of the "unknown God" (Acts 17:23).

**History honestly.** In the **Chinese Rites controversy**, Roman Catholic missionaries argued for a century over whether Confucian and ancestral rites were idolatry; Rome forbade them in the early eighteenth century and relaxed the ban in 1939. **The Orthodox mission in China**, begun by the Russian Church in Beijing in the early eighteenth century, was small and slow. In **1900**, during the Boxer Rising, **222 Chinese Orthodox Christians were martyred**, among them the first Chinese Orthodox priest, **St Metrophanes (Mitrophan) Chang Tzi-tzung**; they are commemorated on **11 June** (on the Church calendar). The Chinese Orthodox Church today survives in small communities, under heavy restriction **as of November 2026**. The question of ancestor veneration among Africans is taken up in Stage 11.

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether reverence for parents and the dead is fulfilled in prayer within the communion of saints, or remains offering to spirits.** Confucianism asks little about God; the Church offers it the Father to whom the ancestors themselves are known.
Vlachos and Rose: Orthodox prayer and Ea:
Many Westerners say that the **Jesus Prayer is the Christian mantra**, and that hesychasm and Eastern meditation are the same thing in different words. Two modern Orthodox writers have answered this at length: **Metropolitan Hierotheos (Vlachos) of Nafpaktos** (born 1945) and **Fr Seraphim Rose** (1934–1982). Their books are in copyright, so this lesson paraphrases.

**The likeness that prompts the question.** Both traditions use a short prayer repeated many times; attention to the breath; a seated posture; the stilling of thoughts; a spiritual guide. **St Gregory Palamas** (Theology Stage 8) defended the hesychasts' bodily method, the head bowed, the breath slowed, the mind drawn into the heart, against Barlaam, who mocked them.

**Vlachos's case** (in his books on Orthodox and Eastern spirituality, paraphrased).

1. **The aim.** In Eastern meditation the aim is to quiet the mind and reach a state, often the experience of one's own deepest self or of an impersonal absolute. In hesychasm the aim is **the healing of the *nous***, the eye of the soul, darkened by sin, so that it may see **the uncreated light of God**, as the apostles did on Mount Tabor.
2. **Created and uncreated.** Eastern meditation, however deep, reaches **created** states of the soul. The Orthodox saint receives **uncreated grace, God's own energy**, which no technique can produce.
3. **Repentance.** Hesychasm begins in **repentance**, the Jesus Prayer is a cry for mercy ("have mercy on me"), and it lives inside the Church: the sacraments, obedience, the commandments. **Remove these and the "method" is not hesychasm.**
4. **Person to Person.** The Jesus Prayer names a Person and speaks to Him. It is not a sound with power in itself.

**Rose's case** (*Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*, 1975, paraphrased). Rose, an American convert who had studied Eastern religions before becoming Orthodox, warned that Eastern meditation brought into Christianity (in "Christian yoga", "Christian Zen" and similar movements of the 1960s and 1970s) **opens the soul to spiritual experiences that are not from God**. Their very calm and pleasantness, he argued, is the danger: the Fathers warn that the enemy can come as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14). **His book belongs mostly to Stage 11**; here its point is that the methods are not neutral.

**Where Orthodox writers differ.** Rose and Vlachos speak sharply. Others, while agreeing that the paths are different, speak more gently of the sincerity of Eastern seekers and stress what the Church shares with them (Lesson 27). **None treats the methods as interchangeable.**

**Their best reply.** Eastern teachers say: the Orthodox method is one of many techniques; "uncreated light" is your name for what we call the clear light of mind; and experience, not doctrine, settles the question.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** **Experience cannot test itself.** The Church tests experience by its fruits (humility, love, repentance) and by its agreement with Christ. The saints who saw the uncreated light were the humblest of men.

**What it finally rests on.**

| | Eastern meditation | Hesychasm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Goal** | a state of mind; the Self; emptiness | the healing of the *nous*, communion with Christ |
| **Means** | technique | repentance and grace; the method only serves |
| **What is reached** | created states | God's uncreated energy, as gift |
Vivekananda, 1893, and the East comes We:
Until the late nineteenth century, few Westerners knew the Eastern religions except from scholars. Then **Hindu and Buddhist teachers came West**, and they brought with them a powerful idea: that all religions are paths to the same goal.

**Chicago, 11 September 1893.** At the **World's Parliament of Religions**, held with the Columbian Exposition, a young Bengali monk, **Swami Vivekananda** (1863–1902), opened his speech with "Sisters and Brothers of America" and received a standing ovation. He presented Hinduism, in the form of **Advaita Vedanta**, as the mother of religions, tolerant of all, and taught that every religion is a path to the same truth. He founded the **Vedanta Society** in New York (1894) and the **Ramakrishna Mission** in India (1897).

**His teacher.** **Ramakrishna** (1836–1886), a Bengali mystic, was said to have practised Hindu, Muslim and Christian devotion in turn and found the same God in each. His followers summed up his teaching as "as many faiths, so many paths" (paraphrased).

**After Vivekananda.**

| Teacher | Movement | In the West |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Paramahansa Yogananda** (1893–1952) | Self-Realization Fellowship | *Autobiography of a Yogi* (1946); presented Jesus as a yogi |
| **D. T. Suzuki** (1870–1966) | Zen | books from the 1920s onward |
| **Maharishi Mahesh Yogi** (1918–2008) | Transcendental Meditation | the Beatles in 1968; marketed as a technique, not a religion |
| **A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada** (1896–1977) | ISKCON | New York, 1966 |
| **The 14th Dalai Lama** | Tibetan Buddhism | in exile from 1959 |
| **Thich Nhat Hanh** (1926–2022) | Vietnamese Zen | "engaged Buddhism", mindfulness |
| **Jon Kabat-Zinn** (born 1944) | Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (1979) | mindfulness in hospitals and schools, presented as secular |

**Their strongest case.** These teachers offered what many Westerners felt Christianity had lost: **practice instead of only belief, experience instead of dogma, stillness in a noisy world, and tolerance instead of exclusive claims**. Many Christians found them gentler than the churches they had left.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **A real hunger.** The Western turn East often came from **a Christianity that had forgotten its own contemplative tradition**. Fr Seraphim Rose and many converts went East first, and then found in Orthodoxy the prayer they had been seeking. **The answer to the hunger is not contempt for it but the Church's own hesychasm.**
2. **Advaita presented as neutral.** Vivekananda's "all paths are one" is **not neutral**: it is Advaita Vedanta, which places personal gods, Christ included, at a lower level of truth. **"All religions are true" here means "all religions are true insofar as they agree with Vedanta".**
3. **"Just a technique."** TM, mindfulness and yoga are often presented as religiously neutral. Some of their practices may be used simply for relaxation; but the Fathers' warning stands that **ways of prayer shape the soul**, and their roots are religious (Lesson 23; Stage 11).

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the East's offer of experience without dogma is itself a dogma**: the perennialist claim that all religions are one, taken up in the next two lessons.
\"All religions are one\": the perennial:
The most common modern answer to the variety of religions is that **they are all the same at heart**: different paths up one mountain, different names for one Reality. In its serious, philosophical form this is called the ***philosophia perennis***, the **perennial philosophy**, and it deserves its strongest statement.

**The name.** The phrase was used by the Renaissance scholar Agostino Steuco (1540) and by Leibniz, and made famous by **Aldous Huxley**'s anthology ***The Perennial Philosophy*** (1945). Huxley argued that the mystics of every faith teach the same thing: a divine Reality underlying the world, the same Reality in the depths of the soul, and the goal of life as union with it.

**The Traditionalists.** A more rigorous school, often called **Traditionalist**, includes **René Guénon** (1886–1951), a Frenchman who became a Sufi Muslim and died in Cairo; **Ananda Coomaraswamy** (1877–1947); and **Frithjof Schuon** (1907–1998), whose ***The Transcendent Unity of Religions*** (1948) argued that every revealed religion has an **outer, exoteric form**, its dogmas and laws, which differ and must be kept, and an **inner, esoteric core**, which is the same in all. **Huston Smith** (1919–2016), author of *The World's Religions*, popularised this view.

**The philosophical pluralist.** **John Hick** (1922–2012), a British philosopher of religion, argued in *An Interpretation of Religion* (1989) that the great religions are different human responses to **"the Real"**, which is beyond all our concepts, personal (God, Allah, Krishna) and impersonal (Brahman, nirvana, the Tao) alike. Each tradition transforms people from self-centredness to Reality-centredness, and since they do so **about equally well**, none can claim to be the only true one.

**The parable.** Pluralists often tell of **blind men and an elephant**: each feels one part and insists the elephant is like a rope, a pillar or a fan. The story is old. It appears in the Pali Canon (*Udāna* 6.4, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, CC0), where a king has the blind of the city shown an elephant, and they quarrel:

> "Saying, 'Such is an elephant, not such! Such is not an elephant, such is!' they punched each other with their fists."

**The strongest case, gathered.**

1. **The mystics agree.** Eckhart, Rumi, Shankara and Zen masters sound alike.
2. **Moral fruits are found in every religion**, and saints too.
3. **Which religion one holds depends mostly on where one is born.** Can God have hidden the truth from most of humanity?
4. **Humility.** Exclusive claims have led to persecution and war; pluralism is the humble, peaceful position.
5. **God is beyond all concepts**, as the Orthodox apophatic Fathers themselves say; so no religion's concepts can be final.

**Orthodox writers who were drawn to it.** The view has had Orthodox sympathisers: **Philip Sherrard** (1922–1995), co-translator of the *Philokalia* into English, wrote for the Traditionalist journal *Studies in Comparative Religion* and was sympathetic to Schuon's ideas while remaining Orthodox. **Most Orthodox writers have rejected it**, as the next lesson shows.
\"All religions are one\" answered:
The Orthodox answer to the perennialists does not deny that there is truth in other religions (Lesson 27). **It denies that they are all saying the same thing.**

**1. They contradict each other, on the main points.** The religions of this stage and the last do not differ only in outward forms; they differ on what the Real is and what salvation means.

| Question | Answers that cannot all be true |
| --- | --- |
| **Is the ultimate personal?** | yes (Christianity, Islam, bhakti, Sikhism); no (Advaita, Theravada, Taoism) |
| **Did Jesus die on the cross?** | yes (Christianity, history); no (the Qur'an) |
| **Is the self real?** | yes (Christianity, Hinduism); no (Buddhism) |
| **One life or many?** | one (Abrahamic faiths); many (Indian faiths) |
| **The end?** | resurrection of the body; absorption; extinction of craving; isolation of spirit |

**To say all are one, the perennialist must treat every one of these answers as merely "exoteric"**, which is to say that the believers of every religion are wrong about what their own religion teaches.

**2. The view from above is itself an exclusive claim.** Hick's "Real" beyond all concepts, Schuon's esoteric unity, Vivekananda's Vedanta: each is **a particular philosophy**, usually close to Advaita or Neoplatonism, which claims to know the truth that every religion only half sees. **It is as exclusive as any creed, but without admitting it.**

**3. The elephant needs a king.** In the Buddha's own parable, the point is that **the king can see the elephant and the blind cannot**.
