The Buddha told it to say that the other teachers were blind, not that all were right. **The parable works only if someone sees the whole.** The Christian claim is that someone does: "No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him" (John 1:18, KJV).

**4. Christ does not fit.** Every other teacher in these stages pointed to a way. **Christ said "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6)**, and the apostles preached "none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). One may reject this, but one cannot make Christ a perennialist without rewriting Him.

**5. Apophatic is not agnostic.** The Fathers say God is beyond all concepts; **they do not say He is unknown**. He has made Himself known in His energies and, above all, in His Son. The apophatic way leads **into** the Trinity, not beyond it (Theology Stage 2).

**6. On birthplace and humility.** That most people believe what they were taught is true of pluralists too, almost all of them modern Westerners. And **humility is not the refusal to say anything is true**, but the readiness to receive truth as a gift. The Church's answer to violence in religion is not relativism but **Christ's command to love enemies** (Stage 9, Lesson 21).

**Their best reply.** The contradictions are at the level of concepts, which all fall short; the mystics who go beyond concepts agree; and John 14:6 can be read of the eternal Word, present in every tradition, rather than of the historical Jesus alone.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** The Church does hold that the eternal Word is at work beyond her walls (next lesson). **But the eternal Word is the historical Jesus**: there is no other Logos behind Him. "The Word was made flesh."

**What it finally rests on.** **Whether the ultimate truth is a Reality beyond every revelation, of which the religions are partial views, or a Person who has revealed Himself and by whom all views are measured.**
Seeds of the Word, and what may be hoped:
If the religions are not all one, what is the truth in them, and what may Christians hope for their followers? Here **Orthodox writers answer differently**, and both views are given at their strongest.

**What the Fathers grant: the seeds of the Word.** Stage 1 read **St Justin Martyr**'s teaching on the *lógos spermatikós*, the "seed-bearing Word" (*Second Apology* 13): every true thing said by anyone belongs to Christians, because the Word sows seeds of truth in all. Here it is applied to the East. Justin's own reason, in *Second Apology* 10 (tr. Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF 1, 1885), is that Christ "was partially known even by Socrates (for He was and is the Word who is in every man...)". And he warns in the same place that those who knew only part of the Word "often contradicted themselves". **St Clement of Alexandria** (about 150–215) went further, calling Greek philosophy a "schoolmaster" to bring the Greeks to Christ, as the Law brought the Jews (*Stromata* 1.5, paraphrased). St Paul himself quoted pagan poets at Athens (Acts 17:28) and began from an altar "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD" (17:23).

**What this means and does not mean.** It means **every true and good thing in the Upanishads, the Buddha, the Gita, Laozi or Guru Nanak belongs to Christ**, because He is the Truth, and Christians may recognise it gladly. It does **not** mean that these religions are paths of salvation equal to the Church. **A seed is one thing, Justin says, and the thing itself is another.**

**What may be hoped for those outside the Church.** Here the disagreement among Orthodox writers is real.

- **The stricter view.** Many Fathers and modern saints insist: **outside the Church there is no salvation**, because salvation is union with Christ in His Body. St Ignatius Brianchaninov (1807–1867) taught this sharply in the nineteenth century, and many Athonite and other writers hold it today. On this view, **charity means telling others the truth plainly**, because their salvation is at stake, and false comfort is cruelty.
- **The more hopeful view.** Others, without denying that the Church is the only ark, stress that **God "will have all men to be saved"** (1 Timothy 2:4), that the Gentiles "shew the work of the law written in their hearts" (Romans 2:15), and that **God is not bound by His sacraments, though we are**. Metropolitan Kallistos Ware put it, in paraphrase: we know where the Church is, but we cannot be sure where it is not. On this view, the faithful pagan or Buddhist is left to the mercy of God, who judges each by the light he was given.
- **What both agree.** The Church is Christ's Body and the fullness of truth; **no one is saved except through Christ**, whether or not they knew His name on earth; the Church must preach Him to all; and judgment belongs to God. **Neither view permits contempt** for anyone, nor the claim that it makes no difference what one believes.

**Their best reply** (the perennialist's). If seeds of the Word are everywhere, why not call the other religions true paths? And if God may save those outside, why must the Church be the only way?

**The Orthodox reply to that.** Because a seed is not the harvest, and a schoolmaster is not the Father. **God may save whom He wills by ways known to Him; He has told us the way He has given us**, and it has a name.

**What it finally rests on.** **That all truth is Christ's, and all salvation is through Christ**: the first lets the Church honour every good thing in the East; the second keeps her from calling it the same.
Looking back: the religions of India and:
This stage has answered the faiths that begin not with a prophet sent by God but with **the self, suffering and liberation**.

**The answers, in one table.**

| Tradition | Its insight the Church can honour | Where it parts from the Church | The root question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Advaita Vedanta** | the One behind the many; the false self | the world and the person as finally unreal | Is otherness illusion or gift? |
| **Bhakti** (Ramanuja, Madhva) | a personal God of love and grace | souls and matter eternal; avatars, not Incarnation | Myth or history? |
| **The Gita** | duty without craving; surrender to God | the Self passing through bodies | One person or a traveller? |
| **Karma and rebirth** | deeds shape the soul | many lives; the body shed | Resurrection or rebirth? |
| **Yoga** | discipline of attention | isolation of spirit from matter | Isolation or union? |
| **Theravada** | suffering and craving diagnosed | no-self; extinction of craving | Empty stream or person? |
| **Mahayana, Pure Land** | compassion, grace | grace beyond history | A principle or a Person? |
| **Zen** | silence, attention | seeing one's own nature | Self or Another? |
| **Tibetan** | compassion under persecution | tantric deities, tulkus | What are the spirits? |
| **Jainism** | reverence for all life | no Creator; self-liberation | Is there grace? |
| **Sikhism** | one God, grace, the Name | God never incarnate | Has God become man? |
| **Taoism** | humility, the nameless Way | an impersonal Way | Is the Way a Person? |
| **Confucianism** | reverence, family, the dead | offerings to spirits | Prayer for the dead or to them? |

**What they share, and what the Church answers.**

1. **The person.** Again and again the question is **whether the human person is real and lasting, body and soul**, or a passing appearance. The Church's answer comes from the Trinity (God is personal) and the Incarnation (God took a body): **the person is God's gift, and will rise.**
2. **History.** The Eastern faiths speak in cycles and myths; the Gospel speaks of **one event**: "crucified also for us under Pontius Pilate". That is why Christ cannot be one avatar or one bodhisattva among many.
3. **Grace.** Where the East speaks of grace (bhakti, Pure Land, Sikhism), the Church rejoices; she adds that **grace has a face**.
4. **Prayer is not neutral.** Hesychasm and Eastern meditation look alike and aim differently (Lesson 23).
5. **All religions are not one.** They contradict on the main points; the perennialist view is itself a particular philosophy; **the elephant needs a king who sees**.

**Where Orthodox writers differ**, and both are honoured: on how generously to read the *Tao*, on how sharply to warn about Eastern practice, and on **what may be hoped for those outside the Church**. All agree: **the seeds of the Word are Christ's, and the harvest is Christ.**

**What to carry forward.**

- **Learn their question before answering.** A Buddhist is not asking which prophet God sent.
- **Honour what is true and good**, by name.
- **Tell the history** of the persecuted honestly: Tibetans, Sikhs, Dalits, and the Chinese martyrs of 1900.
- **Offer the Church's own stillness**, not only arguments.

**Next.** Stage 11 turns to the old gods and the new: African traditional religion and the ancestors, paganism, the occult, Theosophy and the New Age, and Fr Seraphim Rose on "the religion of the future".
Context: the old gods, the occult and th:
The religions of Stages 3 to 10 have scriptures, councils, schools and centuries of argument. This stage turns to something older and something newer: **the gods, spirits and ancestors that people turned to before the Gospel came, and the movements that went back to them after Christianity.**

**Why they belong together.** The ancestors honoured in a Shona village, the gods of a modern Wiccan circle, the spirits a Victorian medium called up and the "higher self" of a New Age workshop seem to share little. What they do share is a **picture of the spiritual world as many powers, reached by technique, offering help, healing, knowledge of the future or a higher state**. Against that picture the Church sets one God, the Creator, known as Father, Son and Holy Spirit, reached by repentance and grace. **The question each lesson asks is: who or what is really being addressed?**

**The map of the stage.**

| Part | Lessons | What is answered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The frame** | idolatry and the demons | how Scripture and the Fathers read the gods |
| **African traditional religion** | the high God, the ancestors, the healers and diviners, the rites of the dead | the faith of Master Roachi's own region, with the Shona and Nguni terms |
| **Paganism revived** | ancient and modern paganism, Wicca | the return of the old gods in Europe and America |
| **The occult** | spiritualism, astrology and divination | contact with spirits; knowing the future |
| **Esoteric movements** | Theosophy, Steiner, the New Age, Fr Seraphim Rose | the modern "wisdom" religions |
| **Freemasonry** | what it is, and the Church's rulings | a fraternity that the Orthodox churches have judged a rival religion |

**What is pointed across, not taught again.** Hinduism, Buddhism, karma and rebirth in their Indian forms, yoga, and the claim that "all religions are one" were answered in **Stage 10**; this stage meets them only in their Western, Theosophical and New Age dress. The Orthodox teaching on angels and demons is in **Theology Stage 2** ("The invisible creation"), the communion of saints and the departed in **Theology Stage 4**, and the African missions of the Patriarchate of Alexandria in **Theology Stage 12** ("Orthodoxy in Africa").

**Two cautions kept throughout.**

1. **Honesty about Christian history.** Missionaries in Africa often condemned everything African together, the drum with the sacrifice, and called that the Gospel. Europe burnt and hanged people as witches. The lessons say so where it belongs.
2. **The people are not the error.** A grandmother who goes to the *n'anga* because her grandson is ill, or a teenager drawn to Wicca because it reveres nature, is not an enemy. **The Fathers wrote against the demons and against idolatry, and for the people held by them.**

**The stage's one sentence.** **Every power that is not God is either a creature to be loved and governed, or a spirit to be tested; only God is to be worshipped.**
Idolatry and the demons: how Scripture a:
Before the Church answers any particular god or spirit, she has a way of reading all of them. It comes from the Septuagint and St Paul.

**The texts.** The Greek Psalter reads Psalm 95:5 (96:5 in the Hebrew numbering): "For all the gods of the heathen are devils: but the Lord made the heavens" (Brenton's Septuagint, 1844). The Hebrew has *elilim*, "nothings" or "idols"; the Greek translators wrote *daimónia* (δαιμόνια). St Paul, writing about meat offered in the temples of Corinth, keeps both sides: an idol is nothing in itself, "But I say, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, and not to God: and I would not that ye should have fellowship with devils" (1 Corinthians 10:20, KJV).

**Two claims held together.**

| Claim | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **The idol is nothing** | there is no Zeus, no god of the river who is a second god beside the Creator; the statue is wood and stone |
| **The worship is not nothing** | spiritual beings who have turned from God receive worship meant for Him, and work through it |

**The word "idolatry".** *Eidōlolatreía* (εἰδωλολατρεία) means "service of an image". In the Fathers it means **giving to anything created the worship (*latreía*, λατρεία) that belongs to God alone**. The Seventh Ecumenical Council (787) drew the line that matters here: icons and saints receive honour and veneration (*proskýnēsis*, προσκύνησις); **worship belongs to God only** (Theology Stage 8).

**How the Fathers used this.** St Justin Martyr (about 100–165) and St Athanasius (about 296–373), in *Against the Heathen*, argued two things at once: the pagan myths are human inventions, and the demons used them to draw people away from the true God. They did not think the pagans stupid. Justin held that the **Word (*Lógos*) had sown seeds of truth** in the best of the Greeks, and Athanasius argued from the order of the world to its one Maker. **The answer to the gods is not contempt for those who served them but the announcement of the God they were looking for**, as St Paul did at the Areopagus (Acts 17; Stage 1).

**The other side's best case.** A thoughtful polytheist or practitioner of a traditional religion will say: the spirits are real and helpful, they answer, they heal; why call them devils? **That is the hinge of this whole stage.** The Orthodox answer is not that nothing happens. It is that spirits are known by their fruit and by what they ask: **a spirit that receives sacrifice and worship, or binds people by fear, is not of God**, however helpful it seems at first (2 Corinthians 11:14).

**What it rests on.** **Whether there is one Creator who alone is to be worshipped, and whether the spiritual beings below Him can be good and still accept worship.** Christians answer the first yes and the second no.

**The practical rule.** For a Christian the line is not between "natural" and "spiritual" but between **honour and worship**. Honour to the dead, to elders, to the land and to one's people is right. Worship, sacrifice and prayer for power go to God alone.
African traditional religion: Mwari, uNk:
African traditional religion is not one religion with one book. It is many peoples' ways of living with God, the spirits and the dead, handed down by custom. This lesson takes the Shona of Zimbabwe and the Nguni peoples (Zulu, Ndebele, Xhosa) as the examples nearest Master Roachi.

**Their own case, at its strongest.** Its best interpreters, many of them African Christians, insist on what outsiders missed. The Kenyan theologian **John Mbiti** (1931–2019), in *African Religions and Philosophy* (1969), argued that **Africans knew God before the missionaries came**, and that religion in Africa is not a separate compartment but runs through birth, marriage, farming, sickness and death. A traditional practitioner would say: we believe in one Creator, we honour our forebears, we keep the land in balance, and our healers know the plants and the spirits.

**The high God.**

| People | Name | Meaning and role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Shona** | ***Mwari*** | the Creator; also called *Musikavanhu* ("maker of people") and *Nyadenga* ("of the sky"); honoured at shrines in the Matopo hills, such as Njelele |
| **Zulu** | ***uNkulunkulu*** | "the great-great one", the first, who brought people out from the reeds |
| **Xhosa** | ***Qamata*** (also *uThixo* in Christian use) | the Creator |

**God far off, spirits near.** In much traditional belief, the high God is **great but distant**. Ordinary needs are taken to the ancestors and spirits, who are closer and more concerned with the family. People rarely pray to *Mwari* directly except in crisis, drought or through the shrine's mediums. This pattern, a remote Creator and near intermediaries, is common across Africa.

**What the Church affirms.** The Church does not say Africans worshipped nothing. Missionaries themselves adopted *Mwari* and *uNkulunkulu* as the name of God in the Shona and Zulu Bibles. That is a judgement that **the Creator they named is the God of Abraham**, known dimly, as St Paul said of the Athenians: "Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you" (Acts 17:23, KJV).

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **God is not distant.** The Creator who seemed far has come near in the flesh: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:14). The deepest change the Gospel brings to African religion is not a new list of rules but **God Himself as the near one**, Father to each believer.
2. **The intermediaries are reordered.** If God is near in Christ, no spirit stands between the believer and God as a gatekeeper. The saints pray with us, but **the way to the Father is through the Son, in the Spirit**.
3. **What is good is kept.** Reverence for elders, the sense of community (*ubuntu*, "a person is a person through other persons"), hospitality and respect for creation are not pagan; they are natural goods the Gospel fulfils.

**Their best reply.** Some African scholars answer that Christianity came with colonial rule and treated African religion as superstition while keeping European customs as if they were the Gospel. **That charge is often true of the history**, and an Orthodox answer should say so.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the Creator has made Himself known personally in Christ**, so that the distance between God and people, which the ancestors filled, has been closed by God Himself.
The ancestors: vadzimu, amadlozi and the:
At the centre of traditional religion in southern Africa are not the gods but **the family's own dead**. This is the point where African Christians most often feel torn, so it needs to be learnt exactly.

**The terms.**

| Term | People | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***mudzimu*** (plural ***vadzimu***) | Shona | a family ancestor spirit, usually a grandparent or forebear who died well, was buried rightly and has been brought home |
| ***mhondoro*** | Shona | "lion" spirits: ancestors of chiefs and founders, guardians of a territory, speaking through a medium |
| ***svikiro*** | Shona | the spirit medium through whom an ancestor speaks |
| ***idlozi*** (plural ***amadlozi***) | Zulu, Ndebele | the ancestors, also called *amathongo* |
| **"the living dead"** | Mbiti's phrase | the recently dead who are still remembered by name and remain part of the family |

**Their case at its strongest.** The ancestors are **not gods**, a traditionalist will say, and are not worshipped as God is. They are elders who have gone ahead, closer to God, who still care for their descendants. They protect the family, are told of births and marriages, receive beer, snuff or an animal at ceremonies, and are angry if forgotten or if the family breaks its customs. Sickness or misfortune may mean an ancestor is displeased, and a diviner can find out why. **The family is one across death.** Seen this way, honouring the ancestors is family loyalty, and a Christian who stops is abandoning his own people.

**Why this matters for an Orthodox answer.** Much of this is close to Christian instinct. The Church too says **the dead are alive in God**, that the family is not broken by death, that we must remember our dead by name. African Christians who become Orthodox often notice at once that the Church **prays for the dead**, keeps the third, ninth and fortieth days and the anniversaries, and has saints who intercede. Protestant missions, which had dropped prayer for the dead, gave Africans nothing in this place; that gap is one reason ancestral rites survived beside church-going.

**Where the line falls.** The Orthodox answer (taught in the next lessons) distinguishes:

| Practice | The Church's judgement |
| --- | --- |
| remembering the dead by name, honouring their graves, telling their stories | **good**, and fulfilled in the memorial services |
| praying *for* the dead | **commanded** by the Church's Tradition |
| asking the departed saints to pray for us | **right**, for those the Church glorifies |
| sacrifice and offerings *to* the dead to win protection or avert anger | **not permitted**: sacrifice belongs to God alone, and Christ's sacrifice is final |
| consulting the dead through a medium or diviner | **forbidden** (Deuteronomy 18:11) |
| fearing that an unappeased ancestor will punish the living | **answered** by the Gospel: the dead are in God's hands, not ours to appease |

**What it rests on.** **Whether the dead are in God's keeping, to be prayed for, or in a world of spirits to be appeased.** Christianity says the first: "he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him" (Luke 20:38, KJV).
The n'anga, the sangoma and the inyanga::
Between the living and the spirits stand specialists. To answer traditional religion well, one must know what each does and not lump them together.

**The specialists.**

| Name | People | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***n'anga*** | Shona | traditional healer and diviner: diagnoses illness and misfortune, often by consulting spirits, and prescribes herbs, rituals or charms |
| ***isangoma*** (*sangoma*) | Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi | diviner called by the ancestors, usually through illness or dreams, and trained in a long initiation (*ukuthwasa*) |
| ***inyanga*** | Zulu | herbalist: knowledge of medicines, less centred on spirit possession |
| ***muroyi*** / ***umthakathi*** | Shona / Zulu | **witch**: one who harms others by secret spiritual power; the healer's opponent |

**Their case at its strongest.** Defenders say: the healer is a doctor of body and community. Illness in Africa is not only a germ; it is also a question of **why** it struck this person now. The *n'anga* or *sangoma* answers that question, restores broken relationships, and uses a pharmacopoeia some of which modern medicine has studied. In Zimbabwe the Zimbabwe National Traditional Healers Association (ZINATHA) was founded in 1980, and traditional practitioners are recognised in law in both Zimbabwe and South Africa. **Many people consult them and also go to church, and see no conflict.**

**The Orthodox answer: three things kept apart.**

1. **Herbs and practical knowledge are creation.** A plant that heals is God's gift. The Church has never forbidden medicine; Sirach 38:4 (Septuagint) says the Lord created medicines out of the earth. Knowledge of plants is not the problem.
2. **Divination and spirit-consultation are forbidden.** Scripture: "There shall not be found among you any one... that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch. Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer" (Deuteronomy 18:10–11, KJV). The canons agree: **Canon 61 of the Council in Trullo (692)** puts those who go to soothsayers and fortune-tellers, and makers of amulets, under six years' penance (tr. Percival, NPNF 2/14, 1900). The reason is not that nothing happens; it is that **seeking hidden knowledge or power from spirits other than God puts the soul in their hands.**
3. **Witchcraft fear is answered by Christ, not by counter-magic.** The *n'anga* fights the witch with stronger charms. The Church says the believer under Christ is not at the mercy of curses: Christ has "spoiled principalities and powers" (Colossians 2:15). The remedy is prayer, the sacraments, holy water and the priest's blessing, not a stronger spirit.

**History told honestly.** Witchcraft accusations do great harm. In parts of Africa today, elderly women, albino people and children have been accused, driven out or killed. And **Christian Europe** hanged and burnt tens of thousands as witches between about 1450 and 1750, while some churches in Africa today run "deliverance" campaigns that name children as witches. **Fear of witches is not cured by a church that feeds it.** The Orthodox answer is to remove fear, not to redirect it.

**What it rests on.** **Whether hidden spiritual power may be sought from anyone but God.** The Church says no, and adds that the one who belongs to Christ need not fear the witch.
The rites of the dead: kurova guva, ngoz:
The hardest pastoral questions in southern Africa come at funerals. Families gather, and the Christian is asked to take part in rites that may include more than mourning.

**The rites.**

| Rite | People | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ***kurova guva*** ("beating the grave") | Shona | about a year after death, a ceremony with beer and often an animal, at which the spirit of the dead is **brought home** to become a *mudzimu* who protects the family |
| ***bira*** | Shona | an all-night gathering with *mbira* music and dancing, in which ancestors are invited to possess a medium |
| ***ukubuyisa*** ("bringing back") | Zulu | the parallel rite of bringing the spirit of the dead home, usually with the slaughter of a beast |
| ***ngozi*** | Shona | the avenging spirit of someone murdered or badly wronged, believed to bring death and misfortune on the offender's family until appeased, sometimes by payment of cattle or even a girl given in marriage |

**Their case.** Without these rites, the traditionalist says, the dead wander, the family loses its protector, and misfortune follows. *Kurova guva* is an act of love and duty; refusing it shames the dead and the living. ***Ngozi*** expresses a real truth: **a wrong done is not forgotten until it is put right.**

**How Christians have answered: three positions.**

| Position | Who has held it | Its argument |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A clean break** | many Protestant and Pentecostal churches, and some Orthodox and Catholic clergy | the rites involve sacrifice to and consultation of spirits; a Christian cannot divide himself; St Paul forbids "the table of devils" (1 Corinthians 10:21) |
| **Christianise the rite** | the Catholic Church in Zimbabwe, which developed a Christian memorial rite (*kugadzira*) to take the place of *kurova guva*; some Anglicans | keep the family's gathering and the remembering, replace the offering to the spirit with a Mass for the dead |
| **Distinguish within it** | many Orthodox clergy in Africa | attend the gathering and grieve with the family; take no part in any offering, invocation or medium; offer the Church's own memorial in its place |

**Orthodox writers and clergy answer this differently.** Some, stressing *akriveia* (strictness, Stage 1), say the faithful should not attend at all, because presence is read as consent. Others, stressing *oikonomia* (pastoral economy), say the Christian should be present as a son or daughter, refuse the ritual acts openly, and let the family see the difference. **Both agree that no Orthodox Christian may sacrifice to or consult the dead.** They differ on presence.

**The Orthodox gift here.** The Church already has what the family is looking for: the **memorial service** (*mnēmósynon*, μνημόσυνον, Russian *panikhida*) on the third, ninth and fortieth days and at one year, with ***kollyva*** (boiled wheat, the seed that dies and rises, John 12:24). **The one-year *kurova guva* falls at the same time as the Church's one-year memorial.** A priest can offer the family a rite that remembers the dead, gathers the clan, and commends the soul to God.

**On *ngozi*.** The Church agrees a murder must be repented of and made right, with restitution where possible. But the remedy is confession and justice, not paying an angry spirit, and **never the giving of a girl as compensation**, which wrongs a living person to appease a dead one.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the rite addresses God about the dead, or the dead as powers.**
The Orthodox answer on the ancestors: th:
The last two lessons named what the Church refuses. This one gives what she offers, because the strongest answer to ancestral religion is not a prohibition but **a better place for the dead**.

**The communion of saints.** The Creed confesses the Church as one, holy, catholic and apostolic. The Church is one body across death: the living and the departed in Christ are one family. **Death does not cut a Christian off from the Church.** This is taught in full in Theology Stage 4; here the point is what it does to the question of the ancestors.

**Three relations to the departed.**

| Relation | Who | What the Church does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **We pray for them** | all the departed, our own family first | memorial services, the Saturdays of the Souls, names read at the *proskomide* in every Liturgy |
| **They pray for us** | the departed generally, in God's love; the saints with certainty | the Church asks the saints for their prayers |
| **We do not appease them** | anyone | there is no offering to the dead; Christ's sacrifice is offered to God for them |

**How this differs from *vadzimu* and *amadlozi*.**

1. **The dead are in God's hands, not ours.** In ancestral religion the dead become powers who need the living to feed and honour them. In the Church the dead **need our prayers**, not our offerings, and are **judged and cared for by God**, not by the family's rites. That relieves the living of fear.
2. **Holiness, not age, makes a saint.** An ancestor gains standing by dying old and being brought home. A saint is one the Church recognises as having **lived in Christ**. A grandfather who was a drunkard does not become a protector by dying; he needs our prayer and God's mercy.
3. **The saints are not family gatekeepers.** They pray for the whole Church, and they point to Christ. The Church glorifies Africans too: the martyrs of the early African Church, and in recent years African Orthodox clergy and faithful killed for the faith (Theology Stage 12).

**The other side's reply.** A traditionalist may answer that the Orthodox simply have **their own ancestor cult**, with candles, food at graves and the names of the dead, and have no right to condemn his. **This deserves a fair answer.** The outward forms are similar, and that is no embarrassment: the Church fulfils human instinct, she does not abolish it. The difference is in **the direction of the act**: the Church's memorial is addressed to God for the dead; the *kurova guva* offering is addressed to the dead for the living.

**The view of the spirits who appear.** What of the spirits that speak through a *svikiro* or appear in dreams demanding a beast? Orthodox writers in the patristic tradition, from the desert fathers to St Ignatius Brianchaninov (1807–1867), hold that **the souls of the departed do not wander or possess the living at will**; spirits that do so and demand offerings are to be treated as deceiving spirits, whatever name they give. Others put it more gently: the Church does not know every case, but she knows **that she must not seek the dead through mediums**, and that is enough to guide practice.

**The practical shape.** An Orthodox family in Zimbabwe or South Africa keeps a **memorial list** of its dead, has the priest serve a memorial at the one-year mark, visits and blesses the graves, and tells the children who their great-grandparents were. **Nothing good in honouring the ancestors is lost.**

**What it rests on.** **Whether Christ's death and resurrection have changed the condition of the dead.** The Church says they have: St John Chrysostom's Paschal Homily, read every Pascha, proclaims (in paraphrase) that Christ is risen, life reigns, and no one dead is left in the tomb.
Paganism, ancient and revived: Julian, H:
The old gods of Greece, Rome and the North did not vanish in a day, and in the last century they have been taken up again on purpose. This lesson covers both.

**The ancient defence.** The pagan case was best made not by peasants but by philosophers. Porphyry (about 234–305) wrote *Against the Christians*; the Emperor **Julian** (ruled 361–363), raised a Christian, returned to the gods and tried to restore them, writing *Against the Galileans*. His case, put at its strongest:

1. The ancestral gods made Rome and Greece great; **abandoning them is ingratitude and novelty**.
2. The Christians have left both Hellenism and the Jewish Law and **belong to neither**.
3. The many gods are powers under a highest principle; the myths are **symbols** for philosophers to read, not crude stories.

That last point matters. Late paganism, shaped by Neoplatonism (Philosophy Stage 5), was **not crude polytheism**. It held a single highest One and many lesser divine powers who ruled nations and things.

**The Orthodox answer then.** St Gregory the Theologian answered Julian in two *Invectives* (Orations 4 and 5); St Cyril of Alexandria wrote a long reply to *Against the Galileans*. Their answers:

| Pagan claim | Christian answer |
| --- | --- |
| the gods are ancestral | antiquity is not truth; the God of Abraham is older than the gods |
| the gods are powers under the One | then the One alone is God, and the powers are creatures, owed no worship |
| the myths are symbols | the symbols were worshipped with sacrifice, and the Fathers held that worship went to demons (previous lessons) |
| Christianity is new | it is the fulfilment of the oldest promise, Genesis 3:15 |

**Modern paganism.** From the nineteenth century, with Romanticism and nationalism, people in Europe began to **reconstruct** the old religions:

| Movement | What it revives |
| --- | --- |
| **Hellenism** (*Hellēnismos*) | the Olympian gods; in **2017** the Greek state recognised the Hellenic ethnic religion as a "known religion" |
| **Heathenry** (Ásatrú) | the Norse and Germanic gods; Iceland recognised Ásatrúarfélagið in 1973 |
| **Rodnovery** ("native faith") | the Slavic gods, strong in Russia, Ukraine and Poland |
| **Druidry** | a reconstructed Celtic spirituality, largely modern in form |

**Their case today.** Modern pagans argue: Christianity was imposed by kings and swords; our ancestors' religion was destroyed; nature is sacred; many gods allow tolerance where one God breeds intolerance. **The first charge contains real history.** Charlemagne forcibly baptised the Saxons in the 770s and 780s; Christian emperors from Theodosius I closed temples by law; Olaf Tryggvason forced Norway's conversion. **An Orthodox answer should not deny it.** The Fathers themselves condemned forced conversion, and the Russian conversion under St Vladimir (988) had its compulsions too.

**The Orthodox answer now.** Coercion was a sin against the Gospel, not part of it. But **the truth of a religion is not settled by how it spread**, and modern paganism is often a reconstruction from fragments, joined to a modern love of nature that Christianity also has. The Church reveres creation as God's work without worshipping it.

**Note.** Some forms of modern European paganism, especially in Germany and among some Rodnovers, are tied to **racial nationalism**. Many pagans reject this. It should be named but not imputed to all.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the divine is one Creator distinct from the world, or many powers within it.**
Wicca: Gardner, the Goddess and the God:
The most widespread new pagan religion in the English-speaking world is **Wicca**, and the most common reason people give for joining it is not demons but nature, freedom and the feminine. It has to be understood in its own terms.

**Origins.** Wicca was made public in England by **Gerald Gardner** (1884–1964), a retired civil servant, in *Witchcraft Today* (1954) and *The Meaning of Witchcraft* (1959). He said he had been initiated in 1939 into a surviving coven in the New Forest. His priestess **Doreen Valiente** (1922–1999) rewrote much of the ritual. Gardner drew on the theory of the Egyptologist **Margaret Murray** (*The Witch-Cult in Western Europe*, 1921) that the witches of the trials were members of a surviving pre-Christian fertility religion.

**What historians now say.** The historian **Ronald Hutton**, in *The Triumph of the Moon* (1999), a sympathetic study, concluded that **Murray's thesis does not stand** and that Wicca is a **new religion of the twentieth century**, drawing on ceremonial magic, Freemasonry, folklore and Romanticism. Many Wiccans accept this and say a religion can be new and true.

**Their beliefs, from their own writers.**

| Belief | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **the Goddess and the God** | the divine as female and male, often the Moon Goddess (maiden, mother, crone) and the Horned God of nature; some Wiccans see all goddesses as one Goddess |
| **the Wheel of the Year** | eight festivals (*sabbats*), including Samhain (31 October), Yule, Beltane (1 May) and the solstices |
| **the circle and magic** | ritual in a cast circle; magic as directing natural energies by will |
| **the Wiccan Rede** | its ethic, usually given as: do what you will, so long as it harms no one (paraphrase) |
| **the threefold law** | many Wiccans hold that what one sends out returns threefold |
| **no single creed** | covens and solitaries vary widely; there is no central authority |

**Why people come.** Its defenders say Wicca offers **the sacredness of nature, a divine feminine, ritual and beauty, personal experience instead of dogma, and an ethic without guilt**. Many come from Christian homes where faith seemed rule-bound and the body and the earth were treated with suspicion. Feminist Wicca (for example the writer **Starhawk**, *The Spiral Dance*, 1979) adds the claim that the Goddess restores women's dignity.

**Their reply to Christian critics.** Wiccans insist they do **not** worship Satan, who is a Christian figure they reject. **This is true and should be acknowledged.** Accusing Wiccans of devil-worship is both inaccurate and uncharitable, and ends any conversation. The European witch trials, which burnt women as Satanists, haunt this subject; Wiccans often call that period "the Burning Times".

**What Wicca rests on.** **That the divine is immanent in nature, polarised as female and male, and approached by ritual and will rather than by revelation and grace.** The next lesson answers it.
Answering Wicca and modern paganism: cre:
The Orthodox answer to Wicca does not begin by condemning; it begins by showing that **what drew the Wiccan is found, truer, in the Church**. Then it names where the paths divide.

**1. Nature is sacred, but not divine.** The Church blesses water at Theophany, fields and fruits at the Transfiguration, homes, boats and wells. Her services sing the psalm that calls on creation: "Let the heavens rejoice, and the earth exult" (Psalm 95:11, Brenton). The Fathers saw the world full of the ***lógoi*** (λόγοι), God's purposes in each thing (St Maximus the Confessor). So the Orthodox answer is not "nature is dead matter". It is: **creation is good, holy and charged with God, because it is made, not because it is God.** Worshipping it, or its powers, puts the gift in the place of the Giver (Romans 1:25).

**2. The feminine is honoured, without a goddess.** The strongest Wiccan claim is that Christianity has only a male God and despises women. The Orthodox answer:

- **God is beyond sex.** "Father" names a relation within the Trinity, not a male body. The Fathers insist that God has no gender in His essence (St Gregory the Theologian, Oration 31).
- **The Church's highest creature is a woman.** The hymn *Axion estin*, sung at every Liturgy, calls the Theotokos more honourable than the cherubim and beyond compare more glorious than the seraphim (paraphrase). No man is honoured so in the Church.
- **Holy women** stand among the apostles' equals: Mary Magdalene, Thekla, Nina of Georgia, Helena, Olga.

**Its best reply.** A Wiccan answers that a woman honoured for obedience is not the same as a Goddess worshipped for power, and that the Church's priesthood is male. **This is a real disagreement**, not a misunderstanding, and should be stated plainly. The Church holds that the dignity of a person is holiness, not power, and that the Theotokos's "be it unto me" is not weakness but the freest act of a creature.

**3. Magic and prayer are opposites.**

| Magic | Prayer |
| --- | --- |
| directs power by will and technique | asks a Person, and accepts His answer |
| the result depends on correct procedure | the result depends on God's love and the soul's state |
| the practitioner is in control | the one who prays surrenders control |

**The Church's objection to magic is not that it is spooky but that it is the opposite of faith.** It seeks to use spiritual reality rather than to be changed by God. St Basil's Canon 65 (Letter 217, tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2/8, 1895) rules: "He who confesses magic or sorcery shall do penance for the time of murder". He and the Trullan canon treat it gravely because it turns the soul from trust to control.

**4. The Rede and the Cross.** "Harm none" is a decent rule, and many Wiccans live it better than many Christians. But it is **an ethic of avoidance**. Christ's commandment is love even to the cross, including enemies. And it leaves untouched the question every person meets: **what of the harm I have already done?** Wicca has no forgiveness that comes from outside the self. The Church offers confession and the Cross.

**History told honestly.** The witch trials were a Christian sin, and they were mostly Western; the Orthodox world had fewer, though Russia had some. **An Orthodox Christian can say to a Wiccan: they should not have killed you, and they were not keeping Christ's commandment when they did.**

**What it rests on.** **Whether the divine is a Person who creates and saves, or a power within nature to be worked with.**
Spiritualism and the séance: contact wit:
In 1848 two girls in a farmhouse in New York State began, they said, to hear the dead knock in reply to questions. Within a few years millions in America and Europe were sitting in séances. **Spiritualism is the occult in its most domestic form**, and it still runs through New Age practice and the wider culture.

**The history.**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1848** | the **Fox sisters**, Kate and Margaret, in Hydesville, New York, report rappings answering questions |
| **1850s** | séances spread through America and Britain; mediums, table-turning, spirit writing |
| **1857** | **Allan Kardec** (pen name of Hippolyte Léon Denizard Rivail, 1804–1869) publishes *The Spirits' Book* in France, founding **Spiritism**, with reincarnation; it became very large in **Brazil** |
| **1882** | the Society for Psychical Research is founded in London to test the claims |
| **1888** | Margaret Fox publicly confesses that the rappings were produced by cracking her toe joints; she later retracts the confession |
| **after 1914–18** | a revival of séances among grieving families after the First World War; Sir Arthur Conan Doyle a leading advocate |

**Their case at its strongest.** Spiritualists argue: **the dead survive, and the proof is that they speak.** Mediums have given grieving families details they could not have known. Spiritualism, they say, offers evidence where churches offer only faith, and comfort where churches offer only doctrine. Many Spiritualist churches add a liberal Christian ethic.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Scripture forbids it** by name: "a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer" are among the practices "abomination unto the LORD" (Deuteronomy 18:11–12, KJV). King Saul's consultation of the woman at Endor (1 Samuel 28) is told as part of his fall.
2. **The Church's teaching on the dead** (Theology Stage 4) holds that after death the soul is in God's hands, awaiting the resurrection. It does not hover at our call.
3. **What, then, speaks in a séance?** The Orthodox tradition gives two answers, both of which can be true in different cases: **fraud and suggestion**, which the Society for Psychical Research exposed many times; and **deceiving spirits**, which can know what the dead knew and imitate them. St John Cassian and the desert fathers warn that the demons know much about a person's life. **Either way the medium is not reaching the dead.**
4. **Comfort is found in the Church.** The grieving mother does not need to hear raps. She has the memorial service, the prayer for her child, the communion of saints, and the promise of the resurrection.

**Their reply.** A Spiritualist will say: you have no evidence that what speaks is a demon; you assume it from your doctrine. **That is fair.** The Orthodox answer is that the Church does not need to identify every voice; it is enough that she has been **told not to seek** them, and that their message, often that there is no judgement and no need of a Saviour, is not the Gospel (Galatians 1:8).

**Where it survives.** Ouija boards, "ghost-hunting" programmes, mediums on television and New Age **channelling** (lesson below) are Spiritualism's heirs. **Priests in many places report that most cases of people troubled by spirits begin with one of these.**

**What it rests on.** **Whether the living may seek the dead, and whether what answers is who it claims to be.**
Astrology and divination: the Fathers ag:
About three in ten American adults say they believe in astrology, in a 2018 Pew survey, and horoscopes run in newspapers across the world. Astrology is the most respectable of the occult arts, and the Fathers answered it directly.

**What astrology claims.** The heavens at the moment of birth (the *horoscope*, from Greek *hōroskópos*, "watcher of the hour") **shape or show a person's character and destiny**. The twelve signs of the zodiac, the planets and their "aspects" to one another are read to forecast events and advise choices. Modern astrologers often soften it: the stars **incline, not compel**, or they are symbols that mirror the soul, not causes.

**Their case at its strongest.** Its defenders say: it is among the oldest human sciences, practised in Babylon, Greece, India and the medieval Christian world; people recognise themselves in their signs; it is a language for self-knowledge, not a religion. Even some medieval Christian thinkers allowed that the stars affect bodies.

**The Fathers' answer.** **St Basil the Great**, in *Hexaemeron* Homily 6 (about 378), took apart "the art of casting nativities". His arguments (tr. Blomfield Jackson, NPNF 2/8, 1895):

1. **The figures change too fast.** The stars' positions shift constantly; the astrologer cannot catch the true moment of birth.
2. **Kings would be born every day.** If the "royal" configuration recurs daily, why is there a hereditary succession rather than kings born at random?
3. **It destroys moral responsibility.** "If the origin of our virtues and of our vices is not in ourselves, but is the fatal consequence of our birth, it is useless for legislators to prescribe for us what we ought to do". The robber is not guilty, the judge is unjust, and Christians "shall see our great hopes vanish".
4. **It blames God.** "For the evil stars throw the blame of their wickedness upon Him Who made them."

**St Gregory of Nyssa** wrote a treatise *Against Fate* on the same lines. **St Augustine** (*Confessions* VII.6) added the argument from twins: Jacob and Esau, born at almost the same moment, lived opposite lives.

**The softer form answered.** If astrology only "inclines", the Orthodox answer is that **the soul's direction comes from the will and from grace**, and seeking to know the future by signs is still **divination**. The canons forbid both the casting of fortunes and consulting those who do (**Canon 61 of Trullo, 692**). The Christian lives by **providence**, not fate: God cares for each person, and the future is in His hand, not written in the sky.

**The Star of Bethlehem.** Astrologers point to the Magi (Matthew 2). The Fathers answered that the star was a **sign given by God**, which led astrologers *out* of astrology to worship Christ. St John Chrysostom (*Homilies on Matthew* 6) argued it was no ordinary star, since it moved and stopped over a house. **Christ came to free them from the stars, not to confirm them.**

**Other divination.** Tarot cards, palmistry, tea leaves, the *I Ching*, and the divining bones (*hakata* in Shona, *amathambo* in Zulu) of a diviner all seek the same thing. **The Church's answer is the same: do not seek hidden knowledge from creatures; ask God, and trust Him.**

**What it rests on.** **Whether human life is governed by fate written in creation, or by a personal God and a free will.**
Theosophy: Blavatsky, the Masters and th:
Almost every idea of the New Age, from karma as cosmic justice to "ascended masters" to the claim that all religions share one hidden wisdom, passed through one nineteenth-century movement: **Theosophy**.

**The founder.** **Helena Petrovna Blavatsky** (1831–1891), born in Ekaterinoslav in the Russian Empire (now Dnipro, Ukraine) and baptised Orthodox, travelled widely, claimed to have studied with hidden **Masters** (*Mahatmas*) in Tibet, and worked as a medium in America. With **Henry Steel Olcott** (1832–1907) and **William Quan Judge** (1851–1896) she founded the **Theosophical Society** in New York in **1875**; its headquarters moved to **Adyar**, near Madras (Chennai), in 1882.

**The books.** *Isis Unveiled* (1877); ***The Secret Doctrine*** (1888), claiming to expound an ancient "Book of Dzyan"; ***The Key to Theosophy*** (1889), a question-and-answer introduction.

**The word.** *Theosophía* (θεοσοφία), "divine wisdom", is an old Greek word (Christian writers used it), which Blavatsky took for a **"Wisdom Religion"** she said lay behind all religions.

**Their own statement.** The Society's three objects, in *The Key to Theosophy* (1889; Project Gutenberg text):

> "(1). To form the nucleus of a Universal Brotherhood of Humanity without distinction of race, colour, or creed. (2). To promote the study of Aryan and other Scriptures, of the World's religion and sciences, and to vindicate the importance of old Asiatic literature, namely, of the Brahmanical, Buddhist, and Zoroastrian philosophies. (3). To investigate the hidden mysteries of Nature under every aspect possible, and the psychic and spiritual powers latent in man especially."

**Its teachings.**

| Teaching | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **no personal God** | the Absolute is impersonal; Blavatsky's character "Theo" says: "We reject the idea of a personal, or an extra-cosmic and anthropomorphic God" |
| **all religions one at root** | each religion is an outer form of the one esoteric wisdom |
| **karma and reincarnation** | the soul (the "Ego") returns in many bodies, under an exact law of retribution |
| **the Masters** | perfected men who guide humanity in secret |
| **root races and cosmic cycles** | humanity evolves through seven "root races"; a scheme later abused by racial theorists |

**Its influence.** Theosophy carried Hindu and Buddhist terms into the West in a Western form; it helped revive Buddhism in Sri Lanka (Olcott) and influenced the Indian independence movement. From it came **Anthroposophy** (Steiner), the **"I AM" movement**, **Alice Bailey's** teaching (which spread the phrase "New Age"), and the young **Jiddu Krishnamurti**, presented as a coming World Teacher, who in **1929** dissolved the order built around him.

**Questions about Blavatsky.** In 1885 a report for the Society for Psychical Research by **Richard Hodgson** concluded that her letters from the Masters were fraudulent. In 1986 another member of that Society, **Vernon Harrison**, published a critique of Hodgson's methods. **The question remains disputed**; the answer below does not depend on it.

**The Orthodox answer in brief.** Theosophy is answered at three points: **the personal God** (Theology Stage 2), **the uniqueness of Christ** against "all religions are one" (Stage 10), and **reincarnation**, which the next two lessons read in Blavatsky's own words and in St Irenaeus. **It repeats, nearly point for point, the Gnostic pattern of Stage 2**: secret knowledge, hidden masters, an impersonal divine, salvation by enlightenment.

**What it rests on.** **Whether God is a Person who reveals Himself, or an impersonal Absolute known by esoteric knowledge.**
Reading: Blavatsky's Key to Theosophy on:
*The Key to Theosophy* (1889) is a dialogue between an Enquirer ("ENQ.") and a Theosophist ("THEO."). In section VIII Blavatsky faces the oldest objection to reincarnation. The text is from the Project Gutenberg edition (eBook 55618), in her own English; it is in the public domain.

**The objection, as she states it:**

> "First of all, you have against this theory of re-incarnation, the fact that no single man has yet been found to remember that he has lived, least of all who he was, during his previous life."

**Her reply begins:**

> "Your argument, I see, tends to the same old objection; the loss of memory in each of us of our previous incarnation. You think it invalidates our doctrine? My answer is that it does not, and that at any rate such an objection cannot be final."

**Read closely: "the same old objection".** She knows it is old. It was made by St Irenaeus in the second century, as the next lesson shows. Blavatsky's answer is to **divide the self**.

**The core of her argument:**

> "Re-incarnation means that this Ego will be furnished with a *new* body, a *new* brain, and a *new* memory. Therefore it would be as absurd to expect this *memory* to remember that which it has never recorded as it would be idle to examine under a microscope a shirt never worn by a murderer, and seek on it for the stains of blood which are to be found only on the clothes he wore."

**What she is claiming.** Memory, for Blavatsky, belongs to the **brain** and the **personality**, which die. What passes on is the **"Ego"**, the higher, permanent self, which does not carry ordinary memories. So the lack of memory proves nothing. To know one's past lives, she says, "one must put oneself in *rapport* with one's real permanent Ego, not one's evanescent memory".

**Then the moral system.** Later in the same section she ties reincarnation to **karma**:

> "We believe in an unerring law of Retribution, called KARMA, which asserts itself in a natural concatenation of causes and their unavoidable results."

And the punishment of sin, she says, is not in hell but "verily on to this earth, the plane and region of his sins, where he will have to atone for every bad thought and deed."

**Questions to bring to the text.**

1. **If the person who sinned and the person who suffers share no memory, no brain and no personality, in what sense is the second punished for the first?** Blavatsky's own image is telling: the clean shirt was "never worn by a murderer". Then why is its wearer being punished?
2. **The appeal to an unprovable "Ego".** Her reply moves the evidence out of reach: memory cannot show reincarnation, only esoteric *rapport* can. That is coherent, but it means **the doctrine cannot be tested** by anything the enquirer can check.
3. **Justice without mercy.** The law of karma is "unerring" and impersonal. It explains suffering as deserved. **Is a child born blind being punished?** Christ was asked this and answered no (John 9:2–3).
4. **Where did it come from?** Blavatsky frames it as the "Wisdom of the Ages". It is a Western, evolutionary reworking of Indian ideas (Stage 10 taught them in their own forms), joined to a Victorian faith in progress.

**What to carry to the next reading.** Her strongest move is **separating the self from its memory**. Irenaeus attacks exactly that.
Reading: St Irenaeus against the transmi:
**St Irenaeus of Lyons** (about 130–202), in *Against Heresies* (about 180), answered Gnostic teachers who held that souls pass from body to body to gain experience of every kind of act. Book II, chapter 33 is the oldest Christian refutation of reincarnation, and Blavatsky's "same old objection" is his. Translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 1 (1885), as given on New Advent.

**His first argument: memory.**

> "We may subvert their doctrine as to transmigration from body to body by this fact, that souls remember nothing whatever of the events which took place in their previous states of existence. For if they were sent forth with this object, that they should have experience of every kind of action, they must of necessity retain a remembrance of those things which have been previously accomplished".

**Read closely.** Irenaeus does not merely say "nobody remembers". He says the doctrine **defeats its own purpose**. If souls return in order to learn, a learner who forgets every lesson cannot learn. They would spend their labour "wretchedly in vain".

**His second argument: the forgetting is invented.** Plato, Irenaeus says, met the objection by inventing a "cup of oblivion" given by a demon before birth. Irenaeus replies:

> "For if the cup of oblivion, after it has been drunk, can obliterate the memory of all the deeds that have been done, how, O Plato, do you obtain the knowledge of this fact (since your soul is now in the body), that, before it entered into the body, it was made to drink by the demon a drug which caused oblivion?"

**Against Blavatsky.** This is precisely her move: the higher Ego knows, the brain forgets. Irenaeus's question applies: **if the forgetting is total, how does the teacher know what was forgotten?** Blavatsky answers by esoteric *rapport*; Irenaeus would answer that this is a claim no one can check, made by the one who needs it.

**His third argument: the soul is not ruled by the body.** To those who say the body itself causes the forgetting, he answers that the soul remembers dreams and visions while in the body, and the prophets remembered what they saw: "The body, therefore, does not cause the soul to forget those things which have been spiritually witnessed; but the soul teaches the body".

**His positive teaching.** The chapter ends with the Christian picture:

> "But, as each one of us receives his body through the skilful working of God, so does he also possess his soul. For God is not so poor or destitute in resources, that He cannot confer its own proper soul on each individual body, even as He gives it also its special character."

And at the resurrection "all those who have been enrolled for life [eternal] shall rise again, having their own bodies, and having also their own souls".

**The two pictures side by side.**

| | Blavatsky | Irenaeus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the self** | a permanent Ego wearing many personalities | one soul with one body, made by God |
| **memory** | belongs to the perishable brain | belongs to the soul, which is not ruled by the body |
| **justice** | karma, impersonal and exact, on earth | the judgement of a personal God, at the resurrection |
| **the goal** | escape from rebirth by evolution of the Ego | **resurrection** of this body and this soul |
| **the person** | passes away; the Ego continues | **each person is unrepeatable** and rises as himself |

**The heart of it.** **For Irenaeus, God loves each person as this person, with this body.** "It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment" (Hebrews 9:27, KJV). Reincarnation, however gentle its modern form, makes the person a temporary costume.
Anthroposophy: Rudolf Steiner and his Ch:
Of all the esoteric movements, Anthroposophy speaks most about Christ, runs schools many Christian parents use, and farms by its own methods. It is the hardest to recognise as a separate religion, which is why it needs its own lesson.

**The founder.** **Rudolf Steiner** (1861–1925), born in the Austrian Empire, edited Goethe's scientific writings and wrote *The Philosophy of Freedom* (1894). He became General Secretary of the German section of the Theosophical Society in 1902. He broke with it in **1912–13**, when its leaders promoted Krishnamurti as a coming World Teacher, and founded the **Anthroposophical Society**. Its centre is the **Goetheanum** at Dornach, Switzerland.

**The word.** *Anthroposophía*, "wisdom of the human being": Steiner taught that by disciplined meditation one can develop organs of spiritual perception and **know the spiritual worlds as clearly as the physical**, a "spiritual science".

**What came from it.**

| Work | Founded |
| --- | --- |
| **Waldorf (Steiner) schools** | 1919, Stuttgart; now well over a thousand worldwide |
| **biodynamic farming** | from lectures in 1924 |
| **anthroposophical medicine**, including mistletoe preparations for cancer | 1920s |
| **The Christian Community**, a church using Steiner's insights, with its own sacraments | 1922, with the Lutheran pastor Friedrich Rittelmeyer |

**His teaching on Christ, from his own lectures.**

- Christ is a **high cosmic being**, the "Sun Spirit", who descended into the man Jesus at the Baptism in the Jordan.
- The **"Mystery of Golgotha"**, the death and resurrection, is the turning point of earth's evolution: Christ's being entered the earth itself.
- In lectures on Luke's Gospel (1909) Steiner taught that there were **two Jesus children**, one from Solomon's line (Matthew) and one from Nathan's (Luke), who later united.
- Humanity is pulled between two opposed spirits: **Lucifer** (pride, escape upward) and **Ahriman** (materialism); Christ holds the balance.
- **Reincarnation and karma** remain, in a Christianised form.

**Their case at its strongest.** Anthroposophists say: Steiner restored the **cosmic Christ** whom modern theology had shrunk to a moral teacher; he joined science and spirit; Waldorf education honours the child's imagination; biodynamic farming treats the land as alive. Many Christians find in his work a richness the churches lost.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Christ is not a cosmic being who entered a man.** The Third and Fourth Ecumenical Councils (431, 451) taught that **the eternal Son of God is Himself the subject of the Incarnation**: one person, from conception, not a spirit descending on Jesus at the Baptism. Steiner's Christology is close to the Gnostic and **Nestorian** patterns of Stage 2.
2. **Knowledge of God is not a technique.** Steiner's "spiritual science" claims that the higher worlds can be seen by training. The Orthodox tradition teaches that **visions sought are dangerous**, and that the knowledge of God comes by repentance, purity and grace (Theology Stage 10). St Ignatius Brianchaninov warns at length against seeking spiritual sight.
3. **Reincarnation contradicts the resurrection** (previous two lessons).

**For parents.** Waldorf schools differ greatly; many families use them without any anthroposophical belief. But **the curriculum and the teachers' training rest on Steiner's spiritual teaching**, including his view of the child as a reincarnating spirit. Parents should know that.

**What it rests on.** **Whether Christ is the eternal Son made flesh, or a cosmic being known by higher clairvoyance.**
The New Age: the Age of Aquarius and spi:
"New Age" names no church and no creed. It is a **loose movement of beliefs and practices** that grew in the West from the 1960s and has now soaked into ordinary life: crystals, energy healing, horoscopes, channelling, manifestation, "the universe" that answers wishes.

**Where the name comes from.** In astrology, the spring equinox moves slowly backwards through the zodiac, spending about 2,100 years in each sign. The Christian era is called the **Age of Pisces**; the coming age is **Aquarius**, expected to bring spiritual awakening. **Alice Bailey** (1880–1949), a former Theosophist, spread the phrase "New Age".

**The milestones.**

| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| **1962** | the **Findhorn** community in Scotland and the **Esalen Institute** in California founded |
| **1970s** | channelling grows: Jane Roberts's "Seth" books; *A Course in Miracles* (1976), dictated, its scribe said, by an inner voice she identified as Jesus |
| **1980** | Marilyn Ferguson, *The Aquarian Conspiracy* |
| **1983** | Shirley MacLaine, *Out on a Limb*, brings the movement into best-seller lists |
| **2006** | *The Secret* popularises the "law of attraction" |

**Its typical beliefs.**

| Belief | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **the divine within** | God is an energy or consciousness in all things; the true self is divine |
| **spiritual evolution** | humanity is moving to a higher consciousness |
| **energy** | crystals, *chakras*, *reiki* and auras work by subtle energies |
| **channelling** | spirits, "ascended masters" or the "higher self" speak through a medium |
| **reincarnation and karma** | souls return to learn |
| **personal choice** | each person builds his own spiritual path from many sources |

**How widespread.** In a **2018 Pew survey** of American adults, about **six in ten** held at least one New Age belief: 42% that physical objects can have spiritual energy, 41% in psychics, 33% in reincarnation and 29% in astrology. **The shares were almost the same among Christians as among those of no religion.** That is why the New Age matters for the Church: it is less a rival than a **solvent**, mixed into the beliefs of baptised people.

**"Spiritual but not religious".** The New Age's social form is the person who says he is spiritual but not religious. **His case at its strongest:** institutions corrupt; dogma divides; experience is what matters; each person must find his own truth; the churches have abused their power. **Much of that charge against the churches is deserved**, and the Orthodox answer should begin by admitting it.

**Why people come.** The New Age offers what modern life lacks: meaning, a sense of the sacred, healing, community, and ritual, **without repentance, authority or a God who makes claims**.

**What the New Age rests on.** **That the self is divine and the measure of truth.** The next lesson answers it.
Answering the New Age: the god within an:
The New Age is hard to argue with because it has no creed to refute. The Orthodox answer works best at the **centre**, where all its forms meet: the claim that **the self is divine**.

**1. Theosis is not the self discovered as God.** The New Age says "you are God". The Orthodox Church also speaks of **deification** (*théōsis*, θέωσις): "For He was made man that we might be made God" (St Athanasius, *On the Incarnation* 54, tr. Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2/4, 1892; Theology Stage 3). The likeness is real; the difference is total.

| New Age | Orthodox theosis |
| --- | --- |
| the self is already divine and needs to awaken | the person is a creature, made from nothing |
| the divine is impersonal energy | God is three Persons, who love |
| union by technique and awareness | union by **grace**, through repentance and the sacraments |
| the self dissolves into the One, or is magnified | the person is **healed and kept**, one with God without confusion |
| no need of a Saviour | **only through Christ**, who joins God and man in His person |

**Union by grace, not by nature.** St Maximus the Confessor and St Gregory Palamas teach that the deified share in God's **energies**, never His **essence** (Theology Stage 2). **The creature never becomes the Creator.** This is the precise line the New Age erases.

**2. Discernment of spirits.** Channelling, angel cards and spirit guides are **contact with spirits**. The Orthodox tradition has a long teaching on discernment (*diákrisis*, διάκρισις): "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God" (1 John 4:1, KJV). The test St John gives is Christ: does the spirit confess that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh? **Channelled messages almost always** say there is no sin, no judgement, no need of a Saviour, and that Jesus was one master among many. The Church reads that as the mark of a deceiving spirit, whatever its warmth. The Fathers call this ***plánē*** (πλάνη), **spiritual delusion**: false experience that flatters the self.

**3. Energy and healing.** Some New Age practices (massage, breathing, rest) do good for natural reasons. The danger is in the **explanation and the opening**: *reiki*, for example, describes itself as channelling a universal life energy and, at higher levels, uses symbols and attunements. Orthodox pastors commonly advise against practices that **open the person to unknown spiritual powers**. Orthodox writers differ on how far to go: some forbid any practice with a non-Christian spiritual origin; others distinguish physical techniques from their spiritual framework (as with yoga, Stage 10).

**4. The God who makes claims.** The deepest answer is not an argument. **The New Age offers a spirituality in which nothing is asked of the self.** Christ asks everything: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me" (Matthew 16:24, KJV). The paradox, which the saints witness, is that **the self found by losing it is truer and freer** than the self worshipped.

**Their best reply.** A New Ager will say the Church just wants control. **Answer with honesty and an invitation**: the Church has sinned; but come and see what the saints were like.

**A Catholic parallel.** In 2003 two Vatican councils published *Jesus Christ, the Bearer of the Water of Life: a Christian reflection on the New Age*, making similar points. It is useful as a careful survey, though not an Orthodox text.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the self is divine by nature, or a creature called to become god by grace.**
Fr Seraphim Rose: Orthodoxy and the Reli:
The most influential Orthodox answer to the New Age was written before the term was common. **Fr Seraphim Rose** (1934–1982), whose life is taught in Theology Stage 12, published ***Orthodoxy and the Religion of the Future*** in **1975**. What follows is a summary and paraphrase; the book is in copyright.

**Rose's own path.** He knew the other side from inside. As a young man he studied Chinese philosophy, read the Traditionalist writers (René Guénon above all, Stage 10) and searched through Eastern religions before becoming Orthodox in 1962. **He wrote as one who had been where his readers were.**

**The argument of the book, in outline.**

| Chapter theme | Rose's claim, paraphrased |
| --- | --- |
| **the spirit of the age** | a new religious consciousness (his phrase) is forming in the West, open to every spiritual experience and closed to none, and it is not neutral |
| **Hinduism and "dialogue"** | Eastern teachers brought to the West a spirituality aimed explicitly at absorbing Christianity |
| **Eastern meditation in the Church** | Christians adopting meditation techniques divorced from repentance are being led into passive spiritual states |
| **UFOs, "signs from heaven"** | the modern UFO and "contact" phenomena, he argued, match in pattern the demonic visions described in Orthodox spiritual literature |
| **the charismatic revival** | he argued that "speaking in tongues" and the experiences of the charismatic movement (Stage 7) show the same mediumistic passivity |
| **the religion of the future** | these converge into a world religion without Christ, which Orthodox tradition associates with the time before Antichrist |

**His central idea: mediumism.** Rose's key term is ***mediumistic*** spirituality: an attitude in which the person **opens himself passively** to whatever spiritual power comes, seeking experience rather than God. He contrasts it with Orthodox prayer, which is sober (*nḗpsis*, νῆψις, watchfulness), humble, distrustful of sensations, and guided by a spiritual father. **This distinction is his lasting contribution**, and many Orthodox who disagree with parts of the book accept it.

**Where Orthodox readers differ about the book.**

| View | Its argument |
| --- | --- |
| **prophetic** | Rose saw clearly what the New Age would become; its rise after 1975 bears him out; his warnings on meditation and passivity are patristic |
| **valuable but overdrawn** | his treatment of the charismatic movement and of UFOs can read as alarmist; he relies on secondary sources for Hinduism; the apocalyptic frame can breed fear rather than discernment |

Both views are held by Orthodox clergy and scholars, and the book remains in print and widely read.

**How to use it.** For polemics, Rose's method matters more than his examples: **ask not only "is this true?" but "what does this practice do to the soul that uses it?"** A spirituality is known by whether it makes a person humble, sober and loving, or passive, proud and hungry for experience.

**What it rests on.** **Whether spiritual experience is neutral, or must be tested by its source and its fruit.** Rose says it is never neutral.
Freemasonry: what it is and what it says:
Freemasonry is not a religion by its own account. It is a fraternity with lodges in most countries, charitable works, and rituals. The Orthodox churches that have ruled on it have nonetheless judged it **incompatible with membership in the Church**. To see why, one must first hear what it says of itself.

**Origins.** Lodges of working stonemasons existed in medieval Britain. From the seventeenth century, gentlemen who were not builders were admitted ("speculative" masonry). On **24 June 1717** four London lodges formed the **Grand Lodge of London and Westminster**, later the Premier Grand Lodge of England. In **1723** the Presbyterian minister **James Anderson** published its ***Constitutions***.

**Their own text.** Anderson's first Charge, "Concerning GOD and RELIGION" (1723; public domain):

> "A Mason is oblig'd by his Tenure, to obey the moral Law; and if he rightly understands the Art, he will never be a stupid Atheist nor an irreligious Libertine. But though in ancient Times Masons were charg'd in every Country to be of the Religion of that Country or Nation, whatever it was, yet 'tis now thought more expedient only to oblige them to that Religion in which all Men agree, leaving their particular Opinions to themselves; that is, to be good Men and true, or Men of Honour and Honesty, by whatever Denominations or Persuasions they may be distinguish'd; whereby Masonry becomes the Center of Union, and the Means of conciliating true Friendship among Persons that must have remain'd at a perpetual Distance."

**Read closely.** Two moves are made. First, Masonry once required the local religion; now it requires only **"that Religion in which all Men agree"**, a natural religion of morality and belief in God. Second, Masonry becomes **"the Center of Union"** for men of every creed. **That is the whole question in one sentence.**

**What Freemasonry is today.**

| Feature | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **the degrees** | Entered Apprentice, Fellowcraft, Master Mason; many further degrees in other rites |
| **the Great Architect of the Universe** | the name under which God is addressed; regular lodges require belief in a Supreme Being |
| **ritual and symbol** | the square and compasses; initiation in a temple; the drama of **Hiram Abiff**, the builder of Solomon's Temple, slain and raised in the Master Mason degree |
| **secrecy** | oaths not to reveal the ritual |
| **the two families** | "regular" (Anglo-American) lodges require belief in God; the Grand Orient of France dropped that requirement in **1877** |

**Their case at its strongest.** Masons say: we are not a religion; we have no sacraments, no doctrine of salvation, no clergy. We ask a man to believe in God and to be good, and we leave his religion to him. Many Christians, including clergy, have been Masons. **Masonry teaches brotherhood across religious divides in a world torn by them.** Grand lodges have rejected the charge that they are anti-Christian as a misreading of symbols.

**Honest history.** Freemasonry has been attacked with forgeries and conspiracy theories, most notoriously the **Taxil hoax** (1885–1897), in which Léo Taxil invented Masonic devil-worship and then confessed. Totalitarian regimes, Nazi and Soviet, persecuted Masons. **The Orthodox case should not rest on such material.** In the Greek world, many prominent men, and some clergy, were Masons in the early twentieth century, which is why the Church ruled on it.

**What it rests on.** **Whether a brotherhood with its own temples, initiations and prayers to a God common to all religions can be morally neutral for a Christian.** The next lesson gives the Church's answer.
The Orthodox Church's rulings on Freemas:
The Orthodox churches have answered Freemasonry not by fear of conspiracy but by a **theological judgement**: that its rites make it a religion, and that a Christian cannot belong to two.

**The rulings.**

| Date | Body | Ruling |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1930** | the Inter-Orthodox Preparatory Commission, meeting at the **Vatopedi monastery on Mount Athos** with representatives of the autocephalous churches | characterised Freemasonry as an anti-Christian and erroneous system |
| **1932** | the Council of Bishops of the **Russian Orthodox Church Outside of Russia** | condemned Freemasonry |
| **12 October 1933** | the bishops of the **Church of Greece**, after a report by four bishops and an opinion of the Theological Faculty of Athens | declared Freemasonry incompatible with Christianity; the faithful must stand apart from it |
| **1972, 1996 and later** | the **Holy Synod of the Church of Greece** | reaffirmed the 1933 ruling |

**The 1933 statement's argument** (paraphrased from an English translation):

1. **Freemasonry is not simply a philanthropic union** but a mystery system, which its own writers trace to the **ancient pagan mysteries**.
2. **Its initiations re-enact a death and rising**: the Master Mason relives the death of Hiram, as the initiates of the old mysteries died with their god.
3. **It has the marks of a religion**: temples with altars, its own rites of adoption, marriage and funeral, a hierarchy and a discipline.
4. **Its tolerance is syncretism.** It seems compatible with every religion because it treats all as equal and itself as **above them**, making a Christian the brother of men of every faith in the lodge while an uninitiated Christian is an outsider.
5. **Therefore** clergy may not join, those who joined unknowingly should leave, and **all the faithful must stand apart from Freemasonry**, for one cannot belong to Christ and seek moral perfection in another mystery.

**The Orthodox answer to Anderson.** Anderson's "Religion in which all Men agree" is exactly the problem. The Church does not deny that non-Christians know God's existence and the moral law (Romans 1–2). But **to make that common religion the "Center of Union", with its own temple and initiations, is to place Christ among the options**. St Paul: "Ye cannot drink the cup of the Lord, and the cup of devils" (1 Corinthians 10:21); the Church applies the principle: one cannot belong to two mysteries.
