**Their best reply.** Masons answer that the Greek bishops misread symbols as sacraments; that the Hiramic drama is a moral allegory, not a rite of salvation; that Christian Masons see no conflict, and that some Orthodox hierarchs themselves were Masons. **Some of this is factually fair.** The membership of certain hierarchs was widely reported in the period, and the rituals of English lodges are milder than the continental texts the 1933 commission quoted.

**The Orthodox reply to that.** The question is not intention but **what the act is**. An oath of secrecy before a God addressed as common to all religions, in a temple, with an initiation into death and rising, is a religious act, whatever a member intends. And the Church judges what may be shared with the Mysteries.

**Pastoral practice, as of November 2026.** In the churches that have ruled, a Mason is asked to leave the lodge before receiving Communion or being received into the Church. Practice in other jurisdictions varies, and not every local church has issued a formal ruling. The Roman Catholic Church also forbids membership (Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, 1983, reaffirmed in 2023); Stage 5 notes it.

**What it rests on.** **Whether a lodge's rituals are religious acts.** If they are, a Christian cannot share them.
Looking back: one God among the gods, sp:
This stage moved from the ancestors of a Shona homestead to the lodges of London, through Wiccan circles, séances, horoscopes, Theosophy and the New Age. **One question ran through every lesson: who or what is being addressed, and on what terms?**

**The pattern, gathered.**

| Movement | What it addresses | What it promises | What it rests on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **African traditional religion** | the ancestors, spirits, a distant Creator | protection, healing, family wholeness | the dead as powers to be honoured with offerings |
| **The healers and diviners** | spirits through the *n'anga* or *sangoma* | the cause of misfortune and its cure | hidden knowledge sought from spirits |
| **Modern paganism and Wicca** | the gods, the Goddess and the God | the sacredness of nature, ritual, freedom | the divine within nature, approached by will |
| **Spiritualism** | the dead through mediums | proof of survival, comfort | the dead within reach of the living |
| **Astrology and divination** | the stars and signs | knowledge of the future and the self | fate written in creation |
| **Theosophy and Anthroposophy** | the Masters, the higher self, a cosmic Christ | esoteric knowledge, spiritual evolution | an impersonal divine; reincarnation |
| **The New Age** | the divine self, energy, spirit guides | awakening without repentance | the self as divine |
| **Freemasonry** | the Great Architect common to all | brotherhood above creeds | a natural religion as the centre of union |

**The Orthodox answer, gathered.**

1. **One Creator, who alone is worshipped.** Every other power is a creature: to be honoured if holy, loved if human, governed if natural, **tested if a spirit**. "All the gods of the heathen are devils: but the Lord made the heavens" (Psalm 95:5, Brenton).
2. **God has come near.** The distance that ancestors, mediums and masters fill is closed by the Incarnation. **No one needs a gatekeeper to reach the Father.**
3. **The dead are in God's hands.** We pray for them; the saints pray for us; no one is appeased (lessons 4 to 7).
4. **Prayer, not technique.** Magic, divination and esoteric training seek control; the Christian asks and trusts.
5. **Each person is unrepeatable.** Against reincarnation, the resurrection of this body and this soul (St Irenaeus).
6. **Theosis by grace, not divinity by nature.** The New Age's deepest claim is answered by the Church's deepest teaching.
7. **Discernment.** Spiritual experience is never neutral; it is tested by Christ and by its fruit (Fr Seraphim Rose; 1 John 4:1).

**Where Orthodox answer differently, as met in this stage.** Whether a Christian may attend the family's rites of the dead (*akriveia* or *oikonomia*); whether some practices with non-Christian origins can be separated from their framework; how far Rose's warnings are prophetic or overdrawn. **On worship, sacrifice to the dead, divination and the lodge, they agree.**

**The history the stage did not hide.** Forced conversions of pagans; missionaries who condemned everything African; the witch trials; churches today that feed witchcraft fear. **The Church's answer to the old gods is stronger when it confesses these.**

**Looking ahead.** Stage 12 turns from too many gods to **none**: atheism and the modern objections. Many who leave the New Age end as sceptics, and many sceptics drift into it; the same person may be met in both stages.
Context: unbelief in the modern world:
Stage 11 answered those who believe in too many powers. This stage answers those who believe in **none**: the atheist, the agnostic, the sceptic, and the many people who simply live as if God were not there.

**How many.** The Pew Research Center's 2025 report on the world's religions estimated that **about 24% of the world's people had no religious affiliation in 2020**, some 1.9 billion, up from about 23% in 2010. About 1.3 billion of them are in **China**. Being unaffiliated is not the same as atheism: many of the "nones" believe in God or a higher power and simply belong to no religion. **As of November 2026** these remain the most recent global figures, and in Europe, North America and Australasia the share of "nones" is still rising, while in Africa it stays very low.

**Why atheism needs its own answer.** Every other stage answered people who agree there is a God and dispute who He is. Here **the existence of God itself** is denied, and with it the meaning of every other stage. The arguments are of four kinds:

| Kind | The claim | Lessons |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Evil and hiddenness** | a good God would not allow this suffering, or would make Himself plain | 3 to 7 |
| **Explaining religion away** | religion is projection, ideology or wish (Feuerbach, Marx, Freud) | 8 to 11 |
| **Evidence and science** | there is no evidence; miracles are incredible; science has replaced God | 12 to 18 |
| **Life without God** | morality and meaning do not need God; or, honestly faced, there is none (Nietzsche) | 19 to 22 |
| **Jesus and the resurrection** | Jesus is a myth, or the Gospels are unreliable, or the resurrection did not happen | 23 to 26 |

**What is pointed across, not taught again.** The **arguments for God** (Aquinas's Five Ways, the ontological argument, the Kalam, fine-tuning, Plantinga) are taught in **Philosophy Stages 6, 7 and 14**. **Hume** on causation and miracles, and his *Dialogues*, are in **Philosophy Stage 9**; **Feuerbach, Marx and Nietzsche** in **Philosophy Stage 11**; Mackie, Plantinga and Rowe on evil in **Philosophy Stage 14**. Genesis and evolution, with both Orthodox views, are in **Theology Stage 5**. This stage uses those lessons and asks the polemical question: **how does the Orthodox Christian answer, and where does the disagreement finally rest?**

**What is distinctive about the Orthodox answer.** Many Christian apologists answer atheism with philosophy alone. The Orthodox tradition uses philosophy but adds two things:

1. **God is not a being among beings.** The God the New Atheists deny is often a very large object inside the universe. The Fathers never believed in that god either. **Apophatic theology** (Theology Stage 2) is the first answer to much modern atheism.
2. **Knowledge of God is not only argument.** "Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8, KJV). The Fathers held that unbelief is often a matter of the heart and of a life, not only of the mind, and that the strongest answer is a saint.

**The rule of charity.** Many atheists are honest, moral and serious, and many have been hurt by Christians. **The lessons give their arguments as their best defenders would**, and they answer the arguments, not the people.
What atheism is: atheism, agnosticism an:
Before answering atheism, it must be defined, because atheists themselves define it differently, and much argument is wasted on the words.

**The words.**

| Term | Origin | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **atheism** | Greek *átheos* (ἄθεος), "without God" | in the older sense, **the belief that there is no God**; in a newer sense, simply **lacking belief** in God |
| **agnosticism** | coined by **T. H. Huxley** in **1869**, from Greek *ágnōstos*, "unknown" | the view that **we do not or cannot know** whether God exists |
| **naturalism** | Latin *natura* | the view that **nature is all there is**: no God, souls or supernatural beings |
| **materialism** | | the stronger view that everything is **matter** and its motions |
| **secularism** | Latin *saeculum*, "age, world" | a political view that the state should not favour religion; not itself atheism |

**A curious history of the word.** The early Christians were called ***átheoi*** by the Romans, because they refused to worship the gods. St Justin Martyr answered (First Apology 6) that Christians were atheists with respect to the false gods, but not with respect to the true God. **Every Christian is an atheist about Zeus**, a point modern atheists sometimes make against Christians. The answer is that **denying one god because he is a creature is not the same as denying the Creator**.

**"Lack of belief" and the burden of proof.** Many modern atheists, following **Antony Flew**'s essay "The Presumption of Atheism" (1972), define atheism as simply not believing, so that **the burden of proof lies entirely on the believer**. Their case: one does not need to disprove fairies to lack belief in them. **The answer**: this makes atheism a psychological state rather than a position. Anyone who claims that the universe is self-existent, or that mind is only matter, is making claims that need defence just as much as theism. **Flew himself, late in life, became a deist** (*There Is a God*, 2007), persuaded largely by the argument from the order of nature; the circumstances of that book are disputed.

**Kinds of unbelief met in practice.**

| Kind | What it looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **convinced atheist** | has thought it through; holds naturalism; often scientifically educated |
| **agnostic** | thinks the question cannot be settled, and lives as if it does not matter |
| **practical atheist** | never thinks about God at all |
| **wounded unbeliever** | lost faith through suffering, a church scandal, or a hard upbringing |
| **"apatheist"** | regards the question as uninteresting |

**Why this matters.** **The arguments of this stage are mostly for the first kind.** For the others, argument is often not the need at all, and Stage 13 takes them up.

**What it all rests on.** **Whether nature is self-explaining, or points beyond itself to a Source.** Naturalism is the real position behind most modern atheism, and it is what the Orthodox answer finally addresses.
The problem of evil: the logical and the:
The oldest and strongest argument against God is the suffering of the world. Every honest believer has felt it. It must be put at full strength.

**The ancient form.** Lactantius (about 250–325) attributes to **Epicurus** the dilemma that Hume made famous (the Reading in this stage gives Hume's words): if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, He is not all-powerful; if able but unwilling, He is not good; if both, whence evil?

**The two modern forms** (taught in full in Philosophy Stage 14).

| Form | Defender | Claim |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **logical** | **J. L. Mackie**, "Evil and Omnipotence" (1955) | an all-good, all-powerful God and evil are **logically incompatible**; believing in both is contradictory |
| **evidential** | **William Rowe**, "The Problem of Evil and Some Varieties of Atheism" (1979) | even if not contradictory, **pointless suffering** is evidence against God; Rowe's example is a fawn burnt in a forest fire, suffering for days with no one to see |

**The state of the debate.** Most philosophers, including many atheists, now accept that **Alvin Plantinga**'s **free will defence** (*God, Freedom, and Evil*, 1974) answers the logical form: it is possible that God has a good reason (the value of free creatures) for permitting evil, so there is no contradiction. **The evidential form is where the argument now lives.** It asks not "is it possible?" but "is it likely?"

**The evidential case at its strongest.** We see vast suffering whose purpose we cannot see: children with cancer, animals over millions of years, earthquakes. If there were a God, we would expect to see the reasons, at least sometimes. **We do not. So probably there is no God.** Atheists add that the believer's answers ("free will", "soul-making") fit some evils but not the scale, nor animal suffering before humans existed.

**The standard replies.**

1. **"Sceptical theism"**: if God exists, we should **expect** not to see many of His reasons, as a child does not see a surgeon's. Our not seeing a reason is weak evidence that there is none (Stephen Wykstra, 1984).
2. **The greater-goods defence**: freedom, love, courage and compassion require a world where real harm is possible (Swinburne, Hick's "soul-making").
3. **The cumulative case**: the evidence of evil must be weighed with the evidence for God (Philosophy Stage 14).

**The replies' weaknesses.** Atheists answer that sceptical theism, if pushed, makes God's goodness unknowable, and that greater goods do not obviously need *this much* evil. **These are serious points.** The next lesson gives the distinctively Orthodox answer, which does not depend on a complete theodicy.

**What it rests on.** **Whether we are in a position to judge that suffering is pointless**, and **whether goodness in God must look like goodness in a manager of a pleasant world.**
The Orthodox answer to suffering: freedo:
The Orthodox Church does not have one official theodicy. She has a **way of seeing suffering**, and its strength is that it does not try to justify each evil but places all of it inside a story that ends in resurrection.

**1. Evil is not a thing God made.** The Fathers, following St Basil (homily *That God Is Not the Author of Evil*) and St Dionysius the Areopagite, teach that evil is **not a substance** but a **privation**, a turning away from the good, as darkness is the absence of light. God made all things good. Evil enters through **the free will of creatures**, angels first and then man.

**2. The fall wounded the whole creation.** Death, disease and the "groaning" of creation (Romans 8:22) are, for the Fathers, the result of creaturely rebellion, not of God's design. Orthodox writers differ on how this relates to animal death before humans (Theology Stage 5): some hold that the fall's effects extend through all time, as God foresaw it; others that the world was made unfinished and is still being brought to its goal. **Both refuse to call death good.** That is a real difference from the atheist, who must call death simply natural, and from some theodicies that call it useful.

**3. God does not explain suffering from outside; He enters it.** This is the heart of the answer. **Christ does not answer Epicurus with an argument; He answers with the Cross.** God the Son takes on flesh, weeps at a friend's tomb ("Jesus wept", John 11:35), is tortured and cries "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46, quoting Psalm 22). **The God of the Christians is not an onlooker.**

**4. Suffering can be transformed.** The saints show that suffering, joined to Christ, becomes a way to God. **St John Chrysostom**, writing from exile, argued that **no one can be harmed except by himself**: loss, sickness and death cannot destroy a soul; only sin can (the second Reading of this stage). This is not indifference to pain. It is the claim that **the deepest good of a person cannot be taken away**.

**5. The end is resurrection.** "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death" (Revelation 21:4, KJV). The Orthodox answer is **eschatological**: the story is not over, and its last word is Pascha.

**The book of Job.** Job is given no explanation. God answers from the whirlwind, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job 38:4, KJV), and Job is satisfied, not because he understands but because **he has seen God**. The Fathers read Job as a type of Christ, the righteous sufferer.

**Their best reply.** An atheist will say: this is not an answer, it is a consolation; it does not show why the fawn burns. **That is fair.** The Orthodox Christian should admit that **he does not know the reason for each evil**. His claim is narrower: that God is good, has entered suffering, and will heal it, and that this is not contradicted by the fact that we cannot see each reason.

**Dostoevsky's question.** Ivan Karamazov refuses any future harmony bought with a child's tears (Philosophy Stage 13). **Dostoevsky answered not with an argument but with the elder Zosima's life.** That is the Orthodox shape of the answer.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the meaning of suffering must be visible now, or can be revealed at the end.**
Reading: Hume's Dialogues, Part X, and E:
David Hume (1711–1776) wrote his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* in the 1750s; they were published after his death, in **1779**. Three characters debate: **Cleanthes**, who argues for God from design; **Demea**, an orthodox believer who argues from human misery to the need of faith; and **Philo**, the sceptic. Part X turns Demea's catalogue of misery against both believers. Text from the Project Gutenberg edition (eBook 4583), public domain.

**Philo's challenge to Cleanthes:**

> "And is it possible, CLEANTHES, said PHILO, that after all these reflections, and infinitely more, which might be suggested, you can still persevere in your Anthropomorphism, and assert the moral attributes of the Deity, his justice, benevolence, mercy, and rectitude, to be of the same nature with these virtues in human creatures?"

**Read closely: "Anthropomorphism".** Philo's target is a particular idea of God: one whose goodness is **the same kind** as human goodness, only bigger. **That is important for the Orthodox answer.** Philo is right that, on that model, the world looks like the work of a poor manager.

**The argument:**

> "His power we allow is infinite: whatever he wills is executed: but neither man nor any other animal is happy: therefore he does not will their happiness. His wisdom is infinite: He is never mistaken in choosing the means to any end: But the course of Nature tends not to human or animal felicity: therefore it is not established for that purpose."

**Read closely: the hidden premise.** The argument assumes that **if God is good, His purpose must be our happiness** in this life. Remove that premise and the conclusion does not follow. Christianity has never held that the purpose of the world is the present "felicity" of animals and men; it holds that the purpose is **communion with God**, which may pass through suffering.

**The famous lines:**

> "EPICURUS's old questions are yet unanswered. Is he willing to prevent evil, but not able? then is he impotent. Is he able, but not willing? then is he malevolent. Is he both able and willing? whence then is evil?"

**Read closely: three options, and a missing fourth.** Philo offers impotence, malevolence or contradiction. The classical Christian reply adds a fourth: God is able and willing to **overcome** evil, but **not by abolishing the freedom** in which love is possible, and **not in a moment, but through a history** that ends in the resurrection. Whether that fourth option is credible is exactly what the debate is about.

**Then Philo on nature:**

> "But what racking pains, on the other hand, arise from gouts, gravels, megrims, toothaches, rheumatisms, where the injury to the animal machinery is either small or incurable?"

**Read closely: natural evil.** Here Philo moves from moral evil (what people do) to **natural evil**: pain built into the "machinery". This is the harder problem, and it is why Rowe's fawn is still discussed.

**Questions to bring to the text.**

1. **Philo's God is a designer who makes a machine for comfort.** Is that the God of the Fathers, or the God of eighteenth-century deism?
2. Does Hume's argument refute God, or **one model of God's goodness**?
3. **What would Philo say to the Cross?** Hume never discusses it here. The next reading gives an answer written by a man in exile and pain.

**Note.** Philo's last position in the *Dialogues* (Part XII) is famously ambiguous: he allows that the cause or causes of order in the universe "probably bear some remote analogy to human intelligence". **Hume's own view remains debated.**
Reading: St John Chrysostom, that no one:
**St John Chrysostom** (about 349–407), Archbishop of Constantinople, was exiled by the Empress Eudoxia's party and died on a forced march in 407. In exile, in poor health, he wrote a treatise for his friend the deaconess Olympias and others: ***No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Harm Himself***. It is the answer to suffering of a man who was suffering. Translation: W. R. W. Stephens, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers 1st series vol. 9 (1889), as given on New Advent.

**He begins by expecting to be laughed at:**

> "I know well that to coarse-minded persons, who are greedy in the pursuit of present things, and are nailed to earth, and enslaved to physical pleasure, and have no strong hold upon spiritual ideas, this treatise will be of a strange and paradoxical kind".

**His method: what is the virtue of a thing?** Each thing, he says, has the evil that ruins it: "iron to rust, wool to moth, flocks of sheep to wolves." **So what ruins a human being?** "Most men think," he continues, that it is "poverty, others bodily disease, others loss of property, others calumny, others death".

**His thesis:**

> "When then neither loss of money, nor slander, nor railing, nor banishment, nor diseases, nor tortures, nor that which seems more formidable than all, namely death, harms those who suffer them, but rather adds to their profit, whence can you prove to me that any one is injured when he is not injured at all from any of these things?"

**Read closely: harm redefined.** Chrysostom is not saying pain does not hurt. He is saying that **the virtue of a human being is the right state of the soul**, and nothing outside can take that away. What Hume's Philo counted as the evidence against God (gout, toothache, misery) Chrysostom counts as **the arena** where the soul is either ruined by itself or crowned.

**The one real harm:**

> "When any one having been beaten by another, or deprived of his goods, or having endured some other grievous insult, utters a blasphemous speech, he certainly sustains a damage thereby, and a very great one, nevertheless it does not proceed from him who has inflicted the insult, but from his own littleness of soul."

**His examples.** Job, whom the devil "had not power to upset or overthrow"; Paul; the three young men in the furnace. And the parable of the two houses: the house on sand fell "not on account of the force of the trials... but on account of his own folly".

**His conclusion:**

> "Thus in no case will any one be able to injure a man who does not choose to injure himself".

**Hume and Chrysostom side by side.**

| | Philo (Hume) | Chrysostom |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the good of man** | happiness, "felicity" | the virtue of the soul, communion with God |
| **suffering** | evidence against a good God | a trial that can crown or ruin, depending on the soul |
| **the real evil** | pain | sin, which only the self can commit |
| **the author's state** | writing in comfort, publishing after death | **writing in exile, sick, near death** |

**Questions to bring.**

1. Is Chrysostom's answer **too hard**? It can sound cruel to a grieving parent. Chrysostom wrote it for those already suffering, as **comfort and courage**, not as a debating point to fling at the bereaved.
2. Does it answer **natural evil** to animals, who have no virtue to keep? Not directly. Its strength is for **human** suffering.
3. **It changes the question.** Hume asks why God allows pain. Chrysostom asks **what pain can do to a soul that belongs to God**, and answers: nothing that it does not allow.
Divine hiddenness: why does God not make:
If God exists and wants a relationship with us, why does He not show Himself unmistakably? This argument, newer in its formal shape, is now one of the most discussed.

**Their case at its strongest.** The Canadian philosopher **J. L. Schellenberg**, in *Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason* (1993), argued:

1. If a perfectly loving God exists, He would always be open to a personal relationship with every creature capable of one.
2. Such openness means no one capable of the relationship would be **non-resistantly** unaware that God exists.
3. But there are **non-resistant non-believers**: honest seekers who would believe if they could, and people in cultures that never heard of such a God.
4. **So a perfectly loving God does not exist.**

**What gives it force.** It does not depend on suffering, and it is personal: many people have prayed for faith and felt nothing. **It must not be brushed aside.**

**Scripture knows the experience.** "Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour" (Isaiah 45:15, KJV). The Psalmist cries "how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" (Psalm 13:1, KJV). The hiddenness of God is not an atheist discovery; **it is a theme of the Bible and the saints**, including the "dark nights" of the spiritual life.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **God is hidden by nature, not by neglect.** In Orthodox theology God's **essence** is unknowable to any creature, ever (Theology Stage 2). He is known in His **energies** and in Christ. The question is not "why is God not visible like an object?" but "**how does the Uncreated make Himself known to creatures?**"
2. **Knowledge of God is personal, so it cannot be forced.** A proof that overwhelmed every mind would leave no room for love freely given. St Gregory the Theologian taught that God's light is given in measure to those being purified (Theology Stage 1). Pascal, a Western witness, said God gives light enough for those who seek and darkness enough for those who do not (*Pensées*, in paraphrase).
3. **God has not been hidden in the decisive way.** Christianity's claim is that God **did** show Himself plainly: "the Word was made flesh" (John 1:14). The hiddenness argument tends to ignore the Incarnation as a claimed event; the Christian answers that **the public evidence is Christ** (lessons 23 to 26).
4. **The "non-resistant" seeker.** The Orthodox Church does not claim to know any soul's heart. She is cautious about claiming that every non-believer is resisting, and she holds out **hope for those who never heard** (a question where Orthodox writers differ, Theology Stage 4). **God's dealings with each person are not finished at any given moment of their life.**

**Their best reply.** Schellenberg answers that even a little evidence, a felt presence, would be given by a loving God to an honest seeker, and many receive none. **Here the debate becomes personal.** The Orthodox answer is that seeking takes the form of **a life**: prayer, the commandments, the Church. Christ's promise is "seek, and ye shall find" (Matthew 7:7, KJV), not "find at once".

**What it rests on.** **Whether God, if He exists, would make Himself known as an object to every mind on demand, or as a Person to those who seek Him in a certain way.**
Feuerbach: God as the projection of man:
In 1841 a German philosopher argued that theology is really a disguised study of humanity. His idea has shaped every later "explanation" of religion.

**Who.** **Ludwig Feuerbach** (1804–1872), a former student of Hegel, published *Das Wesen des Christentums*, ***The Essence of Christianity***, in **1841**. George Eliot (Marian Evans) translated it into English in **1854**. It is taught as philosophy in Philosophy Stage 11; here it is answered.

**His own words** (tr. Marian Evans, from the second German edition; Project Gutenberg eBook 47025):

> "Consciousness of God is self-consciousness, knowledge of God is self-knowledge. By his God thou knowest the man, and by the man his God; the two are identical."

And:

> "Religion is the dream of the human mind."

**His case at its strongest.** Every attribute given to God (love, wisdom, justice, personality) is a **human** quality, taken out of man, perfected, and set up as another being. Religion is **man's earliest and indirect form of self-knowledge**. The believer worships his own nature without knowing it. And this is **alienation**: the more man gives to God, the less he keeps for himself. Feuerbach's programme is to bring these qualities back: theology must become **anthropology**. This is not hatred of religion; it is the claim to **reveal its true content**, which is human.

**Why it is persuasive.** Gods do often look like their worshippers. Feuerbach noticed something real: **people make gods in their own image**, and much religion is self-flattery.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **It assumes what it must prove.** Projection explains belief **if** there is no God. If there is a God, the fact that human goodness resembles Him is exactly what one would expect, since man is made **in His image** (Genesis 1:26). Feuerbach reads the image backwards. **The resemblance is real; the question is which is the original.**
2. **The Christian God is not a flattering projection.** A projected god would look like us at our best. The God of Scripture judges, commands self-denial, and **dies on a cross**. Early Christians found Him, as St Paul says, "unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness" (1 Corinthians 1:23). **No one projects a crucified God.**
3. **Apophatic theology.** The Orthodox tradition already warns that **every concept of God falls short** of Him; St Gregory of Nyssa called concepts of God "idols" when taken for the reality. **The Fathers made Feuerbach's warning first** and drew the opposite conclusion: not that God is man, but that **God is beyond every human image**.
4. **It cuts both ways.** If belief is suspect because it fulfils a wish, so is unbelief, which fulfils the wish to be accountable to no one (lesson 11).

**Their best reply.** A follower of Feuerbach can answer that the "image of God" doctrine is itself a projection. **At this point the argument is circular on both sides**, and it must be decided on other grounds: the arguments for God, and the evidence about Christ.

**What it rests on.** **Whether the likeness between God and man is because man made God, or because God made man.**
Marx: religion as the opium of the peopl:
Feuerbach said religion is projection. **Karl Marx** (1818–1883) asked **why** people project, and answered: because their real lives are miserable.

**His own words** (*Zur Kritik der Hegel'schen Rechts-Philosophie. Einleitung*, 1844; the original German, public domain; the translation is ours):

> "Die Religion ist der Seufzer der bedrängten Kreatur, das Gemüth einer herzlosen Welt, wie sie der Geist geistloser Zustände ist. Sie ist das Opium des Volks."

*"Religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions. It is the opium of the people."*

**Read closely.** Marx is not only sneering. Religion is a **sigh** and a **heart**: a real cry of real suffering. But it is an **opiate**: it dulls the pain instead of curing it. He goes on that abolishing religion as the people's **illusory** happiness is the demand for their **real** happiness. **For Marx, religion will wither once the conditions that need it are changed.**

**His case at its strongest.** Religion has often served the powerful: it has told slaves to obey, the poor to wait for heaven, and has blessed kings and empires. Marx's critique is in part a **moral** one, and many Christians have admitted its force.

**The Soviet experiment.** Lenin went further than Marx: religion must be actively fought. **The Soviet state, from 1917, attempted the most systematic destruction of a church in history.**

| Period | What happened |
| --- | --- |
| **1917–1920s** | Church property seized; Patriarch St Tikhon arrested; clergy shot; the League of the Militant Godless founded (1925) |
| **1930s** | mass closure of churches; by **1939** only a few hundred of the tens of thousands of churches remained open and only a handful of bishops at liberty; tens of thousands of clergy killed, many at places like **Butovo** |
| **1943** | Stalin, in the war, allows a patriarch to be elected |
| **1959–64** | Khrushchev's renewed campaign closes thousands of churches |
| **1988–91** | the millennium of the baptism of Rus' and the end of the USSR |

The Russian Church glorified the **New Martyrs and Confessors of Russia** in **2000**. (History and Theology Stage 11 tell this history.)

**History told honestly.** Marx's critique did not come from nowhere. The Russian Church of the **Synodal period** (1721–1917) was governed by the state; much of the clergy was poor and the hierarchy close to the throne; the Church often blessed the tsar's order uncritically. **An Orthodox answer to Marx should admit that the Church gave him evidence.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **The Gospel is not an opiate.** The Magnificat says God "hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree" (Luke 1:52, KJV). The Fathers, above all **St Basil** and **St John Chrysostom**, preached against the rich more fiercely than most socialists.
2. **The experiment was run.** Marx predicted religion would fade when its conditions changed; the Soviet state tried to change them by force. **Faith survived seventy years**, often most strongly among the poor and the persecuted; it was the atheist state that fell.
3. **The genetic fallacy.** Even if some religion comforts the oppressed, that says nothing about whether it is **true** (lesson 11).

**What it rests on.** **Whether religion is only a response to social misery, or a response to God that also judges social misery.**
Freud: religion as wish-fulfilment and i:
After Feuerbach and Marx comes **Sigmund Freud** (1856–1939), the founder of psychoanalysis. His argument is in copyright in its English translations and is paraphrased here.

**The books.** ***Totem and Taboo*** (1913) traced religion to a supposed primal crime: the sons of a primitive horde killed their father, then felt guilt and worshipped him as a god. ***The Future of an Illusion*** (1927) gave the argument most people know. ***Moses and Monotheism*** (1939) applied the same theory to Judaism.

**His case, paraphrased from *The Future of an Illusion*.**

1. Human beings are helpless before nature, fate and death, as a child is helpless.
2. The child had a **father** who protected him. The adult, still helpless, **longs for a father** greater than his own.
3. Religion supplies one: a heavenly Father who protects, rewards and promises life after death.
4. Religious beliefs are therefore **illusions**: in Freud's technical sense, beliefs **driven by a wish**. An illusion need not be false, he admits, but its source is the wish, not evidence.
5. A mature humanity will give up the illusion and face reality with science, as a child grows up.

**Its force.** The argument is psychologically shrewd. **Belief often is shaped by wishes**, and many believers have a faith that is mostly comfort. Freud was a serious man writing about a serious danger.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **Freud's own concession.** He admitted an illusion **need not be false**. So his argument, even if true, is about **why** people believe, not **whether** it is true. That is the **genetic fallacy** (lesson 11).
2. **It cuts both ways.** The psychologist **Paul Vitz** (*Faith of the Fatherless*, 1999) turned Freud's method around: he studied prominent atheists (Nietzsche, Hume, Russell, Sartre, Freud himself and others) and argued that many had **absent, dead or contemptible fathers**, so that their atheism could equally be called a wish: the wish that there be **no** Father to answer to. **Vitz did not claim this disproves atheism; he claimed Freud's method cannot decide the question.**
3. **The Christian God is not what a wish would make.** Freud's god is a protective father who rewards. The God of the Gospel also **judges**, calls to repentance and the cross, and threatens the comfortable. Hell is not a wish. **A wish-fulfilment would be much more pleasant than Christianity.**
4. **Freud's history has not survived.** *Totem and Taboo*'s primal murder was rejected by anthropologists even in his lifetime; few scholars of religion now defend it.
5. **The longing points somewhere.** C. S. Lewis argued (*Mere Christianity*, 1952, in paraphrase) that creatures are not born with desires unless something exists to satisfy them. St Augustine's "our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee" (*Confessions* I.1, tr. Pusey) says the same: **the longing for the Father is evidence of the Father**, not against Him.

**Their best reply.** A Freudian can say Lewis's argument is itself wishful. **That is true as a matter of logic.** Longing proves nothing either way. The question goes back, again, to evidence.

**What it rests on.** **Whether a belief's emotional usefulness counts against its truth.** Neither side's psychology can settle it.
Answering the projection theories: the g:
Feuerbach, Marx and Freud differ, but their arguments share one shape: **religion is explained by its origin in human needs, so it need not be taken as true.** This lesson answers the shape itself.

**The common form.**

| Thinker | Religion comes from | So it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Feuerbach** | man's projection of his own nature | anthropology in disguise |
| **Marx** | social misery and class rule | an opiate and an ideology |
| **Freud** | infantile helplessness and the father-longing | an illusion |
| **Later evolutionary accounts** (e.g. Pascal Boyer, *Religion Explained*, 2001) | mental tools evolved for other purposes (detecting agents, remembering minds) | a by-product |

The philosopher **Paul Ricoeur** called **Marx, Nietzsche and Freud** the **"masters of suspicion"**, with Feuerbach standing behind them: they taught the modern world to ask, of any belief, **what hidden interest produced it?**

**1. The genetic fallacy.** The **genetic fallacy** is judging a belief true or false by **where it came from** rather than by the evidence for it (Philosophy Stage 1 teaches the fallacies). A man may believe in his wife's fidelity because he wishes to, and she may still be faithful. **A cause of belief is not a reason against it.** Each master of suspicion assumes atheism, then explains belief; **none of them proves atheism**.

**2. The double edge.** Every suspicion turns round.

| Against belief | Against unbelief |
| --- | --- |
| believers want a Father to protect them | unbelievers want no Father to judge them |
| religion serves the powerful | atheism served the Soviet and other states that persecuted |
| believers project their nature | atheists project their own scepticism onto the universe |
| religion is an evolved by-product | then so is the reason that judges it (lesson 18) |

**The Psalmist** saw the second column: "The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God" (Psalm 14:1, KJV). **"In his heart"**: Scripture too says that belief and unbelief have motives. **But the Orthodox answer should not use this to dismiss atheists**, any more than they should use Freud to dismiss believers. It shows only that **motives cannot settle the question**.

**3. What suspicion is good for.** The Orthodox tradition can learn from the masters of suspicion. The Fathers knew that **religion can be an idol**: a comfort, a tool of power, a projection. Christ's sharpest words were for the religious. **Spiritual sobriety (*nḗpsis*) already asks of each spiritual feeling where it came from.** A Christian who has examined his own motives for belief is not threatened by Freud.

**4. The real question.** Once suspicion has done its work on both sides, the question that remains is the old one: **Is there evidence that God exists, and that He has acted in Christ?** That is where the remaining lessons go: to miracles, science, the mind, morality and the resurrection.

**In conversation.** When someone says "you only believe because you were raised to", the honest answer is: **perhaps that is how I came to believe; it is not why I still believe; and how you came to disbelieve does not settle it either. Let us look at the reasons.**

**What it rests on.** **That origin and truth are different questions.** Both sides must answer the second.
Hume on miracles: the argument:
Christianity rests on a miracle, the resurrection. So the most important sceptical argument for this curriculum is **David Hume's** essay "Of Miracles", section X of *An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding* (**1748**). The argument is taught in Philosophy Stage 9; here it is set out for answering. Text: Project Gutenberg eBook 9662, public domain.

**The definition.**

> "A miracle is a violation of the laws of nature; and as a firm and unalterable experience has established these laws, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can possibly be imagined."

**The principle.**

> "A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence."

**The maxim.**

> "That no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact, which it endeavours to establish".

**The argument, in two parts.**

| Part | Argument |
| --- | --- |
| **Part 1: in principle** | the laws of nature are supported by **uniform experience**; a miracle is by definition against uniform experience; so the evidence against any miracle is as strong as evidence can be, and testimony for it can at best balance it |
| **Part 2: in fact** | no miracle has been attested by enough educated, honest witnesses with something to lose; humans love the marvellous; miracle stories flourish among "ignorant and barbarous nations"; the miracles of rival religions **cancel each other out** |

**Its force.** Hume captures a real rule of good thinking: **extraordinary claims need strong evidence**, and people do lie, exaggerate and deceive themselves. Carl Sagan's well-known slogan, that extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence (paraphrase), is Hume popularised. Most modern scepticism about the Gospels begins here, often unknowingly.

**Read closely: two possible readings.** Scholars dispute what Hume meant in Part 1:

1. **The strong reading**: no testimony could **ever** justify belief in a miracle. If so, the argument looks **circular**: it assumes experience is "uniform" against miracles, which is the point at issue, since the Christian claims experience includes the resurrection.
2. **The weaker reading**: testimony for a miracle **must be very strong**, and in practice never is. Then the argument is not a proof but a demand for evidence, and the question becomes **whether the evidence for the resurrection is strong enough** (lessons 25 and 26).

**Hume's own examples.** He discusses the cures reported at the tomb of the Jansenist deacon **François de Pâris** in Paris (from 1727), attested by many witnesses, and dismisses them because "the absolute impossibility or miraculous nature of the events" refutes them. Critics note that this seems to **settle the case before the evidence is heard**.

**What it rests on.** **Whether nature is a closed system whose regularities cannot be interrupted, or the ordered work of a God who may act in it.** If the first is assumed, Hume wins before he starts. The next lesson answers him.
Answering Hume on miracles: what a mirac:
Hume's essay has been answered since the year it appeared. The Orthodox answer uses those replies and adds its own understanding of what a miracle is.

**1. A miracle is not a "violation".** Hume's definition assumes that the laws of nature are rules that God would have to **break**. The Orthodox and patristic understanding is different. **God is the giver of every natural power**; the laws describe how creatures normally act. A miracle is **God acting directly** in His creation, beyond its own powers, for a sign. Nothing is "violated", any more than a man violates the law of gravity by catching a falling cup. St Augustine put it: a miracle happens not against nature but against **what is known of nature** (*City of God* XXI.8, in paraphrase).

**2. The argument is circular in its strong form.** Hume's "uniform experience" against miracles can only be established by **ruling out in advance** the testimony that experience includes them. **George Campbell**, *A Dissertation on Miracles* (1762), and in our time the philosopher of science **John Earman**, in ***Hume's Abject Failure*** (2000), argue this. Earman is not a Christian; he argues on the mathematics of probability that **Hume's maxim, read strictly, would forbid belief in any unprecedented event**, including new discoveries in science.

**3. The probability depends on background beliefs.** Whether a miracle is likely depends on whether **God exists and has reason to act**. If there is no God, a resurrection is almost impossible. If there is a God who has promised to raise the dead and who sent His Son, a resurrection in that context is **exactly what one might expect**. **Hume's argument depends on naturalism; it cannot establish it.**

**4. The Gospel miracles are not like other wonder-stories.** Hume's Part 2 says miracles are reported by credulous people far away. The resurrection was proclaimed **in Jerusalem**, within weeks, by people who **suffered for it**, and opposed by authorities who could have produced the body. **St Paul lists witnesses**, many still alive and able to be questioned: "After that, he was seen of above five hundred brethren at once; of whom the greater part remain unto this present" (1 Corinthians 15:6, KJV). Whether that is enough is a historical question (lessons 23 to 26), not one Hume can settle in advance.

**5. Rival miracles do not cancel out.** Hume says miracles in rival religions refute each other. **Christianity has never claimed that only Christians see wonders.** Scripture records the wonders of Pharaoh's magicians (Exodus 7). The question is not whether wonders happen but **who works them and to what end** (Stage 11).

**6. The Orthodox experience.** The Orthodox Church does not treat miracles as a past age. She venerates **incorrupt relics, wonder-working icons and living saints**, many in the twentieth century (St John of Shanghai, St Nektarios, St Luke of Crimea, a surgeon and archbishop). **The Church is cautious**: she investigates claims and many are rejected. But for her, miracles are **the ordinary signs of God's presence**, not exceptions to be explained away.

**Their best reply.** Sceptics answer: all this grants that miracles are possible but not that any happened; **the evidence for any particular miracle is always weaker than the evidence that people err**. **That is the real dispute**, and it is about the evidence, not the definition.

**What it rests on.** **Whether naturalism is assumed or argued.** Without it, Hume's argument becomes a sensible demand for good evidence, which Christians accept.
The New Atheists: Dawkins, Harris, Hitch:
In the years after the attacks of 11 September 2001, four writers made atheism a bestselling cause. They were called the **"New Atheists"**: new not in their arguments, which were mostly old, but in their tone and confidence.

**The four and their books.**

| Writer | Book | Year | Background |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Sam Harris** (born 1967) | *The End of Faith* | 2004 | neuroscientist |
| **Richard Dawkins** (born 1941) | ***The God Delusion*** | 2006 | evolutionary biologist, Oxford |
| **Daniel Dennett** (1942–2024) | *Breaking the Spell* | 2006 | philosopher of mind |
| **Christopher Hitchens** (1949–2011) | *God Is Not Great* | 2007 | journalist |

**Their case, at its strongest** (paraphrased; their books are in copyright).

1. **Faith is belief without evidence**, and it is a vice: it switches off the critical mind, and so it is dangerous, as religious violence shows.
2. **The God hypothesis is a scientific hypothesis**, and a bad one: the universe looks exactly as it would without God (Dawkins).
3. **Evolution has removed the need for a designer**; the appearance of design in living things is explained by natural selection.
4. **Religion is a natural phenomenon** to be studied like any other (Dennett).
5. **Religion poisons everything** (Hitchens's subtitle): it has justified war, cruelty, the abuse of children and the suppression of women.
6. **Morality does not need God**: we are good because evolution and culture made us so.
7. **Moderate religion gives cover to extremism** (Harris).

**Why they persuaded.** They wrote clearly, with wit, and named real evils: religious terrorism, clerical abuse, the treatment of women and of doubters. **Many Christians had no answer ready.**

**The reception.** The New Atheists were criticised **by other atheists** too. The philosopher **Michael Ruse**, an atheist, said *The God Delusion* would make him embarrassed to be an atheist; the literary critic **Terry Eagleton**, a Marxist, wrote a scathing review in 2006 and a book, *Reason, Faith, and Revolution* (2009). The usual criticism: **they attacked a god no serious theologian believes in** and showed no knowledge of the theology they rejected.

**Where things stand, as of November 2026.** The movement's moment passed in the 2010s. Hitchens died in 2011, Dennett in 2024. In **2024** Dawkins called himself a **"cultural Christian"** who preferred Christian culture to its alternatives while still rejecting belief; **Ayaan Hirsi Ali**, once associated with the movement, announced her conversion to Christianity in **2023**. Several commentators now speak of a "post-New Atheist" moment, with more sympathy for religion among sceptics, though the numbers of the unaffiliated continue to grow in the West.

**The Orthodox answer** is given in the next lesson. In outline: **faith is not belief without evidence** (Hebrews 11:1 means trust grounded in what God has shown); the God they deny is not the God of the Fathers; and the history of religious crimes, which must be admitted, does not touch the question of whether God exists.

**What it rests on.** **Whether God is a hypothesis within the universe that science could test, or the ground of the universe's being.**
Dawkins's central argument: who designed:
*The God Delusion*'s fourth chapter contains what Richard Dawkins calls **the central argument of the book**. It is worth answering carefully, because it is widely repeated.

**The argument, paraphrased.** (The book is in copyright.)

1. The greatest challenge is to explain the **improbable appearance of design** in the universe.
2. The natural temptation is to say there was a designer.
3. But a designer able to design a universe would have to be **even more complex**, and so **even more improbable**, than what he designs. So the designer hypothesis raises the larger problem of **who designed the designer**.
4. Darwinian natural selection explains biological design without a designer, by **cumulative small steps**.
5. We do not yet have the equivalent for physics (the fine-tuning of the constants), but we should expect one, perhaps a multiverse.
6. **Therefore God almost certainly does not exist.**

Dawkins calls this the **"Ultimate Boeing 747" argument**, after the creationist claim that life arising by chance is like a tornado assembling a jumbo jet in a scrapyard. God, he says, is the ultimate 747.

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **God is not complex, and not a being among beings.** The whole of patristic and classical theology holds that God is **simple** (not made of parts), **uncreated**, and **not one item in the universe**. He is not a very large and complicated mind needing an explanation; He is **the source of being itself**. Orthodox theology goes further: God is **beyond being** (*hyperoúsios*, ὑπερούσιος, St Dionysius). **Dawkins's argument applies to a god who is a part of nature; it does not touch the God the Church confesses.** The philosopher **David Bentley Hart**, an Orthodox Christian, has made this point at length (*The Experience of God*, 2013).
2. **"Who made God?" misunderstands the question.** The arguments for God (Philosophy Stage 7) do not say "everything has a cause, so God". They say that **what exists contingently**, that might not have existed, depends on what exists **necessarily**. To ask what caused the necessary being is to ask what caused the uncaused. **The question cannot arise.**
3. **Explanation does not require explaining the explainer.** In science, an explanation is good if it explains, even if we cannot explain it in turn. If archaeologists find a carved inscription, they may infer an engraver without knowing who made the engraver (the Christian philosopher **Alvin Plantinga** made this point in his review of the book; the atheist **Thomas Nagel**, reviewing it too, objected that Dawkins treats God as though He were a complex physical system).
4. **Evolution answers a different question.** Natural selection, whatever its scope, explains how living things change **given** a world with stable laws, matter, and reproduction. **It does not explain why there is a world, or why it is lawful** (lesson 17).

**Their best reply.** Dawkins replied that **divine simplicity is an evasion**: a being who knows everything and acts on everything cannot be simple. **This is the real point of disagreement**, and it is philosophical, not scientific. The classical answer is that God's knowledge is not a store of many items but **one act**, as His being is one. Whether that is coherent is argued in the philosophy of religion; it is not settled by biology.

**What it rests on.** **Whether God is a complex being inside reality who needs explaining, or the simple, necessary ground of all being.** The New Atheists' case largely assumes the first.
Science and scientism: the warfare myth:
Most people now believe that **science and religion have always been at war**. Historians of science say this is a myth, and an Orthodox answer should know the history.

**The warfare thesis.** It was popularised by two books: **John William Draper**, *History of the Conflict between Religion and Science* (**1874**), and **Andrew Dickson White**, *A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology in Christendom* (**1896**). Both told the history of science as a long battle against the Church, especially the Roman Church.

**What historians now say.** The historian **Ronald Numbers** edited *Galileo Goes to Jail and Other Myths about Science and Religion* (2009), in which specialists, believers and not, corrected the common stories:

| Myth | History |
| --- | --- |
| medieval Christians thought the earth was flat | educated Christians knew it was round from antiquity; the flat-earth myth was spread in the nineteenth century |
| the Church burnt Giordano Bruno for science | Bruno (died 1600) was condemned for theological heresies, not for Copernicanism |
| religion held back science | modern science grew in Christian Europe, often among believers: Kepler, Boyle, Newton, Pascal, Faraday, Maxwell, Mendel |

**History told honestly.** The **Galileo affair** was real: the Roman Inquisition condemned Galileo in **1633** and kept him under house arrest until his death. It was a failure of the Roman Church, which Pope John Paul II acknowledged in 1992. **The Orthodox churches had no Galileo case**, but under Ottoman rule the Orthodox world also had little share in the scientific revolution, and some Orthodox writers have treated science with suspicion. **Neither side's history is spotless.**

**The Orthodox view of science.** St Basil's *Hexaemeron* used the best natural science of his day. The Fathers held that **creation is rational because it is made by the Logos**, so it can be understood. Modern Orthodox scientists, from the geneticist **Theodosius Dobzhansky** to many working physicists, see no conflict between the faith and the scientific method. The priest-physicist **Georges Lemaître** (a Catholic), who proposed the expanding universe in 1927, is a reminder that the Big Bang was first a believer's theory.

**Scientism.** The real opponent is not science but **scientism**: the claim that **science is the only way to know anything**. Its best defenders say so openly: the philosopher **Alex Rosenberg**, *The Atheist's Guide to Reality* (2011), argues that physics fixes all the facts and that there is no meaning, purpose or self beyond that.

**The answer to scientism.**

1. **It refutes itself.** "Only scientific claims can be known" is **not a scientific claim**; no experiment can establish it.
2. **Science rests on what it cannot prove**: that nature is orderly, that our minds can grasp it, that truth is worth seeking. These are philosophical, even theological, assumptions.
3. **Whole areas of knowledge lie outside it**: mathematics, logic, ethics, history, the knowledge of persons.

**What it rests on.** **Whether science is one way of knowing, or the only one.** The Orthodox Church welcomes the first and denies the second.
Evolution and the atheist argument: wher:
For many atheists, **Darwin** is the decisive reason to disbelieve: evolution, they say, has made God unnecessary. Orthodox Christians answer this argument, and they answer it **in two different ways**, because they differ on evolution itself.

**The atheist case at its strongest.** Before Darwin, the design of living things was the best evidence for God (William Paley, *Natural Theology*, 1802). Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* (**1859**) showed how that design could arise by **variation and natural selection** without a designer. Dawkins wrote that Darwin made it possible to be an intellectually fulfilled atheist (*The Blind Watchmaker*, 1986, in paraphrase). Add the waste and cruelty of evolution, millions of years of predation and extinction, and the conclusion follows: **if God made the world, He made it by a method no good God would choose; more likely, nothing made it.**

**The Orthodox views** (both taught in full in Theology Stage 5, "Genesis: creation and the fall as the Church reads them"):

| View | Its answer to the atheist argument |
| --- | --- |
| **A literal, patristic reading of Genesis** (Fr Seraphim Rose, *Genesis, Creation, and Early Man*; many Athonite and Russian writers) | evolution by natural selection, as a full account of human origins, **is not true**, and it is no accident that atheists use it; the Fathers teach that **death entered through sin**, so a world of death before the fall is not God's original creation. The atheist is right that Darwinism and the patristic faith conflict; he is wrong to choose Darwin |
| **A reading compatible with evolution** (the geneticist **Theodosius Dobzhansky**, a member of the Orthodox Church; many Orthodox scientists and theologians) | evolution is **how** God made living things, as the Fathers allowed that the earth "brought forth" life at God's command (Genesis 1:24); natural selection explains mechanism, not **why there is anything at all**; the atheist confuses a process with its source |

**Both views agree** on what the atheist argument cannot do:

1. **Evolution does not explain existence.** It presupposes a universe with laws, matter and living things that reproduce. Why any of it exists is a different question (Philosophy Stage 7).
2. **Evolution does not explain the laws' order.** Natural selection cannot explain the mathematical order of physics or its fine-tuning (Philosophy Stage 14).
3. **The fall changes the picture of suffering.** Whether the death in nature is read as entering through the fall, or as part of a creation not yet brought to its goal, **neither Orthodox view calls death good**, and both see creation awaiting healing (Romans 8:21–22).
4. **Man is more than his origin.** Whatever his bodily history, the human person bears **the image of God** and a spiritual soul; that is a theological claim no biology confirms or refutes.

**Where they differ in answering.** The first view **concedes** that Darwinism, if true, would support the atheist, and denies Darwinism; the second **denies** that it would, and accepts evolution. **Each considers the other's answer weaker**: the first says the second has accepted the atheist's premise; the second says the first has tied the faith to a scientific claim. **The Church has not defined this** (Theology Stage 5).

**What it rests on.** **Whether a natural process can explain away its own source.** Both Orthodox views say it cannot.
Naturalism and the mind: consciousness a:
If naturalism is true, the mind is a product of the brain, which is a product of evolution, which aims at survival, not truth. Several philosophers, not all believers, argue that **this undermines naturalism itself**.

**The naturalist's case.** Philosophers like **Daniel Dennett** (*Consciousness Explained*, 1991) and **Paul and Patricia Churchland** argue that the mind **is** what the brain does. Thoughts, feelings and choices are neural processes; there is no soul. Neuroscience increasingly maps mental life onto brain states. **Why posit anything more?**

**Three problems for naturalism** (taught as philosophy in Philosophy Stage 14):

**1. Consciousness.** Why is there **something it is like** to be a person at all (Thomas Nagel, "What Is It Like to Be a Bat?", 1974)? David Chalmers called this the **"hard problem"** (1995): explaining how the brain processes information does not explain why it is **experienced**. Some naturalists answer that consciousness is an illusion (illusionism); critics answer that an illusion is itself an experience.

**2. Reason.** **C. S. Lewis** (*Miracles*, 1947) and later the philosopher **Alvin Plantinga** argued: if our beliefs are produced by blind physical causes selected only for survival, **we have no reason to trust that they are true**. Plantinga's **evolutionary argument against naturalism** (*Warrant and Proper Function*, 1993; *Where the Conflict Really Lies*, 2011): on naturalism plus evolution, the probability that our minds are reliable is low or unknown; so the naturalist has a **defeater** for all his beliefs, including naturalism. **Naturalism undermines the reason that would support it.**

**3. Intentionality and meaning.** Thoughts are **about** things. How can a physical state be "about" anything? This is Brentano's old question (Philosophy Stage 11).

**Thomas Nagel's verdict.** The atheist philosopher **Thomas Nagel**, in ***Mind and Cosmos*** (2012), argued that **materialist neo-Darwinism is almost certainly false** because it cannot account for consciousness, reason and value. He did not become a theist; he sought a third way. **The book was attacked by many naturalists, which shows how central the question is.**

**The Orthodox answer.** The Church does not depend on any one theory of mind. She teaches that the human being is **one person, body and soul**, made in God's image, with a ***nous*** (νοῦς), the spiritual intellect that can know God (Theology Stage 10). The soul is not a ghost in a machine but the **life and form** of the body (a view the Fathers share with Aristotle, Philosophy Stage 4). **Reason can be trusted because it is a gift of the Logos**, the divine Reason who made the world rational and the mind able to grasp it (John 1:1–9). That is why science works, and it is something naturalism must take on credit.

**Their best reply.** Naturalists answer that evolution would select for **true beliefs** because true beliefs aid survival. Plantinga replies that behaviour, not belief, is selected, and false beliefs can produce useful behaviour. **The debate is ongoing**, and many philosophers on both sides think it unresolved.

**What it rests on.** **Whether mind comes from matter, or matter from Mind.** "In the beginning was the Word" (John 1:1, KJV).
Morality without God: the atheist case:
"You don't need God to be good." This is the most common atheist claim in ordinary conversation, and **in one sense it is plainly true**. The question is what follows.

**The atheist case at its strongest.**

1. **Atheists are often good.** Many live honest, generous lives. Christians must not deny this, and Scripture does not: St Paul says the Gentiles "do by nature the things contained in the law" (Romans 2:14, KJV).
2. **Euthyphro's dilemma** (Plato, *Euthyphro*; Philosophy Stage 3): is something good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? If the first, morality is arbitrary; if the second, goodness is independent of God, and we can know it without Him.
3. **Morality has natural sources.** Evolutionary biologists (Frans de Waal, on primates) show the roots of empathy and fairness in animals; secular philosophers ground ethics in well-being (**Sam Harris**, *The Moral Landscape*, 2010), reason (Kant), or agreement (Rawls).
4. **Religious morality is often worse.** Scripture contains commands most moderns find cruel; religious people have done great evil.

**Atheists who disagree with this.** Not all atheists think morality survives atheism unchanged. **J. L. Mackie** (*Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong*, 1977) argued that objective moral values would be "queer" entities that do not fit a naturalist world, so **there are no objective moral facts** (error theory). **Nietzsche** (lesson 21) said that if God is dead, Christian morality has lost its ground and will collapse. The Christian need not prove this; **some of the most rigorous atheists concede it**.

**Three different questions.** Most of the argument here is confused because three questions are run together:

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| **Can atheists be moral?** | **yes**, and many are |
| **Can atheists know what is right?** | often **yes**, by conscience and reason, which God gave all |
| **Can morality be objectively binding if there is no God?** | **this is the real question** |

**The real question.** If the universe is matter without purpose, and humans are products of blind evolution, **what makes cruelty truly wrong**, and not merely disliked by creatures evolved to dislike it? Secular philosophers give serious answers: moral realists such as Derek Parfit and Erik Wielenberg argue that moral facts are **necessary truths**, like mathematics, needing no further ground. **This is the strongest atheist position**, and the next lesson answers it.

**What it rests on.** **Whether moral truth can be objective and binding in a universe that is not itself personal or purposive.**
The Orthodox answer on morality: conscie:
The Orthodox answer to "morality without God" is not that atheists are wicked. It is that **the good they rightly see points to the Good they deny**.

**1. Conscience is God's gift to all.** St Paul: the Gentiles "shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness" (Romans 2:15, KJV). The Fathers call conscience the **voice of God in the soul**. St Dorotheos of Gaza (sixth century) taught that God planted conscience in man at creation, and that it is darkened by sin and brightened by obedience. **So an atheist who knows that cruelty is wrong is not reasoning without God; he is hearing God without naming Him.**

**2. The answer to Euthyphro.** The dilemma assumes **two options**: goodness is either God's arbitrary will or a standard above God. The classical Christian answer, held by the Fathers, is **a third option: the Good is God's own nature.** God commands what is good because He **is** the Good; His commands are not arbitrary, and the standard is not outside Him. St Dionysius the Areopagite names God **"the Good"** before any other name (*The Divine Names* IV). **The dilemma dissolves.**

**3. The answer to "necessary moral truths".** The best atheist position (previous lesson) says moral truths are necessary, like mathematics, and need no ground. The theist answer:

- **Why should a necessary truth bind me?** A mathematical truth tells me what is so; a moral truth tells me **what I ought to do**, and claims authority over my will. **Authority belongs to persons.** Moral obligation is most at home in a universe whose source is personal.
- **Why should evolved minds grasp these truths?** If our moral sense is a product of survival pressure, it would be a coincidence that it tracks necessary moral truths (the "evolutionary debunking" problem, raised by atheist philosophers such as Sharon Street). **The theist has an explanation: the God who is Good made the mind to know the good.**

**4. Orthodox ethics is not a code but a cure.** For the Orthodox Church morality is not mainly obeying rules but **being healed**: the passions purified, the person restored to God's likeness (Theology Stage 10). **The saints are not people who followed the rules best but people who became love.** That is what an atheist morality, at its best, can admire but cannot produce in the same way: it has no grace and no forgiveness from outside the self.

**5. History told honestly.** The atheist's fourth point (religious people do great evil) is true. Christians, including Orthodox Christians, have persecuted, enslaved and killed. **The answer is not to deny it but to say: they sinned against the Gospel, and the Gospel is what judges them.** By what standard does the atheist condemn them? Often by the Christian standard of the dignity of every person, which came into the world through the Gospel (the historian Tom Holland, *Dominion*, 2019, an agnostic, argues this at length).

**What it rests on.** **Whether goodness is a feature of an impersonal universe, or the nature of a personal God.** If the first, it is hard to see why it binds; if the second, it is clear why atheists can still know it.
Nietzsche: the death of God and what it:
The most honest atheist, many Christians have said, was the one who hated Christianity most. **Friedrich Nietzsche** (1844–1900) did not think atheism was easy, and he did not think morality would survive it. His philosophy is taught in Philosophy Stage 11; here he is read as a witness.

**The madman.** In *The Gay Science* (*Die fröhliche Wissenschaft*, **1882**), section 125, a madman runs into the market-place with a lantern in the morning, crying "I seek God!". The unbelievers laugh. He answers (tr. Thomas Common, 1910, as *The Joyful Wisdom*; Project Gutenberg eBook 52881):

> "God is dead! God remains dead! And we have killed him! How shall we console ourselves, the most murderous of all murderers?"

And before that:

> "What did we do when we loosened this earth from its sun? Whither does it now move? Whither do we move? Away from all suns?"

**Read closely.** The madman is not speaking to believers but to **atheists**, who laughed at him. His charge is that **they have not understood what they have done**. To kill God is to lose the sun: up and down, purpose, the ground of value. "Is there still an above and below?" **Nietzsche's atheism is a tragedy, not a relief.**

**His case at its strongest.**

1. **Christian morality depends on Christian faith.** Kindness to the weak, humility, equality of souls, are Christian values; without God they have no ground. The English, he mocked, think they can keep Christian morality without Christ (*Twilight of the Idols*, 1889, in paraphrase).
2. **Christian morality is "slave morality"**: the resentment of the weak against the strong, dressed as virtue (*On the Genealogy of Morals*, 1887).
3. After the death of God, man must **create his own values**; the **Übermensch** ("overman") is the one who can.

**What he got right, from the Orthodox view.** **Nietzsche saw what the New Atheists did not**: that the death of God is not a small change. If there is no God, the dignity of every person, compassion for the weak and the claim of truth are not self-evident leftovers; they lose their foundation. **The Christian and Nietzsche agree on the stakes.**

**The Orthodox answer.**

1. **"Slave morality" misreads the Gospel.** Christian humility is not the resentment of the weak but the **freely chosen self-emptying of the strong**: God the Son, who "made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7, KJV). The martyrs were not weak.
2. **The twentieth century answered.** Nietzsche foresaw (*Ecce Homo*, 1888, in paraphrase) that the collapse of the old values would bring wars such as the earth had never seen. Those wars came. **His sister's edition of his works served the Nazis** (Philosophy Stage 11), and he himself despised antisemitism, but the collapse of Christian value was followed by the worst slaughter in history.
3. **The madman's question has an answer.** "How shall we console ourselves?" The Church's answer is that **God did die, on the Cross, and rose**. On Great and Holy Saturday the Church sings over God lying dead in the tomb in the flesh, and that day is followed by Pascha.

**What it rests on.** **Whether values can survive the death of God.** Nietzsche and the Fathers both say no; they differ on whether God is dead.
Nihilism after Fr Seraphim Rose: the fou:
**Fr Seraphim Rose** (Theology Stage 12; Stage 11 of this curriculum) wrote, in the early 1960s before his monastic life, a long study of modern unbelief. It was published after his death as ***Nihilism: The Root of the Revolution of the Modern Age*** (1994). It is in copyright; what follows is a summary and paraphrase.

**The thesis.** Rose took Nietzsche at his word. The modern age, he argued, is not neutral or secular; it is driven by **nihilism**: the denial that there is any absolute truth. And because truth for Christians is ultimately **Christ**, who said "I am the truth", nihilism is at root a revolt against God.

**The four stages of nihilism** (Rose's scheme, paraphrased):

| Stage | What it holds | How it denies truth |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Liberalism** | truth is a private matter; tolerance of all views; faith kept but softened | **truth is not denied but made unimportant**; one keeps Christian values without Christian conviction |
| **2. Realism** | only what science and the senses show is real (positivism, materialism) | **truth is reduced** to the measurable |
| **3. Vitalism** | life, energy, feeling and the irrational are what matter (Nietzsche, Bergson, much of modern art and the occult) | **truth is replaced** by vitality and experience |
| **4. The nihilism of destruction** | nothing is true, so everything may be destroyed (the revolutions, Bolshevism, Nazism) | **truth is attacked** |

**Read closely: liberalism as the first stage.** Rose's most striking claim is that **polite, tolerant liberalism** is the beginning of nihilism, not its opposite. It keeps the forms of faith while emptying them of claim. Each later stage is the earlier one made honest.

**Its strength.** The scheme explains why **atheism is rarely only an argument**: it is a direction of a whole culture. It links the New Atheism (Realism), the New Age (Vitalism, Stage 11) and the totalitarian regimes (Destruction) as stages of one movement. **It also explains Nietzsche**, who saw the logic most clearly.

**Where Orthodox readers differ.** Some find Rose's scheme **prophetic**: the movement from liberal Christianity to unbelief to the irrational has continued in the West since he wrote. Others find it **too sweeping**: it can treat every liberal as a nihilist, it leans on his reading of German and French writers more than on careful history, and it underrates the Christian inheritance still present in liberal societies. **Both are held**, and Rose himself wrote it before he was a monk and did not revise it for publication.

**The answer Rose gives.** Nihilism, for Rose, is not answered by an argument but by **truth lived**: a Christianity that is not liberal, not a private opinion, but a whole life given to Christ, who is Truth in person. The saints, the Fathers and the Church's services are the alternative to the age.

**For conversation.** The scheme helps place an unbeliever: is he a **liberal** who thinks truth unimportant, a **realist** who trusts only science, a **vitalist** seeking experience, or a **despairing** nihilist? **Each needs a different conversation** (Stage 13).

**What it rests on.** **Whether there is absolute truth, and whether it is a Person.**
The historical Jesus: did he exist?:
A small but loud group of writers claim that **Jesus never existed**. Almost all historians, believers or not, disagree. An Orthodox Christian should know why.

**The mythicist case at its strongest.** The best-known defender is the historian **Richard Carrier**, *On the Historicity of Jesus* (2014); before him **Robert M. Price** and, in the nineteenth century, Bruno Bauer. Their argument:

1. St Paul, the earliest Christian writer, says little about Jesus's earthly life; he speaks of a heavenly Christ.
2. The Gospels are later, theological and full of the supernatural.
3. Non-Christian references are few and late, and some were tampered with.
4. Dying-and-rising saviour myths existed in the ancient world; Jesus may be one, later given a history.

**What historians say.** The agnostic New Testament scholar **Bart Ehrman**, no friend of orthodox Christianity, wrote ***Did Jesus Exist?*** (2012) to refute the mythicists. **The consensus of historians of antiquity is that Jesus of Nazareth existed and was crucified under Pontius Pilate.** The evidence:

| Source | Date | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **St Paul's letters** | the 50s AD | Jesus was a Jew, "made of a woman, made under the law" (Galatians 4:4, KJV); Paul met **"James the Lord's brother"** (Galatians 1:19) and Peter |
| **1 Corinthians 15:3–7** | a creed Paul "received", likely within a few years of the crucifixion | Christ died, was buried, rose, and appeared to named witnesses |
| **The Gospels** | about 65–100 AD in most scholars' dating | four accounts, from different communities, sharing a historical core |
| **Josephus**, *Antiquities* XX.9.1 | about 93 AD | the high priest Ananus brought before the Sanhedrin "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James" (tr. William Whiston, 1737) |
| **Tacitus**, *Annals* XV.44 | about 116 AD | see below |

**Tacitus, a hostile witness.** The Roman historian, describing Nero's persecution after the fire of Rome in 64, writes (tr. Alfred John Church and William Jackson Brodribb, 1876):

> "Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus, and a most mischievous superstition, thus checked for the moment, again broke out not only in Judæa, the first source of the evil, but even in Rome".

**Read closely.** Tacitus despises the Christians; he has no reason to invent Christ. He gives the place, the reign and the governor.

**Josephus's other passage.** A second passage (*Antiquities* XVIII.3.3, the *Testimonium Flavianum*) calls Jesus "the Christ" and mentions his resurrection. **Most scholars think it was expanded by a Christian copyist** but that Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral original. The passage on James is generally accepted as authentic.
